How a GPU Works, and How to Optimize Its Performance

Using one H200 as the example, we zoom from a whole large model down to a single instruction and bit: how the GPU works, where the time goes, and how to make it faster.

A draft GPU tutorial, under review round by round. Every figure is interactive: press the buttons, drag the timeline.

1What Questions Does This Book Answer, and With Which Example?

In this book, we follow one sentence through a 62-layer large language model, derive the three inference regimes, and then open up one layer to see how the hardware runs it and how to push it as fast as it can go.

That comes down to three questions. First, once a sentence enters the model, what steps turn it into the next token? Second, the model has only one set of fixed parameters (called weights), so why does running it to generate output (called inference) split into three regimes? Those regimes are prefill (processing the whole known input at once), decode (token-by-token decoding, generating 1 new token at a time), and verify (speculative decoding verification: guessing a few tokens first and checking them all in one pass). Primer 1, Sections 5 to 7 cover all three. Third, when we open up one layer, what does each step compute, what does it hand to the next step, and how do we push it, step by step, close to the shortest time the hardware allows?

The whole book uses only one example: the 62-layer Muse Spark Open. It is an open-weight Mixture of Experts (MoE) large language model with about 816 billion total parameters, where each layer picks only a few small expert networks out of many to run (see Primer 1, Section 2). Our task comes from a public GPU performance optimization competition. Muse Spark Open runs across 8 NVIDIA H200s (a data-center GPU), and we write the GPU program for one layer on a single card. For each layer type, the task gives the shortest time that the nominal hardware peaks allow, called the lower bound. You can calculate the non-expert part of that bound directly from the full-layer rules in Primer 2, Section 4. The expert part is whatever is left after you subtract everything else from the given bound (see Primer 2, Section 1). We first take apart every step of that single layer on one H200. Then, at the end of Chapter 9, we add the 62 measured single-layer times back up into a full decode pass and state which parts are measured and which are not measured (for how the 8 GPUs split the work, see the opening of Primer 1).

We wrote this book for engineers and students who want to make large language model inference run fast or understand low-level GPU performance. By the end, you will be able to break down one layer's execution time across its stages and calculate whether each step is memory-bound or compute-bound, read GPU machine instructions to locate where time is going, and judge whether a code change pays off or is a net loss at the current token count.

2In What Order Does the Book Dissect the System?

We zoom in through the profiler's six levels, from coarse to fine. Each chapter opens up the part we saw in the previous chapter, and a single matrix-vector multiplication ties the evolution together from chapter to chapter.

The opening three chapters are Primers (Primer 1 to Primer 3), which look in turn at the full model, a single layer, and a minimal GPU program (kernel; see Primer 3). Then we enter Part I (Chapters 1–6), which maps to Level 1 through Level 6 of a profiler (a performance profiling tool that measures the latency and utilization of each hardware unit): Chapter 1 starts at the execution timeline, and each subsequent chapter zooms in one level deeper.

One worked example runs through all of Part I. It is the first matrix multiplication in a layer when the input has only 1 token, which makes it a matrix-vector multiplication, gemv (one matrix times one vector; see Primer 2, Section 2). Primer 3 writes its first version, and each of Chapters 1–6 uses that chapter's new mechanism to make it one step faster. Multi-token GEMM, at 8 to 256 tokens, needs mechanisms that are not all in place until Chapter 6, so we walk through its full evolution in one go in the final section of Chapter 6.

Part II (Chapters 7–9) returns to a layer's two main operators and the full-layer assembly. The two operators are attention, which looks across the context, and Mixture of Experts (MoE), which picks experts to compute for each token (see Primer 1, Section 2 for what they are). The two operators and the full-layer assembly each walk their own evolution chain from slow to fast, and the end of Chapter 9 adds the measured single-layer time back up into the full 62-layer decode pass. In Part III, Chapter 10 summarizes how to take a slow kernel and track down its bottleneck one level at a time. Finally, Appendix A explains what changes in hardware from H200 to the next-generation NVIDIA GPU (B200), Appendix B provides a quick-reference table of machine instructions (the low-level instructions the GPU actually executes), and Appendix C provides the glossary and term index.

4What Prerequisites Do You Need, and What Can You Skip on a First Read?

You only need to know how to read C/C++, multiply matrices, and understand CPU caches and multithreading; we build every GPU concept from scratch.

Before starting this book, you need only four things:

  • Reading C/C++: pointers, arrays, loops, and functions;
  • Multiplying matrices and computing vector dot products;
  • Knowing what a CPU cache is: a small, fast copy of memory sitting close to the compute core;
  • Knowing that multiple threads can read and write the same memory at the same time, and that doing so can cause errors.

You do not need any prior GPU background. Primer 3 writes our first CUDA GPU program from scratch, and Chapters 1–6 open up the GPU hardware one level at a time. Chapter 2, Section 6 explains when data written by one GPU thread becomes visible to other threads, and compares that behavior with common desktop and server CPUs (x86). And you do not need an H200 on hand to read this book.

On a first read, you can skip three parts and come back to them when you need them:

  • The one-line cost breakdown under each step caption in the interactive figures;
  • Multi-token GEMM in the final section of Chapter 6 (Section 8), which draws on all the mechanisms from Chapters 1–6;
  • Chapter 10 and the three appendices, which are meant for reference.

5How Do You Use the Figures and Charts in This Book?

Every figure draws the real hardware units and data paths, and you step through them using the buttons and sliders outside the figure. We plot every measured result as a chart and state how it was measured.

Each interactive figure in this book opens right in the middle of an active execution step. You can use the buttons outside the figure to switch modes, or drag the slider to walk through execution one step at a time; each step's caption card lists the formula, the inputs (tensor shape, data type, and where they live), the outputs (where they are written), what gets handed to the next step, and a single line for the cost of that step.

We plot latencies, speedups, and before-and-after comparisons as charts right under the paragraph they belong to, without separate figure numbers. The main text states only the conclusion and at most one key number. Primer 3, Section 5 and Chapter 10 explain how we measure latencies in this book. Each chart's note states in only one sentence how that chart was measured, and we do not mix results from different measurement setups in the same chart. Finally, the lower-bound line in a chart shows the shortest time that the nominal hardware peaks allow; it is calculated, not measured (see Primer 2, Section 4).

This book works at two reading speeds: skim only the section headings, the bold sentences, and the figure readouts to catch the mechanism of each section, or read the full text to follow one causal chain through the entire derivation.

6How Are Units, Terms, and Formulas Written Throughout This Book?

  • Units: We use decimal units (MB, GB, TB/s) for device memory capacity, weight size, and bandwidth (bytes transferred per second), and binary units (KiB, MiB) for on-chip storage and tile sizes. Memory vendors quote bandwidth in decimal units, whereas on-chip storage is aligned to powers of 2.
  • Token: Throughout this book, we call the basic unit processed by the model a token, and do not shorten it to "word."
  • Operator and kernel: An "operator" is one computation step in the model (such as a single matrix multiplication); we call the function that implements it on the GPU a kernel throughout this book (not a "core"). One operator can be implemented by one or several kernels.
  • Single layer and full model: "single layer" means one decoder layer on a single GPU, with time measured in µs; "full model" means the complete 62-layer network, with time measured in ms.
  • Speedup notation: "~XXX× faster" and "a ~XXX× speedup" mean old time ÷\div÷ new time (the ratio, without subtracting 1). "X%X\%X% faster" means old time ÷\div÷ new time −1- 1−1, and a latency drop is written as "takes X%X\%X% less time."
  • Formulas and tensor shapes: We typeset formulas in math notation; a multidimensional array of numbers is called a tensor, and we write a tensor shape as W :  [rows,  columns]  BF16\shape{W}{\text{rows},\;\text{columns}}{BF16}W:[rows,columns]BF16—the tensor name, the length of each dimension in square brackets, and the element data type in the subscript (for example, BF16 stands for 16-bit floating point, and we explain each data type the first time it appears).
  • Chinese and English terms: We explain each English technical term the first time it appears, and Appendix C at the end of the book provides the glossary and term index.

Takeaway: This book follows a single model on a single H200 from start to finish: first we trace how one sentence passes through the entire model, and then we open up one layer level by level down to instructions and bits.

When you feed a sentence into the 62-layer Muse Spark Open, what steps turn it into the next token, and why do we run the same weights in three regimes: prefill, decode, and verify? Let's answer the second question first: on every forward pass (when processing only a few tokens), a single GPU has to stream about 9.0 GB of fixed weights out of device memory. You pay that bill per forward pass, not per token—so how many tokens you have ready to run together before the pass starts decides which regime you use.

The model runs across 8 H200 GPUs, where the H200 is an NVIDIA data-center GPU. Each GPU stores and computes only a slice of each layer's weights (Primer 2, Section 1 shows how we slice them), and this book looks at only one of those GPUs. The communication that sums or concatenates results across the 8 GPUs does not count toward the single-GPU ledger, and it is not measured in this book (Primer 2, Section 2 shows where each layer exchanges data). Figure P1-1 lays out the whole model from input to output. This chapter and Primer 2 walk through each of its parts in turn; here, let's first look at the order in which they run.

1Inbound: How Does One Sentence Become the Two Inputs to Layer 0?

We first split a sentence into integer token IDs and look up their embedding vectors; RMSNorm then produces two inputs: 32-bit stream_0 and 16-bit x_0.

A GPU only works on numeric arrays, so Step 1 in Figure P1-2 splits the input sentence into tokens and maps each one to its integer ID in the 202,048-entry vocabulary. We call the full trip from embedding lookup all the way to scoring every token in the vocabulary one forward pass (or one pass for short), and we write T for the number of tokens processed together in that pass (our example in this chapter uses a 5-token prompt, so T = 5). Those T IDs form an array ids of shape [T][T][T].

The model represents every token with 8,192 numbers—this width is the hidden size, and every 8192 in the tensor shapes below refers to this same dimension. In Step 2, we use ids to look up the embedding table Wembed :  [202048,  8192]  BF16\shape{W_{embed}}{202048,\;8192}{BF16}Wembed​:[202048,8192]BF16, where BF16 is a 16-bit floating-point format (2 bytes per number). This lookup is not a matrix multiplication: using the ids array, it simply fetches the T corresponding rows and writes them out as e :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{e}{T,\;8192}{BF16}e:[T,8192]BF16. Because each GPU stores only about 1/8 of the embedding table's rows, a GPU fills in zeros whenever an ID falls outside its local 1/8 slice, and the 8 GPUs then sum their local eee tensors so every GPU gets the complete eee. Because the lookup reads only these T rows, it does not count toward the fixed weights read on every forward pass in Section 4.

Next, we compute Layer 0's two inputs from eee. RMSNorm (root mean square normalization) divides a vector vvv by the square root of the mean of its squared elements, RMSNorm(v)=v/1n∑ivi2+ϵ\mathrm{RMSNorm}(v) = v / \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_i v_i^2 + \epsilon}RMSNorm(v)=v/n1​∑i​vi2​+ϵ​ (where ϵ\epsilonϵ is a small constant that prevents division by zero), to keep the numeric range stable. Weighted RMSNorm performs that same division and then multiplies elementwise by a learned scale vector; this scale vector has the same length as the vector being normalized, and each place that uses one has its own copy. The RMSNorm right after the embedding lookup does not multiply by a scale vector: once the division is done, it casts the result to FP32 (32-bit floating point, 4 bytes per number) to produce stream0 :  [T,  8192]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{stream}_0}{T,\;8192}{FP32}stream0​:[T,8192]FP32. Later layers do not overwrite this tensor, but instead add their results onto it (Primer 2, Section 2 shows how), so we call it the residual stream, written stream. In the source code, this post-embedding normalization is called embed_norm; it runs only once at the very start, and after it finishes, each token's vector has an RMS of about 1. From that point on, the residual stream itself is not normalized again.

Why split the data into two copies at different precisions? We store the residual stream in 32-bit FP32: the outputs of all 62 layers accumulate into that same stream, and 32 bits preserve more significant digits than 16 bits. The matrix multiplications inside a layer take 16-bit BF16 inputs instead; BF16 reads fewer bytes and computes faster. So at the end of Step 2, we copy stream_0, run a weighted RMSNorm on the copy, and cast it to BF16 to get Layer 0's matrix-multiplication input x0 :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{x_0}{T,\;8192}{BF16}x0​:[T,8192]BF16 (called input_layernorm in the source code). Every layer prepares its input the same way: it copies the residual stream and normalizes the copy while leaving the residual stream itself untouched. Starting from Layer 1, Layer l−1 computes this input for Layer l during its own final stage, using Layer l's scale vector (Primer 2, Section 2). So the two normalizations at the start are not redundant: the first sets the starting point of the residual stream, and the second builds the input to Layer 0. Throughout this book, we write stream_l and x_l for these two inputs to Layer l.

Each layer merges into the residual stream twice (Primer 2, Section 2 gives the merge equation). At each merge, we first normalize the new term to an RMS of about 1 and multiply it elementwise by a coefficient β\betaβ, while multiplying the old residual stream elementwise by a coefficient α\alphaα. Both α\alphaα and β\betaβ are vectors of length 8,192, computed from a vector that each merge site learns on its own (this book does not cover how). Every position iii satisfies αi2+βi2=1\alpha_i^2 + \beta_i^2 = 1αi2​+βi2​=1; only when βi\beta_iβi​ gets extremely close to 1 does αi\alpha_iαi​ stop at a floor of about 0.03, leaving the identity slightly off. The old residual stream also has an RMS of about 1: Layer 0's starting point comes from the first normalization. As long as the two terms are roughly uncorrelated and each term has about the same magnitude across all 8,192 positions, their sum still has an RMS of about 1. Every merge works this way, so the residual stream stays at roughly the same scale as it accumulates layer after layer. Neither of these two conditions is measured in this book.

2Passing Through 62 Layers: What Goes to the Next Layer, and What Stays for Future Tokens?

Vertically, each layer hands the updated stream and x down to the next layer; horizontally, it writes each token's key and value into the layer's KV cache for future tokens to read.

Why does every layer need to save keys and values? When a token enters Layer l, it first computes three vectors from x_l: a query Q, a key K, and a value V. It then takes the dot product of its own Q with the K of itself and every preceding token to get a sequence of similarity scores sis_isi​, runs softmax (pi=esi/∑jesjp_i = e^{s_i} / \sum_j e^{s_j}pi​=esi​/∑j​esj​) to turn those scores into weights that sum to 1, and takes a weighted sum over those tokens' V vectors—that calculation is attention. Because each token attends only to itself and earlier tokens, we call this causal attention. Once an earlier token computes its K and V, those values never change, yet every subsequent new token has to read them again—so each layer saves the computed K and V in its own dedicated region of device memory, the KV cache (K_cache[l] and V_cache[l]).

If you open up Step 3 in Figure P1-2, each Layer l (l = 0..60) hands stream_{l+1} and x_{l+1} down to the next layer. Only the final layer (l = 61) breaks the pattern: because no layer follows it, it outputs only stream_{62} and skips computing x.

We compute K and V by multiplying x by a narrower weight matrix, so both are much narrower than x. We slice them into segments of 64 numbers each, where each segment is one key-value head (KV head). We slice Q into 64-wide heads the same way, and each KV head is shared across several query heads that each run the attention calculation above (Primer 2, Section 1 covers how many query heads share a KV head and how they are grouped). Each layer has 16 KV heads in total, with each GPU handling 2 of them.

We store every number in the cache in FP8 (8-bit floating point, 1 byte per number), so on a single GPU, one token in one layer takes up one slot (KV cache slot) of 2 (K, V)×2 (heads)×64×1 B=256 B2\ (K,\ V) \times 2\ (\text{heads}) \times 64 \times 1\ \mathrm{B} = 256\ \mathrm{B}2 (K, V)×2 (heads)×64×1 B=256 B.

The second half of every layer is a Mixture of Experts (MoE) block: each layer has 256 experts, and each GPU stores 32 of them (called its local experts). Each expert is a feed-forward network (FFN) made of 3 weight matrices. The first two matrices each project the input into a vector; one of those two vectors passes through an elementwise nonlinear function to become a set of scaling ratios, and then multiplies the other vector elementwise. The third matrix projects that product back out. A tiny scoring matrix scores all 256 experts, and each token uses only its top-scoring 8 experts and takes a score-weighted sum of their outputs (see Primer 2, Section 2). Two more matrices sit around the experts, and every token passes through them: one squeezes the vector narrower before the experts, and the other widens it back up to 8,192 dimensions afterward (Primer 2, Section 1 gives their shapes).

Across all 62 layers, only two things change from layer to layer. First is how far back attention looks: 46 sliding-window layers attend only to the most recent 2,048 positions, whereas 16 full-attention layers attend to the entire history from the start. Second is how we store the expert weights: the middle 60 layers compress expert weights to 4-bit precision at 28.3 MB per expert, while the first and last layers remain uncompressed (Primer 2, Section 1 shows how 28.3 MB is calculated).

3Outbound and Loopback: How Do 8,192 Numbers Turn Back into a Token ID?

We pick out only the rows that need a prediction, normalize them, and project them against all 202,048 vocabulary candidates to produce logits, then feed the chosen token ID back to Step 2 (embedding lookup).

In Step 4 of Figure P1-2, we first pick out only the rows that actually need a prediction—call that row count R. During prefill, the prompt already gives us the next token for positions 1–4, so we take only the last row (R = 1); during decode, we have only 1 row to begin with (R = 1); and during verify, we check predictions across 8 positions at once, so we take R = 8 (see Section 7 for details). We cast those R selected rows of stream_{62} to BF16 and run them through a weighted final RMSNorm to produce hfinal :  [R,  8192]  BF16\shape{h_{final}}{R,\;8192}{BF16}hfinal​:[R,8192]BF16.

Step 5 runs lm_head (vocabulary projection, the matrix that scores every candidate token in the vocabulary). We split the vocabulary evenly by rows across the 8 GPUs so each GPU holds about one eighth, Wlm :  [≈25k,  8192]  BF16\shape{W_{lm}}{\approx 25\text{k},\;8192}{BF16}Wlm​:[≈25k,8192]BF16, which takes up 0.414 GB. Each GPU multiplies h_final by its local shard to compute its local logits z :  [R,  vocabulary/8]  FP32\shape{z}{R,\;\text{vocabulary}/8}{FP32}z:[R,vocabulary/8]FP32, and the 8 GPUs concatenate their shards into the full logits for all 202,048 candidates. Notice the contrast with Step 2: the inbound lookup fetches only T rows by index, whereas outbound scoring has to take the dot product of every candidate with h_final, so every forward pass has to stream the entire 0.414 GB local shard regardless of R.

Step 6 applies the logit softcap: we first multiply each score by a fixed scale factor sss, and then pass it through c⋅tanh⁡(⋅/c)c\cdot\tanh(\cdot / c)c⋅tanh(⋅/c) (where sss and ccc are constants defined by the model) to smoothly squeeze every score into [−c, c][-c,\ c][−c, c] so no individual score grows too large. Once capped, these RRR rows of unnormalized candidate scores are called logits, with shape logits :  [R,  202048]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{logits}}{R,\;202048}{FP32}logits:[R,202048]FP32.

From logits, Step 7 picks the new token ID next_id (the sampling algorithm is outside the scope of this book), and Step 8 feeds next_id right back into Step 2 (embedding lookup) as the row index for the next forward pass, so no further tokenization is needed from this point on.

We call the number of valid slots in the KV cache the committed sequence length, and the next forward pass writes its first token at position (committed sequence length +1+ 1+1). Prefill advances the committed sequence length by T (5 in our example, so the next pass starts at position 6), decode advances it by 1, and verify advances it by the number of tokens accepted in that pass, as we will see in Section 7.

4Forward-Pass Accounting: What Is the Minimum Number of Bytes One GPU Must Read per Pass, and How Long Does That Take?

When you run only a few tokens, every pass still streams ~9.0 GB of fixed weights plus 28.3 MB per active compressed expert, while the KV cache traffic for those few tokens is negligible.

A GPU's main device memory is HBM (High Bandwidth Memory); bandwidth is how many bytes it transfers per second, and the H200 has a nominal peak HBM bandwidth of 4.8 TB/s. Because the weights on a single GPU add up to several gigabytes and cannot fit on-chip, every forward pass has to stream them fresh from HBM (Chapter 2, Section 2 covers how much data fits on-chip).

Let's break the bytes read in one forward pass into three parts, starting with the fixed weights read on every pass. We call the matrices that apply to every token—without any token-dependent routing—dense matrices, and each layer has 5 of them: the matrix that computes Q, K, V, and gating values (a set of scaling coefficients; see Primer 2, Section 2), the attention output projection matrix, the router scoring matrix for experts, and the two matrices that project the vector down before the experts and back up afterward.

Across the three regimes in this chapter, our local GPU reads 138.4 MB of dense weights per layer (Primer 2, Section 1 breaks down each matrix), totaling 8.58 GB across all 62 layers; add the 0.414 GB local shard of lm_head from Section 3 and the bill comes to 8.996 GB (approximately 9.0 GB). Whether you feed 1 token in a pass or batch 5 or 8 tokens side by side, you still read that exact same 9.0 GB.

Even if the GPU did nothing else, just streaming these fixed weights into the chip takes 8.996 GB÷4.8 TB/s≈1.87 ms8.996\ \mathrm{GB} \div 4.8\ \mathrm{TB/s} \approx 1.87\ \mathrm{ms}8.996 GB÷4.8 TB/s≈1.87 ms (excluding experts and cross-GPU communication).

The second part of the bill is the expert weights, which we pay for based on how many experts the pass actually touches. Across the middle 60 layers, each local expert we touch adds 28.3 MB of reads; if we touch 1 local expert per layer on average across those 60 layers, the pass reads an extra 60×28.3 MB≈1.7 GB60 \times 28.3\ \mathrm{MB} \approx 1.7\ \mathrm{GB}60×28.3 MB≈1.7 GB, adding about 0.354 ms at 4.8 TB/s. The experts in the first and last layers are uncompressed, at about 100.7 MB each (Primer 2, Section 1). Here we set them aside for now, so 1.7 GB counts only the middle 60 layers rather than all expert reads. When a pass runs only 1 token, each GPU touches 1 local expert on average, yet whichever GPU touches the most local experts in a given layer (the busiest GPU, or straggler rank) touches more than 1. Throughout this book, we count expert reads by the number of local experts touched per layer on the busiest GPU (Primer 2, Section 1 gives that number). As a pass processes more tokens together, it touches more experts overall, though different tokens often land on the same expert and share a single read of its weights.

The third part is the KV cache, which reads 256 B per visible historical token in each layer (Section 2). Even the largest pass in this chapter (verify in Section 7) reads only a dozen or so slots per layer—well within Section 2's 2,048-token sliding window, so sliding-window layers and full-attention layers read the exact same number of slots. Across all 62 layers, that comes to less than 0.21 MB, which is negligible next to 9.0 GB. That holds only when the history is short; once the history grows to tens of thousands of tokens, it no longer holds (see Primer 2, Section 5).

Once we stream those weights in, how much math do we actually do on them? We write FLOP for the number of floating-point operations, counting one multiply-add as 2 FLOPs. A single BF16 weight takes up 2 bytes, and each of the T tokens in the pass does one multiply-add with it for a total of 2T2T2T FLOPs—which works out to approximately T FLOPs for every 1 byte of BF16 weight read. In the time it takes an H200 to read 1 byte from HBM, its compute units can execute hundreds of FLOPs (see Primer 2, Section 4 for the exact number), so when T is small, the compute units spend most of their time waiting on HBM; Primer 2, Section 5 shows how large T must grow to flip that balance.

5Prefill: Why Can Known Tokens Run in Parallel in a Single Pass?

Under causal attention, each token attends only to itself and earlier tokens whose keys and values we already compute in the same pass, so we can stack all 5 tokens into one matrix pass.

We call the forward pass that processes the user prompt prefill. Before computation begins, all 5 tokens at positions 1–5 are already known (T = 5), so we stack the 5 rows directly into xl :  [5,  8192]  BF16\shape{x_l}{5,\;8192}{BF16}xl​:[5,8192]BF16 and push them through together—each weight matrix multiplies a 5-row matrix at once rather than multiplying a single vector 5 separate times.

On this pass, each layer writes 5 slots (5×256 B5 \times 256\ \mathrm{B}5×256 B) into its KV cache; because the cache starts out empty, there is no prior history to read. Once all 5 rows finish Layer 61, we take R = 1 as in Section 3 to produce token 6. All 5 tokens share that single read of the fixed weights, so each token's share comes to about 1.80 GB. Across the pass, we do about 5 FLOPs for every byte of BF16 weight read (Section 4). When a prompt is very long, we split it into chunks and run them across several passes (see Primer 2, Section 5).

6Decode: Why Can Each Pass Process Only 1 Token, and What Is Its Bottleneck?

Token 7 does not exist until we generate token 6, so decode can feed only 1 token per pass while still streaming all the fixed weights—doing only ~1 FLOP per byte read.

Text generation in a large language model is autoregressive: each new token is computed from the tokens that came before it. From this step on, we enter decode (token-by-token decoding), where the input to the pass is only the token we just generated, token 6 (T = 1). Each layer writes 1 new slot into the KV cache and reads 6 slots: that new slot plus the 5 that prefill left behind. After Layer 61, we take R = 1 to produce token 7. Compared with prefill, the fixed-weight read per token jumps 5× (9.0 GB vs. 1.80 GB). Here we count only the bytes that a single GPU reads from HBM, and cross-GPU communication stays out of the ledger (as noted at the start of this chapter).

When many requests are active online at the same time, we can merge each request's 1 new token into a single pass, and they all share that one read of the fixed weights. As long as we merge 8 tokens or fewer, those fixed weights stay at about 9.0 GB. Once we go past 8 tokens, one dense matrix switches to having every GPU read a full copy, pushing the fixed weights up to about 12.6 GB, after which they stop growing with the token count (see Primer 2, Section 1). Because each request has its own history, each one still reads its own KV cache; once the fixed weights are set, each additional merged request pays only for its own KV reads and any extra experts it touches. As long as the pass is still waiting on HBM, its runtime is determined mainly by how many bytes it reads. So as we merge more requests, pass latency rises only slightly at first, and total throughput scales almost in step with the number of requests (Primer 2, Section 5 covers how multiple requests merge into one pass and how pass latency and the bottleneck shift).

7Verify: How Can One Request Yield More Than 1 Token in a Single Pass?

We draft 7 candidate tokens, stack them with the known token 6 into an 8-row pass, and check them left to right up to the first mismatch—getting 1 to 8 tokens out of a single pass.

verify (speculative decoding verification) is not a step that follows decode, but an alternative regime to decode: it starts from the exact same post-prefill state, with 5 slots in the KV cache and token 6 already known. A separate drafting mechanism (for example, a small draft model, or drafter) first guesses 7 candidate tokens for positions 7 through 13, called draft tokens. Right or wrong, all 8 tokens are known numbers before the forward pass begins—so just like prefill (Section 5), we stack them into xl :  [8,  8192]  BF16\shape{x_l}{8,\;8192}{BF16}xl​:[8,8192]BF16 (T = 8) and push them through in a single pass. Each layer writes 8 slots into the KV cache and reads 13 slots in total (including the existing 5 slots), and at the end we feed all 8 rows into lm_head (R = 8) so we can check the prediction from every row.

Why can a single pass verify all 7 guesses at once? Under causal attention, row i attends only to the first i rows (Section 2), so the output of row i (i = 1..8) gives the large model's prediction for position 6 + i—a prediction that is valid only if the draft tokens at positions 7 through 5 + i are all correct. Because row 1 depends only on the known tokens 1–6, its prediction for position 7 is guaranteed to be valid.

To keep things concrete, assume we select the highest-scoring candidate each time (under probabilistic sampling, the acceptance rule changes to probabilistic acceptance, which this book does not cover). Walking from left to right, we compare the large model's predictions against the draft tokens: we accept all draft tokens before the first mismatch, and at the first mismatch we reject that draft token and directly adopt the large model's own prediction at that position. Even if all 7 draft tokens are wrong, this pass still produces token 7; if the first k draft tokens are correct, the pass yields k + 1 tokens (up to 8).

What happens to the KV cache slots that rejected draft tokens wrote across all layers? We leave them in place: the committed sequence length advances only by k + 1, and subsequent passes read only up to the committed sequence length, so those rejected slots are never read and future passes overwrite them.

This pass still reads the exact same fixed weights, doing about 8 FLOPs per byte of BF16 weight read (Section 4). When we spread that read across the k + 1 tokens produced by the pass, each token's share comes to 9.0 GB÷(k+1)9.0\ \mathrm{GB} \div (k + 1)9.0 GB÷(k+1), dropping from 9.0 GB when all draft tokens are wrong (k = 0) down to 1.12 GB when all 7 are right (k = 7), as shown in the chart below.

Of course, verify is not free—compared with decode, it pays three extra costs: the latency of drafting itself, writing 7 extra KV slots and reading 7 extra KV slots per layer, and any additional local experts touched across 8 tokens (where each extra local expert adds 28.3 MB of reads per layer). If the very first draft token is wrong, the pass yields only 1 token after paying all three extra costs, coming out slower than plain decode. Verify pays off only when the average number of tokens produced per pass beats "(verify pass latency +++ drafting latency) ÷\div÷ decode pass latency"; neither drafting latency nor the number of extra experts touched across 8 tokens is measured in this book.

Now that we have the full-model ledger across all three regimes, notice that they differ only in how many tokens run together in one forward pass, while the main body of every pass repeats the exact same layer structure 62 times. Each layer takes (x_l, stream_l), reads and writes its own KV cache, and hands the updated inputs to the next layer (Section 2), while the inbound and outbound steps happen only at the two ends. That is why the next chapter zooms in on a single layer: once we see clearly what one layer computes and how many bytes it reads as T varies, we understand the main body of all 62 layers.

Takeaway: Every forward pass reads the fixed weights once, so how many tokens we can process in parallel in that pass defines the three regimes: prefill (batching known prompt tokens together), decode (generating 1 token at a time), and verify (drafting 7 candidate tokens and verifying them together).

Next chapter's question: If we open up any one of the 62 layers on a single H200, what steps does it break into, and what is the fastest that each step can run under decode and prefill?

In Primer 1, we treated each layer as a black box that takes in (xl, streaml)(x_l,\ \mathrm{stream}_l)(xl​, streaml​) and hands back (xl+1, streaml+1)(x_{l+1},\ \mathrm{stream}_{l+1})(xl+1​, streaml+1​). Now let's open one of those boxes up: how fast can each stage inside a layer possibly run, and is it waiting on HBM or on the Tensor Core (the dedicated on-chip unit for matrix multiply-accumulate)?

1Why Do the Matrices on a Single GPU Have These Shapes?

Eight GPUs partition attention by head and experts by index while replicating three dense matrices on every GPU; for T≤8T \le 8T≤8, each GPU must read 138.4 MB of dense weights per layer plus the weights of routed local experts.

Let's start with attention, which we split using TP8 (tensor parallelism: partitioning the same matrix by head across 8 GPUs). Q has 128 query heads (head dimension 64; see Primer 1, Section 2); across 8 GPUs, our local GPU gets 16 query heads and 2 key-value heads. On this GPU, every 8 query heads share 1 key-value head — a setup called GQA (grouped-query attention; see Chapter 7, Section 2). Each query element also gets a gate value (a scaling factor that we will use in Section 2). Stack Q, K, V, and the gate together and the projection matrix has 1,024+128+128+1,024=2,3041{,}024 + 128 + 128 + 1{,}024 = 2{,}3041,024+128+128+1,024=2,304 output rows: its tensor shape is Wqkv :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W_{qkv}}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}Wqkv​:[2304,8192]BF16, which takes 37.75 MB. After attention finishes, the output matrix projects those 1,024 columns back to 8,192 dimensions with tensor shape Wo :  [8192,  1024]  BF16\shape{W_o}{8192,\;1024}{BF16}Wo​:[8192,1024]BF16, taking another 16.8 MB.

Now look at the experts, which we split across GPUs using EP8 (expert parallelism: assigning different experts to different GPUs). Dividing all 256 experts in the layer evenly across 8 GPUs leaves 32 local experts on each GPU. Each expert takes a narrowed 4,096-dimensional vector as input (produced by the narrowing matrix pooler in the next paragraph). In Primer 1 we saw that each expert has 3 matrices; here we pack the first two side by side into a single matrix w13w_{13}w13​. That matrix w13w_{13}w13​ projects 4,096 dimensions to 8,192 dimensions, with the first 4,096 columns holding the gate ggg and the last 4,096 columns holding uuu (Section 2, Stage 6 shows how they combine). The down projection w2w_2w2​ then maps 4,096 dimensions back to 4,096 dimensions, so the two matrices together hold 3×409623 \times 4096^23×40962 weights. In the middle 60 layers, we store expert weights in NVFP4 (4-bit floating-point format). Every 16 weights share a 1-byte scale factor while each weight's own 4 bits store its relative magnitude, which works out to 0.5625 B per weight on average (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit layout). That puts 1 expert at 28.3 MB, whereas the first and last layers (layers 0 and 61) keep their experts uncompressed in 2-byte BF16, so 1 expert takes 100.7 MB.

Finally, the last three dense matrices are not split across GPUs: every GPU holds a full copy of each. The small router matrix handles routing (selecting experts for each token) by scoring all 256 experts; we store it in 4-byte FP32 as Wrouter :  [256,  8192]  FP32\shape{W_{router}}{256,\;8192}{FP32}Wrouter​:[256,8192]FP32, which comes to 8.4 MB. pooler (Wpool :  [4096,  8192]  BF16\shape{W_{pool}}{4096,\;8192}{BF16}Wpool​:[4096,8192]BF16) narrows 8,192 dimensions down to 4,096 and takes 67.1 MB. unpooler (Wunpool :  [8192,  4096]  BF16\shape{W_{unpool}}{8192,\;4096}{BF16}Wunpool​:[8192,4096]BF16) projects 4,096 dimensions back up to 8,192, also at 67.1 MB.

Take unpooler next: when T≤8T \le 8T≤8, each GPU computes only 1/8 of the output f (1,024 columns) by reading only 1,024 rows of WunpoolW_{unpool}Wunpool​ (8.4 MB). The 8 GPUs then stitch the full T×8,192T \times 8{,}192T×8,192 result together with an all-gather. Once T>8T > 8T>8, each GPU simply reads the entire 67.1 MB matrix and computes all 8,192 columns locally, skipping that all-gather. Add up the exact byte counts of the five dense weight matrices a single GPU reads per layer at T≤8T \le 8T≤8 and you get 138.4 MB — the exact number we used in Primer 1. For T>8T > 8T>8, the dense weights read per layer climb to about 197.1 MB, which comes to about 12.6 GB across all 62 layers plus lm_head.

How much expert weight data do we read at T=1T = 1T=1? A single token picks 8 experts, so on average one GPU lands 8×32/256=1.08 \times 32 / 256 = 1.08×32/256=1.0 local expert. All 8 GPUs exchange expert results once per layer, though, so any GPU that finishes early has to wait for the slowest one. That means the layer's runtime is set by the busiest GPU (the GPU that hits the most local experts in that layer). If a token picks its 8 experts uniformly at random, the busiest GPU out of the 8 hits about 2.56 local experts on average.

For a sliding-window layer at T=1T = 1T=1, the benchmark specification sets a lower bound (minimum execution time) of 40.0 µs. (Section 4 defines the lower bound.) We can add up everything the layer reads outside the experts directly: 138.4 MB of dense weights, 2,048 sliding-window slots of historical KV cache (0.52 MB), and the intermediate results passed between stages (about 0.1 MB). That comes to about 139 MB in total, which takes about 29 µs at 4.8 TB/s. The remaining 11.03 µs (about 53 MB) is the benchmark's budget for the experts. On the busiest GPU, that works out to about 1.87 local experts per layer. That 1.87 is the benchmark's own load assumption, and it is lower than the 2.56 from uniform random selection. The benchmark does not explain the difference. This book uses the number as given. The benchmark also sets the T=8T = 8T=8 switchover point. This book did not measure the all-gather latency or the crossover point between the two partitioning strategies.

2What Does Each of the 8 Stages in a Layer Compute, and What Does It Pass to the Next Step?

Stages 1–3 compute attention and add the result back into the residual stream; Stages 4–8 split into two branches to select experts and project down the hidden dimension, merge at Stage 6, and add back into the residual stream.

Let's walk through the attention half of the layer first (you can click any stage in Figure P2-2 to see its full step card). Stage 1 (qkv_gate) multiplies qkv=xl Wqkv⊤\mathrm{qkv} = x_l\, W_{qkv}^{\top}qkv=xl​Wqkv⊤​: it takes xl :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{x_l}{T,\;8192}{BF16}xl​:[T,8192]BF16 and produces qkv :  [T,  2304]  BF16\shape{\mathrm{qkv}}{T,\;2304}{BF16}qkv:[T,2304]BF16, then slices that output by column into four pieces — q (1,024), k (128), v (128), and gate (1,024) — and hands them to Stage 2. When T=1T = 1T=1, this stage reduces to a single matrix-vector multiplication y=Wxy = W xy=Wx (gemv), which we will use as our running example all the way through Part I.

Stage 2 (attention, gated attention; see Chapter 7, Section 1) starts by running per-head RMSNorm on q and k. In the 46 sliding-window layers, it then applies rotary position embedding (RoPE; the 16 full-attention layers do not apply RoPE). Each pair of elements rotates by an angle set by the token position, so the position-dependent part of the q–k inner product depends only on the distance between the two tokens. After that, it casts the freshly computed k and v down to 1-byte FP8 and writes them into the layer's KV cache.

Next, Stage 2 pulls in the visible historical KV cache — only the most recent 2,048 tokens in a sliding-window layer, or the entire history in a full-attention layer. Each query head takes its q and computes the inner product against every historical k in its shared key-value head. It then runs softmax (Primer 1, Section 2) to turn that row of scores into weights that sum to 1, and takes the weighted sum over the historical v vectors. One more per-head RMSNorm and an elementwise multiply by σ(gate)\sigma(\text{gate})σ(gate) (where σ\sigmaσ is the sigmoid function mapping values into 0..10..10..1) gives the attention output oattn :  [T,  1024]  BF16\shape{o_{attn}}{T,\;1024}{BF16}oattn​:[T,1024]BF16 for Stage 3.

Stage 3 (o projection and first gated residual) takes the local GPU's 1,024-column attention output to compute a=oattnWo⊤a = o_{attn} W_o^{\top}a=oattn​Wo⊤​, and all 8 GPUs sum their partial aaa tensors with an all-reduce to form the full a :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{a}{T,\;8192}{BF16}a:[T,8192]BF16. Next, we blend that summed aaa into the layer's incoming residual stream stream_in\mathrm{stream\_in}stream_in (that is, streaml\mathrm{stream}_lstreaml​): stream_mid=α1⊙stream_in+β1⊙RMSNorm(a)\mathrm{stream\_mid} = \alpha_1 \odot \mathrm{stream\_in} + \beta_1 \odot \mathrm{RMSNorm}(a)stream_mid=α1​⊙stream_in+β1​⊙RMSNorm(a). Here α1\alpha_1α1​ and β1\beta_1β1​ are two length-8,192 FP32 coefficient vectors — one value per coordinate — derived from a length-8,192 vector learned for Stage 3 (with α12+β12=1\alpha_1^2 + \beta_1^2 = 1α12​+β12​=1 elementwise; see Primer 1, Section 1). Because they do not depend on the token, we read them only once per layer. Finally, Stage 3 runs the pre-FFN normalization h=RMSNorm(stream_mid)⊙(1+wpre_ffn)h = \mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathrm{stream\_mid}) \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{pre\_ffn}})h=RMSNorm(stream_mid)⊙(1+wpre_ffn​) and hands h :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{h}{T,\;8192}{BF16}h:[T,8192]BF16 to both Stage 4 and Stage 5. Because the learned length-8,192 vector wpre_ffnw_{\mathrm{pre\_ffn}}wpre_ffn​ stores an offset relative to 1, the formula multiplies by 1+wpre_ffn1 + w_{\mathrm{pre\_ffn}}1+wpre_ffn​ — the weighted RMSNorm from Primer 1.

At hhh, the dataflow forks into Stage 4 and Stage 5. Because neither branch depends on the other, they can run concurrently (Chapter 9, Section 1 shows how we schedule them). One branch is Stage 4 (router), which scores all 256 experts in FP32 as s=σ(cr⋅hWrouter⊤)s = \sigma(c_r \cdot h W_{router}^{\top})s=σ(cr​⋅hWrouter⊤​), where crc_rcr​ is a fixed scaling constant. To pick the winning experts, we add a learned bias to each expert's score and take the top 8 — but that bias is used only for selection, while the final routing weights still use the unbiased scores. Stage 4 hands two outputs to Stage 6: the chosen expert indices topk_ids :  [T,  8]  int32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_ids}}{T,\;8}{int32}topk_ids:[T,8]int32 (int32 is a 32-bit integer, 4 bytes each) and the normalized routing weights topk_weights :  [T,  8]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_weights}}{T,\;8}{FP32}topk_weights:[T,8]FP32 (the selected unbiased scores divided by their sum).

The other branch is Stage 5 (pooler), which narrows the hidden state via p=RMSNorm(hWpool⊤)⊙(1+wpre_expert)p = \mathrm{RMSNorm}(h W_{pool}^{\top}) \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{pre\_expert}})p=RMSNorm(hWpool⊤​)⊙(1+wpre_expert​) and sends p :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{p}{T,\;4096}{BF16}p:[T,4096]BF16 to Stage 6.

The two branches meet at Stage 6 (expert stage; see Chapter 8, Section 1). Out of the 8 experts a token picks, we compute only the ones that live on the local GPU. For each local (token, expert eee) pair, we run four steps:

  1. Project gu=p W13,e⊤\mathrm{gu} = p\, W_{13,e}^{\top}gu=pW13,e⊤​ to get the first 4,096 columns ggg and the last 4,096 columns uuu.
  2. Apply SwiGLU: inter=silu(g)⊙u\mathrm{inter} = \mathrm{silu}(g) \odot uinter=silu(g)⊙u, where silu(z)=z⋅σ(z)\mathrm{silu}(z) = z \cdot \sigma(z)silu(z)=z⋅σ(z).
  3. Run the down projection y=inter W2,e⊤y = \mathrm{inter}\, W_{2,e}^{\top}y=interW2,e⊤​ back to 4,096 dimensions.
  4. Normalize each yyy and accumulate it weighted by its routing weight: mtok+=wtok,e⋅RMSNorm(y⊙(1+wpost_expert))m_{\mathrm{tok}} \mathrel{+}= w_{\mathrm{tok},e} \cdot \mathrm{RMSNorm}(y \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{post\_expert}}))mtok​+=wtok,e​⋅RMSNorm(y⊙(1+wpost_expert​)). Multiplication by 1+wpost_expert1 + w_{\mathrm{post\_expert}}1+wpost_expert​ comes before division here — the opposite order from Stage 3 — and wtok,ew_{\mathrm{tok},e}wtok,e​ is the token's topk_weights entry for expert eee. Once every local (token, expert) pair finishes, Stage 6 hands m :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{m}{T,\;4096}{BF16}m:[T,4096]BF16 to Stage 7.

From there, Stage 7 (unpooler) computes f=m Wunpool⊤f = m\, W_{unpool}^{\top}f=mWunpool⊤​, projecting back up to f :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{f}{T,\;8192}{BF16}f:[T,8192]BF16 (for T≤8T \le 8T≤8, computing only the local GPU's 1,024 columns; see Section 1) and passing it to Stage 8.

Finally, Stage 8 (second gated residual) blends the expert branch back into the residual stream: stream_out=α2⊙stream_mid+β2⊙RMSNorm(f⊙(1+wpost_ffn))\mathrm{stream\_out} = \alpha_2 \odot \mathrm{stream\_mid} + \beta_2 \odot \mathrm{RMSNorm}(f \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{post\_ffn}}))stream_out=α2​⊙stream_mid+β2​⊙RMSNorm(f⊙(1+wpost_ffn​)), which becomes the streaml+1\mathrm{stream}_{l+1}streaml+1​ passed to the next layer. Just as in Stage 6, multiplication comes before division here, and the coefficients α2\alpha_2α2​ and β2\beta_2β2​ come from a vector learned for Stage 8 with α22+β22=1\alpha_2^2 + \beta_2^2 = 1α22​+β22​=1 elementwise. To finish the layer, Stage 8 computes xl+1=RMSNorm(stream_out)⊙(1+wnext)x_{l+1} = \mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathrm{stream\_out}) \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{next}})xl+1​=RMSNorm(stream_out)⊙(1+wnext​); the final layer skips xl+1x_{l+1}xl+1​.

Because Stage 8 reads no weight matrices — only a few length-8,192 vectors — we only need to look at Stages 1–7 when we calculate minimum execution times below.

Beyond the all-reduce inside Stage 3, the 8 GPUs run a second all-reduce sum on mmm right after Stage 6. When T≤8T \le 8T≤8, they also run an all-gather after Stage 7 to stitch the 1,024 columns from each of the 8 GPUs into 8,192 columns. All three cross-GPU collectives sit on the main chain, so all 8 GPUs must wait for each collective to finish before moving on (their latency sits outside this book's single-GPU accounting; see Primer 1).

3Which Memory Reads Must Wait for the Previous Step to Finish?

In single-request decode, inter-stage activations account for under 0.2% of total bytes read; the five dense weight matrices and historical KV cache can be read from the start, and expert weights can be prefetched as soon as Stage 4 selects the experts.

If we draw these 8 stages by their data dependencies, we get a directed acyclic graph (DAG, where each arrow means "must wait for its result"; see Figure P2-3). The whole layer forms a single serial main chain that forks at hhh into Stage 4 and Stage 5 and merges back at Stage 6. Outside that main chain, there are two extra edges: one sends stream_mid straight from Stage 3 to Stage 8, and the other keeps the KV cache written by this layer horizontally for future tokens.

Every byte a stage reads from memory falls into one of two buckets. The first bucket is activations — the intermediate results just produced by the previous stage in the current forward pass, which do not exist until that previous step finishes (about 0.1 MB in single-request decode; see Section 1). The second bucket is weights and historical KV cache, which are already sitting in HBM before the current forward pass even starts.

How do the expert weights for Stage 6 fit in? Those bytes are also sitting in HBM from the start, with one catch: Stage 6 has to wait for Stage 4 (router) to produce topk_ids before it knows which experts to read. Because Stage 4 runs in parallel with Stage 5 (pooler), the moment Stage 4 finishes we can start prefetching the selected expert weights while Stage 5 is still running. We will see how hardware takes advantage of that overlap in Chapter 1, Section 4 and Chapter 9, Sections 4–5.

4How Fast Can a Stage Possibly Run, and What Is It Waiting On?

Minimum execution time is the slower of byte transfer time and compute time; below 206 FLOP/B the stage is HBM-bound, and above 206 FLOP/B it is Tensor Core-bound.

A single H200 has two hard hardware ceilings: HBM read bandwidth tops out at 4.8 TB/s, and Tensor Core BF16 matrix-multiplication throughput tops out at 989 TFLOP/s (Chapter 5, Section 3 shows how a single instruction works under the hood). Even if you overlap memory transfers and arithmetic completely, a stage can never finish faster than whichever of those two jobs takes longer:

tmin⁡=max⁡ ⁣(bytes transferred4.8 TB/s, FLOP989 TFLOP/s)t_{\min} = \max\!\left(\frac{\text{bytes transferred}}{4.8\ \text{TB/s}},\ \frac{\text{FLOP}}{989\ \text{TFLOP/s}}\right)tmin​=max(4.8 TB/sbytes transferred​, 989 TFLOP/sFLOP​)

That minimum time is the stage's lower bound (floor). For a full layer, the lower bound is whichever of two times is longer: total bytes moved across the layer divided by 4.8 TB/s, or total operations across the layer divided by 989 TFLOP/s. Computing the bound this way assumes that while one stage is running its math, the weights for later stages are already being read in (Section 3). By this definition, the full-layer lower bound is never higher than the sum of the individual stage lower bounds.

Comparing the two terms inside the maximum tells you right away which side is slower. The number of floating-point operations a stage performs per byte transferred is its arithmetic intensity, written I=FLOP/byteI = \text{FLOP} / \text{byte}I=FLOP/byte (in FLOP/B). Divide peak compute throughput by peak memory bandwidth and you get the machine's ridge point, 989/4.8≈206989 / 4.8 \approx 206989/4.8≈206 FLOP/B. Plot achievable compute throughput against arithmetic intensity and you get the roofline model in Figure P2-4.

Whenever I<206I < 206I<206, moving bytes takes longer than doing the math: the compute units sit waiting on HBM, so the stage is memory-bound (HBM-bound). Whenever I>206I > 206I>206, the math takes longer than moving the bytes: data already on chip waits on the Tensor Core, so the stage is compute-bound (Tensor Core-bound).

Let's run the numbers on Stage 1's gemv at T=1T = 1T=1. In Primer 1, Section 4, we worked out that at T=1T = 1T=1 we do only 1 operation per byte of BF16 weight read. That puts the arithmetic intensity at I≈1I \approx 1I≈1 FLOP/B, only about 1/2061 / 2061/206 of the ridge point: even if we use the Tensor Core, we can tap at most 0.5% of its compute throughput (see Figure P2-4). So the lower bound for this step is determined entirely by reading the weights:

37.75 MB4.8 TB/s=7.86 µs\frac{37.75\ \text{MB}}{4.8\ \text{TB/s}} = 7.86\ \text{µs}4.8 TB/s37.75 MB​=7.86 µs

That 7.86 µs lower bound is the target line that every gemv version in Part I tries to reach.

Of course, the lower bound assumes ideal overlap between memory transfers and compute as well as full rated bandwidth, which real hardware runs do not necessarily reach. Launching a kernel (a program executed concurrently by many threads on the GPU; defined in Primer 3, Section 1) also carries a fixed overhead that does not shrink with byte count (we measure how large it is in Primer 3, Section 5). On top of that, getting close to 4.8 TB/s requires keeping enough unanswered read requests in the air at the same time (called in-flight reads; Chapter 2, Section 3 measures how much must be kept in flight). As a result, measured execution time is always higher than the lower bound — and closing that gap is the goal of the chapters that follow.

5As the Token Count T Grows, Which Stages Become Tensor Core-Bound First?

Dense weights are shared across all tokens in the forward pass, historical KV is shared only across new tokens of the same request, and expert weights are shared only across tokens routed to that expert; thus dense stages cross 206 FLOP/B first.

Let BBB be the number of requests batched into a single forward pass and LLL be the number of new tokens per request in that pass, giving T=B×LT = B \times LT=B×L total tokens. In online serving, the very same layer runs across three typical regimes:

  • Regime 1 (decode, T=1T = 1T=1): One request with 80,000 historical tokens generates tokens one at a time, with B=1, L=1B = 1,\ L = 1B=1, L=1.
  • Regime 2 (verify, T=256T = 256T=256): 32 concurrent online requests with varying history lengths each verify 8 draft tokens at once, with B=32, L=8B = 32,\ L = 8B=32, L=8.
  • Regime 3 (chunked prefill, T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384): For a very long prompt, materializing tens of thousands of activation rows at once takes too much device memory. Instead, we slice the prompt into 16,384-token chunks and run them one after another, a technique called chunked prefill. Here we look at chunk 5, where 65,536 tokens are already cached, with B=1, L=T=16,384B = 1,\ L = T = 16{,}384B=1, L=T=16,384.

Why don't all 7 stages cross 206 FLOP/B together? The answer comes down to how many tokens share each byte you pull from HBM:

  • Dense weights (Stages 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7): We read these once and share them across all TTT tokens in the pass, so their arithmetic intensity III scales roughly in proportion to TTT. The dense stages cross 206 FLOP/B once TTT reaches two to three hundred (see Chapter 5, Section 2 for the exact crossover and measurements). Still, when a matrix has fewer rows or columns — for example, o has only 1,024 input columns — the input and output activation bytes per token make up a larger share of memory traffic and pull the arithmetic intensity down slightly. That is why at T=256T = 256T=256, qkv_gate has already crossed 206 while o sits just below 206. As for router, its 4-byte FP32 weights cut its arithmetic intensity to half that of a same-shaped BF16 matrix, and its lower bound is still evaluated against 989 TFLOP/s.
  • Historical KV cache (Stage 2): Every request has its own conversation history, so 1 byte of historical KV cache is shared only across the LLL new tokens of that same request. When L=1L = 1L=1, for each 256 B KV cache slot we read, 16 query heads each run one 64-dimensional inner product and one 64-dimensional weighted sum (64 multiply-accumulates apiece, at 2 FLOP per multiply-accumulate). That totals 2×2×16×64=4,0962 \times 2 \times 16 \times 64 = 4{,}0962×2×16×64=4,096 FLOP and gives an arithmetic intensity of I=4096/256=16I = 4096 / 256 = 16I=4096/256=16 FLOP/B. At L=8L = 8L=8, the arithmetic intensity climbs to 127.5 FLOP/B (about 8×), which is still short of 206.
  • Expert weights (Stage 6): The weights of 1 expert are shared only across the tokens that actually route to that expert. Because H200 Tensor Cores have no native 4-bit matrix multiply, we have to unpack expert weights to BF16 before multiplying (Chapter 6, Section 3 shows how), so the compute ceiling stays at 989 TFLOP/s. Each routed token does 1 multiply-accumulate (2 FLOP) per weight (0.5625 B), which gives an arithmetic intensity of 2/0.5625≈3.562 / 0.5625 \approx 3.562/0.5625≈3.56 FLOP/B per token. Reaching 206 FLOP/B takes roughly 206/3.56≈58206 / 3.56 \approx 58206/3.56≈58 tokens hitting the same expert in the same pass.

Let's start with Regime 1: decode (T=1T = 1T=1). With a single token in flight, no bytes are shared across tokens at all: all 7 stages sit between 0.5 and 16 FLOP/B (see Figure P2-4), well below 206. The 6 non-expert stages add up to about 29 µs, and the expert stage takes the 11.03 µs budget we worked out in Section 1. The chart below breaks down the lower bound stage by stage, where the 7.86 µs bar for qkv_gate is the gemv lower bound from Section 4.

Next, look at Regime 2: verify (T=256T = 256T=256, where B=32B = 32B=32 requests each verify L=8L = 8L=8 tokens). Here the three large dense matrices (qkv_gate, pooler, and the fully read unpooler) cross 206 FLOP/B and become Tensor Core-bound. Meanwhile, o sits right below 206, router stays low because its weights take 4 bytes each, and attention shares KV cache reads only across the L=8L = 8L=8 tokens within each request, stopping at 127.5 FLOP/B.

What happens in the expert stage? Under uniform routing, the 256×8=2,048256 \times 8 = 2{,}048256×8=2,048 hit pairs spread evenly across all 256 experts: our local GPU gets 256 hit pairs, touches nearly all 32 local experts, and feeds each expert only 8 tokens on average.

The benchmark specification instead defines its lower bound under skewed routing (where popular experts attract more tokens; see Chapter 8, Section 1). If we subtract the non-expert memory reads from the benchmark lower bound, the remaining expert budget corresponds to the busiest GPU hitting about 16.0 local experts, fewer than the ~32 experts under uniform routing. Why does skew lower the time bound? Because we read expert weights once per distinct active expert rather than once per token: concentrating hits onto fewer popular experts means the busiest GPU reads fewer distinct experts, which pulls the full-layer lower bound down accordingly. The benchmark does not state how it chose that budget, and this book takes it as given. Under that benchmark lower-bound assumption, the local GPU's 256 hit pairs spread across 16.0 experts — about 16 tokens per expert, still far below the 58 tokens needed to become Tensor Core-bound. At about 57 FLOP/B (see Figure P2-4), well below 206, the expert stage remains HBM-bound, leaving the full layer with 3 compute-bound stages and 4 memory-bound stages.

Even so, when we check the full-layer lower bound, total arithmetic divided by 989 TFLOP/s takes only about 60% of the byte-transfer time, so the full layer as a whole remains memory-bound. Compared with T=1T = 1T=1, the lower bound of a sliding-window layer grows to about 3.6× its T=1T = 1T=1 value, in exchange for processing 255 additional tokens in the same forward pass (see the chart below for the per-layer lower bounds).

Finally, look at Regime 3: chunked prefill (T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, chunk 5 of a long prompt with 65,536 tokens already cached). Under uniform routing, each local expert now receives 16,384×8/256=51216{,}384 \times 8 / 256 = 51216,384×8/256=512 tokens, far above 58, and attention's LLL is 16,384 as well. At this point, all 7 stages cross 206 FLOP/B and become Tensor Core-bound. By the rule from Section 4, once every stage is Tensor Core-bound, the full-layer lower bound is simply the sum of the individual stage lower bounds — about 9.87 ms, which differs by about 0.2% from the benchmark-specified 9.85 ms. For a sliding-window layer on the same chunk, the benchmark-specified 5.66 ms is about 13% higher than the 5.00 ms sum of stages, for reasons that were not determined.

Keep in mind that all lower bounds above count only single-GPU memory transfers and arithmetic, leaving out kernel launch overhead (Primer 3, Section 5) and cross-GPU communication latency (Primer 1). Skewed routing is only the benchmark's load assumption — hit counts under real routing traffic were not measured — and the memory savings and extra forward passes of chunked prefill were also not measured in this book.

HBM-bound stages get faster when you read fewer bytes and pack the available bandwidth more fully (Chapters 2, 3, and 6). Tensor Core-bound stages get faster when you keep the matrix units fed (Chapter 5). Part I starts with the cleanest HBM-bound stage in the layer — gemv at T=1T = 1T=1 — and pushes it step by step toward its lower bound.

Takeaway: What a stage waits on comes down to how many tokens share each byte it reads. In single-request decode, no bytes are shared and all 7 stages are HBM-bound; as the token count and byte sharing grow, the stages become Tensor Core-bound one by one.

Next chapter's question: At T=1T = 1T=1, Stage 1 is a single matrix-vector multiplication y=Wxy = W xy=Wx, and reading WWW takes at least 7.86 µs. If we write that calculation as a minimal CUDA program, what does the code look like, and what does each keyword do?

Primer 2 left us at a lower bound: at T=1T = 1T=1, Stage 1 needs at least 7.86 µs to finish reading WWW. To get anywhere near that bound, we first need code that actually runs on the GPU—so how does a minimal CUDA program put thousands of threads to work together to compute y=Wxy = W xy=Wx?

1How Does CUDA Turn the Row Loop of y=Wxy = Wxy=Wx into Parallelism?

The outer row loop disappears: each of the 2,304 rows goes to a thread block (CTA), and those CTAs reside on the 132 SMs in batches; inside each CTA, 128 threads split up the 8,192 columns and accumulate them in parallel.

We are computing y=Wxy = W xy=Wx from Stage 1 of Primer 2, where both W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 and x :  [8192]  BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16}x:[8192]BF16 sit in HBM and each output row is yr=∑k=08191Wr,k xky_r = \sum_{k=0}^{8191} W_{r,k}\, x_kyr​=∑k=08191​Wr,k​xk​. Let's write M=2,304M = 2{,}304M=2,304 for the number of rows and K=8,192K = 8{,}192K=8,192 for the number of columns. To keep the code short, the listing below writes the output yyy in FP32; the real Stage 1 writes BF16 and slices it into q, k, v, and gate for Stage 2. The arrows at the end of the lines point to the chapters that explain the hardware mechanism behind each line.

// #include <cuda_bf16.h> and device memory allocation omitted; stream is a pre-created CUDA stream
__global__ void gemv_kernel(const __nv_bfloat16* W, const __nv_bfloat16* x,
                            float* y, int K) {
    __shared__ float smem[128];                                // → Chapter 3
    int row = blockIdx.x;                                      // → Chapter 2
    int tid = threadIdx.x;                                     // → Chapter 3
    float acc = 0.0f;                                          // → Chapter 3
    for (int k = tid; k < K; k += blockDim.x) {
        acc += __bfloat162float(W[row * K + k])                // → Chapter 3 (load), Chapter 6 (conversion)
             * __bfloat162float(x[k]);                         // → Chapter 5 (multiply-add)
    }
    smem[tid] = acc;
    __syncthreads();                                           // → Chapter 4
    if (tid == 0) {                                            // → Chapter 4
        float sum = 0.0f;
        for (int i = 0; i < blockDim.x; ++i) sum += smem[i];
        y[row] = sum;
    }
}
gemv_kernel<<<M, 128, 0, stream>>>(W, x, y, K);                // → Chapter 1, Chapter 2

Let's walk through the code from top to bottom. At the start, __global__ marks the function as a kernel—a function launched once by the CPU and executed concurrently by thousands of threads on the GPU. CUDA calls a group of threads that cooperate on a unit of work a thread block (CTA) (short for cooperative thread array, and called block in code), and all CTAs from one launch form a grid. The launch statement on the last line fires up M=2,304M = 2{,}304M=2,304 CTAs at once, with 128 threads in each CTA executing this function from start to finish. Inside the loop, __bfloat162float converts 2-byte BF16 values into 4-byte FP32 values before multiplying and accumulating them into the thread's own acc (Chapter 6 covers what this conversion costs in hardware).

Instead of stepping through the rows one at a time in an outer loop, CUDA flattens that loop into 2,304 CTAs—one per row—and dispatches them onto SM (Streaming Multiprocessor) units to run. An SM is the compute unit that executes instructions: the H200 has 132 SMs, and a single CTA runs on one SM from start to finish. Each SM has an upper limit on how many CTAs can reside on it at the same time, so the remaining CTAs wait until slots free up (Chapter 2, Section 1 and Chapter 3, Section 1 explain how many fit and why).

2What Does the Launch Statement Do, and When Is yyy Ready?

A kernel launch statement merely enqueues a command into a CUDA stream and returns immediately before yyy is computed; by default, a subsequent kernel in the same CUDA stream is guaranteed to see the data written by the preceding kernel.

Take a look at the triple angle brackets on the last line, gemv_kernel<<<M, 128, 0, stream>>>. Inside the brackets, the first argument sets the number of CTAs for this launch to M=2,304M = 2{,}304M=2,304, and the second sets 128 threads per CTA. The third argument sets the dynamic shared memory bytes allocated per CTA for this launch; this example does not use any, so we pass 0. The fourth argument selects the target CUDA stream—a queue of GPU commands that run in enqueue order, written as the variable stream in code. Because a launch call only puts the command into the queue and lets the CPU keep running without waiting for the GPU to finish, we call it an asynchronous launch.

By default, commands in the same CUDA stream run in the order you enqueue them, so the earlier kernel happens-before the next one: without any extra synchronization, the next kernel is guaranteed to see the earlier kernel's writes. A later kernel can also start early; Chapter 1, Section 4 covers the rules for that case. When the CPU itself needs to wait for the result, it calls cudaStreamSynchronize(stream) to wait until this queue finishes running.

3How Does Each Thread Know Which Segment to Compute?

Via built-in hardware thread coordinates: blockIdx.x identifies the CTA index, threadIdx.x identifies the thread index within the CTA, and blockDim.x gives the CTA size used as the loop stride.

Start with row = blockIdx.x: the CTA index runs from 0..2,3030..2{,}3030..2,303 and maps straight to the row of WWW that this CTA handles. Then tid = threadIdx.x (0..1270..1270..127) and blockDim.x (128) divide up the columns across the CTA: on loop iteration rrr (r=1..64r = 1..64r=1..64), thread tid reads column index k=tid+128 (r−1)k = \mathrm{tid} + 128\,(r - 1)k=tid+128(r−1).

Because each row has 8,192 columns split across 128 threads, every thread runs 8,192/128=648{,}192 / 128 = 648,192/128=64 iterations, and together the 128 threads read one full 16 KiB row of WWW along with 16 KiB of xxx. Within the same loop iteration, adjacent threads read adjacent addresses in that row, so all 128 threads cover a contiguous 256 B span. Every 32 adjacent threads form a warp; Chapter 3, Sections 1–2 explain how they issue load instructions together and how the hardware coalesces them.

You can check this formula directly in Figure P3-1 by dragging the sliders to row = 2, tid = 5, and iteration 24 (r=24r = 24r=24): on that iteration, the thread reads column index k=5+128×23=2,949k = 5 + 128 \times 23 = 2{,}949k=5+128×23=2,949, fetching the two elements W[2 * 8192 + 2949] = W[19333] and x[2949].

4How Are 128 Partial Sums Safely Reduced into One Value?

Each thread writes its partial sum to CTA-shared smem, __syncthreads() waits until all 128 threads finish writing, and thread 0 sums the values and writes back yry_ryr​.

The variables row, tid, and acc sit in registers—each thread has its own private copy, and other threads cannot see them. The array __shared__ float smem[128] (128×4 B=512 B128 \times 4\ \text{B} = 512\ \text{B}128×4 B=512 B) sits in on-chip shared memory, where all 128 threads in this CTA can read and write it while other CTAs cannot see it (Chapter 3, Section 1 covers these two levels of on-chip storage). And the arrays W, x, and y sit in global memory in HBM, where all CTAs can read and write them.

Combining many partial sums into a single value is called a reduction. Because acc is private to each thread, the 128 partial sums have to pass through smem first: each thread writes its accumulator with smem[tid] = acc.

Right after that store comes __syncthreads() (a CTA barrier). It holds all 128 threads in this CTA at this line before any of them proceed; once past it, every thread in the CTA can see the values that those 128 threads previously wrote into smem. This guarantee applies only within the same CTA—exchanging data across different CTAs requires separate rules covered in Chapter 2, Section 6. Without __syncthreads(), when thread 0 reads smem[i], thread i may not have written its value yet.

After the barrier, thread 0 adds the 128 values one by one and writes the sum to y[row], while the other 127 threads wait idle. That keeps the code as simple as possible and gives the right yry_ryr​, at the cost of 512 B of shared memory per CTA, 1 CTA barrier, and 128 dependent additions that 1 thread runs serially. Because CTAs in the same batch reach this step at almost the same time, the SM has no other in-flight memory reads left to overlap with it—so this serial addition adds straight to the runtime of each batch. Chapter 4, Sections 5–6 show how to get all 128 threads to run the reduction together.

5How Do We Measure Latency in This Book, and What Part Lies Outside the Kernel?

Before each run we flush the on-chip cache, bracket a single kernel launch with GPU events, and take the median across 500 runs—of which ~4.6 µs is fixed launch and event-recording overhead.

We time every gemv version in Part I of this book the same way. Before each timed launch, we read a large block of unrelated data to flush the chip's small, fast storage (the on-chip cache), so the GPU actually reads WWW from HBM. Then we record one GPU event—a timestamp that the GPU logs in the CUDA stream—before the launch and another one after it. We run 20 warmup iterations and take the median across 500 timed iterations. Flushing the cache before each run matches the single-request decode scenario from Primer 2 (Chapter 2, Section 2 explains why they match).

Timing an empty kernel that does nothing with the same method gives ~4.6 µs, which we call fixed overhead. Every measured latency in Part I includes this overhead without subtracting it out, whereas the 7.86 µs lower bound from Primer 2 does not include it. Consecutive kernels also pay additional overhead between launches; see Chapter 1, Section 1.

6Why Assign a Thread Block per Row Instead of a Single Thread? (gemv v0 → v1)

Assigning one row per thread launches only 18 CTAs, leaving most of the 132 SMs idle, and adjacent threads read addresses separated by an entire row; switching to one CTA per row speeds up execution by ~12.5×.

We number each version of gemv in this book starting from v0. Following the habit of writing CPU loops, v0 has each thread compute one entire row on its own: row = blockIdx.x * 128 + threadIdx.x, launched with <<<18, 128, 0, stream>>> (2,304/128=182{,}304 / 128 = 182,304/128=18 CTAs), so each thread loops across all 8,192 columns of its row from start to finish. v1 is the kernel from Section 1, launched with <<<2304, 128, 0, stream>>>, which assigns one 128-thread CTA to each row:

// v0: each thread computes 1 full row on its own（int row = blockIdx.x * 128 + threadIdx.x;）
for (int k = 0; k < K; ++k) acc += __bfloat162float(W[row * K + k]) * __bfloat162float(x[k]);
// v1: the 128 adjacent threads of 1 CTA cooperate to read one row in segments (full code in Section 1)
for (int k = tid; k < K; k += 128) acc += __bfloat162float(W[row * K + k]) * __bfloat162float(x[k]);

Here is what happens when we time both versions on the H200 using the method from Section 5:

The gap comes from two sources. First, most SMs sit idle: hardware dispatches work to SMs one CTA at a time (for how dispatch works, see Chapter 2, Section 1), so 18 CTAs can keep at most 18 of the 132 SMs busy.

Second, look at the memory access stride. On a GPU, the 32 adjacent threads of a warp issue one load instruction together, and device memory transfers at least a 32-byte segment per transaction (Chapter 3, Section 2 covers coalesced access). In v0, those 32 threads ask for 32 addresses that sit 16 KiB apart from one another: one load instruction brings back 32×32=1,02432 \times 32 = 1{,}02432×32=1,024 B, yet the current iteration uses only 64 B of it. Each 32 B segment holds the next 16 BF16 elements of that row, and the current iteration uses only 1 of them; the other 15 sit unused until the next 15 iterations, when they may still be in the on-chip cache (see Chapter 3, Section 2).

In v1, those same 32 threads read a contiguous 64 B span: memory transfers 2 segments, and the current iteration uses every byte right away.

Moving from v0 to v1 buys us two things: 2,304 CTAs that fill all 132 SMs, and adjacent threads that read contiguous bytes. In exchange, we pay the three costs from Section 4: 512 B of shared memory, 1 CTA barrier, and 128 serial additions.

Also, in v0 every thread in a warp reads the same x[k] on a given iteration, so 32 rows share one read. In v1, each CTA reads all 16 KiB of xxx on its own, so across 2,304 CTAs they read as many bytes of xxx in total as of WWW (Chapter 2, Section 2 shows how the on-chip cache absorbs those repeated reads).

What if the matrix has fewer than 132 rows? Then assigning 1 CTA per row still cannot fill all 132 SMs, so we have to split each row further across multiple CTAs (see Chapter 2, Section 5). Here we measured only the 2,304-row, T=1T = 1T=1 case in this example. How much each of the two factors contributes, and how much of v1's repeated reads of xxx reach HBM, were not measured separately.

Even so, v1 still runs at ~7× the lower bound (see the chart above). Once you subtract the fixed overhead, its effective bandwidth for reading WWW reaches only about one-sixth of 4.8 TB/s. Why is that gap still so wide? Answering that question is the job of Chapters 2–4.

Takeaway: CUDA flattens the outer loop into 2,304 CTAs that go onto the SMs in batches; having a group of adjacent threads work together on a single row is what fills all 132 SMs and lets them read contiguous bytes.

Next chapter's question: A single v1 launch takes tens of microseconds, and part of that is fixed overhead that does not depend on byte count—yet a single model layer has to launch a sequence of kernels in order. Where does the time between consecutive kernels go, and how do we squeeze it out?
