In Primer 3, every timing run of gemv_kernel (v1) included ~4.6 µs of fixed overhead (see Primer 3, Section 5). In a single model layer, though, the GPU doesn't run only that one kernel—it launches a chain of kernels back-to-back along a CUDA stream. Where does the time between two adjacent kernels go, and how can we eliminate it?

Figure I-1 maps out the six levels of Part I, zooming in level by level from the timeline all the way down to instructions and bits. This chapter sits at the outermost level, Level 1: Timeline.

To see what happens on the timeline, let's put gemv_kernel from Primer 3 back where it lives inside a single layer—right after a normalization kernel and right before a post-processing kernel. That gives us the single three-kernel chain we'll use from start to finish in this chapter:

  1. Normalization kernel: takes input x :  [8192]  BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16}x:[8192]BF16, writes output xn :  [8192]  BF16\shape{x_n}{8192}{BF16}xn​:[8192]BF16, and computes xn=x⋅rx_n = x \cdot rxn​=x⋅r, where r=1/1K∑kxk2+ϵr = 1/\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_k x_k^2 + \epsilon}r=1/K1​∑k​xk2​+ϵ​ (see Primer 1, Section 1 for the RMSNorm definition; no weight vector is multiplied here). This step launches 1 CTA of 1,024 threads.
  2. gemv_kernel (v1): computes y=Wxny = W x_ny=Wxn​ from weight W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 into output y :  [2304]  FP32\shape{y}{2304}{FP32}y:[2304]FP32, launching 2,304 CTAs of 128 threads each.
  3. Post-processing kernel: runs elementwise operations on y :  [2304]  FP32\shape{y}{2304}{FP32}y:[2304]FP32 (standing in for the actual per-head normalization and rotary position embedding (RoPE); see Primer 2, Section 2), launching ⌈2304/256⌉=9\lceil 2304/256 \rceil = 9⌈2304/256⌉=9 CTAs of 256 threads each.

All three steps rely only on the building blocks from Primer 3: thread blocks (CTAs), threads, a CUDA stream, and global memory.

1Why Does the GPU Stall Between Two Kernels?

Two types of gaps arise: when CPU launch lags GPU execution, the command queue drains and the GPU waits for the CPU; even when commands are queued, the next kernel must wait for all CTAs of the previous kernel to exit. We call the first one the CPU launch gap and the second one the hardware handoff gap.

Let's start with the first gap. Because a kernel launch statement just drops a command into the CUDA stream and returns immediately (see Primer 3), the CPU acts as the producer, the GPU acts as the consumer, and the CUDA stream is the queue sitting between them. Suppose each kernel runs on the GPU for tgput_{gpu}tgpu​, while the CPU takes tcput_{cpu}tcpu​ to issue a single launch command. Whenever tcpu>tgput_{cpu} > t_{gpu}tcpu​>tgpu​, the GPU finishes the current kernel before the CPU has pushed the next command into the queue. The queue runs dry, the start-to-start spacing between back-to-back kernels stretches out to tcput_{cpu}tcpu​, and the GPU sits idle for ~tcpu−tgput_{cpu} - t_{gpu}tcpu​−tgpu​ every time. Flip that around to tcpu≤tgput_{cpu} \le t_{gpu}tcpu​≤tgpu​, and the CPU stays ahead of the GPU: the queue always holds commands, and that idle wait vanishes.

Small kernels are where this hurts most, because their tgput_{gpu}tgpu​ is only a few microseconds—and in our three-kernel chain, both the 1-CTA normalization kernel and the 9-CTA post-processing kernel are that small. Our benchmark script fires off the three launches one after another from Python, and the first two rows of Figure 1-1 compare two ways of timing them. In "CPU one-by-one launch", the stream queue is empty when the timer starts, and Python issues the three launches one by one. In "Pre-filled command queue", we first enqueue a kernel that keeps the GPU busy for a short window before starting the timer, and the CPU uses that window to queue up all three launch commands.

In our measurements, launching the kernels one by one from the CPU is ~41 µs slower than starting from a pre-filled command queue (see the chart in Section 5). By the queue rule, those 41 µs land in two places: the first launch (when timing starts with an empty queue) and the ①→② boundary (because ① runs for only a few microseconds). While ② runs for ~54 µs, the CPU queues up ③, so the ②→③ boundary no longer waits on the CPU. How large tcput_{cpu}tcpu​ is on its own, how the 41 µs split between those two places, and how much launching from C++ would save were not measured.

Now look at the second row of Figure 1-1, "Pre-filled command queue". Even when all three commands are already waiting in the queue ahead of time, a gap still separates adjacent bars. The CPU has nothing to do with this second gap: a single CUDA stream enforces its ordering guarantee (happens-before; see Primer 3, Section 2) by waiting until the previous kernel has completely finished and all of its writes are visible before starting the next kernel. As a result, crossing every kernel boundary has to step through the full handoff: "the last CTA of the previous kernel exits → writes become visible → CTAs of the next kernel are dispatched onto the 132 SMs" (for dispatch, see Primer 3, Section 1). While the last few CTAs of the previous kernel are still running, the SMs that finished early are already sitting idle; once that last CTA exits, all SMs sit idle until the next kernel is dispatched onto them.

2Which Gap Does CUDA Graph Eliminate, and Which Does It Leave Behind?

CUDA Graph pre-records the entire execution chain and submits it in one call, eliminating CPU launch gaps while leaving a ~1.0 µs hardware handoff gap between nodes.

A CUDA Graph is a pre-recorded sequence of GPU commands and their dependencies, with each kernel in the graph represented as a graph node. Using one takes two steps. First comes recording and graph instantiation (cudaGraphInstantiate): during warm-up before formal timing starts, we record the three kernel launches in order into a single graph, and at instantiation time the driver (the CPU-side software that manages the GPU) validates the graph and does most of the launch setup up front. Second comes replay: at runtime, the CPU makes a single cudaGraphLaunch call (see the code in Section 5) to submit the whole graph at once, without redoing that setup on later launches. Because we pay the CPU launch time tcput_{cpu}tcpu​ only once for the entire chain instead of once per kernel, the first gap from Section 1 disappears (Row 3 of Figure 1-1).

Each graph node is still a separate kernel, though, and back-to-back nodes still have to obey the ordering rule of a single CUDA stream: the next node cannot start until every CTA of the previous node has exited and all of its writes are visible. That leaves the second gap right inside the graph. During full-graph replay, the hardware handoff gap between two adjacent nodes sits at a median of ~1.0 µs (calibrated as the median across 93 node boundaries in a real inference computation graph, rather than a measurement on this chapter's chain).

Compare that with "Pre-filled command queue" from Section 1: pre-filling the queue can hide CPU launch time too, but only as long as the CPU stays ahead of the GPU, whereas full-graph replay does not depend on the CPU keeping up. On our three-kernel chain, full-graph replay also runs slightly faster than a pre-filled command queue (see Section 5 for the measured results).

Here is the trade-off with CUDA Graph:

  • What you gain: it eliminates the CPU launch gap (see Section 5 for the measured speedup on the three-kernel chain).
  • What it costs: you do an extra recording and instantiation pass during warm-up, and every kernel's arguments, tensor shapes, and device memory addresses get baked into the graph—so if the input token count TTT varies, you have to record separate graphs for different values of TTT (or pad the input up to a recorded TTT).
  • When it loses: on this three-kernel chain, full-graph replay beats both stream-launch modes; the extra cost of recording multiple graphs and padding shapes, and whether it loses in other scenarios, were not measured.

3What Do You Save and What Do You Pay When Fusing Two Kernels into One?

Kernel fusion removes one boundary, one launch, and one global-memory round trip. You pay with one more step in the main kernel, and it works only if the next step never makes all CTAs stop and wait for each other.

Kernel fusion puts the work of two adjacent kernels into a single kernel, keeping the intermediate result in registers or on chip instead of passing it through global memory. Every extra standalone kernel costs you more than a Section 2 handoff: it also writes its intermediate result out to global memory, only for the next kernel to read it right back in. When we time each of the three kernels on its own and the full chain (full-graph replay) on the same H200 with the same method, the full chain takes only ~5.8 µs longer than gemv_kernel alone.

Those 5.8 µs are just the gap between two end-to-end timings, so they still include the actual math inside normalization and post-processing. Fusing the kernels doesn't make that math disappear—you still have to run it—which means 5.8 µs is only an upper bound on what fusion can save.

So how do we actually fuse them? First, a quick piece of terminology: the elementwise work that runs after a kernel's main loop finishes and right before it writes out the final result is called the epilogue.

Folding post-processing into the epilogue is straightforward. In gemv_kernel, right after thread 0 of each CTA finishes the intra-CTA reduction for its row's dot product and before it writes out y[row], that value is already sitting in its register. And because elementwise post-processing doesn't need results from any other CTA, thread 0 can just apply it in place before writing the output.

Folding normalization into the front of the kernel takes one more step of reasoning. In xn=x⋅rx_n = x \cdot rxn​=x⋅r, the scale factor r=1/1K∑kxk2+ϵr = 1/\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_k x_k^2 + \epsilon}r=1/K1​∑k​xk2​+ϵ​ depends on the sum of squares across the whole vector xxx, so at first glance it looks as if you have to finish reading all of its elements before the matrix multiply can even begin. But look back at the v1 loop in Primer 3: to compute its own row's dot product, every CTA already reads the entire vector xxx (8,192 elements) from start to finish. Because every CTA reads all of xxx anyway, it can accumulate the sum of squares ∑kxk2\sum_k x_k^2∑k​xk2​ right alongside the dot product in that same loop, compute rrr after an intra-CTA reduction in the epilogue, and multiply it into the dot product at the end to write out y[row]=r⋅∑kW[row,k] xky[\text{row}] = r \cdot \sum_k W[\text{row}, k]\,x_ky[row]=r⋅∑k​W[row,k]xk​. This works because:

y=W(x⋅r)=r (Wx)y = W(x \cdot r) = r\,(Wx)y=W(x⋅r)=r(Wx)

Without a normalization weight vector, these two expressions are algebraically identical; with a weight vector, the expression becomes r W(wnorm⊙x)r\,W(w_{\text{norm}} \odot x)rW(wnorm​⊙x), which still uses only the data read by the current CTA. Numerically, only two things change: you skip one BF16 rounding step from writing xnx_nxn​ out to global memory (rounding a 32-bit float to 16 bits; see Chapter 6, Section 1), and you change the rounding order of the multiply-adds.

Fusion cuts out only the kernel boundaries and global-memory round trips; the computation you fold in still has to run. We measured this on a faster gemv kernel: folding the start of Stage 2 (per-head normalization, RoPE, and writing the FP8 KV cache; see Primer 2, Section 2) into the epilogue of Stage 1 still adds ~1.1 µs inside the kernel itself (see the chart below). In that kernel, each CTA still computes 1 row. Whenever one of a head's 64 CTAs finishes writing, it adds 1 to a counter; the last CTA to increment the counter runs the normalization and position embedding, while the rest exit right away (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for how the counter is written). How that extra 1.1 µs splits across those steps was not measured.

Whether two steps can be fused boils down to one question: can the second step get the data it needs without forcing all CTAs across the GPU to stop and wait for one another? You can fuse in two cases: either the data is already inside the same CTA, or the results from multiple CTAs only need to come together in one place so the last CTA that finishes writing can process them (Chapter 2, Section 6). Normalization fits the first case because every CTA already reads all of xxx (this 16 KiB vector stays in the on-chip cache; see Chapter 2, Section 2). Here is the trade-off with kernel fusion:

  • What you gain: you cut out 2 hardware handoffs and 2 launches, and the intermediate result xnx_nxn​ (16 KiB, which is small at T=1T = 1T=1) no longer gets written to global memory and read back in.
  • What it costs: the main kernel takes on an extra step in its loop or epilogue, the code gets more complex, and all 2,304 CTAs redundantly compute the same rrr (each CTA does 8,192 extra multiply-adds and one extra intra-CTA reduction).
  • When it loses:
    • When every CTA of the second step needs results produced by many CTAs of the first step, cramming both steps into a single kernel forces a device-wide barrier where all CTAs across the GPU stop and wait for the slowest CTA to finish writing. Device-wide synchronization also requires all CTAs to be co-resident on the chip at the same time, or else it will deadlock (see Chapter 2, Section 6). When that happens, keeping two separate kernels is usually better; the next section shows how to overlap them partially.
    • The second fusible pattern above (having the last finishing CTA do the work) can lose too: if the fused step is a small kernel that could otherwise enter early using the method in the next section, fusing forces it to wait until after the very last CTA of the preceding kernel finishes, losing that overlap and running slower in measured runs (see Chapter 9, Section 6).

4Can the Next Kernel Start Before the Previous Kernel Finishes?

Yes. PDL allows the successor kernel to be dispatched onto SMs early to prefetch weights, and then read the predecessor's output once all prior writes become visible.

As we saw in Primer 2, Section 3, static weights don't depend on the activations from the previous step, so you can start reading them early. In our three-kernel chain, the normalization kernel has only 1 CTA, so while it runs it occupies only 1 SM and leaves the other 131 SMs sitting idle. In a standard CUDA stream, though, the hardware ties two things together: the next kernel (which we'll call the dependent kernel (successor)) can start dispatching only after the previous kernel (the primary kernel (predecessor)) has completely finished. Hopper (the H200 architecture) provides PDL (Programmatic Dependent Launch) to split those two events apart, and you use it in four steps (Figure 1-3):

  1. When launching the successor kernel, the CPU passes an extra launch attribute telling the GPU that the successor may dispatch before the predecessor finishes.
  2. Inside the predecessor, each CTA issues a trigger call after finishing its main loop and before writing back its output; once every predecessor CTA has triggered (or exited), the hardware may dispatch CTAs of the successor onto idle SMs (the specification permits early dispatch, though it does not guarantee it).
  3. Once a successor CTA lands on an SM, it starts with work that does not depend on the predecessor's output—at the "normalization → gemv" boundary, it fires off the first batch of weight reads for WWW from HBM. Bytes read before the wait call returns must be buffered on chip until xnx_nxn​ is ready (see Chapter 9, Section 4 for how a single layer prefetches weights), so how much data you can prefetch is bounded by on-chip storage capacity.
  4. Right before reading the predecessor's output, the successor issues a wait call; once the wait call returns, the entire predecessor grid has finished executing and all of the predecessor's global-memory writes are visible to the successor.
// Predecessor: issue the trigger (placement: see below)
cudaTriggerProgrammaticLaunchCompletion();
// Successor: the CPU launches the successor through the launch API with the PDL launch attribute; the successor first issues reads that do not depend on the predecessor, then waits
cudaGridDependencySynchronize();   // read the predecessor's output only after this call returns

In this chapter's pattern, code that reads the predecessor's output must be placed after the wait call—and before the wait call returns, the successor also must not write to any buffer that the predecessor may still be reading (this does not occur in this chapter's chain; see Chapter 9, Section 5 for an example). Where you place the trigger call determines only how early the successor can be dispatched onto SMs.

Reasoning from the timeline, PDL can save at most two pieces: the overlap between the predecessor's epilogue and the successor's independent work (whichever is shorter), plus any amount by which the handoff itself may get shorter. We measured that handoff in a small test program built to time only this one step (which we'll call a microbenchmark). In that test, we chain two kernels with PDL: the successor has only 1 CTA and calls wait the moment it lands on an SM, and the time from the exit of the predecessor's last CTA to the return of the wait call is ~0.64 µs. Because this number and the 1.0 µs from Section 2 come from different experiments, you cannot subtract one directly from the other. How much PDL alone saves across a single boundary was not measured.

Where you place the trigger call depends on how many SMs the predecessor occupies. When the predecessor occupies only a few SMs (like the 1-CTA kernel in our example), triggering at kernel entry has almost no effect on the predecessor (not measured against triggering late). When the predecessor fills all SMs on the GPU, though, triggering at function entry lets early-dispatched successor CTAs stall on the wait call while holding onto SM resources, slowing down the predecessor CTAs that have not yet finished. In measured runs, doing so slowed the predecessor attention kernel by up to ~1.65 µs (Chapter 7, Section 11). Whether the contended resource was registers, shared memory, or CTA slots was not measured separately.

Triggering early only slows execution down; it cannot deadlock. The hardware dispatches the successor's CTAs only after every predecessor CTA has either triggered or exited. By that point, no predecessor CTA is still waiting for an SM: every one that has not yet exited is already running on an SM, so the successor's CTAs cannot block it. So when the predecessor fills all SMs, you should place the trigger call after the predecessor's main loop finishes and before its epilogue writeback.

Here is the trade-off with PDL:

  • What you gain: it overlaps the successor's predecessor-independent reads with the predecessor's epilogue (the latency change from enabling PDL on this gemv chain was not measured).
  • What it costs: the successor has to insert a wait call before its first read of the predecessor's data; if you accidentally place a read before the wait call, it may intermittently read stale values left over from the previous replay without any runtime error (see Chapter 9, Section 5 for measured examples of this bug).
  • When it loses: see above (and see Chapter 7, Section 11 for the measured counterexample).

5gemv Evolution v1 → v2: Recording the Three-Kernel Chain into a Single CUDA Graph

Full-graph replay is ~1.7× faster than CPU launch from an empty queue and ~1.6 µs faster than a pre-filled command queue, while individual kernel durations remain unchanged.

This step changes only how we launch the chain—the three kernels running on the GPU are byte-for-byte identical to v1:

// v1: the CPU puts [normalization, gemv_kernel, post-processing] into the CUDA stream one by one
gemv_kernel<<<2304, 128, 0, stream>>>(W, xn, y, K);
// v2: during warm-up, record these three steps on stream and instantiate them into graph_exec; at runtime, submit once
cudaGraphLaunch(graph_exec, stream);

We use the same timing setup as in Primer 3, Section 5, except here the GPU events bracket the entire three-kernel chain (Row 3 of Figure 1-1 corresponds to v2). Look at the first chart: stepping from the first bar ("CPU one-by-one launch") to the second bar ("Pre-filled command queue") shaves off ~41 µs—the CPU launch gap from Section 1. Stepping from the second bar to the third bar ("Full-graph replay (v2)") trims another ~1.6 µs, whose breakdown was not measured separately. See Section 2 for the costs of using CUDA Graph.

Now look at the second evolution-chain chart: when we time gemv_kernel on its own, the difference between v2 and v1 sits inside measurement noise, so the single-kernel duration hasn't budged. That gives us our starting point for the next chapter.

Takeaway: The dead time between kernels comes from two places—the CPU falling behind on launches, and the hardware waiting for all CTAs of the previous kernel to exit; CUDA Graph wipes out the first, kernel fusion cuts down how often you pay the second, and PDL overlaps the second with useful reads.

Next chapter's question: Even after we strip away the gaps between kernels, gemv_kernel by itself still takes 54.08 µs—~7× above the 7.86 µs bandwidth lower bound. Its 2,304 CTAs already fill all 132 SMs, so where else is that time going?

The Full H200 Chip — 2,304 CTAs Fill All 132 SMs, So Where Does the Time Still Go?

In Chapter 1, we stripped out the gaps between kernels, yet the runtime of a single gemv_kernel itself did not budge. Now let's open up that kernel and zoom in to Level 2: the full H200 chip.

The 2,304 CTAs of v1 fill all 132 SMs, yet gemv takes 54.08 µs whereas reading WWW once requires only 7.86 µs—at the full-chip level, where did that time go?

Throughout this chapter, we follow gemv_kernel from v1 / v2 (weights W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16, input x :  [8192]  BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16}x:[8192]BF16, output y :  [2304]  FP32\shape{y}{2304}{FP32}y:[2304]FP32, launch configuration <<<2304, 128>>>) as our main thread.

1How Are CTAs Distributed Across 132 SMs, and Why Does the Final Batch Hold Back the Entire Kernel?

The full GPU can hold at most 2,112 resident CTAs at once; the remaining 192 CTAs must wait for slots to free up and then execute all 64 serial load iterations from start to finish.

The hardware dispatches work to the 132 SMs in units of CTAs (see Primer 3, Section 1). Each SM has a limit on how many CTAs it can keep resident at once, and for v1 that limit is 16 (see Chapter 3, Section 1 for why it is 16). So the whole GPU can hold at most 132×16=2,112132 \times 16 = 2{,}112132×16=2,112 resident CTAs at once.

This book defines that device-wide concurrent CTA capacity (wave size) as 1 wave. Keep in mind that a wave is the on-chip capacity at any moment, not a batch that has to finish in lockstep before the next batch starts: as soon as any CTA finishes and exits, the next pending CTA immediately fills the slot it freed.

When we launch 2,304 CTAs onto a chip with a capacity of 2,112, we get 2,304=2,112+1922{,}304 = 2{,}112 + 1922,304=2,112+192. The first batch of 2,112 CTAs starts together, and because every CTA in v1 does the exact same amount of work, they finish and exit at almost the same time. Only then do the remaining 192 CTAs fill the freed slots and start running. This final partial batch of less than 1 wave is the tail (tail wave), with remainder r=192r = 192r=192 (Figure 2-1).

Why do those 192 tail-wave CTAs nearly double the runtime of the whole kernel? Look inside a single CTA: each of its 128 threads loads 1 element of WWW per iteration, so walking across one row of 8,192 columns takes 8,192/128=648{,}192 / 128 = 648,192/128=64 iterations. Every iteration has to wait for its loaded data to return before the next iteration can begin, because a thread issues its instructions in order (in-order issue). In v1's compiled loop, the next iteration's load sits behind the current iteration's multiply-add, and that multiply-add stalls until the current iteration's data comes back from global memory. That leaves each thread with only 1 read of WWW in flight at any given time (see Chapter 4, Section 2 for how in-order issue works).

A CPU core hides that wait with out-of-order execution and hardware prefetching. On a GPU, each warp uses in-order issue and does not skip past a wait to fire off later reads; while one warp waits, the SM issues reads from other warps instead. Whether the H200 has hardware prefetching was not measured in this book. Instead, this book modifies the code so each SM keeps more in-flight reads at once: either keep more resident threads (see Chapter 3) or have each thread issue multiple reads at a time (see Chapter 4).

Step back to the full chip, and v1's total runtime looks like two 64-iteration serial load chains laid end to end. The 2,112 CTAs of wave 1 walk the first 64-iteration chain, and the 192 tail-wave CTAs immediately walk a second 64-iteration chain of the exact same length from start to finish. Throughout the tail wave, only 192 of the 2,112 device-wide slots are active (~9%) while the remaining slots sit idle, yet the entire kernel has to wait for those last 192 CTAs to finish all 64 iterations.

Which 192 CTAs end up in the tail wave? The CUDA specification does not guarantee CTA dispatch order. On the H200, however, we recorded each CTA's start timestamp with the device-wide global nanosecond timer inside a 132-CTA kernel (the Stage 6 down projection kernel in Chapter 8): the highest-indexed CTA (CTA 131) started 0.9–3.2 µs later than CTAs with indices below 100. That matches dispatch in ascending blockIdx.x order, and extrapolating that order to v1 puts the 192 highest-indexed CTAs in the tail wave (the measured speedup of v3 in Section 8 also indirectly supports this). Which specific CTAs land in the tail wave for launches exceeding one wave (such as the 2,304 CTAs of v1) was not measured directly; code correctness does not depend on this order, and v3 relies on it only for speedup.

2How Long Does One Read Take to Return from HBM to an SM, and Why Does xxx Not Need to Be Read 2,304 Times from HBM?

An unloaded HBM read round trip takes ~0.33 µs, whereas hitting the device-wide L2 cache takes ~0.18 µs; WWW streams from HBM while xxx stays in L2 for reuse.

Figure 2-2 traces the memory path from off-chip memory into the compute units. For this chapter, we only need the outer two levels: off-chip HBM (High Bandwidth Memory, rated bandwidth 4.8 TB/s; see Primer 1, Section 4) on the outside, and the on-chip L2 cache (shared across all 132 SMs, 60 MiB total capacity) one step in. We'll open up the per-SM L1 cache, shared memory, and registers in Chapter 3, Section 1.

Every global memory read walks this path by checking L2 first. If the data is already sitting in L2 (a cache hit), L2 hands it straight back to the SM; if it is not in L2 (a cache miss), the request goes out to off-chip HBM, pulls the data back through L2, and delivers it to the SM. Because L2 is the only memory level on the GPU shared by all SMs, we'll use it again in Section 6 for cross-SM merge.

To measure the round-trip latency from issuing a read to getting the data back in a register, we first need a hardware time unit: the clock cycle, or one tick of the SM clock. This book converts clock cycles to time at the measured sustained clock of ~1.8 GHz, where 1 clock cycle is ~0.56 ns. When only a single read is in flight across the entire GPU (unloaded), one round trip from HBM takes ~0.33 µs, whereas one round trip that hits in L2 takes ~0.18 µs (see the chart below).

That answers the two questions left open in Primer 3. First, within a single kernel run, each element of the weight matrix WWW (37.75 MB) is read only once by a single CTA, so it does not hit in L2. In a real run, that same WWW is not needed again until the next forward pass. In between, ~9.0 GB of fixed weights (see Primer 1, Section 4) stream through the 60 MiB L2 and evict it long before then, so flushing the on-chip cache before timing matches real execution (see Primer 3, Section 5).

Second, the input vector xxx is only 16 KiB—far smaller than the 60 MiB L2 cache. Inferred from capacity alone, once the first batch of CTAs reads xxx for the first time and pulls xxx from HBM into L2, later reads of xxx by other CTAs should hit in L2 (the L2 cache hit rate on v1 was not measured).

Now plug those numbers back into the serial load chain from Section 1. In each loop iteration of v1, every thread issues one read of WWW (from HBM) and one read of xxx (hitting L2) at the same time, so the wait per iteration is approximately one HBM round-trip latency. Using the unloaded round-trip latency as a rough estimate, a 64-iteration serial chain takes 64×0.33≈21 μs64 \times 0.33 \approx 21\ \mu\text{s}64×0.33≈21 μs—the baseline we'll use in Section 8 to estimate tail-wave duration. Two serial chains back to back take ~42 µs, and adding 4.6 µs of fixed overhead gives ~47 µs, which is ~7 µs below the measured 54.08 µs of v1. This rough model captures only the order of magnitude; where the remaining 7 µs comes from was not measured separately.

3How Many Bytes Must Each SM Keep in Flight Simultaneously to Saturate HBM?

When all SMs read concurrently, round-trip latency grows with bytes in flight; reaching the bandwidth plateau requires ~64 KiB in flight per SM, whereas v1 keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight.

We call the bytes that an SM has requested from memory but not yet received bytes in flight. Bytes in flight, bandwidth, and round-trip latency are tied together by Little's Law:

bytes in flight=bandwidth×round-trip latency\text{bytes in flight} = \text{bandwidth} \times \text{round-trip latency}bytes in flight=bandwidth×round-trip latency

Simply put, for an SM to get its full share of bandwidth, the bytes it keeps in flight at once must cover one round-trip latency.

Let's see how high that target is. When all 132 SMs on the GPU stream continuously from HBM, they hit the measured bandwidth plateau (the region where adding more bytes in flight no longer increases bandwidth) at ~4.54 TB/s, or ~34 GB/s per SM. If we calculated using only the unloaded 0.33 µs round-trip latency from Section 2, each SM would seem to need only 34 GB/s×0.33 μs≈11 KiB34\ \text{GB/s} \times 0.33\ \mu\text{s} \approx 11\ \text{KiB}34 GB/s×0.33 μs≈11 KiB in flight.

We ran a separate bandwidth-sweep microbenchmark: all 132 SMs read HBM continuously, with each SM reading several rows of WWW at once (16 KiB per row; see Chapter 3, Section 8 for how the loads are issued). With only 16 KiB in flight per SM, measured device-wide bandwidth falls far short of the plateau (see the chart below). That gap tells us that when all SMs read together, the average round trip is already much longer than the unloaded 0.33 µs.

Follow the chart to the right: when each SM keeps 64 KiB in flight at once (4 rows of WWW), device-wide bandwidth reaches its knee point and then stays on the ~4.54 TB/s plateau. 64 KiB is the measured knee point; once on the plateau, keeping even more bytes in flight adds no bandwidth, so the round trip from round-trip latency=bytes in flight÷bandwidth\text{round-trip latency} = \text{bytes in flight} \div \text{bandwidth}round-trip latency=bytes in flight÷bandwidth only gets longer. Right at the 64 KiB knee point, Little's Law puts the average round trip at ~1.9 µs, ~6× the unloaded latency. We did not measure which segment of the path takes that extra time; a common explanation is queueing.

Put that knee point next to v1 and the second reason v1 is slow jumps right out. In v1, each thread keeps only one 2 B read of WWW in flight per iteration, so 1 CTA (128 threads) has only 128×2 B=256 B128 \times 2\ \text{B} = 256\ \text{B}128×2 B=256 B in flight, and all 16 CTAs on 1 SM total only 4.0 KiB (Figure 2-3). That doesn't even reach the leftmost 16 KiB bar on the chart, let alone the 64 KiB knee point.

Section 1 explained how long the serial load chain is; this section explains how busy each iteration can keep HBM. Because v1 keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight per SM—far below the plateau—the device-wide read load stays light. That is why the rough model in Section 2 could estimate using near-unloaded round-trip latency (the single-iteration round-trip latency of v1 was not measured directly). Raising bytes in flight per SM from 4.0 KiB to 64 KiB is the job of Chapters 3 and 4; keeping more bytes in flight consumes more registers or on-chip memory, and Chapter 3 works out that budget.

4Can We Tell L2 Which Data to Keep?

Yes. Tagging streaming data as evict-first and reused data as evict-last preserves reused data when L2 thrashing would otherwise evict it, but only adds overhead when it would not be evicted anyway.

In Section 2, we saw that the 16 KiB vector xxx fits easily inside the 60 MiB L2 cache. While gemv runs, though, 37.75 MB of single-use weights WWW also stream through L2—could that stream evict the data we want to reuse? Left to itself, the L2 hardware has no way to know which data will be reused shortly and which data will not be used again after one read. When a large volume of single-use data streams through L2, it may evict data that later CTAs still need to re-read.

To change that default, we can attach an L2 residency hint (cache policy) to each load (see Appendix B for the code syntax): tag single-use streaming data evict_first (telling L2 to evict it first when making room), and tag data re-read repeatedly across CTAs evict_last (telling L2 to keep it until last if possible).

When does this actually help? Look at a standalone microbenchmark (Figure 2-4): first read in 8–32 MB of data to be reused (Figure 2-4 uses 32 MB as the example), then stream through 64 MB of single-use data—more than the 60 MiB L2 can hold—and finally re-read the reused data from the first step. In our measurements, tagging the two reads evict_last and evict_first keeps 98.8%–100% of the reused data in L2. Without hints, we infer from capacity alone that the 64 MB stream evicts the reused data from L2 (we did not measure the retention ratio or relative gain for that unhinted case).

Trade-offs of the L2 residency hint (cache policy):

  • What you gain: Keeps reused data in L2 when heavy streaming traffic would otherwise evict it (see the microbenchmark numbers above).
  • What it costs: Every read has to construct and pass an extra residency hint, making the code more verbose.
  • When it loses: When the reused data would not be evicted anyway, the extra hint only adds overhead. On gemv, because xxx is only 16 KiB and is not evicted in the first place, adding these two hints on top of v3 from Section 8 (denoted v4) instead measured ~1 µs slower, so we do not count it as a standalone step. v5 in Chapter 3, Section 8 still carries both hints, and their individual effect in v5 was not measured separately.

5When Only a Few CTAs Remain in the Tail Wave, How Can More SMs Compute the Same Row Together?

Partitioning a row along the reduction dimension KKK across multiple CTAs and merging is called Split-K; splitting only the tail-wave rows in half is called K-halves, where each half-row runs only 32 iterations.

As we saw in Section 1, the tail wave has only 192 CTAs, yet each one still runs all 64 load iterations while ~90% of the chip's slots sit empty. Since one row's inner product is just a sum of 8,192 terms, we can split it straight in half along KKK:

y[row]=∑k=04095W[row,k] xk⏟first half+∑k=40968191W[row,k] xk⏟second halfy[\text{row}] = \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{4095} W[\text{row},k]\,x_k}_{\text{first half}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=4096}^{8191} W[\text{row},k]\,x_k}_{\text{second half}}y[row]=first halfk=0∑4095​W[row,k]xk​​​+second halfk=4096∑8191​W[row,k]xk​​​

Those two halves don't depend on each other at all: two CTAs on two different SMs can compute them concurrently, each producing one partial sum, and then add the two partial sums together.

Splitting only the tail wave pays off best when the tail-wave remainder rrr does not exceed half of 1 wave capacity (r≤2,112/2=1,056r \le 2{,}112 / 2 = 1{,}056r≤2,112/2=1,056). Then splitting rrr rows into 2r2r2r half-row CTAs packs all 2r2r2r CTAs into the slots that sit idle during the tail wave, without adding another wave. We call splitting only the tail-wave rows in half K-halves (tail-wave half splitting). In v1, r=192r = 192r=192, and splitting in half gives 2r=384≤1,0562r = 384 \le 1{,}0562r=384≤1,056, which satisfies that condition. After splitting, each half-row CTA's serial load chain drops from 64 iterations to 32 iterations, and device-wide bytes in flight during the tail wave double as well (384 CTAs versus 192 CTAs; Mode 2 in Figure 2-5).

Generalize that idea to the whole grid and you get Split-K: when the number of output rows or output tiles is too small to fill even 1 wave capacity, partition the reduction dimension KKK into SSS slices so SSS CTAs collaborate on the same output, multiplying the total CTA count by SSS. See Chapter 5, Sections 6–7 for Split-K on multi-token GEMM, and Chapter 6, Section 8 for measured results along the evolution chain.

Trade-offs of Split-K and K-halves:

  • What you gain: K-halves cuts the serial load chain per CTA in the tail wave in half (from 64 iterations to 32 iterations) and doubles device-wide bytes in flight during the tail wave (see Section 8 for the measured speedup).
  • What it costs: Each split row has to write two 4 B partial sums (8 B total), perform one extra cross-SM merge (measured at ~0.67 µs in Section 6), and use a more complex grid block-index mapping.
  • When it loses: It loses when the remainder rrr exceeds half a wave, or when splitting too finely pushes the total CTA count past 1 wave capacity. Splitting into 4 slices on gemv was not measured; on an expert kernel, splitting into 4 slices measured slower than splitting into 2 slices (see Chapter 8, Section 3).

6When Two SMs Each Compute Half a Row, How Do They Add Them Together Safely?

After writing its partial sum, each half-row CTA performs an atomic add on an L2 counter, and the last arriver (receiving old value 1) sums both halves; the two CTAs need not be co-resident on the chip.

First, why does the handoff have to go through L2? Each SM's L1 cache (the per-SM level-1 cache, covered in detail in Chapter 3, Section 1) is private to that SM, and the hardware does not automatically keep L1 caches coherent across different SMs. As we saw in Section 2, L2 is the only memory level on the GPU shared by all SMs. With the global memory accesses used in this chapter, cross-SM data exchange can only meet in the central L2 cache (see Chapter 7, Section 12 for another cross-SM path).

Step two is deciding who does the addition. For that we use an atomic add: it fuses "read the old value, add the new value, and write back to memory" into one indivisible operation so no other thread can step in between, and it returns the old value from before the add. Once the two half-rows finish, each CTA does an atomic add of 1 on the same counter (int32, 4 B, initialized to 0): the first one there (the first arriver) gets old value 0 and exits right away; the second one there (the last arriver) gets old value 1 and knows the other half has already arrived.

An atomic add alone, though, is not enough. Even though the first arriver writes its partial sum part before adding 1 to the counter in program text, without memory ordering constraints the CUDA memory model does not guarantee that another SM will observe the new value of part before observing the new value of the counter. In hardware, the counter update may reach L2 before part, or the last arriver may read stale data from its own SM's L1 cache.

Before looking at the code, let's define the three memory orderings in plain terms:

  • relaxed: Guarantees only that the atomic operation itself is indivisible, without constraining the order of other reads and writes before or after it.
  • release: Orders all prior reads and writes by this thread before this write, making those prior writes visible to any thread that observes this write via an acquire read.
  • acquire: Prevents any subsequent reads and writes by this thread from being reordered before this read.

Combining release and acquire gives acq_rel. Because the L1 caches on different SMs are not coherent with each other, every synchronization on a GPU also has to specify its memory scope—such as within a CTA, across the whole GPU (device), or across the whole system. Here the two half-row CTAs can be dispatched to any two SMs on the GPU, so the scope must be device (device-wide scope, written thread_scope_device in CUDA C++).

This is a place where a GPU differs sharply from a typical CPU. The x86 TSO memory model permits only one reordering: store followed by load. When a core writes A and then reads B, the read may finish before the write to A becomes visible to other cores, behaving as if the read were reordered ahead of the write. To forbid this, x86 requires an MFENCE, while per-core caches are kept coherent automatically by protocols such as MESI.

The GPU memory model makes none of those guarantees for unsynchronized normal (weak) reads and writes: all four orderings—read-read, read-write, write-write, and write-read—may be reordered. Normal weak reads and writes also differ from relaxed atomic operations, since relaxed still guarantees a consistent modification order on the same address. To constrain ordering across different addresses, we use release / acquire or insert a standalone memory fence (an instruction that constrains the order of reads and writes before and after it). An acq_rel fence (fence.acq_rel) guarantees that prior reads and writes are not reordered after subsequent writes, and subsequent reads and writes are not reordered before prior reads. It does not forbid store-load reordering; the algorithms in this book do not depend on forbidding store-load reordering.

That means the classic "write data first, then write flag" pattern that works directly on x86 has to be written on a GPU with scoped release / acquire operations.

#include <cuda/atomic>
// tail_store (last-arriver merge): thread 0 runs this after the intra-CTA reduction (a __syncthreads() precedes it)
// i = row index within the tail wave (0..191); half = 0 for the first half, 1 for the second half
part[2 * i + half] = sum;                                   // write this half-row's partial sum
cuda::atomic_ref<int, cuda::thread_scope_device> c(cnt[i]);
if (c.fetch_add(1, cuda::memory_order_acq_rel) == 1) {      // got old value 1: I am the last arriver
    y[row] = part[2 * i] + part[2 * i + 1];
    c.store(0, cuda::memory_order_relaxed);                 // used again only by the next launch
}

That short snippet locks down the ordering through four links:

  1. Cumulativity: A thread's release publishes not only its own writes, but also any writes from other threads that it already saw before that release through an acquire or a CTA barrier. That lets a synchronization chain carry across link by link, and each synchronization hop only needs a scope covering its own two endpoints. For example, thread A writes data and hands it to thread B across an intra-CTA barrier. When B does a device-scope release and thread C on another SM does a paired device-scope acquire, C sees A's write. If the B→C link used only CTA scope, the chain would break right at that link.
  2. Intra-CTA merge to thread 0: In tail_store, only thread 0 writes the single scalar part and does the atomic add. Even when many threads in a CTA each write their own partial sums (as in the 256-thread microbenchmark below and in Section 7), we still do not need every thread to do an atomic add. We run one __syncthreads() first (see Primer 3, Section 4) and then have thread 0 do a single release; by cumulativity from item 1, that publishes every prior write from the whole CTA.
  3. Cross-SM pairing: The first arriver's release and the last arriver's acquire operate on the same counter cnt[i]. The atomic read-modify-write chain on that one counter passes the first arriver's release to the last arriver's acquire, so the two work by paired synchronization and guarantee that the last arriver sees the part written by the first arriver. The hardware behavior we observe (not a specification guarantee) is that release pushes this SM's writes out to L2 first, and acquire invalidates this SM's L1 so later reads pull fresh data from L2. The last two bars in the chart below measure that exact cost.
  4. Counter reset: After the last arriver adds the two halves and writes y[row], writing cnt[i] back to 0 only needs relaxed, because the counter will not be used again until the next kernel launch—and kernel completion in between already acts as a stream-order boundary (see Chapter 1, Section 1).

Crucially, this "last arriver merges" pattern does not require both CTAs to be co-resident on the chip. The first arriver exits immediately after its atomic add without waiting for anyone, and the last arriver directly reads and merges both halves upon arrival. No matter how far apart in time the two half-row CTAs are dispatched, they can never deadlock.

By contrast, if one CTA loops and repeatedly reads a flag written by another CTA until a condition holds, that is spin-wait. Unlike operating-system threads, the hardware does not swap a resident CTA off its SM to make room for an undispatched CTA from the same launch. Spin-wait must guarantee that both CTAs are on the chip at the same time: because the CUDA specification guarantees neither dispatch order nor co-residency for a standard launch, once waiting CTAs fill every on-chip slot and do not exit, the CTA that writes the flag can never get an SM.

If you do need one CTA to wait on another, there are two specification-sanctioned deadlock-free solutions. First, put the flag-writing producer in a separate preceding kernel. Second, use cooperative launch, where the driver guarantees that all CTAs of the entire grid are co-resident on the chip at once and rejects the launch outright if they do not fit (see Chapter 3, Section 1 for how many CTAs fit per SM). Under a standard launch, placing the producer at the lowest block indices by relying on the ascending dispatch order observed in Section 1 can also run to completion. However, if the driver or hardware changes dispatch order, it can deadlock silently without reporting an error.

Finally, let's measure the hardware cost of device-wide synchronization. Why is device-wide release / acquire so much more expensive than relaxed? Because per-SM L1 caches are not coherent, a release has to wait until all prior writes issued by this thread have settled in L2 before other SMs can observe them. And after an acquire, the SM can no longer trust stale data in its local L1 cache.

Timing a standalone device-wide acq_rel memory fence by itself (the second chart) makes this even clearer: when a prior write is still in flight, the fence waits ~200 extra clock cycles—the time spent waiting for that write to reach L2.

We also ran a separate microbenchmark: 256 threads in one CTA each write 1 value and hand off via __syncthreads() and a release to an acquire on another SM. The median time for one complete cross-SM handoff is ~0.67 µs.

Trade-offs of last-arriver merge via L2:

  • What you gain: Safely merges across SMs without launching a second reduction kernel and without requiring the two CTAs to be co-resident on the chip.
  • What it costs: Each merge pays ~0.67 µs for a cross-SM handoff—spent waiting for prior writes to reach L2, performing the atomic round trip, and on the last arriver's reads (see the two charts above). Invalidating the local SM's L1 also slows down subsequent re-reads, and you have to allocate an extra counter array and a workspace buffer.
  • When it loses: When the partial sums to be merged are large or numerous, having that single last-arriver CTA read back and sum all partial sums by itself turns that CTA into a new tail bottleneck.

7When There Are Many Partial Sums, How Do We Avoid Making the Last CTA Read Them All Alone?

Two alternatives: either have each of the SSS CTAs reduce 1/S1/S1/S of the rows, or have all CTAs issue non-fetching atomic adds directly into a pre-zeroed output buffer.

In Section 6, gemv only split each tail-wave row in half: one counter tracked 1 row, and the last arriver only had to read back two 4 B scalars. Now suppose we pack many output rows of gemv into a single tile, split that tile into SSS slices along KKK, and have a group of SSS CTAs share one counter—the partial sums that the last arriver must read back on its own multiply accordingly. When we compute multiple tokens at once, that volume grows even larger: for example, with 64 tokens and 1,024 output columns split along KKK across S=4S = 4S=4 CTAs (see Chapter 5, Sections 6–7), the 4 FP32 partial sums add up to 4×64×1,024×4 B=1 MiB4 \times 64 \times 1{,}024 \times 4\ \text{B} = 1\ \text{MiB}4×64×1,024×4 B=1 MiB. If we still followed Section 6 and made that single last-arriver CTA serially read back and sum the other 3 slices (0.75 MiB), that 1 CTA's load chain would become a new long tail (Figure 2-7, Mode 1).

The first alternative is parallel slice reduction (Figure 2-7, Mode 2). Instead of letting the first S−1S - 1S−1 arriving CTAs exit right away, keep all SSS CTAs around so they divide the merge work equally in four steps:

  1. Each CTA writes its partial sums into the global workspace buffer and synchronizes within the CTA.
  2. Thread 0 of each CTA does an acq_rel atomic add on the counter to claim a ticket number ttt (the old value returned by the atomic add, counting up from 0; the paired synchronization rule is the same as in Section 6). The counter is never reset. The reason is that no CTA knows whether the other S−1S - 1S−1 CTAs have all seen the ticket count reach the target and stopped spinning; if any CTA wrote the counter back to 0 at that moment, a CTA still spinning would never see the count reach the target. So each call keeps adding SSS more tickets on top.
  3. When all tickets for this group have been claimed, the counter equals (⌊t/S⌋+1)⋅S(\lfloor t / S \rfloor + 1) \cdot S(⌊t/S⌋+1)⋅S. Thread 0 repeatedly reads the counter with acquire until it is at least that value (the last ticket holder does not need to wait), confirming that all SSS partial sums have been written out. Once thread 0 finishes waiting, it runs another __syncthreads() before the rest of the threads in the CTA start reading (see Chapter 5, Section 7 for how counter wraparound is handled).
  4. Using its own slice index along KKK, each CTA reads back the matching 1/S1/S1/S row slice from all SSS partial sums (16 rows when S=4S = 4S=4), adds them up, and writes out the result.

Because earlier-arriving CTAs now spin-wait for later-arriving CTAs, the co-residency rule from Section 6 applies directly: all SSS CTAs must be resident on the chip at the same time (use cooperative launch from Section 6; it also runs to completion under the observed ascending dispatch order, but the specification does not guarantee that). Trade-offs of parallel slice reduction:

  • What you gain: Spreads the merge reads evenly across SSS CTAs, eliminating the long tail of a single CTA serially reading back all partial sums (see Chapter 6, Section 8 for measured results).
  • What it costs: Still requires a partial-sum workspace buffer, one ticket claim with spin-wait, extra merge code in every CTA, and co-residency of all SSS CTAs.
  • When it loses: When there are very few partial sums to merge (for example, only 2 scalars in Section 6), the time saved by distributing the reads may not offset the spin-wait overhead; this crossover point was not measured.

The second alternative is direct atomic add (Figure 2-7, Mode 3): once each CTA finishes its slice of the inner product, all threads issue a non-fetching atomic add straight to the output array in global memory—only adding without reading back, and not waiting for a return after issuing. That eliminates both the partial-sum workspace buffer and the ticket claim and counter.

To use it safely, though, three prerequisites must hold:

  1. Output buffer must be zeroed before the first accumulation: The specification-safe approach zeros the output in a separate preceding kernel. If dedicated CTAs inside the same kernel zero the output and publish a completion flag, they must use the release / acquire paired synchronization from Section 6 and satisfy the co-residency requirement (see Section 6).
  2. Result is only visible to the next kernel: Inside the current kernel, no CTA knows when all other CTAs have finished accumulating. The final sum of all partial sums becomes visible to the next kernel only after the current kernel finishes (or after the dependent kernel (successor) crosses the wait call in Chapter 1, Section 4).
  3. Output is no longer bitwise deterministic: Because floating-point addition is not associative and the order in which CTAs reach L2 may vary from run to run, the accumulated floating-point results may differ in the last few bits.

Trade-offs of direct atomic add:

  • What you gain: Eliminates both the partial-sum workspace buffer and the counter array.
  • What it costs: The output buffer must be zeroed beforehand, the output is not bitwise deterministic, and when many CTAs atomically add to the same output address simultaneously, requests queue up at L2 (see Chapter 7, Section 12 for measured results and explanation on single-request attention).
  • When it loses:
    • Performing scalar atomic adds directly on BF16 requires a compare-and-swap retry loop: read the old value, compute the new value, and write it only if the memory location has not changed in the meantime—otherwise retry from the beginning. This measures slower (see Chapter 6, Section 8).
    • Zeroing the output on the fly and publishing a flag at the entry of compute CTAs in the same kernel to save a separate zeroing kernel also measures slower (see Chapter 5, Section 7 for the mechanism and measured results).

8gemv Evolution v2 → v3: Splitting the 192 Tail-Wave Rows in Half with K-halves

v3 splits the last 192 rows into 384 half-row CTAs, cutting the tail-wave load chain from 64 iterations to 32 and achieving a ~1.25× measured speedup.

In code, v3 keeps the first 2,112 CTAs (indices 0..2111) computing one full row each, just as before. The next 384 CTAs (indices 2112..2495) share one row per pair, with each CTA computing 4,096 columns. Once done, they use the counter-merge code from Section 6 (tail_store) to merge the two halves through the central L2 and write y[row]. We put the half-row CTAs at the end of the grid because, under the ascending dispatch order observed in Section 1, the highest-indexed batch lands right in the tail wave:

// v3: the first 2,112 rows use 1 CTA per row; the last 192 rows use 2 half-row CTAs per row (grid = 2,496)
gemv_v3<<<2112 + 2 * 192, 128, 0, stream>>>(W, x, y, M, K, part, cnt);

With that change in place, the number of concurrently resident CTAs per SM remains 16 (see Chapter 3, Section 1 for why it does not change). Using the unloaded round-trip latency as a rough estimate, cutting the tail-wave chain in about half saves an estimated ~10 µs (see the readout in Figure 2-8 for the formula).

On the hardware, v3 runs ~1.25× faster than v2, saving slightly more than the simple tail-wave model estimates, for reasons that were not determined. In exchange, each of the 192 tail-wave rows pays for one cross-SM handoff, plus an extra partial-sum workspace buffer and counter array (192×12 B≈2.3 KB192 \times 12\ \text{B} \approx 2.3\ \text{KB}192×12 B≈2.3 KB in total; see Section 5 for when this loses).

Even after reaching v3, the runtime of v3 is still ~5.5× the lower bound (the lower bound is only 18.1% of the total, including fixed overhead). The remaining gap comes straight from the second bottleneck we identified in Section 3: v3 still keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight per SM at the same time.

Takeaway: A kernel finishes when its last CTA exits, and whether HBM reaches saturation depends on how many bytes each SM keeps in flight simultaneously. Splitting the tail-wave rows in half and merging them through L2 brings the runtime of gemv down from 54.19 µs (v2) to 43.34 µs (v3).

Next chapter's question: Saturating HBM requires keeping ~64 KiB in flight per SM (Section 3), whereas v3 keeps only 4.0 KiB per SM. Inside a single SM: what limits how many bytes it can keep in flight, and how does data reach registers and shared memory quickly and safely?

Chapter 3Level 3

Single SM — Once Data Enters the SM, How Does It Reach Registers and Shared Memory Quickly and Safely?

  • Preface

  • Primer 3
  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]
