Chapter 2, Section 3 measured that each SM has to keep about 64 KiB of normal loads in flight to saturate HBM, yet v3 keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight per SM. Inside a single SM: what limits how many bytes it can keep in flight, and how does data reach registers and shared memory quickly and safely?

Once data enters an SM from L2, it takes one of two paths to reach the execution units. The first is the register path: at T=1T = 1T=1, a single thread uses each byte of WWW only once and loads it straight into registers. This chapter follows gemv further along this path. The second is the shared memory (SMEM) path: when TTT tokens share the same block of WWW, many threads in a CTA read that block of WWW repeatedly, so we stage it in SMEM first. We will walk through these on-chip mechanisms using a 16 KiB tile of WWW, and Chapters 5 and 6 will use them directly.

1How Many CTAs Can Reside on One SM Simultaneously?

Whichever of the SM's four fixed resource pools is exhausted first sets the limit; gemv v1 exhausts the 64 warp slots first, so each SM holds 16 CTAs.

The 32 threads in a warp (Primer 3, Section 3) share one instruction stream and issue the same instruction together (Chapter 4, Section 1 shows how the scheduler picks a warp each cycle). An SM has four fixed resource pools, and whichever pool runs out first decides how many CTAs can reside on the SM:

  • warp slot: 64 per SM (2,048 threads).
  • CTA slot (thread block slot): 32 per SM.
  • SMEM (shared memory): Each SM has 256 KiB of on-chip storage, of which at most 228 KiB can go to SMEM, and the driver reserves an extra 1 KiB per resident CTA. The rest serves as the SM's L1 data cache (L1 is not coherent across SMs; see Chapter 2, Section 6).
  • register: 65,536 32-bit registers per SM, up to 255 per thread. Hardware allocates registers in units of 256 per warp, which rounds each thread's register count up to a multiple of 8.

Plug gemv v1 (<<<2304, 128>>>) from Primer 3 into each limit, and each pool gives a CTA count:

  • warp slot: 128 threads per CTA = 4 warps, so 64÷4=1664 \div 4 = 1664÷4=16;
  • CTA slot (thread block slot): 32;
  • SMEM (shared memory): smem[128] takes 512 B, plus the reserved 1 KiB for 1.5 KiB total, giving ⌊228÷1.5⌋=152\lfloor 228 \div 1.5 \rfloor = 152⌊228÷1.5⌋=152;
  • register: The compiled code uses 22 registers per thread, rounded up to 24 (the next multiple of 8), or 24×128=3,07224 \times 128 = 3{,}07224×128=3,072 per CTA, giving ⌊65,536÷3,072⌋=21\lfloor 65{,}536 \div 3{,}072 \rfloor = 21⌊65,536÷3,072⌋=21.

Take the minimum of the four, and you get 16 CTAs, or 16×4=6416 \times 4 = 6416×4=64 resident warps per SM, filling all 64 warp slots. That is where "16 CTAs per SM" in Chapter 2, Section 1 comes from. The number of resident warps on an SM divided by 64 is called occupancy. Computing it from the resource pools above gives the theoretical value, which is 100% for v1. Actual runtime occupancy varies from cycle to cycle and is not measured in this book.

Look at the cutoff for the register pool. As long as each thread uses at most 65,536÷(64×32)=3265{,}536 \div (64 \times 32) = 3265,536÷(64×32)=32 registers, all 64 warps fit. Once a thread goes past 32 registers, the register pool runs out before the warp slots (the slider in Figure 3-1 shows this cutoff). If a thread needs to hold more live variables than its allocated registers, the compiler performs register spilling (spill), moving the excess variables to local memory (private to each thread, but stored in device memory and cached in L1 and L2). Registers sit right next to the execution units and bypass the memory hierarchy. Every access to a spilled variable has to go through the memory hierarchy like a device-memory load, taking about 54 clock cycles on an L1 hit and about 600 clock cycles when it reaches HBM.

At compile time, __launch_bounds__ lets you tell the compiler how many threads each CTA has and the minimum CTAs to place on each SM. The compiler caps per-thread registers accordingly—trading per-thread register cap for higher occupancy. Say a 128-thread CTA needs to hold 40 values per thread at once. At 40 registers per thread, each SM fits ⌊65,536÷(40×128)⌋=12\lfloor 65{,}536 \div (40 \times 128) \rfloor = 12⌊65,536÷(40×128)⌋=12 CTAs (48 warps). Capping each thread at 32 registers fits 16 CTAs (64 warps), but spills 8 values per thread to local memory, adding a memory round trip on every access.

The four resource pools constrain a kernel from both ends. If each CTA takes more registers or SMEM, fewer CTAs fit on each SM, and bytes in flight drop with them. Going the other way and forcing down the register cap to fit more CTAs causes register spilling (spill). Whether the extra warps outweigh the spill round trips has to be measured. Chapter 8, Section 4 gives a real example: at T=256T = 256T=256, forcing the register cap down to 72 spills 12 registers, and Stage 6 runs about 26 µs slower instead.

Since the number of CTAs that can reside on an SM at once is fixed, another common launch style is a persistent kernel. The grid launches only as many CTAs as fit in one wave, and each CTA stays on its SM, looping to claim the next piece of work until everything is done. Written for gemv, that loop is for (row = blockIdx.x; row < 2304; row += gridDim.x), where gridDim.x is the total number of CTAs in the launch. That way each CTA starts only once and no longer waits for new CTAs to land on SMs for later work (the time for that step is not measured). A persistent CTA can also keep state on the SM, or pull work from a counter to split the job more finely.

The tail wave does not go away because of this. Put 2,304 rows on 2,112 CTAs, and at the end 192 CTAs still do one extra row while the other 1,920 sit idle, with the exact same tail-wave shape as in Chapter 2, Section 1. To shorten the tail wave, you still have to split the work more finely (Chapter 2, Section 5) or make the work item count an integer multiple of one wave's capacity.

What a persistent kernel costs is one extra loop in every CTA. When the total work cannot even fill one wave, that loop only adds overhead. When back-to-back steps have an all-to-all dependency, a persistent kernel can wait across the whole GPU inside the kernel, but it still needs cooperative launch (Chapter 2, Section 6) and still waits for the slowest CTA every time (Chapter 1, Section 3).

2How Many Sector Requests Does One Warp Load Instruction Generate?

Hardware requests data in 32-byte sectors, and a warp load instruction sends one request for every sector it lands in; the more contiguous the addresses and the wider each thread reads, the fewer requests go out and the more useful bytes come back.

First separate two hardware sizes: a sector is 32 B, the smallest request unit, and a cache line is 128 B, or 4 sectors. Inside each SM, the LSU (Load/Store Unit) takes the 32 addresses of a warp load instruction and merges all addresses that fall into the same sector into one request. The better the addresses merge, the fewer requests go out—that is coalesced access (coalescing).

Look at one instruction loading WWW in each of the three gemv variants (the three modes in Figure 3-2):

  • v0 and v1: Primer 3, Section 6 worked out that one instruction in v0 lands in 32 sectors, while v1 lands in only 2. In the terms of this section, v0 sends 32 requests, and v1 sends only 2 requests. The 30 B in each sector that v0 does not use on that access are the exact elements the same thread will read over the next 15 iterations. They may still sit in L1 and hit in cache, though the L1 hit rate is not measured.
  • v5 (Section 8 of this chapter): Each thread switches to uint4 (a 16-byte vector load) and reads 16 B (8 BF16 elements) at once. One warp instruction reads 32×16=51232 \times 16 = 51232×16=512 B in total—4 full cache lines, or 16 sectors—and uses 100% of the 512 B fetched on that access.

Put side by side, one instruction in v5 brings back 8× as many useful bytes as v1. To keep the same number of bytes in flight, v5 needs only one-eighth as many load instructions for WWW as v1 (this is the count of load instructions for WWW, not the total instruction count of the whole kernel).

Wide coalesced loads require contiguous data and 16 B address alignment. A 16 B load holds onto its 4 destination 32-bit registers until the data comes back. If one thread keeps kkk such loads in flight at once, they take 4k4k4k registers (Chapter 4, Section 3 uses this fact).

When the rows to read come from an index table and do not sit next to each other in memory, a warp cannot coalesce them (the KV cache in Chapter 7 works this way). Then you can only keep more warps resident, or have each thread keep several loads in flight to hold up bytes in flight (Chapter 4, Section 3).

3How Does a Repeatedly Read Data Block Move into SMEM Without Passing Through Registers?

Use TMA to move regular rectangular tiles into SMEM with a single instruction; use cp.async for indexed gather loads.

When several tokens share the same block of WWW, many warps in a CTA read that block of WWW. So we first place it into SMEM as a tile for all warps to read on chip (Chapter 5, Section 6 shows how Tensor Core uses it). Take a tile of WWW from qkv_gate, Wtile :  [128,  64]  BF16\shape{W_{tile}}{128,\;64}{BF16}Wtile​:[128,64]BF16 = 16 KiB. It has 128 rows of 64 BF16 elements (128 B) each. In device memory, these 128 segments are each 128 B long and sit one full row of 16,384 B apart.

To move this 16 KiB tile into SMEM, the hardware gives us four paths (Figure 3-3; Paths 1–2 take a CTA of 128 threads, or 4 warps):

  • Path 1: Normal load into registers, then store to SMEM. Each thread issues 16,384÷(128×16)=816{,}384 \div (128 \times 16) = 816,384÷(128×16)=8 loads of 16 B. Across the CTA, that comes to 32 warp load instructions plus 32 warp store instructions, or 64 instructions in total. Keeping all 8 loads in flight at once takes 8×4=328 \times 4 = 328×4=32 staging registers per thread; doing them one at a time takes only 4 registers, but pays for 8 serial round trips. Take this path only when the data must change format in registers before entering SMEM.
  • Path 2: Per-thread asynchronous copy (cp.async). Each thread still computes its own addresses and issues warp copy instructions—32 instructions in total—but the bytes go straight from L2 into SMEM without passing through registers (0 staging registers). Hopper's TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) does not support gathering by an index table, so gathering scattered rows by index (see Chapter 7, Section 5) has to take this path.
  • Path 3: TMA 1D bulk copy (cp.async.bulk). Give a start address and a byte count, and TMA copies one contiguous span of bytes; one thread issues one instruction and uses 0 data registers. Because our tile of WWW is not one contiguous span of bytes but 128 segments, using Path 3 takes one instruction per row, or 128 instructions in total.
  • Path 4: TMA multidimensional tensor bulk copy (cp.async.bulk.tensor). On the CPU side, we first build a tensor descriptor that records the full tensor's dimensions, row stride, box size, swizzle mode, and out-of-bounds fill mode. Inside the kernel, one thread gives the tile's coordinates and issues 1 instruction. TMA computes all 128 segment addresses on its own, fills out-of-bounds elements with 0 automatically, and can reorder the data as it lands in SMEM using the XOR rule from Section 7—all while using 0 data registers.

SMEM has two access channels, which the CUDA memory model calls two proxies: normal thread reads and writes take the generic proxy, while TMA reads and writes take the async proxy. There is no automatic ordering guarantee between the two channels, so handing off data across them has to cross a cross-proxy fence (fence.proxy.async).

When reading data into SMEM with TMA, TMA subtracts each batch of bytes it finishes writing from an arrival counter in SMEM (covered in Section 5) and wakes the waiting warps once the count hits 0. By the specification, a completed TMA read carries a built-in cross-proxy fence, so once consumers see the completion signal, they can read SMEM directly and get the new data.

Picking among these paths does not change the HBM bandwidth ceiling: when bytes in flight are high enough, both normal loads and TMA reach about 4.5 TB/s (Chapter 2, Figure 2-3; chart in Section 4 of this chapter). What Path 4 gets you is replacing 32–64 instructions with 1 instruction, taking 0 data registers, and leaving address math and bounds checks to the hardware.

What Path 4 costs is a fixed startup overhead on each TMA transfer, building the descriptor on the CPU ahead of time, and a cap on tile shape: at most 256 elements along each dimension. TMA cannot move data gathered by index; when a tile is very small, the fixed overhead outweighs the saved instructions, and the exact size where that flips is not measured.

4How Many Slots Does a Ring Buffer Need to Overlap Data Movement and Compute?

Partition SMEM into a ring of buffer slots so consumers compute on the arrived slot while remaining slots are in flight; once in-flight slots total ~48 KiB per SM, read bandwidth reaches the plateau.

If SMEM has only 1 slot, moving data and computing on it can only take turns, and every tile waits out a full memory round trip. Cut SMEM into NNN buffer slots and cycle through them as 0,1,…,N−1,0,1,…0, 1, \dots, N-1, 0, 1, \dots0,1,…,N−1,0,1,…, and you get a ring buffer. To match, the warps in a CTA split into two roles: one producer warp only issues TMA loads to move the next tile into an empty slot, while the remaining consumer warps only read arrived slots to compute. Splitting warps by role is called warp specialization.

How many bytes must stay in flight still comes from Little's Law in Chapter 2, Section 3: bytes in flight = bandwidth ×\times× round-trip latency. With TMA loads, measured bandwidth reaches the plateau once each SM keeps about 48 KiB in flight (see the first chart below).

This 48 KiB does not conflict with the 64 KiB in Chapter 2, Section 3. Both numbers are measured knee points: Chapter 2 used normal 16 B loads, and this section uses TMA. Compare them through Little's Law at the same bytes in flight: with 16 KiB in flight per SM, the TMA round trip is about 0.76 µs and normal loads take about 0.94 µs; near the plateau the two are almost equal (see the chart note above for the 48 KiB point). At the same bytes in flight, normal loads have a longer round trip, so they have to keep 64 KiB in flight to reach the knee point. Where that difference comes from is not measured.

Because the 1 slot consumers are currently computing on has already arrived and does not count as in flight, the minimum number of slots needed is:

N=⌈bytes in flight needed per SMbytes per slot⌉+1N = \left\lceil \frac{\text{bytes in flight needed per SM}}{\text{bytes per slot}} \right\rceil + 1N=⌈bytes per slotbytes in flight needed per SM​⌉+1

Plug in 16 KiB per slot, and you get N=⌈48÷16⌉+1=4N = \lceil 48 \div 16 \rceil + 1 = 4N=⌈48÷16⌉+1=4: 3 in-flight slots plus 1 slot being computed on, taking 64 KiB of SMEM in total. This formula assumes consumers finish computing one slot no slower than bandwidth delivers one slot (16 KiB at ~34 GB/s per SM takes ~0.48 µs). Then consumers still wait for data, but they wait on the bandwidth ceiling, no longer on the round trip. If consumers compute a slot slower than that, the bottleneck sits on the consumer side: adding slots cannot reach the plateau, and the slot count has to be measured at the consumers' speed.

If the grid does not fill all 132 SMs, fewer SMs share the full chip's bandwidth, so the bytes in flight needed on each active SM grow in proportion. For example, if only half the SMs are running, each active SM has to keep about twice as many bytes in flight.

What a ring buffer gets you is overlapping data movement with compute, so N−1N - 1N−1 slots in flight push read bandwidth onto the plateau (first chart). What it costs is 16 KiB of SMEM for each extra slot, plus one producer warp for the whole ring. Four slots plus the reserved 1 KiB take 65 KiB, so by the SMEM pool in Section 1 each SM fits at most ⌊228÷65⌋=3\lfloor 228 \div 65 \rfloor = 3⌊228÷65⌋=3 CTAs. In addition, the deeper the ring, the longer each step's data takes from issue until it is readable (see the second chart below, measured on another cp.async ring; a TMA ring was not measured for this). This matches Little's Law from Chapter 2, Section 3: round-trip latency = bytes in flight ÷ bandwidth, so when bytes in flight grow faster than bandwidth, the round trip gets longer. That longer round trip makes consumers wait longer only when the ring is just starting to fill or when the next step's address becomes known late (this was not measured separately).

With only 1 slot in flight (2 slots in the ring), read bandwidth is only 60%–70% of the plateau. Raising in-flight slots from 3 to 4 (5 slots in the ring) adds under 1% bandwidth while taking an extra 16 KiB. The best slot count has to be measured on the actual kernel: the expert kernel in Chapter 8 slows down when cut to 2 slots (Chapter 8, Section 9), while expanding the T=32T = 32T=32 projection kernel in Chapter 9 from 6 slots to 7 speeds up single-layer full-graph replay by about 0.55 µs (Chapter 9, Section 2).

5How Do Producers and Consumers Hand Off a Slot Without Overwriting Data Before It Is Read?

Pair each buffer slot with two mbarrier objects—one for full, one for empty; consumers must not signal empty until the data read from the slot has been consumed.

If you hand off slots with __syncthreads(), the whole CTA has to stop together at every step: the producer warp cannot run ahead on its own, and consumers have to wait for each other. An mbarrier (a hardware-counted barrier) makes only the two sides using that slot wait on each other. It is an 8-byte hardware object in SMEM that tracks two counts: how many threads still need to arrive (arrive), and how many bytes still need to be written (transaction bytes). When both counts hit zero, the round finishes and its phase flips. Hardware uses a parity bit (alternating 0 and 1) to tell adjacent rounds apart, so the same object can be reused round after round.

Pair each slot sss with two barriers: full[s] (ready to read) and empty[s] (ready to write). Figure 3-5 walks through round rrr and round r+1r+1r+1 in time order:

  • producer: First waits for the phase of empty[s] to flip. Then it arrives on full[s], registers 16,384 expected bytes for this pass, and issues TMA. Each time TMA finishes writing a batch of bytes, it subtracts them from full[s]; when both the arrival count and byte count hit zero, full[s] flips.
  • consumer: Waits on full[s] until its phase flips, when the bytes written by TMA are already visible to it (Section 3). Next it issues shared-memory loads from the slot, uses the loaded values in multiply-adds, and finally arrives on empty[s].

Issuing a shared-memory load only hands off a request; the data is written into the destination register tens of cycles later. That gives one rule: Consumers must not arrive on empty[s] before the data loaded from slot sss has been consumed by compute instructions. Arrive early, and the producer thinks the slot is empty. The next round's TMA can write into the slot before those shared-memory loads come back, so the consumer gets data from the next tile. Breaking read-before-write order like this is a write-after-read hazard (WAR). It raises no error; the result simply comes out wrong silently. The expert kernel in Chapter 8 broke this rule, and stress testing (replaying repeatedly and checking outputs) caught the overwrite.

Arriving on empty[s] comes with a CTA-scope release by default (Chapter 2, Section 6), so why didn't it block this overwrite? By specification, the default release should order earlier shared-memory loads before the arrival, yet the compiled arrival instruction did not wait for those loads. Adding an intra-CTA fence (fence.acq_rel.cta) made it wait, for reasons not determined (Chapter 8, Section 11). That overwrite has two possible causes:

  • The default release orders only generic-proxy accesses, while the next round overwrites the slot with TMA on the async proxy (Section 3).
  • The compiler moved the instructions that use the loaded results past the arrival, so the earlier shared-memory loads had not yet returned to registers when the arrival went out.

To close off both possibilities, there are two common safe patterns:

  • First, use the loaded values in compute instructions before arriving, and add an intra-CTA fence so the arrival waits for the shared-memory loads to return (Chapter 8, Section 11). Once the data is back in registers, later writes through either proxy cannot change it.
  • Second, after reading slot sss, hold off on arriving, and arrive on slot sss only after the consumer has waited on full for the next slot (or next stage) and received data. By then, the loads from slot sss have long since been used and returned to registers.

The final expert kernel in Chapter 8 uses the second pattern: overwrites no longer show up in stress testing, at a cost of about 0.4–1.6 µs (Chapter 8, Section 11).

What paired mbarrier objects get you is that only the producer and consumers using that slot wait on each other, while other warps do not stop. A single thread's unloaded arrive-plus-wait round trip takes about 200 cycles, but handshakes across several slots in the ring are in flight at once and overlap, so in steady state each step's handshake adds only about 27 cycles. What it costs is two 8 B counters per slot. Also, when consumers arrive a bit later, the producer refills a bit later, which makes the ring slightly shallower.

6What If Data-Movement Warps Have Excess Registers While Compute Warps Do Not Have Enough?

Reallocate registers per warpgroup at kernel entry using setmaxnreg: the producer warpgroup releases registers back to the CTA pool and consumer warpgroups claim them, keeping total CTA registers within 65,536.

Four consecutive warps (128 threads in all) form a warpgroup. setmaxnreg (per-warpgroup register reallocation) works in units of warpgroups, and all 128 threads of a warpgroup must execute this instruction together.

Say a CTA has 1 producer warpgroup and 2 consumer warpgroups. Because setmaxnreg takes effect per warpgroup, even though only one thread issues TMA (Section 3), the producer still has to fill 1 full warpgroup (128 threads), for 384 threads across the CTA. Now say the consumers accumulate for many tokens at once: for instance, each consumer warpgroup computes a 64-token-row × 256-column FP32 output tile, so each thread has to hold 128 partial sums in registers at the same time, plus addresses and temporaries. One version of this book's single-layer prefill and decode kernels sets consumers to 232 registers, compiling with zero spills; the producer only issues copy and arrival instructions, and is set to 40 registers.

If the whole CTA got the same number per thread, giving 232 registers to all 384 threads would take 384×232=89,088384 \times 232 = 89{,}088384×232=89,088 registers—23,552 more than 65,536—so this CTA would not fit in one SM at all. To fit in, each thread can compile with at most ⌊65,536÷384⌋\lfloor 65{,}536 \div 384 \rfloor⌊65,536÷384⌋ rounded down to a multiple of 8, which is 168 registers. Consumers can only get 168 registers, fewer than the 232 set in the code; whether 168 registers are enough or spill to local memory (Section 1) is not measured.

Reallocating by warpgroup at kernel entry untangles this in four steps (Figure 3-6):

  • At kernel launch: 168 registers per thread, the largest number that fits 384 threads (384×168=64,512≤65,536384 \times 168 = 64{,}512 \le 65{,}536384×168=64,512≤65,536; the next multiple of 8, 176, would take 67,584).
  • Producer releases registers: 1 producer warpgroup uses setmaxnreg to lower its quota to 40, returning 128×(168−40)=16,384128 \times (168 - 40) = 16{,}384128×(168−40)=16,384 registers.
  • Consumer claims registers: 2 consumer warpgroups use setmaxnreg to raise their quota to 232, taking 256×(232−168)=16,384256 \times (232 - 168) = 16{,}384256×(232−168)=16,384 registers.
  • Result: 128×40+256×232=5,120+59,392=64,512≤65,536128 \times 40 + 256 \times 232 = 5{,}120 + 59{,}392 = 64{,}512 \le 65{,}536128×40+256×232=5,120+59,392=64,512≤65,536, with zero spills.

What this gets you is 232 registers for consumers, so all accumulators stay in registers without spilling. What it costs is that the whole warpgroup has to run the instruction together, and the producer is left with 40 registers and cannot do anything else. At the same time, the register pool is nearly full, so each SM fits only 1 such CTA. Making it a persistent kernel (see Section 1 of this chapter) lets it initialize only once and overlap moving the next tile with the epilogue of the current tile (those two gains were not measured separately). A persistent kernel can also lose: Chapter 9, Section 6 has a measured example where the exact same load work runs slower when written as a persistent kernel than when launched the normal way (for reasons not determined).

When does it not pay off? If registers are already enough, putting a cap on the producer buys nothing: one step on the multi-token GEMM in Chapter 6, Section 8 tried this and measured no change. Going the other way and adding two more consumer warpgroups does not work either: 4 consumer warpgroups would need 4×128×232=118,7844 \times 128 \times 232 = 118{,}7844×128×232=118,784 registers, which is still too many even after borrowing (Chapter 8, Section 9).

7Why Does One Warp Reading an SMEM Column Queue Up, and How Can We Stagger It with Zero Space Overhead?

SMEM consists of 32 four-byte-wide banks in parallel; within one load, accesses that hit different addresses in the same bank must queue. XORing the column chunk index with the row index scatters same-column data across different banks without one extra byte of space.

In hardware, SMEM is cut into 32 parallel shared-memory banks, each 4 B wide and sending out one 4 B word per cycle. Consecutive 4 B words land on banks 0, 1, …, 31 in order, so every 128 B spans all 32 banks and the whole SMEM sends out at most 32×4=12832 \times 4 = 12832×4=128 B per cycle. Serving all requests of one load instruction in a single pass is called 1 wavefront. At peak throughput, 1 wavefront takes 1 cycle; in the microbenchmark below, each extra wavefront adds about 2 cycles, and why it is 2 rather than 1 is not measured.

When different threads land on different addresses in the same bank, hardware can only split the instruction into several wavefronts and serve them in turn—that is a bank conflict. If several threads read the exact same address, hardware performs a broadcast directly, which does not count as a conflict. When DDD requests crowd onto different addresses in the same bank, it is called a DDD-way bank conflict.

Conflicts start slowing back-to-back issue from 4-way up: under an 8-way conflict, one warp's SMEM read throughput drops to about a quarter (see the first chart below). For 16-byte loads, hardware checks conflicts in phases of 4 groups of 8 threads each (see the second chart below).

Go back to the WWW tile from Section 3: each row is 128 B, cut into 8 chunks of 16 B indexed by c=0..7c = 0..7c=0..7. Each consumer phase reads the same ccc across 8 consecutive rows (8 threads ×\times× 16 B = 128 B, which is one phase). Without swizzling, the offset of row rrr and column chunk ccc is offset(r,c)=128r+16c\mathrm{offset}(r, c) = 128r + 16coffset(r,c)=128r+16c. Across 8 rows, the same chunk sits 128 B apart and all 8 land on banks 4c..4c+34c..4c+34c..4c+3, causing an 8-way bank conflict: each load takes 8 wavefronts, and reading all 8 columns takes 64 wavefronts in all (Figure 3-7 Mode 1).

Turn on XOR swizzle, and the on-chip offset changes to:

offset(r,c)=128r+16 (c⊕(r mod 8))\mathrm{offset}(r, c) = 128r + 16\,(c \oplus (r \bmod 8))offset(r,c)=128r+16(c⊕(rmod8))

Fix the column chunk index ccc, and across 8 consecutive rows c⊕rc \oplus rc⊕r visits every value in 0..70..70..7. The 8 chunks land on 8 different groups of banks covering all 32 banks: the 8-way conflict drops to 0, each load takes only 1 wavefront, reading all 8 columns takes 8 wavefronts in all, and it takes not a single extra byte of SMEM (Figure 3-7 Mode 2). How much an 8-way conflict slows down 16 B loads was not measured directly.

The cost of XOR swizzle is that both the write side and the read side must use the same formula. When moving data with TMA, picking 128 B swizzle in the CPU-side tensor descriptor makes TMA lay the data out by this rule automatically as it writes into SMEM (Section 3, Path 4). TMA's 128 B swizzle also requires the starting address of the SMEM buffer it writes into to be aligned to 1,024 B.

There is another way to stagger banks: row-stride padding. It fits small tables where 32 threads read the same column of 4 B words across 32 rows. When the row width is 32 words, the same column in different rows all lands on one bank (a 32-way conflict); pad each row by 1 word to a width of 33 words, and the same column in adjacent rows shifts by 1 bank automatically, at a cost of 4 extra bytes per row.

Each method handles its own access pattern. The 128 B swizzle pattern repeats every 8 rows: when reading the same column of 4 B words across 32 rows, rows rrr, r+8r+8r+8, r+16r+16r+16, and r+24r+24r+24 land on the same bank, leaving a 4-way conflict, so that access needs row-stride padding. Counterexamples where swizzling loses under other patterns are not measured. Later, Chapter 7, Section 5 uses XOR swizzle when reading KV, and Chapter 8, Section 6 uses 33-word padding for the routing counter table.

8gemv v3 → v5: Loading 16 Bytes per Thread Raises Bytes in Flight by 8×

v3 → v5 makes two changes: each thread reads 16 B, and the kernel carries over the two L2 residency hints from Chapter 2, Section 4. Together they make the kernel about 2.5× faster; the effect of each of the two hints is not measured separately.

We start from v3 in Chapter 2, Section 8: the inputs are W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 and x :  [8192]  BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16}x:[8192]BF16, and the output is [2304][2304][2304]. The grid launches 2,496 CTAs with 128 threads per CTA, and each thread reads only one 2 B element of WWW per iteration, leaving only about 16×128×2 B=416 \times 128 \times 2\ \text{B} = 416×128×2 B=4 KiB in flight per SM.

v5 switches both WWW and xxx to uint4 loads of 16 B at once (8 consecutive BF16 elements, matching Mode v5 in Figure 3-2). Row addresses must be aligned to 16 B, which rows of 8,192×28{,}192 \times 28,192×2 B satisfy. After each load, the elements are converted to FP32 and accumulated:

acc+=∑i=07FP32(W[row,8k+i])⋅FP32(x[8k+i])\mathit{acc} \mathrel{+}= \sum_{i=0}^{7} \mathrm{FP32}(W[\mathit{row}, 8k+i]) \cdot \mathrm{FP32}(x[8k+i])acc+=i=0∑7​FP32(W[row,8k+i])⋅FP32(x[8k+i])

The three lines of C++ below show one iteration's 16 B loads and the conversion of the first two BF16 elements. uint4 is 16 bytes made of four 32-bit integers, where .x/.y/.z/.w each hold 2 BF16 values, and __bfloat1622float2 converts 2 BF16 values (__nv_bfloat162) into 2 FP32 values (float2) at once. The actual source code converts all four fields of w_vec (8 BF16 values in all) to FP32 for multiply-add:

// v5 sketch: each uint4 load reads 16 bytes of W and x (8 consecutive BF16)
uint4 w_vec = reinterpret_cast<const uint4*>(&W[row * K])[k];
uint4 x_vec = reinterpret_cast<const uint4*>(x)[k];
float2 wf0 = __bfloat1622float2(*reinterpret_cast<const __nv_bfloat162*>(&w_vec.x));

First work out residency using Section 1 (Figure 3-1). Each 16 B load takes 4 registers while in flight, so per-thread registers in v5 rise from 23 in v3 to 30, rounded up to 32 (the next multiple of 8). That lands right on the 32-register cutoff from Section 1, so each SM still fits 16 CTAs and 64 warps. If each thread used 3 more registers (33 registers) and crossed the cutoff, rounding to a multiple of 8 would allocate 40 registers, leaving only ⌊65,536÷(40×128)⌋=12\lfloor 65{,}536 \div (40 \times 128) \rfloor = 12⌊65,536÷(40×128)⌋=12 CTAs per SM (this variant was not measured).

Next work out bytes in flight using Section 2: the number of load instructions for WWW drops to one-eighth, and 64 warps ×\times× 512 B per load instruction gives about 32 KiB/SM, or 8× that of v3.

At 32 KiB in flight per SM, bandwidth reaches only about 83% of the plateau (Chapter 2, Figure 2-3). Estimating from that bandwidth plus fixed overhead is still noticeably faster than the measured time (see the chart note), and the gap was not measured separately. Also, v5 still runs about 1.18 waves: after the 2,112 CTAs of the first wave finish, 384 half-row CTAs still have to run a second wave.

9v5 → v6: Why Does Eliminating the Tail Wave Make Execution Slower?

v6 shrinks each CTA to a single warp; although all 2,304 CTAs fit in one wave, each SM holds only ~17 resident warps on average, dropping bytes in flight to ~8.7 KiB and hurting achieved bandwidth.

v6 shrinks each CTA to 32 threads so one warp computes one row:

gemv_v6<<<2304, 32, 0, stream>>>(W, x, y, K);

The load width is the same as v5, with each thread reading 16 B per iteration; the 32 partial sums of a row are still added through 128 B of SMEM (switching to direct intra-warp exchange is covered in Chapter 4, Section 5).

Work out residency using Section 1 (preset v6 in Figure 3-1): per-thread registers match v5, and each CTA takes 128 B of SMEM plus the 1 KiB reserved. Each CTA has only 1 warp, so warp slots allow 64 CTAs, but CTA slots allow only 32, capping each SM at 32 CTAs and giving the full GPU a single-wave capacity of 132×32=4,224≥2,304132 \times 32 = 4{,}224 \ge 2{,}304132×32=4,224≥2,304. All 2,304 CTAs fit in a single wave, so we no longer need the KKK-halves split and L2 merge of v3.

How many CTAs a pool allows is not how many are actually placed inside. The whole grid has only 2,304 CTAs; spread across 132 SMs, each SM gets an average of only 2,304÷132≈17.452{,}304 \div 132 \approx 17.452,304÷132≈17.45 CTAs, or about 17 warps (compared with 64 in v5), leaving three-quarters of the warp slots empty. At 1 in-flight 16 B load per thread, each SM keeps only 17.45×512 B≈8.717.45 \times 512\ \text{B} \approx 8.717.45×512 B≈8.7 KiB/SM in flight, about a quarter of v5.

The chart below gives the measured result: v6 is slower than v5 instead, in the same direction as the drop in bytes in flight. Each thread in v6 issues only one 16 B load before first using the data (about 8.7 KiB/SM in flight). Subtracting fixed overhead leaves an effective bandwidth of about 2.2 TB/s, higher than the value extrapolated from the round-trip latency in Chapter 2, Figure 2-3 (see the chart note). One possibility is that the round trip is also shorter when fewer bytes are in flight; the cause was not measured separately.

So v6 is a measured counterexample to shrinking CTAs to get rid of the tail wave: removing the tail wave pays off only when it does not cut bytes in flight, and residency math has to count the warps actually placed on the SM, not just the ceiling allowed by the pools. Still, the structure of v6 is worth keeping: one warp computes one row, and it fits in a single wave. It drops the tail-wave split and cross-CTA merge, and keeps the whole row's partial sums inside the same warp so they can later be summed directly in registers without going through SMEM (Chapter 4, Section 5).

For the measured effect of the shared-memory half of this chapter (TMA, ring buffer, mbarrier, XOR swizzle, and setmaxnreg) on the TTT-token qkv_gate matrix multiplication, see Chapter 6, Section 8.

Takeaway: How quickly and safely an SM gets data depends on how many contiguous useful bytes each instruction brings back, how many bytes the actually resident warps keep in flight at once, and whether each SMEM slot is returned only after the data read from it has been used in compute instructions.

Next chapter's question: In v6, each SM has only about 17 warps and 8.7 KiB in flight; how does each sub-partition inside the SM pick a warp to issue an instruction each cycle, and how can one thread keep several loads in flight at once to bring bytes in flight back above 64 KiB?

Chapter 4Level 4

Single SMSP — When Each Cycle Can Issue Only 1 Instruction, How Do We Keep Waiting from Stretching Total Runtime?

  • Preface
  • Primer 1
  • Primer 2
  • Primer 3
  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]
  • Chapter 3 [Level 3]
  • Chapter 4 [Level 4]: Single SMSP
  • Chapter 5 [Level 5]
  • Chapter 6 [Level 6]
  • Chapters 7–9
  • Chapter 10
  • Appendices

At the end of Chapter 3, v6 of gemv shrank each CTA down to only 1 warp computing 1 row, and v6 then ran even slower than v5 because concurrent in-flight reads per SM dropped to ~8.7 KiB (Chapter 3, Section 9). To push bytes in flight back up, we need to open up the next level down inside the SM: the SMSP (SM sub-partition), with 4 SMSPs in every SM.

As we saw in Chapter 3, Section 1, each SM holds at most 64 resident warps; split evenly across the 4 SMSPs, each SMSP gets 1 warp scheduler and holds at most 16 resident warps. An SMSP scheduler can issue only 1 instruction per cycle, while a memory load waits tens to thousands of cycles—how do we keep that wait from becoming total execution time?

To answer that, we will follow a single warp through one full pass: what happens while it waits for data, who waits for whom when 32 threads sharing one instruction stream hit branch divergence, and why only 1 thread ends up doing the work when the warp reduces its per-thread partial sums into a single value.

1With Only 1 Issue Slot per Cycle, Which Waits Actually Add to Total Runtime?

An issue slot goes idle only on cycles when the SMSP has zero eligible warps; whether idle issue cycles add to total runtime depends on whether issue slots are the bottleneck resource.

On every clock cycle, the SMSP warp scheduler scans the warps resident in its sub-partition (Figure 4-1; see Chapter 2, Section 2 for clock cycles): as soon as all operands for a warp's next instruction are ready and the target execution unit is free, that warp is eligible.

Each SMSP has only 1 issue slot per cycle. The warp scheduler picks 1 eligible warp, issues 1 instruction from it, and marks that warp selected. Switching warps takes no time: every resident warp keeps its registers on-chip (Chapter 3, Section 1), so picking warp A on this cycle and warp B on the next does not save or restore any state. That much works just like hardware multithreading on a CPU. What differs is CPU SMT (simultaneous multithreading): a CPU core can issue instructions from several threads in the same cycle, but holds only a few contexts per core (not measured in this book). An SMSP, by contrast, holds 16 warp contexts yet issues only 1 instruction from 1 warp per cycle (fine-grained multithreading).

What about the remaining resident warps that do not issue an instruction on that cycle? Either a warp is not selected—it is eligible, just not the one chosen on this cycle—or it is stalled waiting for data or for an execution unit. A cycle is recorded as no eligible (a cycle with no eligible warp), leaving the issue slot idle, only when the SMSP has zero eligible warps. Even if 15 warps sit not selected on a cycle, as long as 1 warp issues an instruction, that cycle's issue slot is full.

When a thread block (CTA) lands on an SM, its 4 warps are distributed across the 4 SMSPs, with 1 warp assigned to each SMSP. You can see this in Mode 1 of Figure 4-1, which corresponds to v1 from Primer 3: each 128-thread CTA computes 1 row, with each thread loading one BF16 element (2 B) at a time. One SM holds 16 such CTAs, so each SMSP holds 16 warps—one from each of the 16 CTAs—each reading a different row of WWW. After issuing 1 load to the Load/Store Unit (LSU; Chapter 3), each warp quickly stalls waiting for the data to return; once all 16 warps are stuck waiting, most cycles end up no eligible.

2Scoreboards and In-Order Issue: How Does a Warp Avoid Stalling in Place After Issuing a Load?

The scoreboard marks only the pending destination register as not ready, stalling the warp only when it reaches the first instruction that consumes that register; the more independent instructions interleaved in between, the fewer warps are needed to saturate issue slots.

A GPU warp issues instructions in program order (in-order issue) and cannot skip past a stalled instruction out of order. How does it keep moving right after firing a load? It uses a scoreboard (Figure 4-2): when the warp issues a load, the hardware logs an entry on the scoreboard, and the warp keeps issuing subsequent independent instructions that do not touch the loaded result. Only when the warp hits the first instruction that consumes that result does it wait for the scoreboard to clear, at which point the warp scheduler switches to another eligible warp. The compiler encodes ahead of time which scoreboard to wait on and before which instruction to stall, while the hardware tracks at runtime when the data comes back and clears the scoreboard (see Chapter 6, Section 5 for the instruction-word encoding). Global memory loads and shared memory (SMEM) loads use this exact same wait mechanism; only the number of wait cycles differs.

Now apply Little's Law (Chapter 2, Section 3) to a single SMSP, where the target to keep fed is the 1-instruction-per-cycle issue slot. Here we count instructions in flight; Section 3 will count bytes in flight. Suppose one load waits DDD cycles, and a warp can issue nnn instructions (including the load itself) between issuing the load and first using its result. Because the issue slot wants 1 instruction every cycle, keeping it full takes about D/nD / nD/n warps taking turns:

required resident warps≈⌈Dn⌉\mathrm{required\ resident\ warps} \approx \left\lceil \frac{D}{n} \right\rceilrequired resident warps≈⌈nD​⌉

Take a short-latency load first: a conflict-free SMEM load takes ~23 cycles (Chapter 3, Section 7). If each load is followed by 3 independent instructions (n=4n = 4n=4), then ⌈23/4⌉=6\lceil 23 / 4 \rceil = 6⌈23/4⌉=6 warps are enough to hit 0 no eligible cycles (Figure 4-2, Mode 4); if only 4 warps are resident, they cannot cover the whole wait window, and idle cycles remain on the timeline (Mode 3).

In the opposite case, the next address may depend on the value returned by the previous load. Suppose three tables sit in SMEM and we chain lookups: idx = len[i]; p = table[idx]; v = data[p];. Right after each load issues, the very next instruction needs its result, pinning n=1n = 1n=1 at every step. At ~23 cycles per load, 3 chained loads wait ~69 cycles in total, so 1 warp stalls on the scoreboard repeatedly (Figure 4-2, Mode 1). A single serial chain cannot be split apart on its own. If an outer loop wraps it, though, len[i + 1] in iteration i+1i + 1i+1 does not depend on iteration iii. While iteration iii is still waiting, the warp can issue the next iteration's load first and stretch nnn larger (Chapter 7, Section 6). The cost of stretching nnn is register pressure: each extra pending load ties up another set of destination registers, and using more registers may reduce resident warps (Chapter 3, Section 1). The next section checks this when we work out the numbers for v7.

3When Memory-Bound, Should You Saturate Issue Slots or HBM? (The Mechanism Behind gemv v6 → v7)

A memory-bandwidth-bound kernel must saturate SM-wide bytes in flight rather than issue slots, by issuing multiple independent wide loads per thread before consuming the first result.

Let's plug HBM into the issue-slot formula from Section 2. In Chapter 2, Section 2 we measured an unloaded HBM round-trip latency of ~0.334 µs, which works out to ~600 clock cycles at the ~1.8 GHz sustained clock. With 1 pending load per warp and n=4n = 4n=4, filling the issue slot would take 600÷4=150600 \div 4 = 150600÷4=150 warps—far above the limit of 16 warps per SMSP—and under full load the round-trip latency stretches to ~1.9 µs (Chapter 2, Section 3), demanding even more warps. That budget cannot be balanced: in gemv, the issue slots have to sit idle for most of the time.

Here is why that unbalanced budget does not hurt us: two different resources are racing to saturate first—the issue slot at 1 instruction per cycle, and HBM, which hits its bandwidth plateau at ~64 KiB of in-flight reads per SM (Chapter 2, Section 3). Whichever resource saturates first governs total runtime through its own Little's Law equation. Because gemv reads 37.75 MB of weights and uses each loaded weight only once, HBM hits the ceiling first.

Look back at Figure 4-1: both modes spend over 80% of their cycles in no eligible, yet their speeds differ because of how many bytes they keep in flight. In Mode 1 (v1 from Primer 3), each thread loads only 1 BF16 at a time, so 16 warps on an SMSP keep only 1 KiB in flight at once, or 4 KiB across the whole SM. In v6, each thread keeps only one 16 B load in flight, which comes to only ~8.7 KiB across the SM. Mode 2 places 4 warps on each SMSP and has each thread keep eight 16 B loads in flight—16 KiB on that SMSP, and right at 64 KiB across the whole SM. Both Mode 1 and v6 are slow because they have too few bytes in flight, not because the issue slot sits empty. At the ~1.9 µs full-load round-trip latency, Mode 2 will have even more idle cycles than what Figure 4-1 shows.

That is how v6 → v7 pushes bytes in flight back up: by firing wide loads back to back. A warp stalls as soon as it reaches the first instruction that uses a loaded result. Peak concurrent in-flight reads per SM therefore equal resident warps times 32 threads per warp, times the loads each thread issues before first use, times the bytes per load. In Chapter 3, Section 9 we calculated that v6 averages ~17.45 resident warps per SM and issues only one 16 B load of WWW per step before multiplying and accumulating. In v7, each thread first fires 8 independent 16 B (uint4) loads into 8 register groups and only then begins the multiply-accumulate. The compiled machine instructions (SASS; see Chapter 6, Section 2 for how source compiles to SASS) show the same order, with all 8 loads of WWW sitting ahead of the first multiply-accumulate. Peak WWW bytes in flight at one time climb from ~8.7 KiB/SM to ~69.8 KiB/SM, crossing the 64 KiB/SM knee for the first time:

17.45×32×8×16 B≈69.8 KiB17.45 \times 32 \times 8 \times 16\ \mathrm{B} \approx 69.8\ \mathrm{KiB}17.45×32×8×16 B≈69.8 KiB

Keep in mind that 69.8 KiB/SM is the peak concurrent in-flight read volume: each warp computing one row (8,192 elements) runs only 8,192÷(32×8×8)=48{,}192 \div (32 \times 8 \times 8) = 48,192÷(32×8×8)=4 such batches of loads (since each 16 B load holds 8 BF16 elements). Because a warp has to finish the multiply-accumulate instructions for one batch before issuing the next batch, time-averaged bytes in flight stay below this peak (not measured; see Section 6).

What does v7 pay for those extra loads? Buffering 8 groups of 128-bit values pushes per-thread register usage from 30 up to 83, which rounds up to 88 under the 8-register per-thread allocation granularity (Chapter 3, Section 1). Because the register file is partitioned equally across the 4 SMSPs and allocated independently within each SMSP (⌊16,384/(32×88)⌋=5\lfloor 16{,}384 / (32 \times 88) \rfloor = 5⌊16,384/(32×88)⌋=5 warps per SMSP), each SM can still hold up to 20 single-warp CTAs—above the 17.45 CTAs assigned per SM by the grid. So we do not lose a single resident warp, and peak bytes in flight scale by a full factor of 8 (see the chart in Section 6 for the measured speedup). If register pressure pushed the residency cap below the 17.45 warps assigned by the grid, resident warps would drop and bytes in flight would no longer scale by 8×; no such counterexample was measured on gemv.

4When 32 Lanes Share One Instruction Stream, Who Waits for Whom Under Branching?

Short conditionals use predication at almost zero cost; long divergent branches within a warp must execute serially one after the other, whereas branches aligned to whole-warp boundaries do not serialize each other.

Inside a warp, the 32 threads are called 32 lanes. At any given instant, all 32 lanes execute the same instruction: the warp scheduler issues 1 instruction to the entire warp at a time, while individual lanes can be enabled or masked off—an execution model called SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads; see Figure 4-3).

Every thread has several 1-bit predicate registers, such as P0. On a very short conditional like if (tid == 0) y[row] = sum;, the compiler does not emit a branch jump at all—it attaches a predicate (such as @!P0) to the instruction, issues it to all 32 lanes as usual, and lets the lanes where the condition is false suppress their writeback.

Once a branch body is long enough to need a jump, you get branch divergence. The hardware tracks which lanes are enabled with a 32-bit active mask: on any given cycle, the warp scheduler issues instructions down only one branch path while masking off the lanes on the other path. The warp runs the true path first, then runs the false path, and only turns all 32 active lanes back on at the reconvergence point where both paths merge—which means you pay the sum of both paths' runtimes, not the longer of the two.

You can see this directly in Figure 4-3, which compares three branching variants for the post-CTA-barrier epilogue of warp 0 (with machine instruction counts in the figure readout):

  • Variant 1 (predicated store): This does no additions and shows predication on its own. Only the lanes where the condition holds write out the value already in their registers; with a predicate attached, the instruction issues in a single pass with no jump.
  • Variant 2 (one-sided branch if (tid == 0) { 128 additions }, v1 epilogue): The other 31 lanes exit right at the branch entry (since no other work follows, the compiler ends them there), yet the warp cannot leave the SMSP until lane 0 finishes summing smem[0..127]. We measure ~4 cycles before a floating-point multiply-accumulate result is ready for the next instruction (Chapter 5, Section 1), and we estimate a floating-point addition at that same value. Running 128 serial additions therefore takes ~512 cycles, plus ~23 cycles for the first SMEM load (Chapter 3, Section 7). Across those ~535 cycles, only 1 of the 32 lanes is doing work.
  • Variant 3 (two-sided branch, illustrative code if (lane < 16) {…} else {…}, 128 additions per branch): The first 16 lanes and the last 16 lanes run their 128 additions one after the other. Their times add together (~2 × 512 cycles) before all 32 lanes turn back on at the reconvergence point.

By contrast, a branch split along whole-warp boundaries—such as if (warp_id == 0)—gives all 32 lanes the same condition, so the warp never diverges. That is how Chapter 3, Section 5 splits producer warps from consumer warps. The trade-off is that work can be handed out to warps only in 32-thread chunks, and the time cost of that coarser granularity was not measured separately. Also note that __syncthreads() requires every thread in the CTA to reach the same barrier instruction, so it cannot sit inside a branch taken by only some threads. Chapter 7, Section 7 shows how different branches can meet at a shared barrier.

In v1's SASS, each row uses Variant 2 to reduce 128 partial sums (v2–v5 were not inspected separately). By v6 and v7, each CTA is down to only 1 warp and 32 partial sums, yet that same one-lane reduction pattern still burns over a hundred cycles—as we will calculate and fix in the next section.

5Keeping the Reduction Inside One Warp: How Does Warp Shuffle Eliminate Shared Memory and CTA Barriers? (The Mechanism Behind gemv v7 → v8)

A reduction across at most 32 threads can read neighbor registers directly in 5 warp-shuffle steps, bypassing shared memory and the CTA barrier (__syncthreads()).

Now replace v7's SMEM epilogue with a warp shuffle (Figure 4-4, Mode 2). In v8, the source code calls __shfl_xor_sync(0xffffffff, acc, o), which lets each thread read acc directly from the register of thread lane XOR o. The first argument is the lane mask: 0xffffffff means all 32 lanes participate, and the instruction itself reconverges those lanes at that point. Values move straight from one register to another without ever touching memory. In the SMEM version of Figure 4-4, Mode 1, the kernel must wait until all 32 threads finish writing memory and those writes are visible to thread 0, so it keeps a CTA barrier. Because a warp shuffle never writes to memory, it needs no barrier.

The whole reduction finishes in log⁡232=5\log_2 32 = 5log2​32=5 halving steps: stepping o = 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 in turn, each step runs one warp shuffle followed by one addition; after 5 steps all 32 lanes hold the total sum, and lane 0 writes it out. Each warp shuffle still waits on the same scoreboard mechanism from Section 2 before the following addition can use its result.

Let's put the two cycle budgets side by side for reducing those 32 values:

  • v8 warp shuffle: Each warp shuffle takes ~24 measured cycles before the next dependent instruction can use its result, paired with one ~4-cycle addition; 5 steps plus the final writeback come out to 5×(24+4)+1=1415 \times (24 + 4) + 1 = 1415×(24+4)+1=141 cycles in total, using 0 bytes of SMEM and 0 CTA barriers.
  • v7 SMEM epilogue: Having all 32 threads write to SMEM, cross the CTA barrier, and load back the first value takes 44.3 measured cycles in total; thread 0 then runs 32 serial additions in ~128 cycles, plus the final writeback, for ~173 cycles in total.

On the wall clock, though, each row's epilogue saves only ~32 cycles, or ~18 ns at ~1.8 GHz. And because the entire grid fits in a single wave starting from v6 (Chapter 3, Section 9), all warps run their epilogues at the same time, so that 18 ns saving does not accumulate across rows.

Back in gemv, v8 removes v7's 128 B of SMEM and __syncthreads() and replaces them with that 5-step warp shuffle. What we gain is a slightly lower executed instruction count and slightly lower per-thread register usage than in v7, while actual residency stays at 17.45 warps per SM.

What does it cost us? Two things. First, warp shuffle works only within a single warp, so a reduction across more than 32 threads (such as v1) still has to shuffle within each warp first and then merge across warps through SMEM and a CTA barrier. Second, in v8 the compiler issues only 7 loads of WWW before starting multiply-accumulate, tucking the 8th load into the middle of the first multiply-accumulate group. That leaves peak concurrent loads of WWW in flight at most 7 (112 B) per thread, or ~17.45×32×7×16 B≈61.1 KiB17.45 \times 32 \times 7 \times 16\ \mathrm{B} \approx 61.1\ \mathrm{KiB}17.45×32×7×16 B≈61.1 KiB per SM—slightly below the 64 KiB knee point; why the compiler chose this schedule was not determined.

6The gemv Evolution v6 → v7 → v8: Why Does One Step Save So Much and the Next Save So Little?

v7 shortens the memory wait; v8 saves at most ~18 ns by our cycle model yet measures slightly faster still, with the extra gain unexplained.

As our baseline in the evolution chart below, we use PyTorch's matrix-vector multiplication function torch.mv, which calls NVIDIA's matrix library cuBLAS under the hood.

In the chart above, v7 runs ~1.43× faster than v6. Every step of the main loop across the 8,192 columns waits on HBM. As peak bytes in flight rise sharply (time-averaged bytes in flight were not measured; Section 3), that HBM wait shrinks with them. That speedup also puts v7 back ahead of torch.mv (v5 was already faster than it, before v6 slipped back behind).

Going by the Section 5 cycle budget, v8 should not run faster: its epilogue saves at most ~18 ns, executing fewer instructions does not shorten a memory-bandwidth-bound kernel, and its peak bytes in flight are slightly lower. How do we tell whether a one-step change is a real speedup or just run-to-run variation (also called measurement noise)? This book checks two criteria. First, across paired runs in the same round, the difference between the two versions must have the same sign every time. Second, that difference must exceed the largest gap between the medians of a single version within this set of runs—which we call its span below. Chapter 7, Section 1 gives the alternating paired ABBA method and its settings, and Chapter 6, Section 8 gives the noise band for the full-graph replay chain.

Here we ran v7 then v8 and then reversed the order on each of two machines, for 4 runs in total (the chart shows the low and high of each version's 4 medians). Across those 4 runs, v7's own median span is 0.32 µs and v8's is 0.29 µs. Both spans are smaller than the 0.42–0.55 µs margin by which v8 beats v7 in each of the 4 paired runs, and all 4 runs have the same sign—so this step is a real speedup. Where that small extra gain comes from was not determined.

Even though v8's peak bytes in flight come close to the knee, its runtime still sits a fair bit above the lower bound. Inside the kernel body, ~3.6 µs remains on top of moving the weights at steady-state bandwidth (see the chart above). That extra time may come from three places. First are the memory round trips at the start and end, and second is the wait for multiply-accumulate between the 4 load batches of each row, which lowers average bytes in flight. Third, dividing 2,304 rows across 132 SMs gives 18 rows to some SMs and 17 rows to others, so the SMs that finish first sit idle. How much each of the three contributes was not measured.

One last bookkeeping detail: why is the overhead ~2.8 µs here when Primer 3, Section 5 quoted 4.6 µs? They measure two different quantities: 4.6 µs is the total event-timed duration of an empty kernel (including the empty kernel's own execution on the GPU), whereas ~2.8 µs is the extra overhead outside a real kernel's body (primarily launch and event-recording overhead; see Chapter 10, Section 1 for details).

Takeaway: An issue slot stays busy as long as at least 1 warp is eligible each cycle; a memory-bound kernel must saturate SM-wide bytes in flight by having each thread issue multiple independent wide loads back to back.

Next chapter's question: Once data is loaded into registers, it must be unpacked and fed into multiply-accumulate instructions; as TTT grows from 1 to 8, which execution pipeline saturates first?

Execution Pipelines and Tensor Core — As T Grows from 1 to 256, How Does Compute Keep Pace with Weight Loads?
