In Chapter 4's v8, peak in-flight reads already approach the knee point, yet the profiler measures a kernel-wide average of only about 3.19 TB/s (Section 8 chart), below the steady-state bandwidth plateau from Chapter 2, Section 3. Chapter 4, Section 6 laid out why we fall short of that steady-state plateau (three candidates; their individual shares were not measured). Once the data lands in registers, we still have to unpack each BF16 pair and multiply-accumulate it—so which execution pipeline do those instructions actually enter?

As TTT grows from 1 to 256, how does arithmetic keep pace with the weights we read in, and once we split KKK, how do we add the pieces back together correctly into one output? First we look at T=1T = 1T=1 to see why the arithmetic hides inside the time spent waiting on memory. Then we see why the ordinary arithmetic pipelines get busy first once TTT reaches 8, so we must switch to the Tensor Core.

1Which Pipeline Does an Issued Instruction Enter, and Which Bound Governs Loop Speed?

The minimum cycles per loop iteration is governed by the maximum of three lower bounds: issue slots, the busiest execution pipeline, and the dependent-instruction chain.

Look at Figure 5-1: each SMSP has three arithmetic pipelines underneath it. Because these pipelines have different lane widths, they take different numbers of cycles to accept 1 warp instruction (issue interval (initiation interval)):

  • FMA pipeline: 32 lanes wide, so it accepts 1 warp instruction every 1 cycle for single-precision fused multiply-add FFMA, addition FADD, and multiplication FMUL. Because it is built from two halves and integer multiply-add IMAD can enter only one half, IMAD is accepted at 1 instruction every 2 cycles.
  • ALU pipeline: 16 lanes wide, accepting 1 instruction every 2 cycles. Integer addition and subtraction, three-input bitwise logic LOP3, shift SHF, and byte permute PRMT all run here.
  • SFU (Special Function Unit): 4 lanes wide, accepting 1 instruction every 8 cycles. Exponential, reciprocal, and reciprocal square-root instructions run here.

Those cycle counts follow directly from each pipeline's lane width, and microbenchmark measurements match them. What people usually call a CUDA Core is simply this set of SMSP pipelines that run standard floating-point and integer instructions; a program that uses only these pipelines and not the Tensor Core is a CUDA Core kernel. Each SMSP also has an LSU (Load/Store Unit, Chapter 3) for memory reads and writes, which we leave out of the arithmetic accounting below.

Put FMA, ALU, and SFU side by side, and their issue intervals stand in a 1:2:81 : 2 : 81:2:8 ratio. Combine those pipeline rates with the issue slot (Chapter 4, Section 1) and scoreboard dependencies (Chapter 4, Section 2), and the loop cycle lower bound (minimum cycles per iteration) is simply the maximum of three bounds. An out-of-order CPU can look past a stalled instruction and issue later independent instructions first, so only loop-carried dependency chains limit its speed. A GPU issues instructions in order, so even the longest dependency chain inside a single iteration stalls that warp. Only other warps can step in to fill those idle cycles, which is why we divide the third term by the number of resident warps:

min cycles per iteration=max⁡(Ninstr⏟issue slot, max⁡p Np⋅Ip, chain length×dependent-instruction latencyresident warps)\mathrm{min\ cycles\ per\ iteration} = \max\Big(\underbrace{N_{\mathrm{instr}}}_{\mathrm{issue\ slot}},\ \max_{p}\, N_p \cdot I_p,\ \frac{\mathrm{chain\ length} \times \mathrm{dependent\text{-}instruction\ latency}}{\mathrm{resident\ warps}}\Big)min cycles per iteration=max(issue slotNinstr​​​, pmax​Np​⋅Ip​, resident warpschain length×dependent-instruction latency​)

Here, "one iteration" means one warp executing the loop body once, and all three terms count SMSP cycles amortized per warp:

  • NpN_pNp​: the number of instructions routed to pipeline ppp;
  • IpI_pIp​: the issue interval of pipeline ppp;
  • dependent-instruction latency: the number of cycles from issuing an instruction until the next instruction that consumes its result can issue;
  • chain length: the number of instructions along the longest dependency chain in one iteration; other independent chains in the same warp advance in parallel and do not lengthen this term;
  • resident warps: the number of warps taking turns issuing instructions on the same SMSP.

Start with unpacking. In Chapter 4, v8 calls a library helper to convert a 32-bit word holding 2 BF16 values into 2 FP32 values. That helper issues 3 instructions per word: 1 PRMT to pull out the high half-word, then 2 left shifts by 16 bits. But BF16 is already the upper 16 bits of FP32, so converting to FP32 only means placing those bits in the upper 16 bits of a 32-bit register and zeroing the lower 16 bits (see the bit layout diagram in Chapter 6, Section 1). We bitwise-AND the high half-word with 0xffff0000 (LOP3 on the ALU pipeline) and shift the low half-word left by 16 bits—only 2 instructions per word. That is how v9 in Section 8 is written.

Now let's work out the three bounds for this 2-instruction-per-word unpacking loop. Splitting a row of 8,192 BF16 elements across 32 threads gives each thread 8,192÷32=2568{,}192 \div 32 = 2568,192÷32=256 BF16 elements, or 128 32-bit words. We have to unpack both WWW and xxx, which comes to (128+128)×2=512(128 + 128) \times 2 = 512(128+128)×2=512 unpacking instructions per thread on top of 256 FFMA instructions.

Average that per word pair (1 word of WWW paired with 1 word of xxx, or 4 BF16 elements in all): each word pair takes 4 unpacking instructions plus 2 FFMA instructions, or 6 instructions in total. Among the unpacking instructions, 2 LOP3 instructions go to the ALU pipeline. For the 2 left shifts, the compiler emits some as SHF (on the ALU pipeline) and some as multiplication by 2162^{16}216 via IMAD (on half of the FMA pipeline). That averages about 3 ALU instructions per word pair, putting the ALU bound at about 6 cycles. Each 16 B uint4 holds 4 word pairs and takes about 24 ALU cycles, while the FMA pipeline takes only about 16 cycles (8 FFMA × 1 plus about 4 IMAD × 2). The ALU pipeline hits its ceiling first.

How you order those instructions matters too (Figure 5-1, Modes 1 and 2): if ALU and FMA instructions alternate, each word pair finishes in 6 cycles with 0 idle cycles. If 3 ALU instructions issue back-to-back instead, the ALU accepts only 1 every 2 cycles and has no FMA instruction in between to interleave, so the scheduler has to wait. That adds 2 idle cycles per word pair, stretching it to 8 cycles.

Here the compiler turns 122 of the 256 left shifts into IMAD, cutting the ALU unpacking instructions from 512 (if all used SHF) down to 390. That is a standard move at this level: when one execution pipeline saturates while an adjacent one is idle, rewrite with equivalent instructions to offload the work—moving left shifts onto the FMA pipeline is called left-shift FMA offloading. The trade-off: IMAD hands its result to the next LOP3 about 2 cycles later than an all-SHF sequence (measured in a microbenchmark; the cause was not found). If the adjacent pipeline is already full, offloading gains nothing. Chapter 6, Section 3 uses this same move by hand in 4-bit weight decoding.

Now check the dependency-chain bound. A single FFMA has a measured dependent-instruction latency of about 4.1 cycles, and we estimate FADD at the same value. One batch runs 8 independent chains of 8 multiply-adds each (one chain per uint4; see Section 8 for the v9 code). The dependency-chain term is only 8×4.1≈338 \times 4.1 \approx 338×4.1≈33 cycles. Spread across about 17.45÷4≈4.417.45 \div 4 \approx 4.417.45÷4≈4.4 warps taking turns per SMSP (Chapter 4, Section 3), that comes to about 8 cycles per batch—far below the issue-slot bound of about 192 cycles per batch.

Both the issue-slot bound and the ALU bound come out to about 24 cycles per uint4, tying as the tightest bound. At that pace, one SMSP digests the 512 B that a warp loads (1 uint4 per thread) every 24 cycles. Across the full GPU, that works out to about 20 TB/s—about 4× the 4.8 TB/s HBM peak—so arithmetic is not the throughput bottleneck. At T=1T = 1T=1, the arithmetic hides inside the time spent waiting on memory, as the v8 → v9 measurement in Section 8 confirms.

If a loop contains an exponential, the bound shifts to the SFU. With 1 exponential per element and the SFU accepting only 1 instruction every 8 cycles, each element takes at least 8 cycles (Figure 5-1, Mode 3). Attention softmax hits this bound; see Chapter 7, Sections 8–9.

2As T Grows Above 1: Where Does CUDA Core Lose to Tensor Core?

Paper peak throughput predicts a crossover at T≈14T \approx 14T≈14, but the measured crossover occurs between T=4T = 4T=4 and 888: for each FMA pipeline instruction, about 2.2 instructions issue in total, so the issue slots become busy first, at ~70%, and the ALU pipeline at ~60%.

In multi-request decode, speculative decoding verification, and prefill (Primer 1, Sections 5–7), we process TTT tokens in a single pass, taking input x :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{x}{T,\;8192}{BF16}x:[T,8192]BF16 and weights W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 to compute y=xWTy = x W^{\mathsf T}y=xWT. Throughout this chapter, we write NNN for the 2,304 rows of WWW (Primer 3 called it MMM). If we count all the bytes read and written for WWW, xxx, and yyy, the arithmetic intensity (Primer 2, Section 4) is:

I(T)=2TNK2NK+2TK+2TN,N=2304, K=8192I(T) = \frac{2TNK}{2NK + 2TK + 2TN},\quad N = 2304,\ K = 8192I(T)=2NK+2TK+2TN2TNK​,N=2304, K=8192

When TTT is much smaller than N,KN, KN,K, I≈TI \approx TI≈T FLOP/B; as TTT grows, it crosses the 206 FLOP/B ridge point from Primer 2, Section 4 at T≈233T \approx 233T≈233. Estimate first from paper peak throughput. At the driver-reported maximum clock of 1.98 GHz (sustained runs sit about 1.8 GHz, which does not change the conclusion), full-chip FP32 FMA peak throughput is 132×4×32×2×1.98 GHz≈67132 \times 4 \times 32 \times 2 \times 1.98\ \mathrm{GHz} \approx 67132×4×32×2×1.98 GHz≈67 TFLOP/s. Divide 67 TFLOP/s by 4.8 TB/s and you get ≈14\approx 14≈14 FLOP/B: if each weight per token needed only 1 FFMA instruction, you would not reach the CUDA Core ridge point until T≈14T \approx 14T≈14.

Now measure both implementations on H200. Version (a) is a CUDA Core implementation that extends the hand-unpacked inner loop from Section 1 so one warp computes several tokens at once, reading each uint4 of WWW once and multiplying it across those tokens. Version (b) is a Tensor Core implementation: PyTorch torch.matmul, backed by cuBLAS (Chapter 4, Section 6), which uses the Tensor Core at these TTT values. Figure 5-2 plots the data from the two charts below on log-log axes.

Look at the two latency charts above. At T=1,2,4T = 1, 2, 4T=1,2,4, (a) the CUDA Core version is faster; starting at T=8T = 8T=8, (b) the Tensor Core version overtakes it and is already about 1.45× faster at T=8T = 8T=8.

Why does the CUDA Core version lose around 8? Because for every 1 FMA pipeline instruction (FFMA + IMAD) it issues, it has to issue about 2.2 total instructions—the extra instructions are the unpacking and address control counted in Section 1. Scale by issue-slot saturation (14÷2.2≈614 \div 2.2 \approx 614÷2.2≈6), and the CUDA Core version leaves the memory-bandwidth-bound regime around T≈6T \approx 6T≈6. Check the unit-utilization chart above: by T=8T = 8T=8, the issue slots and ALU pipeline are the busiest units at ~70% and ~60% utilization. The FMA pipeline sits at only ~30%, and memory bandwidth reaches only ~30% of peak. What the remaining ~30% idle issue-slot cycles stalled on was not measured separately. The measured crossover falls between T=4T = 4T=4 and 888 (T=5T = 5T=5–777 were not measured).

Does that ~2.2 ratio come down when one warp computes multiple tokens at once? Barely. Call twt_wtw​ the number of tokens one warp computes together (at T=8T = 8T=8, the fastest choice is tw=4t_w = 4tw​=4). When TTT is larger than twt_wtw​, the grid splits the tokens into groups and re-reads WWW for each group. You do get to share the unpacking of WWW across those twt_wtw​ tokens, but every token brings its own xxx vector that still has to be loaded and unpacked on its own. If you count only arithmetic instructions in the source code, the ratio drops from about 2.0 at tw=1t_w = 1tw​=1 to about 1.6 at tw=4t_w = 4tw​=4. Yet the measured ratio of "total instructions ÷\div÷ FMA pipeline instructions" goes from 2.24 to 2.21, barely budging with twt_wtw​; the gap comes from address, loop, and load instructions, which were not broken down instruction by instruction.

Switching to the Tensor Core has a trade-off. cuBLAS stays flat around 19 µs from T=1T = 1T=1 through 32; for T≤4T \le 4T≤4, the CUDA Core version runs below that line, so cuBLAS comes out slower (see the latency chart). From T=1T = 1T=1 to 128, each cuBLAS torch.matmul call launches 2 kernels: one using Split-K (Chapter 2, Section 5) to compute partial matrix products, and a second to sum those partial results. That adds an extra kernel launch and an inter-kernel handoff gap (Chapter 1, Section 1). How much of the ~19 µs plateau comes from that extra launch and gap—and what accounts for the rest—was not profiled item by item.

From here on, we split single-layer execution by the token count TTT of qkv_gate into three regimes and use these names directly in later chapters:

  • Regime I: T<8T < 8T<8 (measured at T=1,2,4T = 1, 2, 4T=1,2,4). CUDA Cores are still faster here, so our T=1T = 1T=1 gemv kernel stays on CUDA Cores throughout the book; the bottleneck is the weight bytes we have to read.
  • Regime II: 8≤T<2338 \le T < 2338≤T<233 (measured at T=8…128T = 8 \dots 128T=8…128), where arithmetic intensity stays below the 206 FLOP/B ridge point. We have to switch to the Tensor Core here, even though the full GPU is still memory-bandwidth-bound.
  • Regime III: T≥233T \ge 233T≥233, where arithmetic intensity reaches 206 FLOP/B or higher. Our sweep here only measured up to T=256T = 256T=256; working from the arithmetic-intensity formula, a chunked-prefill chunk of T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384 (Primer 2, Section 5) also falls in this regime (see Chapters 7–9 for larger TTT).

3How Large a Tile Does One Tensor Core Instruction Compute, and Where Do Its Operands Come From?

Each SMSP is paired with a Tensor Core; SM-wide, Tensor Core throughput is 16× that of the FP32 FMA pipeline and needs no unpacking, at the cost of a fixed instruction row height of 16 or 64.

A single Tensor Core does 1,024 FLOP per cycle (BF16 multiplication with FP32 accumulation; see Figure 5-3). With 4 per SM, a full SM delivers 4,096 FLOP per cycle, compared with 128×2=256128 \times 2 = 256128×2=256 FLOP per cycle across the SM's FP32 FMA pipelines (16×). Because the hardware takes BF16 directly, all 512 per-thread unpacking instructions from Section 1 vanish, and the ALU pipeline is no longer the bound.

The mMnNkK tag in the instruction name tells you the exact tile shape: one instruction multiplies an [m, k]×[k, n][m,\ k] \times [k,\ n][m, k]×[k, n] tile and accumulates the product into an [m, n][m,\ n][m, n] tile. Hopper gives us two families of Tensor Core instructions:

The first family is mma.sync (m16n8k16), issued by a single warp on its own with a minimum row height of 16. Threads must first load both the left matrix AAA and the right matrix BBB from SMEM into registers. On H200, back-to-back issue takes 1 instruction every 6 cycles, reaching only about 67% of peak throughput. It fits cases where valid rows do not fill 64 rows, or where registers are too tight to spread across 128 threads (Chapter 8, Section 3 uses it when each expert gets only a few tokens).

The second family is wgmma (m64nNk16), which must be issued together by 1 warpgroup (Chapter 3, Section 6: 4 contiguous warps, or 128 threads). Why must all 4 warps issue it together? Because the 4 warps sit on the 4 SMSPs (Chapter 4, Section 1): each SMSP's Tensor Core computes only the 16 rows for its own warp and leaves the result in that warp's registers, and the 4 pieces combine into 64 rows. So all 4 warps must reach this instruction; just like __syncthreads(), you cannot place it inside a branch that only some threads take (Chapter 4, Section 4).

Its row height mmm is fixed at 64, while its column width nnn can be any multiple of 8 from 8 to 256. In BF16, k=16k = 16k=16, and once n≥64n \ge 64n≥64, the back-to-back issue interval comes close to n/2n / 2n/2 cycles (m64n64k16 measures about 32 cycles, or about 99.8% of peak). FP8 Tensor Core throughput is 2× that of BF16: each instruction takes kkk from 16 to 32 while the issue interval stays the same.

Whenever the hardware reads a matrix operand out of SMEM, it uses a matrix descriptor: a 64-bit value that encodes the starting address and layout of that matrix tile in SMEM. Depending on where the left operand AAA lives, wgmma runs in one of two modes:

  • SS mode: Both AAA and BBB sit in SMEM. The hardware reads both directly through two matrix descriptors, using zero operand registers and writing only the FP32 accumulators into registers.
  • RS mode: AAA sits in registers across the 128 threads (4 32-bit registers holding 8 BF16 values per thread), while BBB sits in SMEM.

Look at the issue-interval chart above: SS mode is slightly faster when n≥64n \ge 64n≥64, while RS mode actually pulls ahead when n≤32n \le 32n≤32. Down at n=8n = 8n=8, SS takes ~18 cycles and RS takes ~17 cycles; the interval stops shrinking as n/2n / 2n/2 because we hit the per-instruction floor.

So when should you reach for RS mode? Only when AAA is already sitting in registers:

  • Intermediate result of chained matrix multiplications: Once attention computes P=softmax(QKT)P = \mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\mathsf T})P=softmax(QKT), PPP already sits in registers, so the second matrix multiplication reads it straight from registers in RS mode (Chapter 7, Sections 9–10). Switching to SS mode would force you to write PPP out to SMEM first and add the cross-proxy fence from Chapter 3, Section 3.
  • Compressed weights decoded to BF16 in registers and fed directly to Tensor Core: This requires putting the weight matrix WWW on the left-operand AAA side (the next section shows how). It pays off only when decoding a weight tile takes less time than reading that 16-bit weight tile from HBM; otherwise it is slower (see Chapter 6, Sections 1–2 for the encoding and Chapter 6, Section 4 for measurements and counterexamples).

For standard dense BF16 matrix multiplication (like our qkv_gate tiles at T≥128T \ge 128T≥128 in this book), we use SS mode.

Switching to Tensor Core instructions comes with costs: the row height is fixed at 16 or 64, which wastes work when valid rows do not fill the tile (next section); wgmma requires 4 warps to issue together, raising register use across all 128 threads at once, and RS mode takes extra operand registers on top. It loses in two places. First is Regime I (Section 2 latency chart). Second is when each expert gets only a few tokens, where the extra registers and SMEM used by wgmma lower occupancy (see the measurements in Chapter 8, Section 4).

4When T Is Only 8 to 32, How Do We Fill the 64-Row Left Matrix? (swap-AB: Swapping Operands A and B)

Using yT=WxTy^{\mathsf T} = W x^{\mathsf T}yT=WxT places the thousands of rows of WWW on the fixed 64-row operand-A side and the TTT rows of xxx on the variable-nnn operand-B side so all 64 rows contain valid data; at small batch sizes, the key saving is accumulator registers.

Take the standard layout first: put x :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{x}{T,\;8192}{BF16}x:[T,8192]BF16 on the left (m=64m = 64m=64 rows) and W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 on the right (n=64n = 64n=64). The fraction of those 64 rows that hold useful rows is the row fill ratio. At T=8T = 8T=8, only 8 of the 64 rows hold real tokens and 56 rows are padded with zeros, wasting 87.5% of compute. Likewise, T=16,32T = 16, 32T=16,32 waste 75% and 50% (Figure 5-4, Mode 1).

The fix is swap-AB (swapping operands A and B, Figure 5-4 Mode 2). Once you swap the two sides, rows of WWW occupy the mmm side (filling all 64 rows at 100%), while xxx moves to the nnn side with n=Tn = Tn=T. When TTT is not a multiple of 8 (such as T=5T = 5T=5), we pad nnn up to 8. By T=128T = 128T=128, xxx already fills two 64-row tiles on its own, so swapping operands saves no cycles (Figure 5-4, Mode 3).

Both instructions do the exact same amount of useful work (8 tokens × 64 rows of WWW), and m64n8k16 runs about 1.76× faster per instruction than m64n64k16 (see the issue-interval chart in Section 3). Still, in the early part of Regime II (T=8–32T = 8\text{–}32T=8–32), the full chip is memory-bandwidth-bound, so those instruction cycles are already hidden behind the time spent reading weights. What swap-AB really buys us here is registers: per-thread FP32 accumulators drop from 32 down to n/2n / 2n/2, needing only 4 registers at n=8n = 8n=8. The price you pay is that the accumulators now hold yTy^{\mathsf T}yT, so you have to transpose the tile through SMEM once before writing it back; and once T≥64T \ge 64T≥64, swap-AB brings no gain at all. Neither the gain from saving registers nor the time spent on the transpose was measured separately; in our multi-token GEMM evolution chain, swap-AB is measured together with another change in a single step (Chapter 6, Section 8).

5Asynchronous wgmma: How Do We Keep the Tensor Core Busy While Preparing the Next Input Group?

Using wait_group<1> keeps 1 commit group executing on the Tensor Core while waiting for the next buffer slot and issuing the next group, at the cost of releasing each SMEM slot one step later.

Issuing a group of wgmma instructions takes four steps. First issue wgmma.fence (so the accumulator registers can be handed over to the Tensor Core), then issue several wgmma instructions in a row, seal them into a commit group with commit_group, and finally call wait_group<N>, which waits until at most NNN commit groups are still unfinished.

Sections 5–7 use this book's hand-written multi-token qkv_gate kernel as the running example (Chapter 6, Section 8 walks through its evolution). Each CTA has 1 producer warp that fills an SMEM ring buffer via TMA (Chapter 3, Sections 4–5) and 1 or 2 consumer warpgroups that issue wgmma. Tiled matrix multiplication steps along the inner dimension KKK by a fixed column width each time (such as 64 columns); each step is a K-step. On every K-step, the consumer reads a tile of xxx and WWW from one slot of the ring and does four things in order: wait for the slot to arrive (full barrier, Chapter 3, Section 5), issue SS-mode wgmma, wait on the commit group, and return the slot (empty barrier).

Compare the two modes in Figure 5-5:

  • wait_group<0> (Mode 1: synchronous drain): Every step waits until the current group finishes and writes its results back to registers before waiting for the next slot and issuing the next group. Every step exposes an extra drain latency—measured at about 53 cycles for 64-column SS mode from issuing the last instruction until all results are written back.
  • wait_group<1> (Mode 2: 1-group in-flight overlap): After issuing group iii, the consumer waits only for group i−1i - 1i−1 to finish and moves on. While group iii is still running on the Tensor Core, the consumer is already waiting on slot i+1i + 1i+1 and preparing to issue the next group. Drain latency is exposed only on the final step.

Watch the buffer-slot lifetime. In SS mode, both AAA and BBB sit in SMEM, so the in-flight group iii is still reading slot iii. Therefore, the consumer returns slot i−1i - 1i−1 to the producer only after wait_group<1> returns and confirms that group i−1i - 1i−1 is done. Slot iii stays held by the consumer until the next step, so the producer has "slots − 1" in-flight slots to rotate through. In RS mode, what you must protect is the operand-AAA registers, using two register sets written in alternation (double buffering); the cross-iteration overlap of P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V in Chapter 7, Section 10 uses this pattern.

So the price of this overlap is 1 fewer rotatable ring-buffer slot in SS mode, or 1 extra set of operand-AAA registers in RS mode. And if preparing the next group takes longer than the matrix multiplication itself, overlap cannot hide that preparation time and the Tensor Core stalls anyway (Chapter 6, Section 4 shows a measured weight-decoding counterexample). Neither the isolated speedup of this step on qkv_gate nor a counterexample where those extra registers cause register spilling was measured separately.

6The K Loop of One Tile: How Deep Must the Ring Be and How Much Must Each Slot Hold So the Tensor Core Never Waits for Data?

The number of in-flight buffer slots times the MMA time per slot must cover the buffer-slot round-trip time. That round trip includes a fixed intercept that does not shrink when a slot gets smaller, so widening the tile to double the compute per slot covers it more easily than adding more slots.

Start with the layout of one K-step (Figure 5-6 Mode 1, our qkv_gate tile at T=128T = 128T=128). Tile height BM\mathrm{BM}BM runs along token count TTT and tile width BN\mathrm{BN}BN runs along output columns NNN: each CTA computes a BM=128\mathrm{BM} = 128BM=128 row × BN=64\mathrm{BN} = 64BN=64 column output tile, stepping along KKK by BK=64\mathrm{BK} = 64BK=64 at a time, while KKK is partitioned with Split-K = 3 (Chapter 2, Section 5). Inside the CTA, 1 producer warp and 1 consumer warpgroup share an 8-slot ring buffer.

One buffer slot holds an xxx tile xtile :  [128,  64]  BF16\shape{x_{\mathrm{tile}}}{128,\;64}{BF16}xtile​:[128,64]BF16 plus a WWW tile Wtile :  [64,  64]  BF16\shape{W_{\mathrm{tile}}}{64,\;64}{BF16}Wtile​:[64,64]BF16, or 24,576 B in total. The producer waits for a slot to open up, sets the expected transaction bytes, and fires off two TMA copies; once the bytes land, the full barrier flips phase (Chapter 3, Section 5). The consumer cuts BK=64\mathrm{BK} = 64BK=64 into four k=16k = 16k=16 slices; the upper and lower 64-row half-tiles each take 4 instructions, giving 8 SS-mode m64n64k16 instructions in all (~256 cycles). It then seals those into a commit group, calls wait_group<1> (Section 5), and hands back the previous slot i−1i - 1i−1. Each thread holds 64 FP32 accumulators, each pinned to a fixed cell of the output tile (see the layout card in Figure 5-6 Mode 1).

Now trace the buffer-slot round-trip time for a single slot: the clock starts when the consumer hands back an empty slot at the empty barrier, runs while the producer fires TMA and the bytes land in SMEM, and stops once the full barrier flips phase so the consumer can use that slot again. We get the round-trip formula from two tile shapes measured under full load at T=256T = 256T=256 (BN=64\mathrm{BN} = 64BN=64 and a second tile shape not covered in this book). Both runs are limited by the slot round trip, so their main-loop times give us two equations that solve to a slot round-trip time ≈1.12 µs+slot bytes÷172 GB/s\approx 1.12\ \text{µs} + \mathrm{slot\ bytes} \div 172\ \mathrm{GB/s}≈1.12 µs+slot bytes÷172 GB/s (the intercept was not measured separately). Next, we use this formula to check whether 3 in-flight slots are enough to cover the round trip at BN=128\mathrm{BN} = 128BN=128 (see the chart in this section). That 1.12 µs intercept holds only under this T=256T = 256T=256 load; it is longer than the unloaded round trip, and the extra time may be queueing (Chapter 2, Section 3; not measured). The 172 GB/s slope is the arrival rate at a single CTA: because many CTAs share the xxx tile and mostly hit in L2, multiplying the single-CTA rate by the CTA count comes out higher than HBM bandwidth.

Apply Little's Law (Chapter 2, Section 3) to this ring buffer: the in-flight slots held by the producer must cover the slots the consumer uses during one round trip. For the Tensor Core not to wait for data, we need

(in-flight slots)×(per-slot MMA time)≥per-slot round trip(\mathrm{in\text{-}flight\ slots}) \times (\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ MMA\ time}) \ge \mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ round\ trip}(in-flight slots)×(per-slot MMA time)≥per-slot round trip

Here per-slot MMA time depends on the work per slot, and in-flight slots = slots − 1 (Section 5); the per-slot interval is whichever of the two terms is larger:

per-slot interval=max⁡(per-slot MMA time, per-slot round tripin-flight slots)\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ interval} = \max\Big(\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ MMA\ time},\ \frac{\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ round\ trip}}{\mathrm{in\text{-}flight\ slots}}\Big)per-slot interval=max(per-slot MMA time, in-flight slotsper-slot round trip​)

Compare two tile widths at T=256T = 256T=256 (BM=256\mathrm{BM} = 256BM=256, BK=64\mathrm{BK} = 64BK=64). Here the 8 warps of two consumer warpgroups map onto the same 4 SMSPs and share the 4 Tensor Cores (the cards in Figure 5-6 Modes 2 and 3 list the bytes and cycles per slot):

  • BN=64\mathrm{BN} = 64BN=64 (Figure 5-6 Mode 2): SMEM fits at most 5 slots, leaving 4 slots in flight, and the slot round-trip time is ~1.36 µs. Each slot runs 16 wgmma instructions in ~513 cycles (converting cycles to µs across this section at a ~1.8 GHz sustained clock gives ~0.285 µs). Those 4 in-flight slots cover only ~1.14 µs in total, which cannot hide the ~1.36 µs slot round-trip time.
  • BN=128\mathrm{BN} = 128BN=128 (Figure 5-6 Mode 3): Per-slot MMA compute (1,025 cycles) doubles to ~0.57 µs, while the formula above predicts that the slot round-trip time rises only slightly to ~1.41 µs. SMEM fits 4 slots, leaving 3 slots in flight that cover 3×0.57=1.71 µs≥1.41 µs3 \times 0.57 = 1.71\ \text{µs} \ge 1.41\ \text{µs}3×0.57=1.71 µs≥1.41 µs, which hides the round trip. We need 2.5 in-flight slots, so 3 in-flight slots are enough with about half a slot of headroom.

Widening from BN=64\mathrm{BN} = 64BN=64 to BN=128\mathrm{BN} = 128BN=128 halves the output column tiles from 2,304÷64=362{,}304 \div 64 = 362,304÷64=36 to 18. To keep the total CTA count close to one wave across the 132 SMs (Chapter 2, Section 1), we also raise Split-K from 3 (108 CTAs) to 7 (126 CTAs). That step is to keep a single wave, not to hide the round trip.

Along KKK, there are 8,192÷64=1288{,}192 \div 64 = 1288,192÷64=128 K-steps in total. Because 128 is not divisible by 3 or 7, the heaviest slice gets 43 steps and 19 steps respectively, and runtime follows the busiest slice (Chapter 2, Section 1). BN=64\mathrm{BN} = 64BN=64 is one of the two points used in the fit (from an earlier run; this run measures 14.33 µs). At BN=128\mathrm{BN} = 128BN=128, the measured 11.16 µs is close to the 10.8 µs predicted at a ~1.8 GHz sustained clock. That confirms only that 3 in-flight slots cover the slot round-trip time; this measurement does not test the intercept or the slope.

Look at the chart above: widening the tile speeds up the main loop by about 1.28×, and Tensor active cycles on the busiest SM climb to 88% of main-loop cycles (see Chapter 6, Section 8 for where this step sits in the multi-token GEMM evolution chain). Roughly half of the time saved comes from the busiest CTA doing ~12% less work (19 steps × 128 columns vs. 43 steps × 64 columns, or 2,432 vs. 2,752), and the other half comes from finishing that same work faster. Between the two bars, all three parameters change together, and the full kernel saves less time than the main loop does (that gap may come from adding the extra partial sums under Split-K = 7; see Section 7). How much queueing adds to the intercept, how the savings split between the two halves, and how much each of the three changes contributes were not measured separately.

Here is the trade-off when you widen BN\mathrm{BN}BN: you double the MMA compute per slot and cut the total grid-wide bytes moved from L2 into SMEM by ~40%, in exchange for three costs:

  • Per-thread FP32 accumulators double from 64 to 128 (eating 64 more registers per thread; Chapter 3, Section 1).
  • Each SMEM slot gets larger, so the ring shrinks from 5 slots to 4.
  • Split-K goes from 3 to 7, more than doubling the partial sums we have to add together at the end (Section 7; see Chapter 6, Section 8 for numerical accuracy).

Push the slot size too far, though, and SMEM cannot hold enough slots to cover the round-trip latency, slowing the kernel down instead (you will see measured counterexamples in Chapter 9, Section 2 and Chapter 9, Section 7).

7After One Tile Finishes: How Are Partial Sums from Multiple Slices Accumulated Back into the Same Output Tile?

Partial sums are converted to BF16 and written to SMEM, and a single TMA tile reduction adds them to the output in L2; before the addition, each slice first confirms through a release/acquire chain that Slice 0 has zeroed the output.

Split-K cuts the inner dimension KKK into segments, with one CTA per segment; below we call one segment and its CTA a K-slice (split-K partition), with Slice 0 computing the first segment. Earlier versions in our multi-token evolution chain (Chapter 6, Section 8) use parallel slice reduction (Chapter 2, Section 7). Here we compare against a simpler baseline: each consumer thread packs its accumulators in pairs (two adjacent BF16 values in one 32-bit word, BF16x2) and issues element-by-element global atomic adds to the output. Hardware supports this instruction directly rather than spinning in the compare-and-swap retry loop of Chapter 2, but 128 threads each firing 32 scattered atomic adds into L2 drags out the epilogue and uses extra registers. Because the reduction adds onto the existing contents of output yyy, we must zero out this output tile (at T=128T = 128T=128, ytile :  [128,  64]  BF16\shape{y_{\mathrm{tile}}}{128,\;64}{BF16}ytile​:[128,64]BF16) before adding to it.

The new implementation takes three steps (Figure 5-7):

  • This kernel writes BF16 output, so each thread first rounds and packs its 64 in-register FP32 accumulators pairwise into 32 BF16x2 words;
  • Next, 8 stmatrix instructions (each writing several 8×88 \times 88×8 submatrices from warp registers into SMEM) write the ytile :  [128,  64]  BF16\shape{y_{\mathrm{tile}}}{128,\;64}{BF16}ytile​:[128,64]BF16 tile (16,384 B) into Slot 0 of the ring buffer. By this point all K-steps are done, so the slot can be reused;
  • Finally, 1 thread issues 1 TMA tile reduction, telling TMA to atomically add those 16,384 B element-by-element into the output in L2 (the whole tile is not a single atomic operation, so additions from different slices can interleave). It waits until TMA finishes reading SMEM before exiting, without launching a separate reduction kernel.

How do we make sure the output tile has been zeroed before any slice adds to it? The main chain is "zero-init → release → acquire → cross-proxy fence → TMA tile reduction", built on the cross-scope cumulativity from Chapter 2, Section 6:

  • Prologue: The same kernel replays repeatedly inside a CUDA Graph (Chapter 1), so each output tile keeps a ticket counter and a "zeroing complete" flag that both only increase and are never reset to zero. On each call, exactly SSS slices (SSS is the Split-K count) each do a relaxed atomic add on the counter to claim a ticket ttt, giving the call index n=⌊t/S⌋n = \lfloor t / S \rfloorn=⌊t/S⌋. Once Slice 0 zeros the output tile, it adds 1 to the flag, and every slice (including Slice 0) waits until the flag is >n> n>n.
  • Slice 0 publishes zero-initialization:
    1. Before entering the main loop, the 128 consumer threads zero the output tile.
    2. Inside the main loop, before returning an empty slot each time, the 128 consumer threads first pass a named barrier. The named barrier gates only these 128 consumer threads without blocking the producer warp; once past it, all 128 threads have finished writing zeros. Thread 0 alone then arrives on the empty barrier. Arriving on an mbarrier carries CTA-scope release semantics, while waiting on that barrier carries acquire semantics. That way the empty barrier still waits for only 1 arrival, and by the specification that single arrival carries the zero-initialization writes of all 128 threads. This chain was not verified in SASS.
    3. By the time the producer has issued all TMA loads for its slice, it has already waited on a slot return from the consumers (acquire). Right then, it issues a red.release.gpu on the global-memory "zeroing complete" flag: a non-fetching atomic add with device-wide (device scope, written .gpu in the instruction name; Chapter 2, Sections 6–7) release semantics. The end of this section explains why we pick this timing.
  • Every slice (including Slice 0) writes back:
    1. After finishing the main loop, the 128 consumer threads first pass a named barrier to confirm they are done with the ring-buffer slots.
    2. Thread 0 repeatedly reads the flag with acquire until the current call's zero-initialization is published.
    3. Thread 0 immediately issues a global cross-proxy fence fence.proxy.async.global, ordering the zero-initialization writes it just acquired before the upcoming TMA reduction.
    4. All consumer threads write their partial sums into SMEM with stmatrix, issue the shared-memory cross-proxy fence fence.proxy.async.shared::cta (Chapter 3, Section 3) so those normal stores are visible to TMA's subsequent SMEM read, and pass another 128-thread named barrier.
    5. Thread 0 issues the TMA tile reduction and waits until TMA finishes reading SMEM.
  • Validity condition:
    1. Only consumers waiting on the flag spin-wait; Slice 0's producer never waits on another CTA. The grid has at most 132 CTAs (each CTA's ring takes 192–200 KiB of SMEM, so at most 1 CTA fits per SM; Chapter 3, Section 1), and no long-running kernel on another stream or in another process holds SMs. When both hold, Slice 0's CTA can get an SM and will not deadlock. This is an operating condition under single-layer deployment, not a specification guarantee like cooperative launch in Chapter 2, Section 6.
    2. Slice 0 must run more K-steps than there are slots in the ring buffer; otherwise the producer has not waited for a slot return, and the zero-initialization writes are not on the chain.
    3. The counter and flag use 32-bit signed integers that only increase, so a continuously running service must reset them before wrap-around; switching to 64-bit counters removes this requirement. This book's kernel stays on 32-bit.
    4. Each (T,S)(T, S)(T,S) configuration has its own counter and flag buffer, and a given buffer is used with only one SSS. If two SSS values shared a buffer, ⌊t/S⌋\lfloor t / S \rfloor⌊t/S⌋ would no longer be the call index; this book does not use it that way. Each buffer is also used by only one call at a time, which sequential replay on a single stream satisfies.

Look at the epilogue chart above: at both TTT values, the epilogue shrinks to about one-third of what it took before.

Now weigh the trade-offs of this change. Compared with per-thread BF16x2 atomic adds, the epilogue shrinks to about one-third, and the only new cost is one extra 128-thread named barrier per K-step. Compared with launching a separate reduction kernel that adds slices in a fixed order, we save one kernel launch at two costs. First, each slice rounds its partial sum to BF16 before adding. Second, the addition order depends on arrival order at L2, so the result is not guaranteed to be bitwise deterministic (see Chapter 2, Section 7 on floating-point non-associativity and Chapter 6, Section 8 for measured output error). Neither the gap between the epilogue time saved and the full-kernel time saved nor the standalone cost of adding one named barrier per K-step was measured separately.

Two measured counterexamples show why the timing of this release matters. In the first counterexample, Slice 0 zeros the output and issues red.release.gpu right at kernel entry. Under memory-ordering semantics, a release only requires earlier writes to become visible before the flag; by itself, it does not block later reads. Yet this release compiles down to a device-scope memory fence instruction (for its cost, see Chapter 2, Section 6). When measured, the producer warp that issues it stalls completely, even though the producer itself never wrote to global memory; which writes that fence is waiting on was not verified. While the producer warp sits stalled, none of the TMA loads after it can issue, so this CTA ends up slower. In the second counterexample, waiting until the entire main loop finishes before issuing the release forces the other slices to wait longer, which is why we place it right after the producer finishes issuing all of its loads. Moreover, if the consumers write this flag in the middle of the instruction sequence that issues wgmma, the compiler stops overlapping those wgmma instructions and slows down the main loop (measured in Chapter 6, Section 6).

8gemv Evolution v8 → v9: A Quarter Fewer Instructions, So Why No Time Saved?

At T=1T = 1T=1, runtime is set by the weight bytes read and the bytes in flight; both versions read the same bytes with the same reads in flight, and the arithmetic cycles we save were already hidden inside the time spent waiting on memory.

Compare the inner loops of v8 and v9 (Figure 5-8), and v9 changes two things:

  • Unpacking implementation: It switches to the hand-written unpacking from Section 1, cutting each word from 3 instructions down to 2.
  • Accumulation method: For every loaded uint4, v8 starts an 8-multiply-add chain from 0 and adds it into acc with 1 FADD. v9 instead keeps 8 accumulators running across batches and merges them only at the end, cutting the merge FADD count as well.

Both versions fully unroll the loop and issue the exact same number of WWW loads per batch; v9 does not hoist the next batch's loads ahead of the current batch's multiply-adds.

Look at the two charts above: across 4 paired runs, two tie and two leave v9 slightly slower; the difference does not keep the same sign, so by the criterion in Chapter 4, Section 6 it does not count as a speedup. Instruction count drops by about a quarter, yet v9 reads the exact same bytes from HBM as v8, with the same occupancy and the same reads in flight (Chapter 4, Section 5), and HBM throughput is almost unchanged. At T=1T = 1T=1, all three arithmetic bounds from Section 1 sit below the limit set by the weight bytes read and bytes in flight (Chapter 4, Section 3), so lowering the arithmetic bound leaves runtime unchanged—making this step a direct measured example of saving arithmetic without saving time.

Its payoff comes once TTT grows: every token has to repeat unpacking and multiply-add, and the v9 inner loop is the starting point for the CUDA Core curve in Figure 5-2. The cost is writing hand-crafted bitwise unpacking code; no extra hardware-resource cost was measured.

Inside a single kernel at T=1T = 1T=1, since cutting arithmetic instructions cannot save time, the next move is to shrink the bytes each weight takes up (Chapter 6, Section 7; see Chapter 9 for cross-kernel launch overhead).

Takeaway: At T=1T = 1T=1, the arithmetic hides inside the time spent waiting on memory; once TTT reaches 8, the issue slots and the ALU pipeline get busy first, so we must switch to the Tensor Core. Once on the Tensor Core, we need asynchronous overlap and enough work per slot to keep it from waiting on data, and after splitting KKK, we also have to add the pieces back together correctly into one output.

Next chapter's question: When TTT is small, runtime comes right back down to the weight bytes read; how can we store each weight in fewer bits and reconstruct it with a handful of integer instructions?
