At the end of Chapter 5, v9 cut instructions by about one quarter, and runtime did not budge: at T=1T = 1T=1, your execution time tracks the bytes you read from HBM (see Chapter 5, Section 8). Once your in-flight reads are already near the 64 KiB/SM knee point, the most direct way to go faster — besides pushing even more reads in flight — is simply to read fewer bytes.

Level 6 zooms all the way in to a single machine instruction and the bits inside a 32-bit register. Here we work out three things: how many bits we can shave off each weight (using a lossless 12-bit format or the model's native 4-bit format), how many integer instructions it takes to unpack those weights back inside 32-bit registers, and whether those decoding instructions eat back the time we saved on memory. Answering that third question means we also have to read the actual machine code scheduled by ptxas and check whether it serializes instructions that should overlap — that is the other half of Level 6 (Sections 5 and 6). Finally, Section 8 walks through the full multi-token GEMM g0 → g5 progression, tying each step back to the chapter where its mechanism lives.

1Which of the 16 Bits in BF16 Can We Skip Storing? (C12 Lossless Weight Format)

The low byte of BF16 must be kept intact; when the top 7 exponent bits fall within a window of 8 adjacent values, the high byte needs only 1 sign bit plus a 3-bit offset, compressing each weight to 12 bits.

Before we touch any bits, we need to know what the accuracy rules allow. Expert weights ship in a lossy 4-bit format from the start (Section 3; Chapter 8, Section 1), but the dense projection weights have to enter the math at their exact published BF16 values. Our correctness test enforces this with two checks. The first leaves only one non-zero element in xxx, which pulls out a single column of WWW as the output, and requires each column's relative error to stay within 0.001 — no lossy quantization can survive that. The second feeds general inputs and checks that the full output's relative L2 error against the exact FP64 product (the square root of the sum of squared errors divided by the square root of the sum of squared exact values) does not exceed 0.01, which leaves headroom for parallel accumulation rounding (we will use that in Section 8).

So if we can't lose precision, where can we save bits? Look at how the floating-point bit fields line up in Figure 6-1. An FP32 number has a 1-bit sign sss, an 8-bit exponent eee (with bias 127), and a 23-bit mantissa mmm. BF16 keeps only 7 mantissa bits — it is literally the top 16 bits of FP32, with the exact same exponent width and bias — so it represents

w=(−1)s 2e−127 (1+m/27)w = (-1)^s\,2^{e-127}\,(1 + m/2^7)w=(−1)s2e−127(1+m/27)

That bit-field alignment is why, back in Chapter 5, Section 1, shifting a BF16 value left by 16 bits gave us a valid FP32 number right away.

Now split a 16-bit BF16 weight right down the middle into two bytes:

  • high byte: the 1-bit sign sss plus the top 7 bits of the exponent (e≫1e \gg 1e≫1).
  • low byte: the lowest 1 bit of the exponent plus the 7-bit mantissa mmm.

Let's trace a concrete weight w=0.02w = 0.02w=0.02 from qkv_gate (the weight matrix WWW from our main gemv running example; see Primer 2, Section 1 for its tensor shape). Its BF16 encoding is 0x3CA4, or 0 01111001 0100100 in binary: the sign bit is s=0s = 0s=0, the 8-bit exponent is e=121e = 121e=121, and the top 7 exponent bits give e≫1=60e \gg 1 = 60e≫1=60. The low byte is 0xA4, where the top bit 1 is the lowest bit of the exponent and the other 7 bits are the mantissa.

Of those two bytes, the low byte is distributed randomly across weights, so there is no way to compress it losslessly. The regularity sits in the 7 bits of the high byte. Both the NyoomFloat12 paper (Together AI, 2026) and nf12 (an open-source 12-bit weight library built on the same idea) rest on one premise: in trained large-model weights, e≫1e \gg 1e≫1 concentrates in 8 adjacent integer values [base, base+7][\text{base},\ \text{base}+7][base, base+7] (corresponding to 16 adjacent BF16 exponents [2 base, 2 base+15][2\,\text{base},\ 2\,\text{base}+15][2base, 2base+15]). We call the smallest integer of this 8-bin window the exponent window base (base), and we pick one base per matrix offline so that the fewest weights fall outside the window.

We tested this distribution only on normal random weights with mean 0 and standard deviation 1/K1/\sqrt{K}1/K​ — all timings in this chapter use those same random weights, and real model weights were not measured. For these weights, the chosen window starts at base=54\text{base} = 54base=54, which covers magnitudes in [2−19, 2−3)[2^{-19},\ 2^{-3})[2−19, 2−3), or roughly 1.9×10−61.9\times10^{-6}1.9×10−6 to 0.1250.1250.125, so typical weights like 0.020.020.02 land squarely inside the window.

With that 8-bin window in place, we can define our own 12-bit weight format, C12 (12-bit lossless weight format):

  • For a weight that lands inside the window, the high byte keeps only the 1-bit sign plus the 3-bit window offset d=(e≫1)−based = (e \gg 1) - \text{base}d=(e≫1)−base (4 bits in total). Together with the 8-bit low byte kept as-is, each weight takes 12 bits. For w=0.02w = 0.02w=0.02 above, base=54\text{base} = 54base=54 gives d=60−54=6d = 60 - 54 = 6d=60−54=6, so its 4-bit code is 0 110.
  • For an escaped weight (outlier) whose e≫1e \gg 1e≫1 falls outside the window, open-source nf12 uses whole-group escape: as soon as 1 weight in a group of 8 escapes, it marks the entire group as escaped and reads back all 8 original BF16 values from a separate escape table, keeping the decoded weights bit-exact. C12 does not do this: in the main table we fill the escaped weight's offset ddd with 0, record its position and true value in a separate side table, and add the difference back into the output after the multiply-accumulate finishes (Section 2).

Let's run the byte math for qkv_gate. Packing every 8 weights into 12 B instead of 16 B cuts the footprint to 75% of the original size: the main table for W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 drops from 37.75 MB to 28.31 MB, plus a side table of about 0.07 MB under the random weights above. At H200's 4.8 TB/s peak HBM bandwidth (see Primer 2, Section 4), the lower bound for reading WWW once from HBM drops from 7.86 µs to (28.31+0.07) MB÷4.8 TB/s≈5.91 µs(28.31 + 0.07)\ \text{MB} \div 4.8\ \text{TB/s} \approx 5.91\ \text{µs}(28.31+0.07) MB÷4.8 TB/s≈5.91 µs. Keep in mind that this ~1.95 µs difference is only the gap between two theoretical lower bounds, not a measured speedup — we will look at the measured numbers in Section 7.

In HBM, we pack every 8 C12 weights into three 32-bit words: two low-byte words la (the low bytes of weights 0–3) and lb (the low bytes of weights 4–7), plus one codeword (cd) holding the 4-bit codes for all 8 weights. We do this packing once offline before running the model. Of course, if a matrix had widely scattered exponents, more weights would escape and the side table would grow accordingly; we have not measured such matrices. Over the next three sections, we will count the extra instructions needed to unpack these weights at runtime and see where the trade-off flips as TTT grows.

2How Do 9 Integer Instructions Decode 8 C12 Weights into BF16?

Eight weights are reconstructed into four BF16x2 registers in 9 ALU instructions: shift to align, mask, add the exponent window base, and permute bytes.

In a 32-bit register, two BF16 values sit side by side as a single BF16x2 (as we saw in Chapter 5, Section 7, with one weight in the low 16 bits and one in the high 16 bits). Our job is to turn the three 32-bit words la, lb, and cd back into four BF16x2 registers. The trick is how we lay out the bits inside cd offline: in byte iii of cd (i=0..3i = 0..3i=0..3), bits 2..02..02..0 hold the 3-bit offset of weight iii, and bit 7 holds the sign of weight iii. That leaves the middle bits free, so we pack the 3-bit offset of weight 4+i4+i4+i (from the second half of the 8-weight group) into bits 6..46..46..4, and we tuck the sign of weight 4+i4+i4+i into bit 3 of the next byte (with byte 3 wrapping around to byte 0).

Once cd is packed in this layout, walking through the four steps in Figure 6-2 (9 instructions in total) reconstructs all 8 BF16 weights. We write those 9 instructions directly in the C++ source using PTX (Parallel Thread Execution ISA), NVIDIA's virtual instruction set — a style known as inline PTX (asm). When CUDA C++ compiles, it first lowers to PTX, and the backend assembler ptxas (PTX optimizing assembler) then compiles that PTX into SASS (Streaming Assembler machine code), the actual machine instructions executed by the GPU. We count pipeline cycles on the compiled SASS (Section 5):

  1. 1 funnel right shift (SHF) (rotating cd right by 4 bits to get rt): SHF concatenates two 32-bit inputs into a 64-bit value and slices out 32 bits, so passing cd as both inputs gives us a 32-bit rotate. Rotating right by 4 bits drops the 3-bit offset of weight 4+i4+i4+i right into bits 2..02..02..0 of each byte in rt, while pulling its sign bit from bit 3 of the next byte down into bit 7 of the same byte — now aligned with the exact bit positions that weight iii occupies in cd.
  2. 2 three-input logic instructions (LOP3) bitwise-ANDed with 0x87878787 (one on cd, one on rt): the single-byte mask 0x87 = 1000 0111b keeps only the sign at bit 7 and the 3-bit offset in the low 3 bits, clearing the middle 4 bits to zero.
  3. 2 integer additions (VIADD) adding EXP_BASE: the constant EXP_BASE=base×0x01010101\texttt{EXP\_BASE} = \text{base} \times \texttt{0x01010101}EXP_BASE=base×0x01010101 packs one copy of the exponent window base base\text{base}base into each of the 4 bytes. After masking, each byte looks like s|0000|d; adding base\text{base}base turns it into s|(base + d), which is the exact high byte of BF16. Call the resulting word ha for the first 4 weights and hb for the last 4 weights. Because base+7≤127\text{base} + 7 \le 127base+7≤127, adding the low 7 bits never carries into the sign bit at bit 7, so a single 32-bit addition sums all 4 bytes in parallel without byte-to-byte interference.
  4. 4 byte permutes (PRMT): PRMT takes two 32-bit source registers (8 bytes total: source bytes 0..3 from the first register, 4..7 from the second) and picks 4 bytes using a 4-digit hexadecimal byte-permute selector mask to build a new 32-bit word, where the lowest hex digit (low 4 bits) selects byte 0 of the result. Reading from low byte to high byte, selector mask 0x5140 grabs source bytes 0, 4, 1, 5 — that is la byte 0, ha byte 0, la byte 1, and ha byte 1 — zipping low and high bytes together into the two BF16 values for weight 0 and weight 1; selector mask 0x7362 grabs bytes 2 and 3 to build weight 2 and weight 3. Running the same pair of PRMT instructions on lb and hb produces weights 4–7.

Follow w0=0.02w_0 = 0.02w0​=0.02 (0x3CA4) from Section 1 along red circle 1 in Figure 6-2 to see this in action: in byte 0 of cd, the low 3 bits are 110 and bit 7 is 0; bitwise-ANDing with 0x87878787 leaves byte 0 as 0x06; adding base=54\text{base} = 54base=54 (0x36) reconstructs the high byte 0x3C; and finally, the low 16 bits of PRMT(la, ha, 0x5140) stitch byte 0 of ha (0x3C) onto byte 0 of la (0xA4) to produce 0x3CA4, giving us back the exact BF16 weight.

How much does this 9-instruction sequence cost on the execution pipelines? All 9 SASS instructions (1 SHF, 2 LOP3, 2 VIADD, and 4 PRMT) run on the ALU pipeline. At 2 cycles per ALU instruction (16 lanes; see Chapter 5, Section 1), unpacking 8 weights costs 18 ALU cycles. In terms of registers, the sequence reads 3 input registers and writes 4 output registers; although the C++ source declares 3 extra temporary registers, the disassembled SASS reuses registers so well that the whole block touches only 7 physical registers (see Figure 6-5).

How do we handle escaped weights that fall outside the window? Notice that the 9-instruction sequence above has zero branches: it blindly decodes the d=0d = 0d=0 placeholder stored in the main table, feeds the resulting wrong weight w^\hat{w}w^ straight into the FFMA multiply-accumulate (Chapter 5, Section 1), and fixes the result afterward by adding an escaped-weight correction term to the output:

yr=∑kw^rk xk+∑k∈Er(wrk−w^rk) xky_r = \sum_k \hat{w}_{rk}\,x_k + \sum_{k \in E_r} (w_{rk} - \hat{w}_{rk})\,x_kyr​=k∑​w^rk​xk​+k∈Er​∑​(wrk​−w^rk​)xk​

Here ErE_rEr​ is the set of escaped column indices in row rrr. In our C12 gemv kernel (where each warp computes 1 row; see Section 7), each warp checks the side table before entering the main K-loop, reads xkx_kxk​ at the escaped indices for its row, and accumulates the correction sum; once the main loop finishes, it adds that correction into the output yry_ryr​. That way, every weight inside the window is decoded bitwise-exact, and every escaped weight has its exact difference added back at the end. Mathematically, the result equals direct BF16 multiplication, though the lowest bits can differ slightly because the floating-point additions happen in a different rounding order (this error was not measured separately). On top of the 18 ALU cycles and temporary registers we counted above, the price you pay is reading and summing that side table before the main loop.

3How Do We Decode 4-Bit Weights (NVFP4) into BF16 in Registers?

Shifting the 4-bit code's sign to BF16 bit 15 and its magnitude to bits 8..68..68..6 yields the exact value times 2−1262^{-126}2−126; after offline nibble permutation, decoding 8 weights takes only 8 instructions.

In Chapter 8, Section 1, the model's expert weights ship in the 4-bit NVFP4 format, where every 16 weights share 1 scale factor (see Primer 2, Section 1). Here is how those bits are laid out:

  • Each 4-bit weight uses E2M1 bit fields: a 1-bit sign sss, a 2-bit exponent eee (exponent bias 1), and a 1-bit mantissa mmm. Across the 8 possible values of the 3-bit magnitude code ccc, the non-negative numbers v[c]v[c]v[c] are {0,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,6}\{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6\}{0,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,6}.
  • The block scale sblocks_{\text{block}}sblock​ shared by every 16 weights uses FP8 E4M3 bit fields (1-bit sign, 4-bit exponent with bias 7, and 3-bit mantissa), and the entire tensor then multiplies by one FP32 scale stensors_{\text{tensor}}stensor​. Put together, a weight's numerical value is

w=± v[c]⋅sblock⋅stensorw = \pm\,v[c]\cdot s_{\text{block}}\cdot s_{\text{tensor}}w=±v[c]⋅sblock​⋅stensor​

Inside each byte, the low 4 bits hold the even-indexed weight w2iw_{2i}w2i​ and the high 4 bits hold the odd-indexed weight w2i+1w_{2i+1}w2i+1​ — get those two nibbles backward and your matrix columns will be scrambled.

Hopper has no hardware instruction that converts 4-bit values straight into BF16, so we have to do it with bitwise ops in registers. Look at the bit alignment in Step 0 of Figure 6-3: if we drop the E2M1 sign bit into BF16 bit 15, the 2 exponent bits into bits 8..78..78..7, and the 1 mantissa bit into bit 6, and fill every other bit with 0, what BF16 number did we just build? By the formula from Section 1, that BF16 bit pattern evaluates to 2e−127(1+m/2)2^{e-127}(1 + m/2)2e−127(1+m/2), while the true E2M1 value is 2e−1(1+m/2)2^{e-1}(1 + m/2)2e−1(1+m/2). The two differ by the exact constant factor 2−1262^{-126}2−126.

Wait — does that still hold when the exponent bits are 0? A BF16 number whose 8 exponent bits are all 0 is a subnormal number, where values sit at uniform steps around 0 with magnitude 2−126⋅m/272^{-126}\cdot m/2^72−126⋅m/27. When you take the E2M1 code for 0.50.50.5 (0 00 1, so e=0e = 0e=0 and m=1m = 1m=1) and shift it into those same bit positions, you get 0x0040. That lands right in the BF16 subnormal range with value 2−126⋅0.52^{-126}\cdot 0.52−126⋅0.5 — the exact same 2−1262^{-126}2−126 factor (you can check the remaining magnitude codes in the Step 0 readout of Figure 6-3). That means we need zero special cases when the exponent is 0: for every weight, each BF16 halfword just keeps the 4 bits selected by mask 0x81C0 (bit 15 plus bits 8..68..68..6).

If we unpack weights directly from the published raw layout (where the low 4 bits of each byte hold the even index), the low nibble of byte jjj (j=0..3j = 0..3j=0..3) goes into the low halfword of BF16x2 and the high nibble goes into the high halfword. Each nibble's sign and 3-bit magnitude need their own shift-and-mask step:

uint32_t b  = x >> (8 * j);
uint32_t lo = ((b & 0x7u) << 6)  | ((b & 0x8u) << 12);   // w[2j]
uint32_t hi = ((b & 0x70u) << 18) | ((b & 0x80u) << 24); // w[2j+1]
D[j] = lo | hi;                                           // = BF16x2 × 2^-126

Why is that so instruction-heavy? Each BF16x2 has 4 separate fields — the sign and magnitude of both the low and high halfwords — and in the raw byte layout, all 4 fields sit at different bit distances from where they need to go, forcing a separate shift per field. When you compile that loop to SASS (Section 5), unpacking 8 weights (j=0..3j = 0..3j=0..3) balloons to 31 integer instructions: 16 three-input logic instructions (LOP3), 9 integer multiply-add left shifts (IMAD.SHL), and 6 funnel right shifts (SHF), or about 8 instructions per BF16x2.

We can cut that down dramatically by rearranging the nibbles offline when we pack the weights. In the expert kernels of Chapter 8, offline weight permutation places nibbles so that a single shift lines up multiple fields at the same time, shrinking the SASS sequence to 8 instructions per 8 weights: 4 shifts plus 4 three-input logic instructions (LOP3), where each LOP3 emits a finished BF16x2 (we skip the bit-by-bit permutation layout here; the bottom of Figure 6-3 shows a schematic view). The chart below compares the instruction counts before and after offline permutation.

Inside those 8 instructions, we write 2 left shifts as IMAD.SHL to move them onto the FMA pipeline (bottom timeline of Figure 6-3). That is the same left-shift offloading we saw in Chapter 5, Section 1: it cuts the ALU cost per 8 weights from 8×2=168 \times 2 = 168×2=16 cycles down to (2+4)×2=12(2 + 4) \times 2 = 12(2+4)×2=12 cycles. Chapter 8, Section 3 covers the measured gains and counterexamples across the expert kernel sizes.

Once we have the four decoded BF16x2 registers, we multiply them by the block scale using paired BF16 multiplies (HMUL2 on the FMA pipeline), which produces this thread's register slice of the left matrix AAA for warp-level mma.sync — its operand-A register fragment (see Chapter 5, Section 3). There is one catch: we still have to cancel the 2−1262^{-126}2−126 factor from our bit alignment, and multiplying the block scale by 21262^{126}2126 all at once would overflow the BF16 maximum (~21282^{128}2128). So we split that compensation across two steps:

  1. pre-multiplying the block scale by 2642^{64}264: when we unpack the FP8 block scale into BF16, we add an offset to its exponent that multiplies the block scale by 2642^{64}264. Because HMUL2 handles subnormal numbers normally without flushing them to 0, multiplying by 2642^{64}264 lifts the subnormal BF16 values for code ±0.5\pm 0.5±0.5 back into the normal BF16 range, leaving each scaled weight at "exact value ⋅sblock×2−62\cdot s_{\text{block}} \times 2^{-62}⋅sblock​×2−62".
  2. multiplying by 2622^{62}262 in the epilogue: after the matrix multiplication accumulates in FP32, the epilogue already has to multiply by the per-tensor FP32 scale stensors_{\text{tensor}}stensor​, so we fold an extra 2622^{62}262 into that FP32 multiply to cancel the remaining 2−622^{-62}2−62.

4When Does Compressing Weights Pay Off, and When Does It Lose?

12-bit weights pay off only when per-step decoding takes less time than reading 16-bit weights from HBM; on qkv_gate, C12 is used only for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, falling back to 16-bit BF16 for T≥128T \ge 128T≥128.

To see when weight compression helps and when it hurts, break a single K-step into three times (Figure 6-4): the time HHH to read one weight tile from HBM (which depends only on the byte count, not on TTT), the time DDD that the decoding threads spend, and the matrix multiplication time MMM (which grows with TTT). When those three stages run on separate hardware units with buffering in between, the step time is simply the maximum of the three; when the same group of threads runs two stages back-to-back, their times add together (Mode B of Figure 6-4). Now, the number of pure decoding instructions depends only on the number of weights and is independent of TTT. But in an RS mode kernel that feeds wgmma directly from registers, the same consumer threads have to both decode the weights and issue the wgmma instructions one by one, so DDD changes with both the number of consumer warpgroups and TTT.

That gives us a clean comparison. A 16-bit kernel does zero decoding, so one K-step takes max⁡(H16,M)\max(H_{16}, M)max(H16​,M); a 12-bit kernel takes max⁡(H12,D,M)\max(H_{12}, D, M)max(H12​,D,M). For T≤128T \le 128T≤128, both MMM and H12H_{12}H12​ are smaller than H16H_{16}H16​, which means the 12-bit kernel wins only when D<H16D < H_{16}D<H16​.

Let's put cycle numbers on H16H_{16}H16​ for a 64-row × 128-column tile of qkv_gate (8,192 weights; the unpooler kernel measured below also uses a 64 × 128 weight tile per K-step). In 16-bit BF16, that tile is 16,384 B; in 12-bit C12, it drops to 12,288 B. Across all 132 SMs on the GPU (see Primer 3, Section 1) running at ~1.8 GHz, the 16-bit MMA loop hits a measured ~4.15 TB/s (~17.5 B per SM per cycle), so reading one 16-bit weight tile takes H16≈936H_{16} \approx 936H16​≈936 cycles per step.

How fast can the ALU pipelines decode those 8,192 weights? If we look at raw ALU peak throughput, the 4 ALU pipelines on one SM can unpack at most 4×32×8=1,0244 \times 32 \times 8 = 1{,}0244×32×8=1,024 C12 weights (1,536 B) every 18 cycles, so 8,192 weights would take only 144 cycles at peak. What happens in the real 12-bit Tensor Core kernel is very different: in every K-step, each consumer thread has to decode its 64 assigned weights and issue RS-mode MMA instructions one by one (estimated at ~250 instructions from the disassembly), while only 1 to 2 consumer warps per SMSP take turns issuing instructions. As we saw from the formula in Chapter 4, Section 2, 1 to 2 warps cannot hide dependent-instruction latency, so decoding becomes latency-bound and runs nowhere near the ALU pipeline peak. (An alternative design where dedicated warps decode weights into SMEM and feed wgmma in SS mode was not measured.)

When T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32, the operator sits in the first half of Regime II (Chapter 5, Section 2), where cutting 25% of the weight bytes can save at most 25% of H16H_{16}H16​. Our 12-bit Tensor Core kernel for T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32 uses 2 consumer warpgroups that take turns on adjacent K-steps. As inferred from measured latency (rather than read directly from hardware counters), each warpgroup handles every other step: from the start of one of its steps to the start of its next step takes ~1,730 cycles (including the time spent waiting for the other warpgroup), so alternating between the two warpgroups averages ~865 cycles per K-step. That cuts the per-step time by only ~8% (1−865/9361 - 865/9361−865/936) — well short of the 25% ceiling. At T=1T = 1T=1, gemv also sees only a ~7% measured speedup, though for a different reason that we will unpack in Section 7.

At T=128T = 128T=128, the operator is still in Regime II (arithmetic intensity ~120120120 FLOP/B, below the 206206206 FLOP/B ridge point), yet the 12-bit kernel actually runs slower. Why? Not because we ran out of Tensor Core FLOPS, but because the longest bar in each K-step shifts from HBM reads to the decoding threads. When decoded weights feed wgmma directly from registers (RS mode; see Chapter 5, Section 3), the same thread group has to decode weights first and then issue 8 wider (n=128n = 128n=128) RS-mode MMA instructions one after another (Mode B of Figure 6-4). In each K-step, those 128 decoding threads take 1,393 cycles to finish — a figure measured directly by the profiler on the unpooler kernel (T=128T = 128T=128, 1 consumer warpgroup). Even when we switch to 2 alternating warpgroups, the average time per K-step drops only to 1,260 cycles, because nearly half the time stalls on barrier synchronization with almost zero overlap between the two warpgroups. Since 1,393>9361{,}393 > 9361,393>936, each K-step of the 12-bit kernel takes ~1.5× longer than the 16-bit kernel. We did not build a 12-bit RS version of qkv_gate for T=128T = 128T=128, but we ran paired measurements on unpooler and o in the same layer: the full unpooler kernel ran ~40% slower (see the chart below).

Once T≥233T \ge 233T≥233 and the operator crosses into Regime III, the 16-bit kernel's matrix multiplication time MMM already exceeds H16H_{16}H16​. At that point the kernel is compute-bound, so reading fewer bytes saves zero time and decoding only adds work. For larger TTT, the 12-bit format never wins again.

Our practical fix is dispatching the kernel by (operator, TTT): on the host side, we index a lookup table by operator and TTT to pick which kernel to launch, adding zero runtime branching. On qkv_gate, we launch the 12-bit weight kernel for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, and switch at T≥128T \ge 128T≥128 to the 16-bit weight SS mode kernel, which reads both operands straight from shared memory (Mode C of Figure 6-4) with 0 decoding instructions. The intermediate range 32<T<12832 < T < 12832<T<128 was not measured separately; the other dense projections follow the same rule, using 12-bit weights only at the TTT values where they win in measurement.

5How Does Our Code Become 128-Bit Machine Instructions, and Why Do We Need to Read SASS?

ptxas allocates physical registers and reorders instructions to emit 16 B SASS words; hardware executes strictly according to the stall counts and scoreboard wait masks encoded in SASS, which is why we must inspect SASS.

All the instruction counts we used in Sections 2 and 3 — 9, 31, and 8 instructions — are compiled SASS counts, not lines of C++ or PTX. As we saw in Section 2, CUDA C++ compiles to PTX first and then ptxas assembles that PTX into SASS; let's look at what ptxas actually does under the hood and what sits inside a single SASS instruction word.

At the PTX level, your code is still written against an unlimited supply of virtual registers (%r1, %r2, …), with no physical register numbers and no final instruction order. When ptxas takes over, it does three jobs (Figure 6-5):

  1. register allocation: it maps virtual registers onto physical registers, which sets how many registers each thread uses and, in turn, how many warps can stay resident on each SM at the same time (see Chapter 3, Section 1).
  2. instruction scheduling: it reorders instructions to hide latency.
  3. SASS code generation: it lowers each PTX instruction into 0, 1, or several SASS machine instructions.

Sometimes that lowering is one-to-one. Our 9 lines of inline PTX for C12 decoding in Section 2 compile through ptxas into 9 SASS instructions (main panel of Figure 6-5).

Now look at examples that are not a simple one-to-one copy (side panel of Figure 6-5). The first is cvt.f32.bf16, which converts BF16 to FP32. In SASS it turns into a PRMT or a shift instruction. This ties back to Section 1: BF16 is the top 16 bits of FP32, so converting the type is just moving bytes. The second is wgmma. Its SASS mnemonic is HGMMA, and wgmma.commit_group, which commits a group of matrix multiplications, has no SASS instruction of its own at all. It is only a group tag on the last HGMMA of the group, so that a later wait_group can wait by group (Section 6).

Every SASS instruction that comes out of ptxas is 128-bit (16 B) wide. Right next to the opcode and physical register numbers, those 16 bytes pack a control word (stall count and scoreboard wait mask) written by ptxas: it tells the hardware which earlier results must finish before this instruction is allowed to issue, and how many cycles at minimum must pass after it issues before the next instruction can go. (NVIDIA does not publicly document the bit encoding of this control word.)

Back in Chapter 4, Section 2, we saw that the compiler pre-encodes which scoreboard to wait on and before which instruction to wait — this 16 B control word is the exact place where that happens. At runtime, the warp scheduler (Chapter 4, Section 1) simply reads the scoreboard mask and stall count out of the control word to decide when the instruction can issue. If ptxas stamps a wait onto an instruction, the execution pipeline stalls right there (ptxas will even reshuffle the instruction order you wrote by hand if it thinks doing so will save registers; see Chapter 8, Section 8). So if you want to verify that your machine code actually overlaps the way you intended, you have to run disassembly (turning the compiled binary back into readable SASS text) and check the SASS yourself.

6Why Does One Extra Normal Instruction Inside an Async MMA Region Slow the Main Loop by More Than 2×?

When predicated normal instructions are mixed into an async wgmma region, ptxas inserts a drain barrier after every HGMMA, slowing the main loop by 2.35×.

Let's call the instruction bracket from Chapter 5, Section 5 the async wgmma region: you open with wgmma.fence, fire off several wgmma.mma_async instructions back to back, and close with commit_group and wait_group. Inside this async wgmma region, the accumulator registers belong to the Tensor Core, and multiple HGMMA instructions can overlap in flight.

What happens if you slip a normal instruction into the middle of that region? Look at a real bug we hit in Figure 6-6. In our T=128T = 128T=128 GEMM kernel for qkv_gate (one of the kernels on the multi-token GEMM evolution chain in Section 8; see Chapter 5, Section 6 for its tiling), each K-step issues 8 HGMMA.64x64x16 instructions. In an early version of the cross-slice readiness flag from Chapter 5, Section 7, we put the release-ordered global store st.release (Chapter 2, Section 6) right inside the async wgmma region. Only consumer thread 0 ran that store on one specific iteration (in the final version, we moved the release flag write outside the region to the producer warp).

When we compiled that early version, ptxas printed a serialization warning (warpgroup.mma serialized), claiming that a non-wgmma instruction defined an accumulator register inside the async region. Because this is a performance warning rather than a compile error, ptxas hides it by default — it shows up only when you turn on verbose ptxas output. Now, a global store does not write to registers at all, yet dropping that conditional-branch flag write into the async wgmma region tripped ptxas's conservative serialization rule and stopped the wgmma instructions from overlapping. (NVIDIA does not publicly document the internal heuristic ptxas uses for this check.)

Look at what changes in the SASS. In the normal case (Mode 1 of Figure 6-6), each K-step contains only 1 WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x1 (the wait instruction compiled from wait_group<1> in Chapter 5, Section 5). Here gsb0 is the scoreboard that tracks unfinished wgmma groups, and 0x1 allows the newest 1 wgmma group to keep running, so the pipeline does not drain. Once serialized (Mode 2 of Figure 6-6), every HGMMA is followed by 1 drain barrier WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0 (corresponding to wait_group<0>), which has to wait until no group is running and costs about 53 cycles each time (Chapter 5, Section 5). The chart below shows the main-loop runtime.

The takeaway is simple: put only the matrix multiplication instructions themselves inside the async wgmma region. Move any flag stores and branches outside the region and hand them to the producer warp (Chapter 3, Section 5) — that out-of-region pattern is what we showed in Chapter 5, Section 7, and it corresponds to the step in Section 8 of this chapter that switches to TMA tile reduction. Watch out for thread divergence too: any branch that diverges across threads inside the same warpgroup will also make ptxas serialize HGMMA instructions one by one (see Chapter 8, Section 9 for measured numbers on the expert kernel).

Our routine check comes down to two steps: turn on verbose ptxas output to see whether the serialization warning appears, and count how many DEPBAR instructions show up per K-step in the disassembled SASS.

7The Final gemv Step v9 → v10: Why Do 25% Fewer Bytes Yield Only a 7% Speedup?

Measured latency includes ~2.8 µs of launch and event-recording overhead, and reshaping the grid in v10 reduces in-flight reads and HBM throughput, leaving a net speedup of only ~7%.

In v9, peak in-flight reads per SM reach ~61.1 KiB, right up near the 64 KiB/SM knee point from Chapter 2, Section 3 (see Chapter 4, Section 5 and Chapter 5, Section 8). For v10 (Figure 6-2 in Section 2), we launch 576 CTAs with 4 warps per CTA, reading the three words la, lb, and cd for every 8 weights and unpacking them in 9 instructions; each thread keeps at most three 16 B loads in flight, which drops the per-SM peak to ~26.2 KiB. We took this grid and CTA shape from our final qkv_gate kernel.

Because v10 changes both the CTA shape and the weight format at the same time, we build a control variant v10c to separate the two effects: it uses v10's CTA shape while keeping BF16 weights. Even v10c actually changes two things at once: the CTA shape changes, and the in-flight reads get shallower (at most four 16 B loads in flight per thread, for a peak of 34.9 KiB/SM). Also note one output difference: from Primer 3 through Chapter 5, v0 → v9 wrote FP32 outputs, whereas all three versions in the first chart below write BF16 outputs, which we mark by adding an n suffix to their names.

Before looking at the measured bars, let's work out the best-case speedup we could hope for. If we subtract the ~2.8 µs of launch and event-recording overhead from v9n's latency in the chart below and scale all of the remaining time down to 75% in proportion to the bytes read, we save at most ~20%. And because part of that remaining time does not scale with bytes read (Chapter 4, Section 6), the real saving has to be smaller than 20%.

Our back-of-the-envelope ceiling says ~20%, yet the measured speedup is only ~7% (see the chart above). Where did the rest of the speedup go? Look at the HBM throughput reported by the profiler in the chart below: both v10cn and v10n drop to the same lower bandwidth plateau, well below v9n. When you compare v10n against v10cn at that same bandwidth, v10n reads ~25% fewer bytes and its kernel body runs ~25% faster (see the chart note below), so it cleanly beats the control variant; when you compare v10n against v9n, however, losing HBM throughput from the shallower in-flight reads eats back most of the byte-saving win.

There is also an instruction-count cost: unpacking C12 weights makes v10n execute ~40% more instructions than v9n, while both kernels sit at a measured occupancy of ~17.45 resident warps per SM (~one quarter of the 64-warp hardware limit, capped by grid size). In short, three candidate factors eat into the 25% byte reduction: shallower in-flight reads (a peak of 26.2 KiB/SM is less than half of the 64 KiB/SM knee point; see Chapter 2, Section 3), a higher dynamic instruction count, and the 4-warp CTA shape. How much each of these three factors contributes, and what the time-averaged bytes in flight look like, were not measured separately.

One more detail stands out in the control variant v10cn: of the ~4.5 µs by which v10cn trails v9n, roughly half (~2 µs) happens outside the kernel body. Its CUDA event time exceeds its kernel-body time by ~4.9 µs, whereas v9n exceeds its kernel body by only ~2.6 µs (what causes that extra ~2 µs was not measured). If we look strictly at the kernel body, switching to the new CTA shape costs ~2.2 µs, and switching to 12-bit weights wins back ~3.5 µs, leaving a net kernel-body saving of ~1.3 µs. (Applying 12-bit weights directly to v9's single-warp CTA shape was not measured.)

Stepping back to look at the entire gemv progression: from v0 → v9 (with FP32 output), we sped the kernel up by ~45× across the evolution charts in Primer 3 through Chapter 5; v10n switches to BF16 output and adds the final step against v9n, which also writes BF16 output.

8Multi-Token GEMM g0 → g5 (T = 8..256): How Do the Mechanisms from Five of Levels 1–6 Stack Up Step by Step?

From g0 to g5, mechanisms from Levels 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 combine to beat cuBLAS across all four TTT values: ~1.41× faster at T=8T = 8T=8 and ~1.07× faster at T=256T = 256T=256.

We measured this evolution chain only on qkv_gate across the four settings with T≥8T \ge 8T≥8 (see Chapter 5, Section 2 for the shapes). Every number in the first four charts below is the average of 4 medians from full CUDA Graph replays, and each includes about 4.964.964.96 µs of empty-graph replay overhead. Note that this overhead is not the same quantity as the ~2.82.82.8 µs launch and event-recording overhead for gemv in Chapter 4, Section 6. Because this series recorded only the 4-run average without run-by-run pairing, we apply only the second criterion from Chapter 4, Section 6. Several steps along the chain modify only one TTT while leaving the code for the other three TTT values unchanged, so two versions with unchanged code act as two measurements of the same version. Across those unchanged pairs, the largest gap is 0.340.340.34 µs (at T=256T = 256T=256). Taking that gap as our spread, we set the noise band for this section at 0.350.350.35 µs and mark any change within the band as noise.

The step names below keep our original experiment version IDs rather than mapping one-to-one to hardware levels. You will notice g3 is missing — that is because the Level 4 mechanisms from Chapter 4 are already superseded here by TMA and Tensor Core instructions rather than forming a separate step:

  1. g0: cuBLAS (see Chapter 4, Section 6). At T=8/32/128T = 8 / 32 / 128T=8/32/128, cuBLAS uses Split-K (see Chapter 2, Section 5) and launches two back-to-back kernels — a main kernel that writes partial sums, followed by a second reduction kernel that adds them up — while at T=256T = 256T=256, cuBLAS runs a single kernel.
  2. g1a (fusing two kernels into one): launches only a single kernel where the last arriving CTA of each output tile sums that tile's partial sums in its epilogue (Chapter 1, Section 3 and Chapter 2, Section 6):
    • T=8/32T = 8 / 32T=8/32: uses wgmma with swap-AB (putting WWW on the 64-row operand-A side; see Chapter 5, Section 4) and launches 288 CTAs. This step both saves one launch and changes the MMA shape, so it runs faster; how much each change contributed was not measured.
    • T=128/256T = 128 / 256T=128/256: launches only 72 CTAs (36 output tiles × Split-K 2), which runs 0.25 µs slower than g0 at T=128T = 128T=128 (within the noise band) and ~46% slower at T=256T = 256T=256. Two reasons explain the slowdown: first, 72 CTAs leave 60 SMs sitting idle (Chapter 2, Section 1); second, the single last-arriving CTA of each of the 36 output tiles has to read back and sum the FP32 partial sums of both split-K slices on its own — reading back 64 KiB per output tile at T=128T = 128T=128 and 128 KiB per output tile at T=256T = 256T=256 (Chapter 2, Section 7).
  3. g1 (Chapter 2 + Chapter 3): at T=128/256T = 128 / 256T=128/256, raises Split-K to 3 and expands the grid to 108 CTAs, cutting idle SMs from 60 down to 24. We also switch the epilogue to parallel slice reduction (Chapter 2, Section 7) so each CTA claims 1/31/31/3 of the tile rows to sum in parallel, and upgrade data movement to a dedicated TMA producer warp, an mbarrier ring buffer (8 buffer slots at T=128T = 128T=128 and 5 buffer slots at T=256T = 256T=256; see Chapter 3, Sections 4–5), and 128 B XOR swizzle (Chapter 3, Section 7). All three changes went in together in the same version and were not measured separately. With g1, T=128T = 128T=128 beats cuBLAS for the first time, while T=256T = 256T=256 still trails cuBLAS (the cause was not measured). Here is a counterexample: Why not have each split-K slice atomically add its partial sum directly into the BF16 output? If you write that in this kernel, the compiler lowers scalar BF16 atomic adds into the compare-and-swap retry loop from Chapter 2, Section 7: because two adjacent BF16 columns share one 32-bit word, atomic adds to neighboring columns fight over the same 32-bit word, and the more threads contend, the more retries pile up. On the 12-bit weight qkv_gate kernel (T=16/32T = 16 / 32T=16/32), a scalar BF16 atomic-add epilogue makes the entire kernel about 2–3× slower than a tile-reduction epilogue (see the final chart in this section). To avoid that contention trap, split-K reduction has to use either parallel slice reduction, paired BF16x2 atomic adds, or TMA tile reduction (see Chapter 5, Section 7).
  4. g2 (Chapter 3, Section 6, setmaxnreg): a controlled experiment that drops the register cap of the producer warpgroup to 24 registers per thread (setmaxnreg applies at warpgroup granularity). That change yielded no speedup (landing inside the noise band), so we did not adopt it; we collected no profiler counters on this version, and why it yielded no gain was not measured.
  5. g4a (waves from Chapter 2, Section 1 + ring buffer from Chapter 3, Section 4): modifies only T=32T = 32T=32 — replacing the 3-slot cp.async ring buffer (Chapter 3, Section 3) with 1 TMA producer warp plus a 9-slot ring buffer, dialing Split-K down from 8 to 3, and shrinking the grid from 288 CTAs (2.2 waves) to 108 CTAs. Because this kernel's SMEM ring buffer fits 1 CTA per SM, all 108 CTAs now run inside a single wave. (Swap-AB was already in place back in g1a rather than added in this step.)
  6. g4b (Chapter 5, Section 7 + Section 6 of this chapter): replaces the reduction at T=128/256T = 128 / 256T=128/256 with TMA tile reduction (Chapter 5, Section 7), accumulating in place in L2. Following the rule from Section 6, we hand the readiness flag writes to the producer warp outside the async wgmma region. That shaves ~1.3 µs off T=128T = 128T=128 and ~1.5 µs off T=256T = 256T=256 (see the charts below). Because we are comparing against g4a's parallel slice reduction here rather than the BF16x2 atomic add from Chapter 5, Section 7, the speedup numbers differ from Chapter 5. Against the exact FP64 product, the relative L2 error of the full output creeps up from 1.6e-3 to 2.7e-3 — still well under the 1e-2 limit of our second correctness check in Section 1. That error bump matches what we expect from rounding each split-K slice to BF16 before accumulation (Chapter 5, Section 7), though we did not verify that pre-accumulation rounding is the sole cause.
  7. g4 (Chapter 5, Section 6): at T=256T = 256T=256, widens the tile column width BN from 64 to 128 (with Split-K = 7, a 4-slot ring buffer, and 126 CTAs), doubling how much Tensor Core work each buffer slot feeds (Chapter 5, Section 6 measured this same step and saw the whole kernel save about 1.35 µs, slightly less than here; Chapter 5 used paired runs and took the median of 60 replays, whereas here we average 4 medians without run-by-run pairing, so the two savings need not be the same). With g4, all four TTT values now beat cuBLAS. The output relative L2 error rises to 3.65e-3 (for the same reason as g4b; it was not determined separately).
  8. g5 (this chapter): brings in three changes together:
    • kernel rewrite: g1a through g4 were written in a high-level Python DSL whose compiler emitted the descriptors and barrier code; g5 rewrites the kernels straight in CUDA C++ with inline PTX (Section 5), building the matrix descriptors, TMA tensor descriptors, and barrier phases explicitly in source code.
    • switching to 12-bit weights (C12) for T=8/32T = 8 / 32T=8/32: switches to the 12-bit weight kernel (with one offline weight permutation pass before execution), reading 25% fewer bytes and sharing the unpacked weights on chip across all 8 or 32 tokens. At T=8T = 8T=8, if we run the same upper-bound estimate from Section 7 on g4 → g5 (subtracting the 4.96 µs empty-graph replay overhead and scaling the rest of the time to 75% in proportion to bytes read), it predicts a ~2.7 µs saving, and we measure 2.95 µs (see the chart below). The ~0.2 µs gap between those two numbers sits inside our 0.35 µs noise band, so it does not count as an extra saving; on top of that, this step also rewrote the kernel in CUDA C++ (see the bullet above), and the two changes were not measured separately. Here at T=8T = 8T=8, the 16-bit baseline g4 is still g1a's 3-slot cp.async ring (288 CTAs) rather than the 16-bit loop of Section 4, so the ~8% estimate from Section 4 does not carry over.
    • keeping 16-bit weights (BF16) for T=128/256T = 128 / 256T=128/256: following the crossover boundary from Section 4, T=128T = 128T=128 stays on 16-bit weights and matches g4's latency; T=256T = 256T=256 also stays on 16-bit weights while switching to a BM = 128, BN = 192, 5-slot ring-buffer tiling with Split-K = 5 and 120 CTAs total. Those 120 CTAs fit into a single wave across the 132 SMs (leaving 12 SMs idle) and shave off a bit more time. The tiling change and the CUDA C++ kernel rewrite were not measured separately.

Takeaway: Compressing weights by a few bits saves HBM bytes at the cost of integer instructions in registers; the trade pays off only when decoding outruns HBM delivery without stalling the Tensor Core. How those instructions are actually scheduled in the end can only be seen by reading the SASS.

Next chapter's question: Part I dissected a single matrix multiplication all the way from the full GPU down to individual bits. In the next chapter, we zoom back out to a single layer of the model: how much historical KV cache does Stage 2 attention have to read at each step, and which of our six hardware levels bottlenecks it first?

Position in the 8-stage single-layer pipeline: Stage 1 qkv_gate → [Stage 2: Paged Attention] → Stage 3 o and gated residual → Stage 4 router ∥ Stage 5 pooler → Stage 6 routed experts → Stage 7 unpooler → Stage 8 second gated residual

In Part I, we followed a single operator — gemv (qkv_gate in Stage 1 at T=1T = 1T=1) — down through all 6 hardware levels, and at the end of Chapter 6 we scaled that same projection up to T=256T = 256T=256 with multi-token GEMM (g0 → g5). Now Part II puts those same hardware mechanisms to work across the rest of the layer. Stage 1 hands off the qkv tensor (which packs query, key, value, and gate together) as the input to Stage 2. Where are the bottlenecks of Stage 2 paged attention under single-token decode, 8-token verification, and long-sequence prefill, and how does the kernel remove the slowest bottleneck step by step?

1What Does Stage 2 Compute, and What Quantity Governs Its Bottleneck?

Stage 2 turns qkv into the gated attention output; its bottleneck is governed by how many query rows share each key-value row.

Before we trace the math, let's get the basic numbers on the board. BBB is the number of concurrent requests, LLL is the number of new tokens per request in this forward pass, and T=B×LT = B \times LT=B×L is the total number of tokens in this forward pass (see Primer 2, Section 5). In token-by-token decode, L=1L = 1L=1; in verify, L=8L = 8L=8, where we stack 1 committed token and 7 draft tokens from the drafting mechanism into 8 rows and run them together (see Primer 1, Section 7); in prefill, LLL runs into the thousands. Each GPU holds 16 query heads and 2 KV heads (denoted g=0,1g = 0, 1g=0,1), with 64 dimensions per head. Because every 8 query heads share 1 KV head (GQA; see Primer 2, Section 1), each key-value row of a given KV head is shared across nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L query rows.

Stage 2 takes qkv :  [T,  2304]  BF16\shape{\mathrm{qkv}}{T,\;2304}{BF16}qkv:[T,2304]BF16 as input and slices it by column into q :  [T,  16,  64]  BF16\shape{q}{T,\;16,\;64}{BF16}q:[T,16,64]BF16, k :  [T,  2,  64]  BF16\shape{k}{T,\;2,\;64}{BF16}k:[T,2,64]BF16, v :  [T,  2,  64]  BF16\shape{v}{T,\;2,\;64}{BF16}v:[T,2,64]BF16, and gate :  [T,  16,  64]  BF16\shape{\mathrm{gate}}{T,\;16,\;64}{BF16}gate:[T,16,64]BF16, with column widths 1024+128+128+1024=23041024 + 128 + 128 + 1024 = 23041024+128+128+1024=2304.

Request lengths keep changing, and allocating contiguous device memory leaves fragments and forces data copies. So we store each request's historical keys and values in a paged KV cache, where each page can live anywhere in device memory. A page table page_table :  [B,  max_pages]  int32\shape{\mathrm{page\_table}}{B,\;max\_pages}{int32}page_table:[B,max_pages]int32 maps each request to its pages: each row corresponds to one request, and max_pages is the number of columns in the page table (no less than the page count of the longest request in the batch). Row b, column i records which physical page slot holds request b's page i; a new token can be appended to any free slot. Our workload sets each page to 1 token (page_size = 1), so reading every historical token takes a page-table lookup first. Section 6 deals with that wait.

In memory, the cache tensors have shape K_cache, V_cache :  [pages,  1,  2,  64]  FP8 E4M3\shape{K\_cache,\ V\_cache}{pages,\;1,\;2,\;64}{FP8\ E4M3}K_cache, V_cache:[pages,1,2,64]FP8 E4M3 (page slots, tokens per page, KV heads, head dimension), paired with sequence lengths seq_lens :  [B]  int32\shape{\mathrm{seq\_lens}}{B}{int32}seq_lens:[B]int32. Every historical token takes 2×2×64×1 B=256 B2 \times 2 \times 64 \times 1\ \mathrm{B} = 256\ \mathrm{B}2×2×64×1 B=256 B per layer on each GPU. A single token's K row packs 64 B from each of the two KV heads into 128 B total (and the same goes for the V row); a kernel that computes only one KV head reads only 64 B of that row, which we call a half-row (64 elements) below. Turning qkv into o_attn takes five steps:

  1. per-head RMSNorm (unweighted, computed in FP32; see Primer 1, Section 1 for the formula): q^=rmsnorm(q), k^=rmsnorm(k)\hat q = \mathrm{rmsnorm}(q),\ \hat k = \mathrm{rmsnorm}(k)q^​=rmsnorm(q), k^=rmsnorm(k); v is not normalized.
  2. RoPE (rotary position embedding): applied only in the 46 sliding-window layers and skipped in the 16 full-attention layers (for RoPE, see Primer 2, Section 2): rotate adjacent dimensions (2i,2i+1)(2i, 2i+1)(2i,2i+1) in FP32 by an angle determined by the token position.
  3. FP8 cast and KV cache write: cast q to E4M3; cast new k and v to E4M3 with saturation, clamped within the E4M3 maximum ±448\pm 448±448 (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit layout), and write them into the cache by page slot index.
  4. GQA attention: for a token at position ppp, a full-attention layer attends to all keys in 0..p0..p0..p, whereas a sliding-window layer attends only to the most recent 2,048 keys (max⁡(0,p−2047)..p\max(0, p-2047)..pmax(0,p−2047)..p); the LLL new tokens of the same request use a lower-triangular causal mask among themselves: oraw=softmax ⁣(5.4738 qfp8K⊤)Vo_{raw} = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{5.473}{8}\, q_{fp8} K^{\top}\right) Voraw​=softmax(85.473​qfp8​K⊤)V Here the model also multiplies the dot product by 5.4735.4735.473 (an attention scaling factor fixed in the model configuration); combined with 1/64=1/81/\sqrt{64} = 1/81/64​=1/8, this folds into a single multiplier 0.6840.6840.684 applied to the dot product rather than to q.
  5. gated attention output: oattn=rmsnorm(oraw)⊙σ(gate)o_{attn} = \mathrm{rmsnorm}(o_{raw}) \odot \sigma(gate)oattn​=rmsnorm(oraw​)⊙σ(gate) producing o_attn :  [T,  1024]  BF16\shape{\mathrm{o\_attn}}{T,\;1024}{BF16}o_attn:[T,1024]BF16 for Stage 3.

Read one KV head of one historical token (K 64 B + V 64 B = 128 B), and nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L query rows use it; each query row does one 64-dimensional dot product and one 64-dimensional weighted sum, for 2×64+2×64=2562\times64 + 2\times64 = 2562×64+2×64=256 FLOPs in total. Divide that by the 128 B read, and you get the operations per byte read (arithmetic intensity; see Primer 2, Section 4): arithmetic intensity≈256nq128=2nq=16L FLOP/B\text{arithmetic intensity} \approx \frac{256 n_q}{128} = 2 n_q = 16L\ \mathrm{FLOP/B}arithmetic intensity≈128256nq​​=2nq​=16L FLOP/B In decode, L=1L = 1L=1 (nq=8n_q = 8nq​=8), so the arithmetic intensity is 16 FLOP/B. That 16 already sits above the ~14 FLOP/B ridge point of CUDA Cores (Chapter 5, Section 2), so CUDA Cores cannot keep up. On the Tensor Core, FP8 runs at twice the throughput of BF16 (Chapter 5, Section 3), which puts the ridge point at about 2×206=4122 \times 206 = 4122×206=412 FLOP/B (for 206, see Primer 2, Section 4), so the Tensor Core is still waiting on data. When we run decode on the Tensor Core, its lower bound is therefore the time to read KV. Move to 8-token verify (L=8L = 8L=8, nq=64n_q = 64nq​=64), and the arithmetic intensity rises to about 128 FLOP/B: CUDA Cores still cannot keep up, and on the Tensor Core the kernel remains bandwidth-bound. Move further to long-sequence prefill (LLL in the thousands), and the intensity shoots far past the ridge point into the compute-bound regime. As LLL grows, the bottleneck shifts the same way qkv_gate did with TTT in Chapter 5, except the horizontal axis here is nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L rather than TTT: the same T=32T = 32T=32 can be 32 decode requests (nq=8n_q = 8nq​=8) or 4 verify requests (nq=64n_q = 64nq​=64).

Two lower bounds anchor the two ends of this spectrum. Take decode first: for 1 request in a full-attention layer with 80,000 historical tokens, reading 20.5 MB of keys and values at 4.8 TB/s gives a bandwidth lower bound of about 4.3 µs. Decode has only 8 query rows, so the Tensor Core spends most of its time waiting on three things: at CTA entry, reading seq_lens first and then the page table, after which each page waits only for the page-table load to return (Section 6); fixed prologue and epilogue work per CTA (Section 4); and merging after splitting across segments (Section 3). Even after we tune the split count, the profiler clocks the attention kernel at about 13.8 µs on this shape, more than 3× the bandwidth lower bound: decode is latency-bound and cannot reach the pure bandwidth lower bound.

Now look at the other end, prefill: on a full-attention layer that appends 16,384 new tokens after 65,536 cached tokens, under the causal mask each new token attends to an average of nˉkey≈65,536+16,384/2=73,728\bar n_{key} \approx 65{,}536 + 16{,}384/2 = 73{,}728nˉkey​≈65,536+16,384/2=73,728 keys. Each query-key pair performs 4×644\times644×64 FLOPs, which adds up to 16 heads×16,384×nˉkey×64×4 FLOP≈4,948 GFLOP16\ \text{heads} \times 16{,}384 \times \bar n_{key} \times 64 \times 4\ \text{FLOP} \approx 4{,}948\ \text{GFLOP}16 heads×16,384×nˉkey​×64×4 FLOP≈4,948 GFLOP. In the final version of this chapter, both QK⊤Q K^{\top}QK⊤ and PVP VPV run in FP8; the FP8 peak is twice the BF16 peak of 989 TFLOP/s, or about 1,979 TFLOP/s (see Chapter 5, Section 3), which puts the compute lower bound at about 2.50 ms. Reading the KV cache for those 65,536 tokens once from HBM takes only about 3.5 µs, but every query tile has to re-read the keys it attends to from L2; we will calculate that L2 traffic in Section 4 once we have the tile count.

We evaluate every version in this chapter across 12 shapes: decode and verify with 1, 16, and 32 requests each (single-request history is 80,000 tokens, while 16- and 32-request histories are distributed within 80,000±7.5%80{,}000 \pm 7.5\%80,000±7.5%), with each workload split between sliding-window layers and full-attention layers. Shape labels below follow the pattern "decode / verify + request count + full-attention / sliding-window"; for example, "verify 32-request full attention" means 32 requests with 8 new tokens each (T=256T = 256T=256) on the 16 full-attention layers. The latency of each workload equals 46×46 \times46× sliding-window layer latency +16×+ 16 \times+16× full-attention layer latency, giving the 62-layer attention total for one step; we then take the geometric mean (the 6th root of the product of the 6 numbers) across the 6 workloads as the representative latency for the entire suite.

Every single-shape latency in this chapter comes from a paired ABBA benchmarking comparison of the attention operator in isolation: within the same process, we capture each shape as a CUDA Graph and replay it in full, flushing L2 before each replay. The old and new versions alternate in symmetric A, B, B, A order for multiple rounds (round count not recorded), and we take the median of each before subtracting; alternating within the same process shares the exact same inputs and cancels slow thermal and clock-frequency drift during the run. The noise-band rules follow Chapter 4, Section 6. Running two identical copies of the code as A and B through the same paired harness produces single-shape variation within about 0.4 µs; any change with a smaller delta is recorded as "within the noise band."

In production, we run this model on the open-source inference framework SGLang, and our baseline for this chapter is SGLang's stock attention implementation, which splits the five steps above into 5 separate kernels launched sequentially. The evolution versions in this chapter launch them as a PDL chain instead, where each kernel reads the output of the preceding kernel only after the wait call (see Chapter 1, Section 4).

2a0 (Part 1): Why Stack the 8 Query Heads of the Same KV Head as Matrix Rows?

Each CTA handles one KV head and stacks all query rows sharing that head into operand A, so each key-value tile is loaded into the SM once to multiply against all query rows.

Suppose you launch one CTA for each query head: then 8 separate CTAs all have to read the exact same KV row. Because many of those 8 reads hit the 60 MiB L2 cache (see Chapter 2, Section 2), the bytes read from HBM are not necessarily 8× higher — what you definitely cut is the number of transfers into the SM and the number of load instructions, dropping from 8 copies down to 1.

So for a given KV head ggg, we stack all nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L query rows that share it into Qg :  [8L,  64]  FP8\shape{Q_g}{8L,\;64}{FP8}Qg​:[8L,64]FP8; in verify, each query head has 8 new tokens, giving 64 rows in total. Each time a 64-token KV tile is loaded (K takes 4 KiB, and K plus V takes 8 KiB in total), we multiply QgQ_gQg​ by the transpose of Ktile :  [64,  64]  FP8\shape{K_{tile}}{64,\;64}{FP8}Ktile​:[64,64]FP8 to compute the entire score tile S :  [8L,  64]  FP32\shape{S}{8L,\;64}{FP32}S:[8L,64]FP32 in one pass.

That row count nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L also decides which Tensor Core instruction family we use (see Chapter 5, Section 3 for the two instruction families). In token-by-token decode (L=1L = 1L=1), there are only 8 rows; placing them into the 16 rows of mma.sync leaves half the rows as padding. Even so, decode runs on the Tensor Core (Section 1) while its bottleneck is reading the KV cache (Section 1: latency-bound), so the Tensor Core has plenty of idle cycles and those 8 wasted rows stay off the critical path. In verify, 64 rows fill m=64m = 64m=64 of wgmma to the brim; early versions first step through 16-row groups with mma.sync, and Section 5 (a2) switches over to wgmma.

While we are at it, we also run the first matrix multiplication Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ directly in FP8: K in the cache is already FP8 E4M3 (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit layout), so once q is cast to E4M3 as well, the multiplication can consume the bytes of K directly and skip unpacking K to BF16 first. The trade-off is that casting q to FP8 introduces rounding error (accounted for in Section 8); how many HBM bytes this saves, and on which shapes it is a net loss, were not measured separately.

3a0 (Part 2): Before All Keys and Values Are Read, How Is the Softmax Denominator Computed on the Fly, and How Are Split Segments Merged Exactly?

Online softmax tracks only the running maximum, denominator, and unnormalized output, rescaling prior values by the exponential difference as each new key tile arrives and merging split-KV segments via log-sum-exp weights.

First, let's switch the exponential base to 2: the hardware transcendental instruction ex2 computes 2x2^x2x directly on the SFU (the machine instruction is MUFU.EX2; see Chapter 5, Section 1 for the SFU pipeline). If we multiply the dot product by 0.684×log⁡2e0.684 \times \log_2 e0.684×log2​e (log⁡2e≈1.4427\log_2 e \approx 1.4427log2​e≈1.4427) before taking 2x2^x2x, we get the exact same math as base eee. Every score sss below already bakes in this factor.

The naive way to compute softmax makes two passes over memory: pass one finds the full-row maximum m=max⁡kskm = \max_k s_km=maxk​sk​ and the denominator l=∑k2sk−ml = \sum_k 2^{s_k-m}l=∑k​2sk​−m (subtracting mmm prevents exponent overflow), and pass two computes ∑k2sk−mvk/l\sum_k 2^{s_k-m} v_k / l∑k​2sk​−mvk​/l. Doing that forces us to read the keys and values twice. The single-pass method (online softmax) fuses both passes into one sweep: whenever a new key tile arrives, we find the tile maximum mtilem_{tile}mtile​ and update mnew=max⁡(mold,mtile)m_{new} = \max(m_{old}, m_{tile})mnew​=max(mold​,mtile​). Because our running lll and OOO were scaled against moldm_{old}mold​, multiplying both by the rescaling factor α=2mold−mnew\alpha = 2^{m_{old}-m_{new}}α=2mold​−mnew​ shifts them onto mnewm_{new}mnew​: l←α l+∑k∈tile2sk−mnew,O←α O+∑k∈tile2sk−mnew vkl \leftarrow \alpha\, l + \sum_{k\in tile} 2^{s_k-m_{new}},\qquad O \leftarrow \alpha\, O + \sum_{k\in tile} 2^{s_k-m_{new}}\, v_kl←αl+k∈tile∑​2sk​−mnew​,O←αO+k∈tile∑​2sk​−mnew​vk​ Once all tiles have streamed through, a final division gives o=O/lo = O / lo=O/l. Packing the 2sk−mnew2^{s_k-m_{new}}2sk​−mnew​ values within a tile into a matrix gives the attention score weight matrix P, which turns the two recurrences into l←αl+P1l \leftarrow \alpha l + P\mathbf{1}l←αl+P1 and O←αO+PVO \leftarrow \alpha O + P VO←αO+PV. Both "P · V" and "BF16 P" below refer to this matrix.

Let's trace a small example you can check by hand (and play tile by tile in Figure 7-3): take one query row, 3 key tiles with 2 keys per tile, and base-2 pre-scaled scores Tile 1 =[1,3]= [1, 3]=[1,3], Tile 2 =[2,5]= [2, 5]=[2,5], Tile 3 =[0,4]= [0, 4]=[0,4], where each key has a 1-dimensional value v: Tile 1 =[4,2]= [4, 2]=[4,2], Tile 2 =[0,8]= [0, 8]=[0,8], Tile 3 =[6,2]= [6, 2]=[6,2].

After Tile 1 arrives: m=3m = 3m=3, l=2−2+20=1.25l = 2^{-2} + 2^{0} = 1.25l=2−2+20=1.25, O=2−2⋅4+1⋅2=3O = 2^{-2}\cdot 4 + 1\cdot 2 = 3O=2−2⋅4+1⋅2=3.

With the intra-tile recurrence in place, we can add Split-KV (partitioning along the key dimension): slice the visible keys of a request into SSS segments assigned to SSS CTAs. Each segment writes its partial results into a global-memory region called the workspace buffer, which typically stays hot in L2 right after being written (for the general pattern of merging partial sums across CTAs, see Chapter 2, Sections 6–7). Segment iii runs the recurrence above on its own slice and outputs oi=Oi/lio_i = O_i / l_ioi​=Oi​/li​ along with the log-sum-exp (lse) lsei=mi+log⁡2li\mathrm{lse}_i = m_i + \log_2 l_ilsei​=mi​+log2​li​. Because 2lsei=2mili2^{\mathrm{lse}_i} = 2^{m_i} l_i2lsei​=2mi​li​ is segment iii's exact unshifted denominator relative to 0, the total log-denominator across all keys is lse=log⁡2∑i2lsei\mathrm{lse} = \log_2 \sum_i 2^{\mathrm{lse}_i}lse=log2​∑i​2lsei​, and the merge step accumulates o=∑i2lsei−lse  oio = \sum_i 2^{\mathrm{lse}_i-\mathrm{lse}}\; o_io=i∑​2lsei​−lseoi​ Multiplying by 2lsei−lse2^{\mathrm{lse}_i-\mathrm{lse}}2lsei​−lse swaps out segment iii's own denominator and replaces it with the denominator across all keys. Now split the example above into two segments (Figure 7-3 Mode 2). Segment A holds Tiles 1–2: mA=5m_A = 5mA​=5, lA=1.4375l_A = 1.4375lA​=1.4375, 2lseA=32×1.4375=462^{\mathrm{lse}_A} = 32 \times 1.4375 = 462lseA​=32×1.4375=46, oA=8.75/1.4375≈6.087o_A = 8.75/1.4375 \approx 6.087oA​=8.75/1.4375≈6.087.
