The total denominator is 46+17=63=25×1.9687546 + 17 = 63 = 2^5 \times 1.9687546+17=63=25×1.96875, the merge weights are 46/6346/6346/63 and 17/6317/6317/63, and the weighted sum is 4663oA+1763oB=280+3863≈5.048\tfrac{46}{63} o_A + \tfrac{17}{63} o_B = \tfrac{280 + 38}{63} \approx 5.0486346​oA​+6317​oB​=63280+38​≈5.048, which is mathematically identical to no splitting; when the floating-point summation order differs, the last bit of the result may differ, and this only becomes important in Section 12.

Together, online softmax and Split-KV let us read the keys and values only once while spreading work across multiple CTAs. In exchange, we pay two costs: each tile adds one maximum reduction, one ex2, and an elementwise multiplication on OOO (Section 8 removes most of this); and splitting across segments writes an extra (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i)(oi​,lsei​) per segment and runs an extra merge step. Meanwhile, Steps 1–3 of Section 1 (per-head RMSNorm, RoPE, and FP8 cast plus KV cache write) run in a separate kernel launched before the main kernel, called the prologue kernel. Put all of these together and we get our starting point a0: separate prologue kernel + GQA query-row stacking + FP8 Q⋅K⊤Q\cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ + fixed-split Split-KV + separate merge kernel, where the split count in a0 is fixed — for example, decode 1-request full attention is fixed at 128 segments.

4a0 → a1: Into How Many Segments Should One Request's Keys Be Split, and How Should They Be Balanced?

Split more finely at low concurrency to keep enough reads in flight, and less finely at high concurrency to avoid multi-wave CTA launch/exit overhead, while balancing work by actual sequence lengths.

Every split segment launches one CTA. Fitting the profiler readings on the decode 16- and 32-request shapes (fitting method not recorded) shows that each CTA spends about 2.04 µs per 64-key tile, plus about 6.6 µs of entry/exit overhead to read the page-table start offset, load Q, and write back (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i)(oi​,lsei​) (distinct from the kernel launch gap in Chapter 1). Because most of this 6.6 µs is spent waiting on memory rather than saturating issue slots, CTAs within the same wave (see Chapter 2, Section 1) wait in parallel across the chip, and critical-path launch/exit overhead is bounded by approximately "waves × 6.6 µs" rather than "CTAs × 6.6 µs". On top of that, the merge step reads back one partial result per segment, which we account for separately.

So whether to raise or lower the split count SSS comes down to whether all CTAs already fit inside 1 wave. When they fit, splitting further adds no wave entry/exit overhead; once they spill past 1 wave, each additional wave pays the fixed per-CTA entry/exit overhead (about 6.6 µs) one more time. At this stage, the single-KV-head split kernel used for decode and verify places 8 CTAs per SM, giving a 1-wave capacity of 132×8=1,056132 \times 8 = 1{,}056132×8=1,056 CTAs (see Chapter 3, Section 1 for how residency is calculated). For each 64-key tile it reads, each CTA randomly gathers 8 KiB of KV via the page table (referred to simply as gather below). This single-KV-head kernel gathers only a 64 B half-row at a time; in the isolated gather-only microbenchmark in Section 5 below, such 64 B half-row gather reaches 2.6–3.1 TB/s. Below 1 full wave, there are not enough bytes in flight to saturate HBM (see Chapter 2, Section 3): at low concurrency (decode 1-request full attention, with only 2 KV heads), 128 segments launch 256 CTAs — just 0.24 waves — and measured gather bandwidth crawls at about 1.3 TB/s; splitting into 256 segments (512 CTAs, 0.48 waves) keeps all CTAs within 1 wave while doubling in-flight reads, which makes execution faster.

At high concurrency, the math flips and we must split into fewer segments instead. Take decode 16-request full attention: keeping 128 segments launches 4,096 CTAs, or 3.88 waves; consolidating to 32 segments (1,024 CTAs, 0.97 waves) pulls the grid inside 1 wave, saving about 3 waves of entry/exit overhead and cutting the partial results read by the merge step to 1/4. Multiplying 3 waves × 6.6 µs predicts a maximum saving of about 20 µs, and the measured saving is about 12 µs; the source of the difference was not measured separately. Decode 32-request full attention and verify 16- and 32-request full attention likewise consolidate their segment counts, running faster by executing fewer waves or reading half as many partial results in the merge step (the time saved on each shape is shown in the chart below).

Conversely, cutting verify 32-request full attention further from 16 segments (0.97 waves) down to 8 segments (512 CTAs, 0.48 waves) makes it much slower (see the note in the chart below). Our explanation (unverified): once all CTAs already fit within 1 wave, cutting further saves zero waves and only drops co-resident CTAs per SM from about 8 to about 4 — halving in-flight reads — while doubling the number of tiles each CTA processes serially. Consolidating verify 16-request full attention from 32 segments to 16 segments also drops to 0.48 waves yet saves time overall, with most of the saving in the merge step (see the note in the chart below); why the main kernel did not slow down was not determined.

Verify 1-request sliding window has a neat boundary quirk of its own: the latest of the 8 new tokens attends to 7 more keys than the earliest, so at most 2,048+7=2,0552{,}048 + 7 = 2{,}0552,048+7=2,055 keys are visible, requiring ⌈2,055/64⌉=33\lceil 2{,}055 / 64 \rceil = 33⌈2,055/64⌉=33 tiles of 64 keys — 1 more than 32. Originally, each KV head was split into 32 segments, forcing 1 CTA to process 2 tiles serially while all CTAs maintained a 2-slot ring buffer (see Chapter 3, Section 4). We switch to launching 33 single-tile CTAs per KV head. Those 66 CTAs are still far below 1 wave, all 33 tiles are in flight simultaneously, and each CTA loads only 1 tile, eliminating both the serial wait for a second tile and the ring buffer. The cost is that the merge step now reads 33 (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i)(oi​,lsei​) pairs (see the chart below).

Requests in the same batch often have different lengths: in this workload suite, historical lengths lie within ±7.5%\pm 7.5\%±7.5% of the mean, so the longest request is about 16% longer than the shortest (1.075/0.925≈1.161.075 / 0.925 \approx 1.161.075/0.925≈1.16). When segments are divided equally per request, CTAs for the longest request run about 16% longer than those for the shortest, holding up the last SMs at the tail. To fix this, we concatenate the keys of all requests into a single logical strip and partition it evenly across all CTAs by actual key count; the trade-off is that one segment may span two requests, requiring extra work in the merge step (measured results on verify appear in Section 7).

Prefill also needs to balance its tail, using a different kernel: each CTA has 1 producer warpgroup and 3 consumer warpgroups (Chapter 3, Sections 4 and 6). Each consumer warpgroup computes 64 query rows, so one CTA handles 24 tokens × 8\times\ 8× 8 query heads =192= 192=192 query rows for one KV head; its shared-memory and register usage allows only 1 CTA per SM, making 1 wave equal to 132 CTAs. At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, the grid launches ⌈16,384/24⌉×2=683×2=1,366\lceil 16{,}384 / 24 \rceil \times 2 = 683 \times 2 = 1{,}366⌈16,384/24⌉×2=683×2=1,366 query-tile CTAs in total.

Each of those 1,366 query-tile CTAs streams all KV entries visible to it from L2: 1,366 CTAs ×\times× an average of about 73,728 visible keys ×\times× 128 B per key per KV head, totaling about 12.9 GB. At the 7.33 TB/s L2 read bandwidth measured by a microbenchmark on the same GPU, streaming through once takes about 1.76 ms, or about 70% of the 2.50 ms FP8 compute lower bound from Section 1: because this is shorter than the compute lower bound, prefill remains compute-bound, though L2 bandwidth has only about 30% headroom left.

We launch these 1,366 CTAs in descending order of work from heaviest to lightest. As explained in Chapter 2, Section 1, CTAs do not switch in lockstep waves — as soon as an SM frees a slot, the next CTA is dispatched; under the causal mask, earlier query tiles attend to fewer keys and do less work, so the last CTAs dispatched onto SMs are the lightest 40 query tiles (80 CTAs). Once the dispatch queue drains, SMs that finish early sit idle waiting for this last batch of CTAs to complete. Splitting each of the lightest 40 query tiles into 4 segments along the key dimension (40 and 4 were tuned empirically) expands the grid to (683−40+40×4)×2=1,606(683 - 40 + 40\times 4) \times 2 = 1{,}606(683−40+40×4)×2=1,606 CTAs. We pay the entry/exit and merge overhead of 240 extra CTAs, and in return the final batch of CTAs takes only 1/4 of the original time, letting the tail SMs finish earlier and saving 345 µs at 65K history (see the chart below).

What if we replace static key-count balancing with dynamic claiming, where each CTA claims its next tile from a global counter? In measured runs, that is actually slower (about 23 µs slower on verify 32-request full attention). One key tile takes only about 1–2 µs, so adding an intra-CTA barrier and handoff on every claim raises the per-tile cost by about 10% and breaks the pipeline that prefetches the next tile's page-table entries (see Section 6). At the same time, static imbalance is at most about 16% to begin with and is already tiny once we split evenly by key count, so dynamic claiming has very little ceiling left to recover.

With a fixed segment count, short requests or sliding-window boundaries can also produce empty segments (start ≥\ge≥ end). An empty segment writes only lsei=−∞\mathrm{lse}_i = -\inftylsei​=−∞ and skips writing an all-zero output; because 2−∞=02^{-\infty} = 02−∞=0, the formula in Section 3 holds naturally, and when the merge step sees −∞-\infty−∞, it skips that segment directly. We did not measure the time saved by skipping empty segments separately.

Because no single combination of kernel and split count wins across all shapes, a1 looks up a per-shape table: at this stage, both decode and sliding-window verify use the single-KV-head mma.sync split kernel (one CTA computes one KV head, with 8 CTAs per SM). Per-shape table lookup cuts the 6-workload geometric mean defined in Section 1 by about 8%; because this version also switched several kernels at the same time, not all 8% comes from table lookup alone (the final kernel assignment for each shape appears at the end of Section 12).

5a1 → a2 (Part 1): When Two KV Heads Share the Same 128 B K Row, How Should the Two Halves Be Read?

Launching the two CTAs that read the two halves of the same row back-to-back saves ~12 µs on 32-request full-attention verification; having a single CTA gather the full 128 B row raises gather bandwidth by 30%–50%+ in an isolated gather microbenchmark.

Because the page table scatters each token into an arbitrary page slot, the kernel sees a stream of random addresses and can only gather them row by row using 16 B cp.async instructions (for the difference between TMA and cp.async, see Chapter 3, Section 3). One token's K row is 128 B wide (see Section 1): 8 threads issuing one 16 B cp.async each can gather the full 128 B row at once, whereas the single-KV-head split kernel has only 4 threads issue one instruction each to fetch only the 64 B half-row for its own head. In an isolated gather-only microbenchmark, gathering the full 128 B row at once hits about 4 TB/s of random-row gather bandwidth — about 30% to 50%+ faster than gathering two 64 B half-rows separately (see the chart below).

The lightest fix is to reorder the grid dimensions so that two CTAs with adjacent blockIdx values handle the two KV heads of the same token segment: launching them back-to-back places the reads of the two halves of the same row right next to each other in time (see Chapter 2, Section 2; whether the second read hits L2 was not measured, only the latency). This relies on the measured behavior from Chapter 2, Section 1 — H200 dispatches CTAs in increasing blockIdx order. It takes zero registers and zero shared memory, at the cost of depending on an unspecified dispatch order; even if that dispatch order changes, the numerical result is still right. On verify 32-request full attention, this saves about 12 µs (and leaves verify 16-request full attention unchanged).

In the decode (L=1L = 1L=1) kernel, the two KV heads of one token together have only 2×8=162 \times 8 = 162×8=16 query rows, so a small 4-warp (128-thread) CTA using mma.sync can compute both heads together. Having one CTA gather the full 128 B row into shared memory — applying a 128 B XOR swizzle on write to avoid bank conflicts (see Chapter 3, Section 7) — lets both heads read from the same buffer. Capping each CTA at 128 registers per thread and 48 KiB of shared memory (3 buffer slots ×\times× 8 KiB each for K and V) places 4 CTAs per SM (compared with 8 for the single-KV-head split kernel); at the cost of an extra shared-memory buffer shared by the two heads, this saves about 16 µs on decode 32-request full attention.

In verify (L=8L = 8L=8), a single KV head already has 64 query rows and must use wgmma. So full-attention verify switches to a 3-warpgroup (384-thread) two-KV-head fusion (merging 2 KV heads per CTA) kernel: 1 producer warpgroup gathers one full K row and one full V row (256 B in total) per token and feeds 2 consumer warpgroups, one per KV head (for warp specialization, see Chapter 3, Section 4). That saves about 5 µs on verify 32-request full attention (see the chart below). Sliding-window verify uses a sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel where each CTA computes one KV head (1 producer warpgroup plus 1 consumer warpgroup; its standalone gain was not measured). The trade-off of two-KV-head fusion is that the total CTA count is cut in half and each SM holds only 2 CTAs. What if we copy this heavy 384-thread two-KV-head fusion structure over to token-by-token decode (L=1L = 1L=1)? Decode 16- and 32-request full attention run about twice as slow (see the note in the chart below). Our explanation (unverified): the 128-thread small CTA places 4 CTAs per SM whereas the 384-thread heavy structure places only 2, cutting in-flight gather reads per SM in half; at L=1L = 1L=1, 56 of the 64 rows in wgmma are also padding.

The half-row versus full-row bandwidth chart above came from a standalone microbenchmark that only does gather. The gather microbenchmark below copies the structure of the two-KV-head fusion kernel: 2 CTAs per SM, 1 producer warpgroup gathering into a shared-memory ring buffer, and consumer warpgroups that simply return ring slots without doing any compute. When we measure its gather bandwidth with a real page table, even laying out all addresses completely contiguously saves only a little over 10% of the gather time (see the chart below). Next, inside the real verify kernel, we turn off the consumers' matrix multiplies and softmax and leave only the producer gathering KV (which we call the producer-only microbenchmark below): runtime is still 92%–94% of the full kernel, so the kernel really is bottlenecked on gather. This two-KV-head fusion gather microbenchmark achieves lower bandwidth than the standalone microbenchmark; how much of that drop comes from having fewer bytes in flight was not measured separately.

6a1 → a2 (Part 2): When Reading Each KV Page Requires a Three-Hop Pointer Chain First, How Do We Hide That Wait?

Prefetching page-table entries 4 tiles ahead into registers hides the page-table lookup round trip inside the pipeline; issuing sequence-length and page-table loads concurrently at batch size 1 yields a change within the noise band.

When each page holds only 1 token, reading a single KV row has to walk a three-hop pointer chain first: Hop 1 reads seq_lens[b], Hop 2 uses the resulting logical page index to read page_table[b, i], and Hop 3 uses the physical page slot to compute addr=base+slot×128\mathrm{addr} = \mathrm{base} + \mathrm{slot} \times 128addr=base+slot×128, fire the first cp.async, and wait for the KV data to land. On the lightly loaded verify 1-request full-attention shape, the measured time from launch until the first tile's data lands is about 2.4 µs (see Figure 7-6 Mode 1 for the duration of each hop); this 2.4 µs is entry latency, distinct from the 6.6 µs full-load overhead in Section 4. Where does that wait land? Right on the integer multiply-add instruction that first computes a memory address from the physical page slot: the profiler shows that warps at this instruction stall mostly on the scoreboard waiting for the page-table load to return (for the scoreboard, see Chapter 4, Section 2). The multi-slot ring buffer from Chapter 3, Section 4 can hide data transfer latency, but it cannot hide address latency — cp.async cannot issue until the address is known.

To pull that per-tile page-table round trip off the critical path, we prefetch the page table several tiles ahead: before entering the main loop, we load the page slots for Tiles 0..3 into registers; upon entering iteration jjj, we use the ready page slots to issue cp.async for Tile j+1j+1j+1 while issuing the page-table load for Tile j+4j+4j+4. The number of tiles ahead is the prefetch distance (lookahead depth): it must cover at least one page-table round trip (about 640 ns). At about 1–2 µs per tile (Section 4) — already much larger than 640 ns — 1 tile is enough, whereas under light load each tile runs faster and requires more tiles ahead. Here we use 4 tiles, and page-table loads also carry the "keep in L2" residency hint (see Chapter 2, Section 4 for the mechanism). On full-load decode 16-request full attention, this step saves up to about 1.6 µs (see the chart below). The trade-off is that in-flight page slots consume registers; other lookahead depths and the exact number of extra registers used were not measured separately.

For a single request, we can also avoid waiting on the sequence length. The kernel launch parameters already include the page-table column count max_pages (Section 1); at B=1B = 1B=1, this usually equals the request's own page count, though the page table may also be pre-allocated to a larger cap, so seq_lens[0] must still be read. For 1-request decode, the kernel computes the segment range from max_pages first and issues the page-table loads for the first 4 tiles concurrently with seq_lens[0]; once seq_lens[0] returns, it verifies before actual use whether the true range matches (re-reading only on a mismatch; the check itself has zero measured cost). Turning three hops into two changes decode 1-request full attention by about 0.26 µs — smaller than the 0.4 µs noise band from Section 1, so no gain is visible (see the chart below) — and the change applies only to B=1B = 1B=1. On verify 1-request full attention there is no gain: starting at Tile 3, the producer must wait for the consumer to free a ring-buffer slot, so the small head start won at entry is absorbed by Tile 3.

Push prefetching past the register limit, however, and it turns into a loss. In the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel of Section 7, the producer has only 32 registers at runtime (reduced to 32 via setmaxnreg in Section 7; see Chapter 3, Section 6 for the mechanism); pushing the page-table prefetch distance beyond 4 tiles overflows the available registers with in-flight page slots and spills to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1), making verify 32-request full attention about 2.4%–2.6% slower instead.

Prefetching across the memory-queue boundary brings no gain either. The preceding prologue kernel writes only q and K/V for the new tokens of this pass. The old historical pages were written earlier and are already ready before the wait call, so we could kick off main-loop prefetching early — yet measured runs show no gain (0.13–0.56 µs slower, with the lower end inside the 0.4 µs noise band; see the chart below). The reason is probably queueing delay: those non-critical requests enter the SM's memory request queue first, ahead of the critical Tile 0 requests, making Tile 0 wait longer.

Prefetching across the L2 residency boundary brings no gain either. The L2 prefetch instruction only pulls a range of data from HBM into L2 without bringing it into the SM. If we issue it before the wait call to prefetch the page table, those prefetched lines may be evicted by KV data streaming through L2 before they are used, forcing a second read from HBM; in measured runs, this is 0.03–0.53 µs slower (with the lower end inside the noise band; see the chart below).

7a2 → a3: Once Multi-Token Attention Enters wgmma, How Do the Producer and Two Consumer Warpgroups Split Registers and Stagger the Pipeline?

Placing the producer warpgroup on the fall-through branch and computing addresses inside the branch eliminates live registers across setmaxnreg.dec 32 and reduces register spills to zero; two named barriers then stagger the two consumer warpgroups by half a step on the Tensor Core.

Inside the "two-KV-head fusion" kernel used for verify, one CTA packs 3 warpgroups totaling 384 threads — 1 producer warpgroup plus 2 four-warp consumer warpgroups; the query tiles Q0, Q1 :  [64,  64]  FP8\shape{Q_0,\ Q_1}{64,\;64}{FP8}Q0​, Q1​:[64,64]FP8 for the two KV heads stay resident in shared memory, and the producer gathers 256 B per token into the ring buffer (see Section 5). At compile time, we allocate 80 registers per thread, so one CTA uses 384×80=30,720384 \times 80 = 30{,}720384×80=30,720 registers and the 65,536 registers of one SM can hold at most 2 CTAs (for residency, see Chapter 3, Section 1); at runtime, setmaxnreg trims the producer to 32 registers per thread and hands the freed registers to the two consumer warpgroups, raising each consumer thread to 104 registers (128×32+256×104=30,720128 \times 32 + 256 \times 104 = 30{,}720128×32+256×104=30,720; see Chapter 3, Section 6).

Register usage sets residency, and residency sets how many CTAs fit in 1 wave: at 2 CTAs per SM, 1 wave is 2×132=2642 \times 132 = 2642×132=264 CTAs. So verify 32-request full attention launches 264 CTAs directly and uses the method from Section 4 — "concatenate the keys of all requests into a single logical strip and partition it evenly by key count" — to fill 1 wave exactly. This step saves about 3.9 µs net; the trade-off is that a segment may span two requests, adding about 1.5 µs to the merge step (already deducted from the net saving).

Remember from Section 5 that the producer-only microbenchmark accounts for 92%–94% of total runtime, so any slowdown in the producer directly drags down the entire kernel. To avoid register spills in the producer, one invariant has to hold: every value still live when setmaxnreg.dec 32 executes must fit inside 32 registers. After compilation, one branch of an if statement runs sequentially right after the branch instruction — the fall-through branch (referred to below as the default fall-through branch) — while the other branch takes a jump. Originally, we put the consumers on the default fall-through branch, and during optimization the compiler hoisted an intermediate KV-row address value above the if statement; that value stayed live across the jump to setmaxnreg.dec 32 in the producer branch, overflowed the 32-register budget, and spilled 8 B to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1), adding a local-memory load wait every time it was used. Moving the producer onto the default fall-through branch and pushing the segment and address calculations inside producer_loop() (after role splitting) leaves zero live variables across setmaxnreg.dec 32:

// Before (illustrative): consumers take the default fall-through branch; the compiler hoists the address calculation in producer_loop above the if, crossing dec 32 and spilling 8 B
if (wg_id > 0) { setmaxnreg_inc<104>(); consumer_loop(); }
else           { setmaxnreg_dec<32>();  producer_loop(); }

// After: the producer takes the default fall-through branch; segment bounds and addresses are set up inside each role branch after splitting, no longer crossing dec 32, with 0 spills
if (wg_id == 0) { setmaxnreg_dec<32>();  producer_loop(); }
else            { setmaxnreg_inc<104>(); consumer_loop(); }

On verify 32-request full attention, measuring this branch flip together with "splitting out the unmasked loop" drops local-memory spills to zero and saves about 15.8 µs (the two changes were not measured separately): key tiles that fall completely inside the visible range run a tight main loop without mask checks, leaving only the last few tiles to run a masked tail loop (splitting out the unmasked loop was measured separately on verify 16-request full attention; see the chart below). Why the compiler hoists the address calculation above if only when the producer takes the jump branch was not determined. The catch is that this behavior holds only under the current compiler: the role-branching code is fragile to branch ordering, swapping the branches can reintroduce spills, and changing the compiler version requires a re-check.

Inside that same CTA loop, scalars that are identical across all 32 threads of a warp — such as the ring-buffer slot index, phase bit, and matrix descriptor — can live in a uniform register (UR), a scalar register shared across the entire warp (see Figure 7-7 Mode 4). General-purpose registers store one copy per thread and force all 32 threads to compute the same value redundantly; in a uniform register, the entire warp computes it once. The limitation is that uniform registers apply only to values identical across all 32 lanes of a warp and are bounded by the per-warp uniform-register limit; the latency gain was not measured separately on this kernel.

Now look at what happens inside each loop iteration: a consumer warpgroup first issues the wgmma for Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤, then runs the elementwise softmax operations (on the ALU/FMA and SFU pipelines), and then issues P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V (for P, see Section 3). If both consumer warpgroups execute the same phase at the same time, they fight over the Tensor Core simultaneously and then leave it idle simultaneously. We stagger them with two named barriers (see Chapter 5, Section 7): each barrier synchronizes the 256 threads of the two consumer warpgroups, while the producer warpgroup in the same CTA does not participate. A named barrier provides two instructions: bar.arrive adds 128 to the arrival count without blocking so the calling warpgroup keeps running, whereas bar.sync adds 128 to the arrival count and blocks until the count reaches 256. Two named barriers (Barrier 0 and Barrier 1) stagger the two consumer warpgroups by half a step in three moves:

  1. Before entering the loop, the 128 threads of Group 1 issue a non-blocking bar.arrive on Barrier 0. Next, the 128 threads of Group 0 execute bar.sync on Barrier 0, bringing the arrival count to 128+128=256128 + 128 = 256128+128=256 so Group 0 passes immediately and starts the first MMA stage [Q⋅K(0)][Q\cdot K(0)][Q⋅K(0)]; meanwhile, the 128 threads of Group 1 execute bar.sync on Barrier 1, where only 128 threads have arrived so far, causing Group 1 to wait at Barrier 1.
  2. Once Group 0 finishes issuing its MMA window, its 128 threads issue a non-blocking bar.arrive on Barrier 1, bringing Barrier 1's arrival count to 256 to release Group 1 while Group 0 moves on to compute softmax.
  3. From then on, the two groups alternate: after issuing its combined MMA window [P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)][P\cdot V(j),\ Q\cdot K(j+1)][P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)], each group issues bar.arrive on the other group's barrier to release it and moves on to softmax; before its next MMA window, it executes bar.sync on its own barrier to wait until the other group arrives and brings the count to 256.

We pay one extra 256-thread barrier synchronization per iteration and serialize the MMA issue windows of the two groups; in return, we save about 2.3 µs on verify 32-request full attention (see the chart below). Conversely, locking only the Q⋅KQ \cdot KQ⋅K segment instead of combining [P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)][P\cdot V(j),\ Q\cdot K(j+1)][P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)] into a single window adds extra per-iteration waiting that slows verify 32-request full attention by about 4.5–4.8 µs.

8a3 → a4: When the Softmax Between the Two Matrix Multiplications Accounts for Over Half the Instructions, How Do We Lighten It?

After RMSNorm, the base-2 attention scores have a bounded upper limit so BF16 weights cannot overflow, allowing per-tile rescaling to be skipped entirely and row sums to be offloaded onto the idle Tensor Core.

An SMSP can issue only 1 instruction per cycle (see Chapter 4, Section 1). Look at the compiled 64-key loop of the verify kernel: it takes 288 machine instructions in total, and softmax accounts for 58% of them — the intra-tile maximum reduction, ex2 to compute α\alphaα, multiplying every element of OOO by α\alphaα, and the row-sum reduction. Because the 4 warps of the producer warpgroup sit across the 4 SMSPs, they share each SMSP's 1-instruction-per-cycle issue slot with the warps of the two consumer warpgroups; every instruction a consumer avoids issuing is one fewer cycle in which a producer cp.async can be blocked from issuing. The producer-only microbenchmark accounts for 92%–94% of total runtime, and part of the remaining about 6%–8% is the cost of consumers occupying issue slots and delaying producer cp.async instructions. Those percentages come from the version in Section 5; after Section 7 eliminates producer register spills, the producer-only share will drop, and reducing consumer instructions saves correspondingly more time (the new share was not measured).

Rescaling on every tile in Section 3 existed solely to prevent 2s−m2^{s-m}2s−m from overflowing. After unweighted RMSNorm, each row has a root mean square of 1, so a 64-dimensional vector has Euclidean length 64=8\sqrt{64} = 864​=8; RoPE is a rotation and preserves length. Across all versions in this chapter, the prologue kernel finishes RMSNorm and RoPE in FP32 before casting q and k directly to FP8 E4M3, and historical keys in the cache were written the same way: with a 3-bit mantissa, round-to-nearest has a relative error of at most 2−42^{-4}2−4, which stretches vector length by at most a factor of 1.06251.06251.0625. Because the dot product of two vectors cannot exceed the product of their lengths (the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality), ∣q⋅k∣≤8×8×1.06252=72.25|q\cdot k| \le 8 \times 8 \times 1.0625^2 = 72.25∣q⋅k∣≤8×8×1.06252=72.25; multiplying by 0.6840.6840.684 and then by log⁡2e\log_2 elog2​e gives: ∣s∣≤72.25×0.684×1.4427≈71.3|s| \le 72.25 \times 0.684 \times 1.4427 \approx 71.3∣s∣≤72.25×0.684×1.4427≈71.3 That is a worst-case upper bound, not a statistical estimate.

Like FP32, BF16 has an 8-bit exponent with an upper limit of about 21282^{128}2128. When the weights P are stored in BF16 and we compute p=2min⁡(s, 72)p = 2^{\min(s,\ 72)}p=2min(s, 72) directly, the largest value is only 2722^{72}272. Since 80,000≈216.380{,}000 \approx 2^{16.3}80,000≈216.3, summing across all 80,000 keys reaches at most about 2882^{88}288, which fits in the FP32 denominator; the smallest value, 2−71.32^{-71.3}2−71.3, also sits well above the smallest normal BF16 number (about 2−1262^{-126}2−126). So we do not need a reference maximum at all: the per-tile max reduction, α\alphaα, and the rescaling of OOO all disappear. That saves about 6.7 µs on verify 32-request full attention (see the chart below). The trade-off is that we now depend on the upper bound above: it holds only along the "unweighted RMSNorm + FP8 rounding" path, and must be re-derived if the model or data type changes. Because that bound sits below 72, the clamp at 72 never triggers and acts only as a safety guard. The baseline implementation splits the five steps into separate kernels. What if we used this no-rescaling scheme on that split pipeline? On the 46 sliding-window layers that run RoPE, q and k are written back to BF16 once after RMSNorm and again after RoPE, adding two extra BF16 roundings that push the upper bound up to about 72.4. At that point, the clamp at 72 may trigger; once it does, the output changes silently. Full-attention layers skip RoPE, so they add only one extra rounding, with an upper bound of about 71.9.

Next, in the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel, we move the row-sum reduction onto the Tensor Core (the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel in the same version does this too). Each tile's contribution to the denominator lll is the row sum of P, which equals P×1P \times \mathbf{1}P×1. Doing that sum on the ALU/FMA pipeline takes 38 additions plus 4 warp shuffles. Instead, we place a constant all-ones matrix in shared memory and issue 4 wgmma.m64n8k16 instructions (64 keys =4×k16= 4 \times k16=4×k16, BF16 input; see Chapter 5, Section 3), saving a net 38 instructions per tile at the cost of extra Tensor Core cycles and an all-ones block in shared memory. This only works if the Tensor Core has idle cycles: this kernel is bottlenecked on gather and issue slots. We did not measure the standalone gain of this change on a single operator; Section 9 covers how the FP8 version uses it.

In the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma verify kernel (Section 5), removing the Tensor Core row-sum reduction and reverting to ALU/FMA row sums changes verify 32-request sliding window by about 0.26 µs — smaller than the 0.4 µs noise band from Section 1, showing neither a gain nor a loss (see the chart below); on which workloads it would become a loss was not measured. Inferring from the pipeline rules of Chapters 4 and 5, offloading row sums onto the Tensor Core pays off only when the ALU/FMA pipeline saturates first while the Tensor Core still has idle capacity.

One more attempt brings zero gain: using the half-precision paired instruction ex2.approx.f16x2 in hopes of halving SFU time. Because the Hopper SFU executes scalar operations one lane at a time (see Chapter 5, Section 1), the compiler expands this instruction into 2 MUFU.EX2.F16 instructions plus 1 byte-permute PRMT (for PTX-to-SASS translation, see Chapter 6, Section 5) — saving zero SFU time, adding 1 extra instruction, and yielding zero gain.

9a4 → a5 (Part 1): After Compressing the Weight Matrix P to 1-Byte FP8, How Do We Compute Exponentials Quickly Without Overflowing?

Leaving exponent headroom triggers rescaling via a warp-vote instruction only when a tile exceeds the threshold, and computes E4M3 bytes directly on the FMA/ALU pipelines via the linear approximation 8(y+7)8(y+7)8(y+7).

To run the P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V multiplication in the next section on the FP8 Tensor Core, we first have to store P in E4M3. The catch is that the upper bound of E4M3 is only 448 (see Section 1), and when the exponent field is all zeros its value is (j/8)⋅21−7(j/8)\cdot 2^{1-7}(j/8)⋅21−7 (where jjj is the 3-bit mantissa value) with a minimum positive subnormal value of 2−92^{-9}2−9 (for subnormal numbers, see Chapter 6, Section 3) — so P must be scaled into this narrow range.

Rescaling historical accumulators only when a tile threatens to overflow is called lazy rescaling. Keeping the row maximum of Tile 0 as the reference mrefm_{ref}mref​, we write the weights as P′=2 8−τ⋅2 s−mrefP' = 2^{\,8-\tau}\cdot 2^{\,s-m_{ref}}P′=28−τ⋅2s−mref​ where τ\tauτ is the headroom reserved for lazy rescaling (a base-2 exponent). As long as a new tile's maximum satisfies mtile≤mref+τm_{tile} \le m_{ref} + \taumtile​≤mref​+τ, we have P′≤28−τ⋅2τ=256<448P' \le 2^{8-\tau}\cdot 2^{\tau} = 256 < 448P′≤28−τ⋅2τ=256<448, so it cannot overflow and mrefm_{ref}mref​, OOO, and lll remain untouched. On each iteration, the entire warp executes just one vote instruction: __any_sync(…, m_tile > m_ref + τ). Here __any_sync asks all 32 threads (lanes) of a warp whether the condition holds for any lane; if even one lane is true, every lane receives true. Only when some row exceeds the threshold does the warp update mrefm_{ref}mref​ and multiply by α\alphaα. Because E4M3 has a narrow range and every tile must check whether mtilem_{tile}mtile​ exceeds the threshold, the intra-tile maximum reduction eliminated in Section 8 returns here, along with the cost of one vote instruction and occasional rescaling (when no row exceeds the threshold, computing α\alphaα and rescaling OOO are still skipped). At τ=4\tau = 4τ=4, the per-tile trigger rate is only 7%–18%; relaxing it to τ=6\tau = 6τ=6 saves another ~1.4 µs on verify 32-request full attention.

However, the headroom τ\tauτ also has a bound at the other end: the larger τ\tauτ is, the smaller 28−τ2^{8-\tau}28−τ becomes, and the sooner small weights drop below 2−92^{-9}2−9 and flush to 0. In the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel, before adopting τ=6\tau = 6τ=6 we tried pushing τ\tauτ directly from 4 to 8: that caused too many small weights to underflow, pushing the output error beyond the numerical tolerance (the maximum error allowed relative to the reference implementation; see Chapter 10, Section 4), so it was rejected (even though it ran about 3.7 µs faster). Yet the same τ=8\tau = 8τ=8 passes inside the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel (Section 5) and saves about 0.83 µs (see the chart below). One possible explanation is that full-attention layers attend to about 80,000 visible keys (versus at most 2,055 in sliding-window layers), so more small weights get flushed to 0; why one kernel exceeds the tolerance while the other passes was not determined.

In prefill, the bottleneck shifts to the SFU. The SFU accepts only 1 warp instruction every 8 cycles — an issue interval 8× that of FMA (see Chapter 5, Section 1); in the 128-key loop, each consumer warp issues 66 MUFU.EX2 instructions per tile, driving SFU pipeline utilization to 77.3%. Because softmax sits right between the two matrix multiplications, any slowdown on the SFU directly delays the start of the subsequent P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V stage.

How can we offload the exponential from the SFU? Look at the E4M3 byte code of the target weight 2y2^{y}2y: it is approximately a linear function of yyy (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit fields). Write the base-2 exponent yyy as an integer part plus a fractional part, y=n+fy = n + fy=n+f (0≤f<10 \le f < 10≤f<1): the 4-bit exponent field holds n+7n + 7n+7, which shifted left by 3 bits gives 8(n+7)8(n+7)8(n+7); the 3-bit mantissa field uses the linear approximation 2f≈1+f2^{f} \approx 1 + f2f≈1+f to hold 8f8f8f. Combined, the byte code is c≈8(y+7)c \approx 8(y + 7)c≈8(y+7). Let's check one byte by hand: take y=2.5y = 2.5y=2.5 (n=2, f=0.5n = 2,\ f = 0.5n=2, f=0.5), which gives 8(2.5+7)=768(2.5+7) = 768(2.5+7)=76, or 0100 1100 in binary. Here the exponent field is 1001 =9=2+7= 9 = 2 + 7=9=2+7 and the mantissa field is 100 =4=8×0.5= 4 = 8 \times 0.5=4=8×0.5; decoding gives 22×(1+4/8)=62^{2}\times(1 + 4/8) = 622×(1+4/8)=6, compared with the exact value 22.5≈5.662^{2.5} \approx 5.6622.5≈5.66. For normal weights 2y≥2−62^y \ge 2^{-6}2y≥2−6, the worst-case relative error is only about 6% (at f≈0.44f \approx 0.44f≈0.44, 1.441.441.44 versus 1.361.361.36), which is on the same order as the 3-bit mantissa rounding error of E4M3 itself (at most 6.25%); below 2−62^{-6}2−6 the error grows larger, and below 2−72^{-7}2−7 the byte code goes negative and is clamped to 0.

Because c=8(y+7)c = 8(y+7)c=8(y+7) is a linear function, there is no need to queue on the SFU — we can compute the byte directly on the FMA and ALU pipelines. To encode every 4 values, we first use a saturating multiply-add FFMA.SAT (where .SAT clamps the result to [0,1][0, 1][0,1], clamping negative byte codes to 0 right here) to compute the normalized value u=(y+7)/15∈[0,1]u = (y+7)/15 \in [0, 1]u=(y+7)/15∈[0,1]. Next, cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 converts into a half-precision pair (f16x2), and a half-precision multiply-add computes 1024+120u=1024+c1024 + 120u = 1024 + c1024+120u=1024+c. Because half precision (FP16: 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, 10 mantissa bits) has an exact unit step size of 1 on the interval [1024,2048)[1024, 2048)[1024,2048), the integer c∈[0,120]c \in [0, 120]c∈[0,120] lands directly in the low 8 mantissa bits of the FP16 value. After register moves (MOV), PRMT packs the 4 low bytes into a 32-bit word: every 4 values issue 9 to 10 instructions in total (the exact breakdown by instruction type was not measured). This step cuts MUFU.EX2 instructions per tile from 66 down to 2 (see the Figure 7-9 readout for the change in SFU utilization), and the profiler measures about an 18% latency reduction on the full-attention kernel at 65K prefill history (see the third chart at the end of the chapter). The trade-off is that every 4 weights consume 9–10 issue slots — 5–6 more issue slots than the original 4 MUFU instructions — shifting pressure from the SFU to the issue slots while introducing piecewise-linear approximation error. Because the denominator lll multiplies those exact same bytes by the all-ones matrix (the method from Section 8), the numerator and denominator use the exact same approximated values, so the error does not appear on only one side.

Next, we use the subnormal range of FP16 to drop that half-precision multiply-add step. FP16 has an exponent bias of 15, and its all-zero-exponent subnormal range is evenly spaced: its values are 21−15⋅m/210=m×2−242^{1-15}\cdot m/2^{10} = m \times 2^{-24}21−15⋅m/210=m×2−24 (where mmm is the 10-bit integer mantissa), with a minimum step size of 2−242^{-24}2−24. We multiply the byte code c=8(y+7)c = 8(y+7)c=8(y+7) by 2−242^{-24}2−24, folding the factor 8×2−24=2−218 \times 2^{-24} = 2^{-21}8×2−24=2−21 straight into FFMA.SAT. The lower bound 0 of .SAT handles the negative-bytecode clamp from above (E4M3 could represent down to 2−92^{-9}2−9, but this small range of tiny weights is flushed to 0); meanwhile, the maximum ccc of 120 times 2−242^{-24}2−24 stays far below the upper bound 1. Next, calling cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 converts two values to FP16 at once with round-to-nearest, so the hardware rounds ccc directly into the low 8 mantissa bits of FP16; PRMT then packs the 4 bytes into a 32-bit register. That cuts 4 instructions per 4 values (2 half-precision multiply-adds and 2 MOV instructions) and saves about another 78 µs on the 65K-history full-attention kernel (see the third chart at the end of the chapter).

In the final prefill version of a5, an all-f16x2 formulation replaces the 2−212^{-21}2−21 scaling above: before finding the intra-tile maximum, cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 converts the raw FP32 scores in pairs to f16x2. Because FP16 has a step size of 1 on [1024,2048)[1024, 2048)[1024,2048) and the low 8 mantissa bits of 1024+c1024 + c1024+c equal ccc directly, both the intra-tile maximum reduction and the linear encoding 1024+c1024 + c1024+c (clamping negative values to 1024) execute on f16x2 at two half-precision values per instruction. This saves a net 28 instructions per tile, at the cost of rounding the scores to FP16 once before finding the maximum. The standalone latency change of this step on the 65K single operator was not measured separately (and is not plotted in the third chart at the end of the chapter); Section 10 next eliminates that initial batch of conversions as well. By contrast, approximating exp2 with an FMA polynomial issues about 7.5 extra instructions for every MUFU instruction it replaces, which runs slower in a loop where issue slots are already tight.

10a4 → a5 (Part 2): How Do the Two Matrix Multiplications Consume Narrower Inputs and Hide the Transpose of V Inside the First Stage's Background Execution Window?

Compute P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V directly with native FP8 wgmma, hiding the 17 byte-transpose instructions for V inside the asynchronous wait window of the first MMA stage.

Originally, we had to convert V to 16-bit in shared memory before running 16-bit wgmma for P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V — which both added a chain of conversion instructions and consumed twice as much shared memory. Once both P and V are in E4M3, we can issue the native FP8 instruction wgmma.m64n64k32.f32.e4m3.e4m3 directly: a 64×6464 \times 6464×64 tile with inner dimension k=32k = 32k=32 per step, E4M3 inputs, and FP32 accumulation (see Chapter 5, Section 3). In the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel, switching to FP8 P (τ=4\tau = 4τ=4; see Section 9) and FP8 P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V together saves about 8.8 µs on verify 32-request full attention; the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel (Section 5) switches to FP8 P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V in the same way (see the chart below). Each tile also saves 8–16 KiB of shared memory; the trade-off is that FP8 P introduces the approximation error discussed in Section 9.

FP8 wgmma requires the right-hand matrix in shared memory to be contiguous along the inner-product dimension: bytes from the same feature dimension at different key positions must sit next to each other. This layout is called K-major layout (inner-dimension major), where K is the matrix-multiply inner-product dimension — which in P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V is the key position. In the KV cache, however, V packs the 64 features of a single key contiguously, so every tile needs a byte transpose. For this we use the shared-memory matrix load instruction ldmatrix, which lets a warp load 8×88 \times 88×8 tiles from shared memory into registers. Each tile's transpose takes 1 ldmatrix, 8 byte-permute PRMT instructions (see Chapter 6, Section 2), and 8 shared-memory stores STS, for 17 instructions in total. After writing to shared memory, the warpgroup also issues a fence.proxy.async and waits on the named barrier from Section 7 for its turn. Those two steps order the generic shared-memory writes from the warpgroup's 4 warps ahead of the asynchronous reads of wgmma (see Chapter 3, Section 3). Both steps are present before and after the change below, so they do not affect the comparison.

Once issued, wgmma executes asynchronously in the background, and its results are not needed until wait_group (for commit and wait, see Chapter 5, Section 5). Inserting these 17 transpose instructions between the commit point of Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ and wait_group<0> runs them concurrently with the matrix multiplication. The transpose still issues all 17 instructions, but they hide inside the background execution window of Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ and no longer sit on the critical path, saving about 1.8 µs on verify 32-request full attention.

When registers have headroom left, we can go one step further with cross-iteration overlap: remove the wait for P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V at the end of each tile so that Tile jjj's P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V crosses the loop back-edge and stays in flight alongside Tile j+1j+1j+1's Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ (wait_group<1>). On verify 16-request full attention, overlapping the transpose with Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ plus cross-iteration overlap saves about 1.7 µs in total (see the chart below). Why not do the same in the 264-CTA kernel for verify 32-request full attention? Because each consumer thread there already uses all 104 registers reallocated in Section 7, and keeping an extra set of P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V input fragments across the loop back-edge spills 20 B to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1); that kernel therefore overlaps the transpose with Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ without enabling cross-iteration overlap.

In prefill, Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ can also switch to half-precision (f16x2) accumulation. Section 8 showed that ∣q⋅k∣≤72.25|q\cdot k| \le 72.25∣q⋅k∣≤72.25, which sits far below the FP16 maximum of 65,504, and FP16 has 11 significand bits — plenty of precision for softmax scores (keeping results within the numerical tolerance). The all-f16x2 approach at the end of Section 9 still had to issue 34 cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 instructions per tile first (32 instructions for the 64 FP32 scores per thread, plus 2 for encoding-constant conversions) to pack scores into f16x2; now the accumulator of wgmma.m64n128k32.f16.e4m3.e4m3 produces f16x2 directly, saving both those 34 conversion instructions and 32 accumulator registers. Applying this only on unmasked full tiles cuts the runtime of the 65K-history full-attention prefill kernel by 14.5%–16.8% (see the chart below). We also tested splitting softmax and P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V into a two-stage pipeline or splitting 128 keys into 64-key subtile pipelines, but neither yielded a gain because the compiler scheduled more instructions.

11a5 → a6 (Part 1): Should the Prologue and the Gating Epilogue Each Take a Separate Kernel?

Prefill fuses the prologue into a one-CTA-per-token kernel; decode and single-request verify fuse the prologue into each split-KV CTA and fuse the gating epilogue into the final kernel that writes o_attn.

Remember from Section 1 that our original baseline splits the five steps into 5 separate kernels, where each additional kernel adds one launch and one "write back to HBM or L2 and read it out again" round trip (see Chapter 1, Section 3). An early fused prologue for prefill split the 20 heads of each token (16 q, 2 k, and 2 v) across 5 CTAs per token; a6 consolidates this into 1 CTA per token (3 warps totaling 96 threads): RMSNorm, RoPE, casting q to FP8, and writing the new K/V entries all happen inside this single CTA, with each head's sum of squares reduced in registers via warp shuffles without using shared memory or a CTA barrier. With 4 threads per head, 96 threads cover 24 head slots; because there are only 20 actual heads, the extra 4 head slots leave 16 threads idle (register usage and residency were not measured separately). At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, prologue latency drops from about 53 µs to about 31 µs (see the chart below).

For decode and single-request verify, launching a separate prologue kernel just for a few rows of q and the new tokens' K/V isn't worth the boundary cost. Because one KV head has only 8 rows × 64\times\ 64× 64 dimensions per token, each split-KV CTA can read qkv directly to recompute the q rows it needs; each segment whose key range contains the new token positions computes and writes only the K/V entries for the new positions falling inside its own range, crosses a CTA barrier, and then reads them back. Why does this work without any cross-CTA synchronization? Because each segment reads only the keys and values in its own key range: the segment covering the new positions uses the values it just computed, and all other segments read only older historical cache entries that were already written in prior passes. Dropping the prologue kernel eliminates one launch and one dependency edge, saving about 1.8 µs on decode 1-request full attention (see the chart below).

At the other end of the pipeline, the gating epilogue rmsnorm(oraw)⊙σ(gate)\mathrm{rmsnorm}(o_{raw}) \odot \sigma(gate)rmsnorm(oraw​)⊙σ(gate) cannot run until the complete orawo_{raw}oraw​ is ready, and it no longer launches as a separate kernel either. In prefill, unsplit query tiles compute it directly, while for the 40 light query tiles split into 4 segments in Section 4, whichever of the 4 CTAs finishes last merges the segments inside the main kernel and then computes the gating epilogue (using ticket numbers; see the second path in Section 12). Shapes that merge inside the main kernel in Section 12 likewise compute the gating epilogue inside the main kernel before writing out, while shapes that still keep a separate merge kernel compute the gating epilogue at the end of the merge kernel after summing the partial results. The trade-off of fusing the prologue and epilogue is that every split segment recomputes q and the code becomes tightly coupled; the time saved by fusing the epilogue alone and any extra register or shared-memory usage were not measured separately.

Where a separate merge kernel remains (such as decode 1-request full attention), the main kernel hands off to the merge kernel via PDL (see Chapter 1, Section 4 for the mechanism). Comparing the three modes — "no PDL", "trigger after the main loop", and "trigger at function entry" (see the chart below) — shows that placing the trigger at function entry is actually the slowest: the merge-kernel CTAs enter too early, occupy SMs while sitting idle at the wait call for about 7.5 µs, and slow down the main kernel as well, probably because CTAs from both kernels co-reside on the same SMs and contend for slots (unverified). Because every shape with a separate merge kernel behaves this way, this chapter places the trigger after the main loop and before writeback.

12a5 → a6 (Part 2): Without a Separate Merge Kernel, How Are the Partial Results of Each Segment Summed Inside the Main Kernel?

Multiplying each segment's numerator and denominator by 2mi2^{m_i}2mi​ converts them to a common zero reference so they can be accumulated directly without waiting for the global denominator (light prefill tiles still merge in fixed order using lse\mathrm{lse}lse weights), finishing via one of three reduction paths selected by grid size.

Why did the merge in Section 3 need lse\mathrm{lse}lse? Because each segment's Oi,liO_i, l_iOi​,li​ were scaled by its own mim_imi​. If each segment instead outputs Oi2miO_i 2^{m_i}Oi​2mi​ and li2mil_i 2^{m_i}li​2mi​ (the true numerator and denominator referenced to 0), that problem goes away: the totals are simply ∑iOi2mi\sum_i O_i 2^{m_i}∑i​Oi​2mi​ and ∑ili2mi\sum_i l_i 2^{m_i}∑i​li​2mi​, followed by a single division o=Ototal/ltotalo = O_{total} / l_{total}o=Ototal​/ltotal​ at the end. In Section 8 we derived the upper bound ∣mi∣≤71.3|m_i| \le 71.3∣mi​∣≤71.3, so 2mi2^{m_i}2mi​ stays far below the FP32 upper limit of about 21282^{128}2128. Below, three in-kernel merge paths split the workload by grid size and segment count per request. Each path notes at the start of its paragraph which shapes it handles, and the list at the end of this section covers the shapes that still use a standalone merge kernel.

The first path is L2 atomic add + grid barrier + per-row normalization epilogue, used only on the verify 16- and 32-request full-attention shapes (264 CTAs). All CTAs atomically add their partial sums into the L2 workspace buffer defined in Section 3, then increment the same arrival counter in L2 and wait until it reaches the total count — this device-wide wait across all CTAs is a grid barrier. Its causal chain has three steps:

  1. Each consumer thread atomically adds its numerator into the L2 workspace buffer using the non-fetching vector atomic add red.global.add.v4.f32, and likewise for the denominator; red means write-only without fetching the old value, and .v4.f32 adds 4 FP32 values in one instruction (see Chapter 2, Section 7). Next, the 256 threads of the two consumer warpgroups cross a named barrier; in the memory model, that barrier orders the atomic adds of all threads in both consumer warpgroups before the representative thread's release (without requiring the atomic adds to have already landed in L2).
  2. A single representative thread for the CTA (thread 0 of consumer warpgroup 0) executes one atom.acq_rel.gpu addition on the global arrival counter and then polls it with ld.acquire.gpu until all CTAs have arrived.
  3. Once the representative thread observes that all CTAs have arrived, the 256 threads of the two consumer warpgroups cross a second named barrier so that all consumer threads are ordered after that acquire.gpu; the 264 CTAs then partition the rows among themselves: read the accumulated numerators and denominators, divide, apply RMSNorm, multiply by σ(gate)\sigma(gate)σ(gate), write out o_attn, and zero their own slice of the workspace buffer for the next launch. Normal global loads after acquire.gpu observe the results published to L2 by every CTA's release without reading stale L1 lines on the local SM (Chapter 2, Section 6).

Why can a single thread's release represent the entire CTA? Because a release operation publishes all prior writes that the releasing thread has already observed (for cumulativity, see Chapter 2, Section 6) — without that first named barrier, the representative thread's release would not cover the atomic adds issued by the other consumer threads.

Who zeroes the arrival counter for the next launch? Nobody does. The 32-bit counter only ever increments, and the total increment per launch must divide 2322^{32}232 evenly so that launch boundaries stay aligned across wrap-around; because 264 does not divide 2322^{32}232, we set the per-launch total to 65,536 and partition it across the 264 CTAs: 64 CTAs add 249 and 200 CTAs add 248, so the weights sum to 65,536 per launch. Each CTA adds its own weight to the old value returned by its atom and rounds up to the next multiple of 65,536 as the target value to wait for on this launch; using a signed difference for the comparison avoids any need to zero the counter across graph replays.

Why does reusing the same counter across launches never mix two launches? Because the single-layer PDL chain enforces a strict handoff invariant: every PDL kernel executes its own wait call before finishing (see Chapter 1, Section 4), and the next kernel that uses this counter touches it only after its own wait call — which guarantees that the previous launch has completely finished and all its writes are visible.

What keeps this spin-wait from deadlocking? Every CTA is guaranteed to see the counter complete only if all 264 CTAs achieve co-residency (simultaneous residency). By resource usage, each SM holds 2 CTAs, and 264=2×132264 = 2 \times 132264=2×132 equals the exact capacity of 1 wave. Formally, CUDA guarantees full-grid co-residency only under cooperative launch (see Chapter 2, Section 6). Here we skip cooperative launch and rely on three prerequisites plus the empirical dispatch behavior observed on hardware (the CUDA specification does not promise to dispatch all 264 CTAs onto SMs at once):

  1. The grid does not exceed the capacity of 1 wave.
  2. No other work occupies the SMs for an extended period, including kernels on other streams in the same process (such as cross-GPU communication kernels) and other processes; the preceding PDL kernel does not count — because the current kernel enters only after every CTA of its predecessor has either triggered or exited (Chapter 1, Section 4), all predecessor CTAs are already on SMs, do not wait on us, and will exit.
  3. The main kernel waits until the entire grid has arrived at the barrier before issuing the PDL trigger call to release the next kernel, preventing CTAs of the next kernel from entering SMs early and taking slots.

In the single-layer graph of this book, kernels such as router run on a side CUDA stream, but they start only after Stage 3 (Chapter 9, Section 1), and cross-GPU communication does not overlap with the single-layer graph (Chapter 9, Section 7), so no other kernel occupies SMs while Stage 2 runs and Prerequisite 2 holds; in an environment where multiple streams or processes share SMs, cooperative launch must be used instead (see Chapter 2, Section 6). In single-request trials on this operator, cooperative launch added about 1.2–1.8 µs of launch overhead. Avoiding cooperative launch saves that overhead in exchange for accepting a risk: if any prerequisite or dispatch behavior above fails to hold, the kernel will hang silently without reporting an error (Chapter 2, Section 6).

Folding this merge step in eliminates the separate merge kernel, saving a net ~3.0 µs on verify 32-request full attention (see the chart and note below).

Because the arrival order of cross-CTA floating-point atomic adds in the first path varies with scheduling, two runs on the exact same input can differ in the last few bits (with a relative difference below 10−410^{-4}10−4, within the numerical tolerance), whereas a separate merge kernel produces bitwise-identical results every run. How this last-bit difference affects the draft acceptance rate (see Primer 1, Section 7) was not measured.

The second path is last-arriver merge, used where the segment count is small or the grid spans multiple waves (decode 16- and 32-request shapes in the single-layer pipeline of Chapter 9, as well as the 40 light query tiles split in prefill in this chapter), so earlier CTAs do not spin-wait in place. On the decode 16- and 32-request shapes in the single-layer pipeline of Chapter 9, each segment likewise accumulates its 2mi2^{m_i}2mi​-scaled numerator and denominator into the workspace buffer via floating-point atomic adds, crosses a CTA barrier, and has thread 0 claim a ticket via atom.acq_rel.gpu (the same mechanism as Chapter 2, Sections 6–7). Every earlier CTA exits as soon as it claims its ticket. The CTA that draws the final ticket crosses a second CTA barrier, reads the full row's numerator and denominator, writes 0 back to both that row of the workspace buffer and the ticket counter for that row, and finishes the division and gating epilogue. Plain stores suffice for that zeroing step: the next consumer of that row is the next launch, and the PDL invariant above guarantees that the two launches execute strictly one after the other. Because no CTA waits on another CTA, this path cannot deadlock even when the grid spans multiple waves; because it uses cross-CTA floating-point atomic adds whose order varies with scheduling, it does not guarantee bitwise-identical results by construction.

The 40 light query tiles split in prefill also merge in the last-arriving CTA via ticket numbers (where the final ticket writes 0 back to the counter), but without floating-point atomic adds: the 4 segments each write their own (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i)(oi​,lsei​), and the CTA that receives the final ticket merges them in the fixed segment order 0–3 using the lse\mathrm{lse}lse weights from Section 3 before computing the gating epilogue; that leaves no accumulation workspace buffer to zero and keeps the result bitwise deterministic.

Verify sliding-window and 1-request sliding-window shapes (2–16 segments per request) take the third path: direct cross-CTA write to remote shared memory (DSMEM) within the same cluster. A thread block cluster declares several CTAs as a group that hardware guarantees to keep co-resident simultaneously. Physically, a GPC (Graphics Processing Cluster) is a group of adjacent SMs on the die wired together by its own inter-SM interconnect, and all CTAs of a cluster must fit inside the same GPC (scattered slots across different GPCs cannot form a cluster); how many SMs each GPC contains on H200 is not publicly documented.

DSMEM (Distributed Shared Memory) lets one CTA in a cluster directly read and write the shared memory of another CTA in the same cluster over the intra-GPC interconnect without going through L2. The st.async instruction asynchronously writes a block of data into the shared memory of another CTA in the same cluster and records the arrived byte count on the receiver's mbarrier (see Chapter 3, Section 5); as soon as the receiver's expected byte count is reached, it knows all segments have arrived.

Concretely, we declare the split-segment CTAs of the same request as a cluster, and as each segment finishes it uses st.async to push its partial results directly into the receiver CTA's shared memory. On 1-request sliding window, fusing the prologue, split-KV main loop, and cluster merge into a single 3-in-1 kernel collapses 3 launches into 1 and saves about 1.6 µs on verify 1-request sliding window (see the chart below). We measured this 3-in-1 kernel in the standalone attention benchmark of this chapter; the full-layer chain in Chapter 9 still keeps a separate attention merge step there.

Verify 16- and 32-request sliding window use the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel (Section 5) and declare the segments of the same request as a cluster (unlike the 8-CTA-per-SM mma.sync split kernel in Section 4). This kernel uses 72 registers per thread and 256 threads per CTA, so each SM holds at most 3 CTAs. Look at verify 16-request sliding window: 16 requests × 2\times\ 2× 2 KV heads =32= 32=32 clusters, each containing NS split-KV CTAs. Under the sliding window, each request sees 2,055 keys, or 33 tiles; when NS = 8, assigning ⌈33/8⌉=5\lceil 33/8 \rceil = 5⌈33/8⌉=5 tiles per segment means the first 7 segments already cover all 33 tiles, leaving the 8th segment with 0 tiles while still occupying a CTA slot.

At 3 CTAs per SM, the full chip can hold at most 132×3/8≈49132 \times 3 / 8 \approx 49132×3/8≈49 clusters of 8 CTAs; because a cluster cannot span GPC boundaries, 49 is only an upper bound, and how many 8-CTA clusters the chip can actually hold is neither publicly documented nor measured here. Those 32 clusters total 256 CTAs, which fit in one wave. When NS = 8, measured runs place 3 CTAs on 16 of the SMs, and those SMs finish last and drag out the tail. Changing to NS = 7 drops the empty segment and shrinks each cluster to 7 CTAs, for 32×7=22432 \times 7 = 22432×7=224 CTAs in total. Each cluster fits inside a single GPC more easily, no SM has to hold a 3rd CTA in measured runs, and latency drops by about 1.3 µs (see the chart below); the trade-off is that with 7 segments, merging must partition 64 output rows across 7 segments, which no longer divides evenly.

Applying in-kernel merge in the wrong regime causes a loss (see the chart below). On single-request full attention, the in-kernel merge tail is more than twice as slow as a standalone merge kernel, making decode 1-request full attention about 3.0 µs slower — probably because all 256 segment CTAs contend on atomic adds to the exact same output row address. On verify 32-request sliding window (64 clusters of 4 CTAs, totaling 256 CTAs), each SM originally holds up to 3 CTAs, fitting all 64 clusters in 1 wave. Expanding each CTA to 2 consumer warpgroups or increasing shared memory drops residency to at most 2 CTAs per SM; querying cluster occupancy shows that at 2 CTAs per SM the GPU can co-reside at most 62 clusters of 4 CTAs, pushing the last 2 clusters into a 2nd wave and stretching the tail. In addition, inlining the epilogue reduction code directly into the function containing the main loop disrupts compiler scheduling of the main loop and slows execution down.

By this point, both the head and the tail have been pulled into the main kernel. In the final standalone operator of this chapter, each shape runs its corresponding kernel:

  • 1-request sliding window: runs the 3-in-1 cluster kernel (fusing prologue, split-KV main loop, and cluster merge).
  • verify 16/32-request sliding window: sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma cluster kernel (up to 3 CTAs per SM, with intra-cluster DSMEM direct-write merge).
  • verify 16/32-request full attention: two-KV-head fusion wgmma kernel (2 CTAs per SM, with in-kernel L2 atomic-add merge).
  • decode 16/32-request full attention and sliding window: prologue fused into each split-KV CTA, followed by a separate merge kernel in the standalone operator of this chapter; the single-layer pipeline in Chapter 9 switches these shapes to the second path (last-arriver merge).
  • decode 1-request full attention and verify 1-request full attention: prologue fused into each split-KV CTA, followed by a separate merge kernel.
  • prefill: 1-CTA-per-token prologue kernel followed by the 1-CTA-per-SM, 3-consumer-warpgroup main kernel; the lightest 40 query tiles are each split into 4 segments and merged inside the main kernel by whichever of the 4 CTAs finishes last (via ticket numbers, the second path in Section 12).

Stage 2 Paged Attention Evolution Chain (a0 → a6)

Across this chapter, a0 → a6 groups our optimizations by the bottleneck each mechanism removes. The three charts below follow the chronological order in which versions were developed; because a single version often bundles several steps together, the a labels in the second chart interleave. In same-session paired ABBA runs against original SGLang, the final version runs about 2.7–2.8× as fast as the baseline (with the final step inside the noise band; see the second chart).

  • a0 (Sections 2–3): launch a separate prologue kernel, stack 8 query heads as matrix rows, and run Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ in FP8, with fixed-split Split-KV followed by a separate merge kernel (corresponding to Bar 1 of the first chart).
  • a1 (Section 4): tune split count to the concurrent request count, balance segments by actual key count, and look up configurations per shape, cutting the 6-workload geometric mean by about 8% (corresponding to Bar 2 of the first chart and Bars 1–3 of the second chart).
  • a2 (Sections 5–6): reshape how the two halves of the same K row are read and prefetch the page table 4 tiles ahead to hide the three-hop wait; bundled into the same version as fewer segments at high request counts and decode prologue fusion, this cuts time by about 33% at Bar 2 of the second chart, while single-request sequence-length bypass lands in Bar 10 (inside the noise band).
  • a3 (Section 7): size residency by register allocation, balance 264 CTAs evenly by key count, place the producer on the default fall-through branch to eliminate spills, split out the unmasked loop, and stagger the two consumer warpgroups via named barriers (landing in Bars 3, 4, and 8 of the second chart).
  • a4 (Section 8): skip per-tile rescaling altogether for BF16 P using the score upper bound, and offload row sums onto the Tensor Core when it has spare capacity. The same version also rewrites the main kernels to emit inline PTX directly inside CUDA C++ (for explicit control over registers, barriers, and instruction scheduling) and bundles the 1-request sliding-window 3-in-1 cluster merge into Bar 4 of the second chart, cutting time by about 17% (the share attributable to the PTX rewrite cannot be separated).
  • a5 (Sections 9–10): compress P to FP8 with lazy rescaling, move exponential encoding onto the FMA/ALU pipelines, overlap FP8 P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V with the transpose, and use half-precision accumulation in prefill; this cuts prefill kernel time by about 19% in the third chart and lands in Bars 5–7 and 9–10 of the second chart.
  • a6 (Sections 11–12): fuse the prologue, gating epilogue, and segment merge into the main kernel (landing in Bars 2, 4, 5, 8, and 10 of the second chart).

Takeaway: The bottleneck of paged attention is governed by how many query rows share each KV row (nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L). When nqn_qnq​ is small, the job is filling all 132 SMs and hiding the page-table round trip; when nqn_qnq​ is large, the challenge shifts inside each CTA to registers, the SFU, and issue slots. Each step of a0 → a6 removes only whichever bottleneck is slowest at that point.

Next chapter's question: After passing through the o projection in Stage 3 and the fork of Stages 4 and 5, the attention output arrives at Stage 6, the stage with the largest byte volume in a single layer: 32 local NVFP4 experts per GPU under 8-GPU expert parallelism. Why is the expert-by-expert dequantizing reference implementation slow, and how do we move the bottleneck onto the Tensor Core during prefill?

Position in the 8-stage single-layer pipeline: Stage 1 qkv_gate → Stage 2 paged attention → Stage 3 o and gated residual → Stage 4 router ∥ Stage 5 pooler → [Stage 6: Routed Experts] → Stage 7 unpooler → Stage 8 second gated residual

Stage 6's 32 local NVFP4 experts hold the largest share of weights in a single layer. Why is the reference implementation that dequantizes one expert at a time so slow? And as the total token count TTT grows from 1 to 16,384, why does Stage 6 ultimately split into three distinct kernels by TTT, and how does each generation evolve from the last?

1What Five Steps Does Stage 6 Compute for Each Hit Pair, and How Does MeM_eMe​ Split Stage 6 into Two Regimes?

When the token count MeM_eMe​ routed to an expert is less than about 58, reading weights is slower than matrix multiplication: decode, verify, and T=753T = 753T=753 prefill fall below this threshold, whereas T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012 prefill lies above it.

Stage 6 takes p :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{p}{T,\;4096}{BF16}p:[T,4096]BF16 from Stage 5, along with the routing indices topk_ids :  [T,  8]  int32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_ids}}{T,\;8}{int32}topk_ids:[T,8]int32 and routing weights topk_weights :  [T,  8]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_weights}}{T,\;8}{FP32}topk_weights:[T,8]FP32 from Stage 4. In each row, the 8 routing weights sum to 1 (see Primer 2, Section 2). All 256 experts in the model are split across 8 GPUs, and this GPU's 32 local experts stay resident in HBM (see Primer 1, Section 2); once Stage 6 finishes, it outputs m :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{m}{T,\;4096}{BF16}m:[T,4096]BF16 to Stage 7. Among the 8 slots slotslotslot of a token toktoktok, only a slot that lands on a local expert eee on this GPU counts as a hit pair (tok,slot,e)(tok, slot, e)(tok,slot,e); if all 8 slots of a token miss this GPU, its output row is all zeros.

For the MeM_eMe​ tokens that hit local expert eee on this GPU (one row per hit pair (tok,slot,e)(tok, slot, e)(tok,slot,e)), Stage 6 runs five steps in order:

H200 Tensor Cores do not accept 4-bit inputs. After 4-bit codewords are loaded onto the chip, the kernel must decode them to BF16 before feeding them into the matrix multiply. Each weight is w=c⋅sblock⋅stensorw = c \cdot s_{block} \cdot s_{tensor}w=c⋅sblock​⋅stensor​: a 4-bit codeword ccc multiplied by a block scale and then by a tensor scale (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit layout and decoding instructions). Counting the bytes, each codeword takes 0.5 B0.5\text{ B}0.5 B, every 16 weights share a 1 B1\text{ B}1 B block scale (0.0625 B0.0625\text{ B}0.0625 B per weight), and each expert carries one FP32 tensor scale, totaling 0.5625 B0.5625\text{ B}0.5625 B per weight. Within each expert, the gate half and the up-projection half share a single FP32 tensor scale (Section 13 explains why storing one scale is enough).

When we report Stage 6 latency below, we are measuring Stage 6 in isolation using alternating A/B paired runs within the same benchmark invocation before and after a change (see Chapter 7, Section 1 for the paired protocol and Chapter 4, Section 6 for the variation criterion). Unless noted otherwise, the timing mode of the charts in this chapter was not recorded. Single-layer latency, by contrast, covers all eight stages of a full layer in Chapter 9. Take the geometric mean of Stage 6 latency across the 6 decode (T=1,16,32T = 1, 16, 32T=1,16,32, with 1 new token per request) and verify (T=8,128,256T = 8, 128, 256T=8,128,256, with 8 new tokens per request) workloads and multiply by 60 (the middle 60 layers use 4-bit experts; see Primer 1, Section 2): that gives the 60-layer total. We use that number to compare against the baseline SGLang implementation, which calls a 4-bit GEMM library function one expert at a time (see the first chart at the end of the chapter). Prefill at T=753,3,012,16,384T = 753, 3{,}012, 16{,}384T=753,3,012,16,384 is shown separately in the second chart at the end of the chapter; intermediate token counts outside these 9 points were not measured.

Along the evolution chain, decode and verify start out sharing two kernel generations (m1 and m2), before the final deployment splits into three branches by TTT: m3 for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, m4 for T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256, and m5 for prefill.

Why split by TTT at all? Because the row count of an expert's matrix multiplication equals the number of tokens MeM_eMe​ routed to that expert. At 3.56 FLOP/B3.56\text{ FLOP/B}3.56 FLOP/B per token against the H200 ridge point of 206 FLOP/B206\text{ FLOP/B}206 FLOP/B, an expert needs Me≈58M_e \approx 58Me​≈58 tokens before matrix-multiply compute time catches up with the time to read its weights once from HBM (Primer 2, Section 5). Which 8 experts each token picks is the routing distribution: spreading tokens evenly across experts is uniform routing, clustering them onto a few experts is skewed routing, and our single-operator benchmarks generate multiple random routing distributions. That Me≈58M_e \approx 58Me​≈58 line splits the workload into two regimes:

  • decode and verify (T=1..256T = 1..256T=1..256): Under uniform routing at T=256T = 256T=256, almost all 32 local experts on this GPU get hit, leaving each expert with an average of only 8 tokens. Under skewed routing, tokens pile onto fewer experts, so fewer experts get hit than under uniform routing. By the task lower-bound accounting in Primer 2, Section 5, at T=256T = 256T=256 the busiest GPU reads the equivalent of about 16.0 local experts of weights (about 452 MB452\text{ MB}452 MB); spreading an average of 256 local hit pairs across those 16 experts gives about 16 tokens per expert, still far below 58. Only a few hot experts at T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256 receive several dozen tokens, which we handle in Section 9. Throughout this regime, weight reads set the physical lower bound: the reference implementation m0 is slowed down by its per-expert loop (Section 2), while the first four kernel generations (m1 → m4) strip away on-chip decoding instructions, tail waves, and synchronization overhead step by step to approach that weight-read lower bound.
  • prefill (T=753,3,012,16,384T = 753, 3{,}012, 16{,}384T=753,3,012,16,384): Under uniform routing, each local expert receives an average of 8T/256=T/328T / 256 = T / 328T/256=T/32 tokens—about 24, 94, and 512 tokens across the three points. T=753T = 753T=753 still sits below the ridge point, but T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012 crosses 58, shifting the bottleneck of our fifth-generation kernel (m5) onto the Tensor Cores and instruction pipelines.

A pair of lower bounds makes this crossover clear. During prefill, all 32 local experts on this GPU get hit (906 MB906\text{ MB}906 MB in total), so reading their weights once at 4.8 TB/s4.8\text{ TB/s}4.8 TB/s takes at least 188.7 μs188.7\ \mu\text{s}188.7 μs. By T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, the roughly TTT hit pairs on this GPU perform 16,384×2×3×40962≈1,649 GFLOP16{,}384 \times 2 \times 3 \times 4096^2 \approx 1{,}649\text{ GFLOP}16,384×2×3×40962≈1,649 GFLOP. At the BF16 peak throughput of 989 TFLOP/s989\text{ TFLOP/s}989 TFLOP/s (4-bit weights are decoded to BF16 on chip before multiplying), the compute lower bound hits 1,668 μs1{,}668\ \mu\text{s}1,668 μs—nearly 9× the weight-read lower bound. In decode and verify, by contrast, we read only the hit experts, so the weight-read lower bound stays much smaller than 188.7 μs188.7\ \mu\text{s}188.7 μs. At T=256T = 256T=256, for the 16.0 experts in the task lower-bound accounting, the weight-read lower bound is about 94.4 μs94.4\ \mu\text{s}94.4 μs, while the compute lower bound is only about 26.1 μs26.1\ \mu\text{s}26.1 μs (Primer 2, Section 5). A full 8-GPU deployment also has to wait for the slowest GPU and run a cross-GPU reduction; this chapter measures single-GPU latency under the routing load of the busiest GPU, excluding that cross-GPU reduction.

2Why Does the Reference Stage 6 Take Tens of Milliseconds, and Why Is the First Grouped-GEMM Step m1a ~80× Faster?

m0 loops over experts one by one, launching small kernels and decompressing weights to FP32 in HBM; m1 switches to a single grouped-GEMM launch per projection with on-the-fly in-register decompression.

m0 is our reference implementation for checking correctness, not the kernel that baseline SGLang runs in production. It steps through the hit local experts one by one in a Python loop: every time an expert is hit, m0 decompresses that expert's entire weight set into a 201.3 MB201.3\text{ MB}201.3 MB FP32 dense matrix, writes it back to HBM, and then multiplies against that dense matrix.
