Look at the HBM byte accounting for a single hit expert: the useful weights are only 28.3 MB28.3\text{ MB}28.3 MB, yet reading the 4-bit weights, writing out the dense FP32 matrix, and reading that dense matrix back moves at least 28.3+201.3+201.3=431.0 MB28.3 + 201.3 + 201.3 = 431.0\text{ MB}28.3+201.3+201.3=431.0 MB—about 15× the useful bytes.

Across the 6 benchmark cases, m0 takes a measured geometric-mean Stage 6 latency of about 37.8 ms37.8\text{ ms}37.8 ms. Scaled by the average number of hit experts per case, that HBM round trip alone still costs about 1 ms1\text{ ms}1 ms even at full HBM bandwidth; its actual share was not measured separately (see the chart below). Beyond that round trip, each hit expert in the per-expert loop also runs two dequantizations (producing temporary FP32 tensors), two FP32 matrix multiplications, SwiGLU, normalization, and a small launch that adds the result back into the output by token index. The share of each item was not measured. m1a drops the HBM round trip, the per-expert loop, the temporary tensors, and the repeated small launches all at once, running about 80× faster than m0.

m1 removes that extra round trip in two steps. First (m1a in the first chart at the end of the chapter), we run token bucketing (grouping tokens that hit the same expert together) and then launch a single grouped GEMM grid per projection instead of launching once per expert. A grouped GEMM is a single launch where each CTA processes one token tile for one expert. Stage 6 now runs in four parts: "token bucketing → gate/up grouped GEMM (with SwiGLU) → down-projection grouped GEMM → post-expert RMSNorm and weighted accumulation." Once an expert's 4-bit codewords and block scales arrive on chip, we decode them to BF16 right in registers and feed them straight into the matrix multiply without writing back any dense weights; HBM reads the 4-bit weights only once. This step is faster on all 6 benchmark cases (see the first chart at the end of the chapter).

Second (m1 in the first chart at the end of the chapter), we interleave the gate and up projections in 32+3232 + 3232+32 rows so the gate and up outputs for the same row land in the same tile and can run SwiGLU directly. At the same time, we switch weight decoding to branchless bitwise unpacking (see Chapter 6, Section 3) and turn on Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL; see Chapter 1, Section 4) so the next kernel launches early to prefetch static weights. Even with those improvements, m1 still takes about 1.6× the latency of baseline SGLang, and only overtakes the baseline with m2 in the next section. What we pay for m1 is maintaining a fixed-shape token-bucketing index table ahead of the matrix multiplications; the overhead of that table and the individual shares of the three items in Step 2 were not measured separately.

3When MeM_eMe​ Is Only a Handful to a Dozen Tokens, How Do We Pipeline Weight Loads?

For T≥16T \ge 16T≥16, m2 switches to a pipelined wgmma tiled kernel, splitting along K at small batch sizes to fill SMs and using a multi-slot weight ring buffer to hide weight loads behind compute.

Step 1 replaces the kernel: m2 switches to Hopper's asynchronous wgmma instruction, placing the in-register decoded weights in operand A and the tokens on the operand-B side (swap-AB; see Chapter 5, Sections 3–5). This is a full kernel rewrite that lands multiple changes together; see m2a in the first chart at the end of the chapter for the change in the 60-layer total. m2 uses different MMA instructions at different TTT: T≤8T \le 8T≤8 keeps warp-level mma.sync (Section 4 explains why), whereas T≥16T \ge 16T≥16 uses wgmma. Running wgmma with operand A in registers (RS mode; Chapter 5, Section 3) has a catch: weight decoding consumes ALU cycles and registers, and when ALU decoding cycles exceed Tensor Core cycles, operand supply cannot keep up (see Chapter 6, Section 4 for a counterexample). In the Me<58M_e < 58Me​<58 regime, once decoding instructions are compressed tightly enough, this does not happen; in early m2 (m2b), however, the decoding sequence is still too long, and ALU decoding latency is the bottleneck that holds Stage 6 above the weight-read lower bound.

Step 2 raises the tile count. The down projection has only 4096 output columns, half of the 8192 columns of the gate/up projection, so at T≤32T \le 32T≤32 there are not enough tiles to fill all 132 SMs. Using Split-K from Chapter 2, Section 5, we split the down projection along K into 4 slices for T≤8T \le 8T≤8 and 2 slices for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, writing the partial sums into an intermediate BF16 matrix that the post-expert RMSNorm kernel sums along the way. At T=1T = 1T=1, even the gate/up projection runs short of tiles, so we split it along K into 2 or 3 slices as well. A separate reduction kernel sums those partial sums at first, before we fuse that reduction into the GEMM kernel in Section 6 (Figure 8-5). What Split-K costs us is writing and reading an extra buffer of partial sums and running the reduction additions, plus the lower precision of BF16 partial sums compared to FP32. Splitting too finely loses performance—cutting the T=16T = 16T=16 down projection into 4 slices makes it slower (see the second chart below).

Step 3 keeps weight reads in flight continuously. Following the multi-slot ring buffer of Chapter 3, Section 4 (Figure 3-4), we allocate 3 weight slots in shared memory so the kernel sustains the bytes in flight needed to saturate HBM (Chapter 2, Section 3; Chapter 5, Section 6). This version also switches to paired 4-bit nibble decoding (each instruction decodes a pair of 4-bit codewords into a pair of BF16 values, BF16x2, at once; see Chapter 6, Section 3), cutting the 60-layer total by more than half (see m2c in the first chart at the end of the chapter). If we remove just the 3-slot ring buffer, Stage 6 at T=16T = 16T=16 and T=32T = 32T=32 slows down by only 5–6 µs; the rest of the gain comes from paired 4-bit nibble decoding and other minor changes in the same version, which were not measured separately.

We then extend the 3-slot ring buffer to T=8T = 8T=8 (in the same version, we also lower registers per thread to raise occupancy) and add a weight-only 2-slot ring buffer at T=128T = 128T=128 and T=256T = 256T=256, saving about 19 μs19\ \mu\text{s}19 μs in Stage 6 at T=256T = 256T=256 (see the chart below). Opening too many ring slots consumes extra shared memory and drops occupancy (see Section 4; for the counterexample where too few slots leave insufficient bytes in flight, see Section 9). We also tried refilling ring slots early inside the loop, where the compiler inserted a CTA barrier between refilling and dequantization and made the kernel slower (see the second chart below).

Step 4 offloads the decoding left shift onto the FMA pipeline (left-shift FMA offloading; see Chapter 5, Section 1). That speeds up 5 of the 6 benchmark cases and saves up to about 9.4 μs9.4\ \mu\text{s}9.4 μs in Stage 6 at T=128T = 128T=128; at T=8T = 8T=8, however, the loop is too short to hide the ~2 extra cycles of latency (measured in Chapter 5, Section 1), so it runs slower.

4Why Does the Same Occupancy Change Turn from Faster to Slower Under a Different Routing Distribution?

As the number of active experts varies with routing, the total tile count varies too; changing per-SM occupancy alters the wave count only for routing distributions that cross a full-wave capacity step.

Back in Chapter 2, Section 1, we calculated wave counts: when each SM holds kkk resident CTAs at once, a single wave fits 132k132k132k CTAs, and total runtime is approximately ⌈Ac/(132k)⌉×\lceil A c / (132 k) \rceil \times⌈Ac/(132k)⌉× the duration of one wave. The expert kernel adds a moving variable: the number of active experts AAA is not constant, because different routing distributions hit different numbers of local experts, so the device-wide tile count AcA cAc (where ccc is the CTAs per expert) fluctuates with the routing distribution. Any change that alters kkk shifts the capacity step 132k132k132k. Routing distributions whose tile counts land between the old and new steps run one wave more or one wave fewer, shifting latency by several to over ten microseconds; distributions that do not cross a step see only the small intrinsic cost or benefit of the change itself.

We have a direct measured example at T=8T = 8T=8. We replace mma.sync with wgmma (see Chapter 5, Section 3); each expert launches c=128c = 128c=128 CTAs (gate/up projection 8,192 columns÷64 columns/CTA8{,}192\text{ columns} \div 64\text{ columns/CTA}8,192 columns÷64 columns/CTA), per-SM occupancy drops from k=9k = 9k=9 to k=8k = 8k=8, and a single wave shrinks from 1,1881{,}1881,188 CTAs to 1,0561{,}0561,056. The two routing distributions with A=9A = 9A=9 have 9×128=1,1529 \times 128 = 1{,}1529×128=1,152 CTAs, so they drop right across the boundary from 1 wave into 2 waves and slow Stage 6 down by over 10 μs10\ \mu\text{s}10 μs. The other three routing distributions (A=8A = 8A=8, still within 1 wave) run slightly faster instead (see the chart below). The same thing happens at T=16T = 16T=16 and T=32T = 32T=32 when we expand the weight ring buffer from the previous section from 3 slots to 4 slots and per-SM occupancy drops from 8 to 7: averaged across multiple routing distributions it is about 1.9 μs1.9\ \mu\text{s}1.9 μs faster, yet at each workload size one routing distribution crosses the step and slows down.

That directly sets a rule: every occupancy or register change to an expert kernel must be benchmarked across multiple routing distributions simultaneously; a change that wins on only one distribution is rejected (benchmarking across multiple routing distributions also multiplies test time by the number of distributions). To stop a change from moving the wave step 132k132k132k, we pin each CTA's register and shared-memory usage to the exact quota that fits kkk CTAs per SM (Chapter 3, Section 1), isolating the change's own gain or loss. We pinned occupancy this way in two places: pinning the T=1T = 1T=1 weight ring buffer at 6 CTAs per SM, and pinning the new weight-only 2-slot ring buffer of the T=16T = 16T=16 down projection at 7 CTAs per SM. Both flipped from a slowdown to a speedup (see the chart below). At T=1T = 1T=1, we also switched from a 3-slot ring to a 2-slot ring in the same change, and the two changes were not measured separately; why T=1T = 1T=1 slowed down without pinned occupancy was not measured either.

The cost of pinning occupancy is a tighter per-thread register cap. Push the compiler attribute __maxnreg__(N) too low and the compiler spills excess values to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1). Switching to wgmma at T=8T = 8T=8 and capping registers at 56 spills 8 registers per thread and slows Stage 6 by about 62 μs62\ \mu\text{s}62 μs; capping at 80 or 72 registers at T=256T = 256T=256 also causes slowdowns from register spilling (see the chart below).

Adding warps per CTA does not necessarily pay off either. Expanding each CTA from 8 warps to 16 warps at T=32T = 32T=32 (from 2 to 4 warps per SMSP) saves only about 0.85 μs0.85\ \mu\text{s}0.85 μs, which sits right around the run-to-run variation of the same configuration (about 0.78 μs0.78\ \mu\text{s}0.78 μs) and shows no clear gain, while costing an extra 8 warps of registers per CTA.

5How Do Blank Padding Rows in the Tail Tiles of Light Experts Stop Burning Tensor Core Cycles?

Check the valid row count at tile entry and step the MMA row height down through 32→16→832 \to 16 \to 832→16→8 for partially filled tail tiles.

Because token bucketing in Section 2 requires all tokens in a tile to belong to the same expert, we have to pad each expert's token count up to a multiple of the tile height BMBMBM (BMBMBM is the number of tokens per tile, which maps to nnn of wgmma after swap-AB). Under skewed routing, many light experts receive only a few tokens, and the last tile of a heavy expert (its tail tile, a partially filled M-tile) often holds only a few valid rows as well; the extra rows padded at the bottom are called padding rows. If we do nothing, every matrix multiplication issues at the full tile height.

Tail-tile M-dimension trimming checks the valid row count at tile entry and picks a narrower MMA instruction shape whenever a tail tile has fewer than 32 valid rows. Because swap-AB puts tokens on the nnn side of wgmma (see Chapter 5, Section 4), and the instruction shape m64nNk16 fixes m=64m = 64m=64 while letting nnn take any multiple of 8 (see Chapter 5, Section 3), a tail tile can step down through three heights: 32→16→832 \to 16 \to 832→16→8.

How much tail-tile trimming saves varies with MeM_eMe​. On verify workloads (MeM_eMe​ around a dozen), tail tiles make up a large share of all tiles: trimming the gate/up projection to 16 rows at T=256T = 256T=256 saves about 26 μs26\ \mu\text{s}26 μs in Stage 6 in a single step, and extending trimming to the down projection and the 8-row step at T=128T = 128T=128 and T=256T = 256T=256 saves more still (see the chart below). As MeM_eMe​ grows larger, on the other hand, the tail tile is only a small fraction at the end of a long queue, so the gain from trimming shrinks (the prefill kernel applies the same trimming; see Section 15).

What you pay for tail-tile trimming is generating extra narrow-tile code branches in the kernel and running one valid-row check at tile entry; at what workload size it loses performance was not measured.

6At T = 1..32, How Are Multi-Launch Round Trips Folded into a Persistent Kernel?

Fold bucketing, gate/up projection, and down projection into a persistent kernel with 132 resident CTAs; for T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32, split back into two PDL-chained kernels to avoid the grid barrier.

In Stage 6, m2 launches token bucketing, the gate/up projection, the down projection, and post-expert RMSNorm one after another, paying a tail wave on every launch. As we saw in Section 3, at T=1T = 1T=1 even the gate/up projection uses Split-K, where each slice writes out partial sums first. Late in m2 (m2g in the end-of-chapter chart), T=1T = 1T=1 takes three steps to cut down the launch count. First, the last-arriving CTA of the gate/up projection sums the Split-K partial sums inside the same kernel (see Chapter 2, Section 7 for ticket numbers and last-arriver reduction), eliminating the separate reduction kernel launch. Second, we drop the standalone bucketing kernel and fold bucketing into the GEMM kernel. Third, the last-arriving CTA reduces the down-projection Split-K partial sums inside the kernel as well. Together, those three steps save about 3.4 μs3.4\ \mu\text{s}3.4 μs (see the chart below).

In the third generation (m3), Stage 6 moves to a persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1): 132 CTAs stay resident on the SMs, and each CTA grabs the next tile instead of exiting when a tile finishes. Inside the kernel, Phase 0 runs token bucketing, followed by the gate/up projection with SwiGLU and then the down projection, streaming weights through a TMA ring buffer (see Chapter 3, Sections 3 and 4). Matrix multiplication inside m3 uses warp-level mma.sync (see Chapter 5, Section 3) rather than wgmma. Because m3 keeps 132 CTAs resident, it has no wave capacity steps (the Section 4 example where occupancy dropped from 9 to 8 and crossed a wave step was measured on m2's non-persistent grid); why mma.sync was still chosen was not determined. Each MMA tile holds at most 8 tokens, and experts with more than 8 tokens are split across multiple passes (see virtual passes below). At T=8T = 8T=8, moving to this persistent kernel saves about 16 μs16\ \mu\text{s}16 μs in Stage 6 (see the chart below).

Phase 0 token bucketing inside the kernel also makes two changes. First, instead of one thread serially scanning 256 slots (for example, 32 tokens×8 slots32\text{ tokens} \times 8\text{ slots}32 tokens×8 slots at T=32T = 32T=32), 8 warps scan 32 slots each in parallel. __ballot_sync collects a yes/no predicate from each of a warp's 32 lanes into a 32-bit integer where bit iii holds lane iii's answer, and __popc counts the set bits in that integer to tell us how many lanes in this warp hit. Each warp writes its hit count n to shared memory; after an intra-CTA barrier, summing n across the preceding warps gives this warp's write offset base:

hit  = (topk_id[slot] == e);              // each lane tests whether its slot hits expert e
mask = __ballot_sync(FULL, hit);          // FULL = 0xffffffff (all 32 lanes participate)
n    = __popc(mask);                      // number of hits in this warp
pos  = base + __popc(mask & lanes_below); // lanes_below = (1u << lane) - 1 (mask of lower-numbered lanes)

That whole bitmap scan takes about 40 cycles; its speedup was measured together with the entry staggering in Section 7, and their individual shares were not measured (see the second chart below).

Second, in the bucketing count table, when 32 threads write to the same column at once, all 32 words land in the same shared-memory bank and trigger a 32-way bank conflict. Padding each row by 1 word (a 33-word row stride, adding only 128 B128\text{ B}128 B of shared memory) staggers the banks (see Chapter 3, Section 7 for the mechanism). Both the small-batch persistent kernel here and the persistent wgmma kernel in Section 9 use this 33-word-stride count table; the third chart below shows its single-layer speedup, while its break-even boundary was not measured.

Next, how do we handle hot experts? At T=16T = 16T=16 and T=32T = 32T=32, we split experts receiving more than 8 tokens into 8-token virtual passes, while experts with at most 8 tokens run a single pass and skip the pass loop on the single-pass fast path. The catch with virtual passes is that a hot expert re-reads its weights on every extra pass. Why not widen each pass to 16 tokens instead? We tried that: per-step instructions grew by 16%, slowing execution down on routing distributions with many active experts at T=16T = 16T=16 and T=32T = 32T=32. By T≥128T \ge 128T≥128, hot experts need many passes and re-read their weights on every pass, which is why we switch kernels in Section 9.

Once the gate/up projection and the down projection are merged into a single persistent kernel, the down projection has to wait until the entire GPU finishes writing gu. Because CUDA guarantees full-grid co-residency only under cooperative launch (see Chapter 7, Section 12 for the conditions required without cooperative launch), the T=1T = 1T=1 persistent kernel uses cooperative launch; all 132 resident CTAs synchronize once at a grid barrier, which takes about 1.4 μs1.4\ \mu\text{s}1.4 μs in a microbenchmark. Because T=1T = 1T=1 has no tail-wave imbalance, splitting the kernel buys nothing, so we keep 1 cooperatively launched persistent kernel.

For T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32, however, splitting the gate/up projection and the down projection into two kernels chained back-to-back with PDL pays off. Because each kernel uses over 118 KiB118\text{ KiB}118 KiB of shared memory, the two kernels cannot co-reside on the same SM. Still, as soon as a gate/up CTA exits an SM, that SM immediately accepts a down-projection CTA, preloads its weight ring buffer into shared memory while the other SMs are finishing, and then pauses at the synchronization point. Splitting into two kernels costs one extra PDL edge of about 0.64 μs0.64\ \mu\text{s}0.64 μs (see Chapter 1, Section 4) and pays off only when tail-wave skew leaves time to preload before the wait, netting under 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs in Stage 6 (see the chart below).

Can we stay in a single kernel and avoid the grid barrier? We tested fine-grained tile counters (where each finished gu tile increments its own counter so the down projection waits only for the tiles it needs) and in-band payload readiness flags (encoding the readiness flag and the gu payload in the same word). Every fine-grained counter handoff requires a device-wide memory barrier—the device-scope acq_rel memory fence from Chapter 2, Section 6: the issuing warp stalls until all prior writes reach L2, while other warps and SMs keep running. That slowed down several benchmark cases, and in-band payload readiness flags also slowed T=1T = 1T=1 by about 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs (the exact causes of the slowdown in both approaches were not measured separately).

The post-expert RMSNorm kernel reads back y, skips non-local slots, and completes Steps 4 and 5 of Section 1; it already overlaps with the main kernel via PDL. Fusing it into the tail of the main kernel hurts the main kernel's occupancy and tail wave, making execution slower. Section 10 explains how late-arriving CTAs get assigned less work after this split.

7At Persistent Kernel Startup, Why Does Activation p Wait in Line Behind Weights?

At kernel entry, all 132 SMs issuing 3 weight slots simultaneously flood the memory queue with ~14 MB of requests; issuing p and Slot 0 first while delaying Slots 1–2 by a few hundred nanoseconds prevents p from queueing behind weights.

At T=1T = 1T=1, activation p is only a few kilobytes, yet kernel-entry timestamps show that loading p takes about 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs longer than loading p in isolation. Why? Because normal global loads (LDG) and TMA requests (see Chapter 3, Section 3) contend for the same queue along the memory path (whether the bottleneck sits in L2 or in the HBM controller was not measured). That is queueing delay (see Chapter 7, Section 6): a small request of a few kilobytes gets stuck in line behind roughly 14 MB14\text{ MB}14 MB of bulk weight requests.

To fix it, we flip the issue order: issue the load of p and Slot 0 weights first, and then spin-wait on the GPU nanosecond timer for a few hundred nanoseconds before issuing Slots 1 and 2. This technique is called open-loop staggering (using a fixed delay without checking whether the data has arrived). At T=1T = 1T=1 (a single cooperative kernel), the delay is 500 ns500\text{ ns}500 ns; the same version also preloads tensor scales into shared memory and caps registers per thread at T=1T = 1T=1 so the post-expert RMSNorm CTA can co-reside on the same SM. Together, that saves about 1.1 μs1.1\ \mu\text{s}1.1 μs in Stage 6 (in the same benchmark round, T=8,16,32T = 8, 16, 32T=8,16,32 include only tensor-scale preloading; see the second chart below). Once T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32 are split into two PDL kernels, the next round adds issuing p first and staggering to the gate/up kernel: T=8T = 8T=8 uses 600 ns600\text{ ns}600 ns, whereas T=16T = 16T=16 and 323232 only issue p first with a 0 ns0\text{ ns}0 ns delay (at T=32T = 32T=32, adding a delay produced a delta within that round's A/A run-to-run variation).

Because this is an open-loop wait, we cannot stretch the delay too far—waiting too long just artificially delays the weights. Sweeping the delay at T=8T = 8T=8 (see the chart below) shows the tradeoff: 0 ns0\text{ ns}0 ns (only issuing p first) captures only about half the gain, the three settings across 300–800 ns300\text{–}800\text{ ns}300–800 ns perform similarly (with 600 ns600\text{ ns}600 ns chosen in the end), and by 1,200 ns1{,}200\text{ ns}1,200 ns the saving drops back again.

The catch with open-loop staggering is that the best delay shifts with TTT, so each TTT needs its own sweep; a closed-loop alternative ("wait until p arrives, then issue Slots 1 and 2") was not measured. On the T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256 kernel (Section 9), delaying Weight Slots 1 and 2 moves the first MMA instruction earlier by only about 0.4 μs0.4\ \mu\text{s}0.4 μs, and the upper bound on remaining savings at kernel entry is less than 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs, so we stopped here.

8In the SASS of the Post-Expert RMSNorm Kernel, What Did the Compiler Schedule Poorly, and What Can Be Loaded Before Waiting?

An empty asm volatile statement blocks rematerialization, and issuing loads via asm volatile blocks instruction sinking; both are only effects observed with the current compiler, not guarantees of the specification.

The first compiler rewrite we run into is rematerialization: instead of keeping a value that has already been computed, the compiler throws it away and recomputes it every time it is needed. Take this 4-line example: outside the loop, the kernel unpacks 16 BF16 weights w[i] to FP32 (Chapter 6, Section 1), adds 1.0f, and stores them into nw[i], then reuses nw[i] repeatedly inside the loop:

float nw[16];
for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) nw[i] = 1.0f + float(w[i]);
for (int step = 0; step < steps; ++step)
    for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) acc[i] += x[step][i] * nw[i];

To save those 16 registers, ptxas may throw nw[i] away and unpack the BF16 w[i] to FP32 and add 1.0f again on every loop iteration. The numerical result stays identical, but every iteration runs 16 extra unpacks and 16 extra additions.

To stop ptxas from doing that, we place an empty inline-assembly barrier (asm volatile) asm volatile("" : "+f"(nw[i])); right after the precomputation:

for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) {
    nw[i] = 1.0f + float(w[i]);
    asm volatile("" : "+f"(nw[i]));
}

Because this empty assembly statement declares that it "reads and writes nw[i]," the compiler must treat nw[i] as the output of an opaque instruction that cannot be rematerialized from w[i]. At runtime it emits 0 instructions, at the cost of holding 16 FP32 registers (64 B per thread) live throughout the loop; when registers are already tight, occupancy may drop by one step (not measured).

The second compiler rewrite is instruction sinking (code sinking), where the compiler moves instructions to a later point in the schedule. In Chapter 1, Section 4, the call cudaGridDependencySynchronize() that waits for the predecessor kernel compiles to griddepcontrol.wait in PTX and ACQBULK in SASS. Before that wait, the kernel can issue loads for data that the predecessor kernel does not write (such as this kernel's own static weights), overlapping those loads with the wait:

uint4 w0 = w_ptr[idx];              // load issued early
cudaGridDependencySynchronize();    // PTX: griddepcontrol.wait / SASS: ACQBULK
use(w0);                            // consumed only after the wait

griddepcontrol.wait is an acquire barrier (Chapter 2, Section 6): accesses ordered after the acquire cannot move ahead of it, but moving normal loads ordered before the acquire down past the wait is completely legal. Once those loads sink past ACQBULK, the overlap between loading and waiting is gone. When we issue those loads with asm volatile, the SASS from our build shows that the loads stay ahead of the wait. Still, the PTX specification makes no such promise, so you need to inspect the SASS again after changing compiler versions.

There is a strict correctness boundary here: data written by the predecessor kernel (its output tensors and the routing results it computed) is guaranteed to be visible only after griddepcontrol.wait. Loading predecessor outputs early is valid only when both grids belong to the same memory synchronization domain (the CUDA grouping that determines which kernels share fence synchronization; all kernels share the default domain unless configured otherwise) and the predecessor kernel finishes writing and executes a GPU-scope release fence before triggering the successor (see Chapter 9, Section 5 for the complete rules and measured data-race violations). Instruction sinking itself affects only speed, not correctness.

Stage 6's post-expert RMSNorm kernel ran into both compiler rewrites at once. First was instruction sinking: in the single-operator benchmark, the kernel entry originally used ld.global.nc (routing loads through the SM's read-only cache path). It issued 6 pre-wait 16 B16\text{ B}16 B loads—2 each for w_post, topk_weights, and topk_ids—which ptxas sank past ACQBULK. Switching to normal global loads issued via asm volatile kept all 6 LDG.E.128 instructions ahead of ACQBULK, saving up to about 0.7 μs0.7\ \mu\text{s}0.7 μs in Stage 6 at T=16T = 16T=16 (see the chart below). The tradeoff is bypassing the read-only cache path, which pays off only when the main kernel does not occupy all 132 SMs and leaves an overlap window for the post-expert RMSNorm kernel. At T=128T = 128T=128, the main kernel occupies all SMs, leaving no overlap window and making execution slower (so the final single-operator version enables this only for T≤32T \le 32T≤32).

All 6 prefetches are safe together only in the single-operator benchmark, where none of the 3 inputs has a predecessor writer. Once integrated into the full layer in Chapter 9, topk_weights and topk_ids are written by the Stage 4 kernel; without a predecessor release fence, reading them before the wait causes the data race described in the correctness boundary above. The final full-layer version therefore keeps only the static weight w_post ahead of the wait and moves topk_weights and topk_ids back after the wait (see Chapter 9, Section 5 for the rule governing what can be read before wait).

Second was rematerialization: the 16 values nwi=1+wpost,inw_i = 1 + w_{post,i}nwi​=1+wpost,i​ that the post-expert RMSNorm kernel precomputed outside the loop were pulled back into the inner loop and recomputed, adding 321 FADD instructions and 162 unpacking instructions. Adding the empty inline-assembly barrier cut static SASS from 1,603 instructions down to 1,120; for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, the latency delta is at most about 0.3 μs0.3\ \mu\text{s}0.3 μs, which lies within run-to-run variation and shows no certain speedup (see the chart below; larger TTT values were not measured).

9At T = 128..256, Why Switch to a Persistent wgmma Kernel?

A persistent wgmma kernel with 132 resident CTAs lets up to 64 tokens routed to a hot expert share a single tile so weights are read only once, while eliminating full-kernel handoff waits between bucketing, gate/up projection, and down projection.

m3 suffices for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, but by T=128,256T = 128, 256T=128,256, hot experts receive several dozen tokens each. Continuing with 8 tokens per pass would re-read a hot expert's weights on every pass, while falling back to m2's 4-kernel tiled scheme would pay 4 tail waves and force the down projection to wait for the entire gate/up kernel to finish before reading gu.

The fourth generation (m4) switches to a single persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1): 132 CTAs claim work from a shared global subtask table (assigned at a fixed stride at first, and switched to atomic dynamic claiming in the next section), completing in-kernel bucketing, the gate/up projection with SwiGLU, and the down projection in one launch. One subtask covers at most 64 token rows × 256 output columns of one expert. That lets a hot expert's tokens fit into a single tile so its weights are read from HBM only once, while gu is written to a global intermediate matrix that the down-projection phase reads directly (Section 11 explains how the down projection confirms that the gu tiles it needs have finished writing). The instruction family also switches back from mma.sync in m3 to wgmma: when token counts reach several dozen rows, only wgmma issued collectively by 4 warps can keep the Tensor Cores fed (see Chapter 5, Sections 3 and 5). At T=256T = 256T=256, this persistent wgmma kernel ultimately saves about 22 μs22\ \mu\text{s}22 μs in Stage 6 over the 4-kernel tiled scheme (see the chart below); its costs are having only 96 registers per thread, adding 2 producer warps per CTA, and maintaining the global subtask table.

In the initial version, each CTA has 18 warps (576 threads). During the kernel entry phase, 4 consumer warpgroups (512 threads) gather the activations of tokens hitting this GPU and write them into a global buffer; once the main loop begins, they dedicate themselves to matrix multiplication, while the other 2 warps serve exclusively as producers. Warp 16 uses TMA to feed the 3-slot shared-memory weight ring buffer. Warp 17 uses TMA to feed activations from the global buffer into the shared-memory activation ring buffer: the gate/up projection reads the gathered p, and the down projection reads the gu written by the gate/up projection. Slots in both ring buffers synchronize via full and empty mbarrier signals (see Chapter 3, Sections 3–5).

Only 96 registers per thread: in the Chapter 3, Section 6 example (1 CTA per SM, 2 consumer warpgroups), each consumer thread got 232 registers; here we have 4 consumer warpgroups, and 4×128×232=118,784>65,5364 \times 128 \times 232 = 118{,}784 > 65{,}5364×128×232=118,784>65,536 does not fit. When the compiler computes the register cap from __launch_bounds__, it rounds the thread count up to a multiple of 128: 576 threads are billed as 640, giving 65,536/640=102.465{,}536 / 640 = 102.465,536/640=102.4, which rounds down to a multiple of 8 to land on 96. That differs from the per-warp allocation formula in Chapter 3, Section 1, which would give 112 registers for 576 threads.

When this kernel was first built, profiling exposed two issues. First, non-MMA stores were interleaved inside the wgmma pipeline region, so ptxas reported that it could not pipeline the region and serialized wgmma (inserting a wait after every HGMMA; see Chapter 6, Section 6 for the mechanism); moving those stores out of the region removed the problem. Second, activation gathering at kernel entry initially wrote scalars, which we changed to 16 B16\text{ B}16 B coalesced wide stores (see Chapter 3, Section 2 for the principle). The same version also eliminated register spills and parallelized Phase 0 bucketing. Both initial rounds were slower than the 4-kernel tiled scheme (the scalar-gather round was about 19 μs19\ \mu\text{s}19 μs slower; see the second chart below for the other round). Only after removing serialization and switching to 16 B16\text{ B}16 B coalesced wide stores did the persistent kernel overtake the tiled scheme, saving about 13 μs13\ \mu\text{s}13 μs. The optimizations in Sections 10 and 11 then built on top of this to reach the roughly 22 μs22\ \mu\text{s}22 μs saving shown in the first chart of this section.

In addition, each slot of this kernel's weight ring buffer takes 36 KiB36\text{ KiB}36 KiB (32 KiB32\text{ KiB}32 KiB of codewords plus 4 KiB4\text{ KiB}4 KiB of block scales for 256 columns×inner dimension 256 elements256\text{ columns} \times \text{inner dimension } 256\text{ elements}256 columns×inner dimension 256 elements). By the rule in Chapter 3, Section 4, while 1 slot is being computed, the remaining N−1N - 1N−1 slots are in flight: a 3-slot ring keeps 2 slots (72 KiB72\text{ KiB}72 KiB) in flight, whereas shrinking to 2 slots leaves only 1 slot (36 KiB36\text{ KiB}36 KiB) in flight—below the roughly 48 KiB48\text{ KiB}48 KiB per SM required to saturate HBM. Shrinking the ring alone therefore slows Stage 6 by about 1.2–1.3 μs1.2\text{–}1.3\ \mu\text{s}1.2–1.3 μs at T=128T = 128T=128 and T=256T = 256T=256 (see the third chart below).

The same 256-column wide tile, however, is a poor fit at T=128T = 128T=128. One token tile (M-tile of routed tokens) holds up to 64 hit pairs of the same expert, so each of the 32 local experts contributes ⌈cnt/64⌉\lceil \text{cnt}/64 \rceil⌈cnt/64⌉ token tiles; the T=128T = 128T=128 routing distribution in the single-operator benchmark produces 22 token tiles in total. The down projection has 4096 columns÷256=164096\text{ columns} \div 256 = 164096 columns÷256=16 column tiles, giving 22×16=35222 \times 16 = 35222×16=352 tiles in total. Because 352/132≈2.67352 / 132 \approx 2.67352/132≈2.67, the 132 resident CTAs take 3 passes, leaving only two-thirds of the CTAs with work in the third pass (see Chapter 2, Section 1 for tail waves). That fractional pass cancels the gain of the single wide tile, and the measured result is a tie. Making CTAs poll a global flag before starting the down-projection phase to confirm that all gate/up tiles have finished writing (a polling barrier, distinct from the per-tile completion flags in Section 11) makes execution slower still (see the first chart of this section).

10How Do All 132 Resident CTAs Finish Together?

All five optimizations target tail latency: longest-processing-time-first ordering, atomic producer work claiming, reverse-order down-projection assignment, tail K-halves splitting, and reduced work quotas for late-arriving CTAs.

The duration of a persistent kernel equals the duration of its last-exiting CTA. When full heavy subtasks and light 8-row tail tiles (which still read an entire weight tile, taking about 17 μs17\ \mu\text{s}17 μs) are mixed together, whichever CTA lands a heavy task near the end stalls the entire GPU. Each of the five changes below pays off only when there is a tail skew to trim:

First is LPT (Longest Processing Time first scheduling), which we already used in prefill attention in Chapter 7, Section 4: we sort subtasks in descending order of padded token count so heavy subtasks run first and short 8-row subtasks fill the remaining gaps across SMs at the end. The cost is maintaining a global sort permutation; when almost all 32 experts consist of full tiles (T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 and 16,38416{,}38416,384), there are no short tail tiles left to pack, and the gain drops to zero (see the fourth chart below).

Second is dynamic work claiming (atomic ticket). Here we look at another T=128T = 128T=128 routing distribution from the full-layer benchmark (not the one in Section 9): 16 token tiles, each with 32 gate/up subtasks and 16 down-projection subtasks, for 768 subtasks in total. With fixed-stride static assignment, 108 CTAs get 6 subtasks and 24 CTAs get 5. That one-subtask gap comes from integer division and cannot be eliminated. The real saving comes from uneven subtask durations: gate/up and down-projection subtasks take different amounts of time, and so do full tiles versus short 8-row tail tiles. Under a fixed stride, a CTA that happens to draw several slow subtasks in a row drags out the tail, while SMs assigned only 5 subtasks finish early and sit idle. Instead, while the current subtask is running, each CTA's weight-producer warp uses a single atomic add to claim the next subtask from the global queue in LPT order (the latency of a single atomic add was not measured). Dynamic work claiming pays off only when single-subtask duration far exceeds claiming overhead and claiming introduces no extra intra-CTA barrier: here a single subtask runs for over ten microseconds, and the claimed ticket rides along with the weight ring slot to the consumers without adding a barrier. In Chapter 7, Section 4, by contrast, one attention key tile takes only about 1–2 μs1\text{–}2\ \mu\text{s}1–2 μs, and every claim would add an extra intra-CTA barrier and handoff, which loses performance.

Third is reverse load-rank assignment. In the earlier version, the gate/up projection and the down projection claimed subtasks in the same alternating sweep order, so the heaviest down-projection subtasks landed on the exact CTAs that had just finished the heaviest gate/up subtasks, stacking two heavy phases onto the same SMs. Recording each CTA's load rank during the gate/up phase lets the down projection assign work in reverse order: the CTAs with the lightest gate/up load claim the heaviest down-projection subtasks first. On the T=256T = 256T=256 sliding-window layer, this speeds up single-layer latency by about 5%5\%5% (see the third chart below; when reverse assignment would lose performance was not measured).

Fourth is tail K-halves splitting (see Chapter 2, Section 5 for the K-halves mechanism). Two conditions trigger it: the final wave of the down projection has at most 66 subtasks left (no more than half of 132), and the fifth-from-last subtask has only 8 rows (because subtasks are sorted from most rows to fewest, the last 5 subtasks are all short 8-row tiles). When both conditions hold, we split each of the last 66 subtasks in the table in half along K, creating 2 × 66 half-K tasks that divide evenly across all 132 SMs. Chapter 2, Section 5 splits only the subtasks left over in the final wave; here we also split subtasks from the end of the second-to-last wave to fill out a full set of 66. The first half writes out an FP32 partial sum and sets a readiness flag (release), and the second half waits on that flag (acquire) and adds its half in (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for the ordering rules of cross-SM partial-sum merging). That wait is guaranteed to finish: every first half sits ahead of its second half in the table, and persistent CTAs claim subtasks in table order. So the earliest unfinished subtask in the table only ever waits on subtasks that have already finished, never on a later subtask. With the split, the other half of the SMs, which would otherwise sit idle, get work too. The cost is an extra partial-sum matrix and a set of flags. Routing distributions that do not trigger splitting still pay for the branch and flag check and slow down (see the second chart below), so we enable splitting only when both conditions above hold.

Fifth is reduced quota for late-arriving CTAs. Once T=16T = 16T=16 and T=32T = 32T=32 are split into two kernels, hardware dispatches CTAs of the down-projection kernel in blockIdx.x order (see Chapter 2, Section 1), so the last-entering CTA 131 arrives about 2 μs2\ \mu\text{s}2 μs later than the earliest CTAs; assigning less work to CTAs 100–131 along a quadratic curve gives later CTAs progressively smaller quotas. Stage 6 saves another ~0.3 μs0.3\ \mu\text{s}0.3 μs; the confidence intervals across 80 routing distributions lie entirely above 0, while unmodified cases in the same benchmark round shift by at most 0.05 μs0.05\ \mu\text{s}0.05 μs (see the chart note below). This adjustment is enabled only on routing distributions where at least one expert runs two virtual passes (receiving 9–16 tokens; see Section 6); enabling it unconditionally on routing distributions without two-pass experts overloads the earlier CTAs and slows execution (see the second chart below).

11Why Do Consumers Stall on Synchronization, and How Do We Move GPU-Scope Releases Off the Critical Path?

When every consumer thread pays its own GPU-scope release, Stage 6 is measured about 93 µs slower; the fix has only one thread per warp issue the release once, and then hands the GPU-scope release to a dedicated warp.

In the persistent wgmma kernel, every time the consumer warpgroups finish a gate/up subtask, they set a completion flag to tell the down-projection phase that this gu tile has been written. The first bottleneck is having every thread issue its own release: all 512 consumer threads issue red.release.gpu on an L2 counter, so every thread pays a GPU-scope write drain while a large number of atomic operations queue up at the same L2 address. How much each of the two effects contributes was not measured separately; together they slow Stage 6 down by about 93 μs93\ \mu\text{s}93 μs. Instead, each warp first aligns with __syncwarp (making prior writes by threads in the same warp mutually visible) and lets only lane 0 issue the release once, dropping the count from 512 to 16. This works by cumulativity (see Chapter 2, Section 6): once a thread observes the writes of the other threads in its group across a barrier, its single release publishes all of those writes together.

The remaining problem is that every GPU-scope release runs a device-wide memory barrier between subtasks (fence.acq_rel.gpu compiles to a sequence of several SASS instructions including MEMBAR.ALL.GPU). L1 caches across SMs are not automatically coherent. On the writer side, each device-wide memory barrier has to wait for all prior global writes to drain to L2, measuring 0.6–1.3 μs0.6\text{–}1.3\ \mu\text{s}0.6–1.3 μs per barrier under full load. On the reader side, once a thread reads the flag with acquire.gpu, subsequent normal loads from that same thread see all prior writes published by the release (Chapter 2, Section 6). To publish completion flags and activation readiness, m4 makes four changes:

Step 1: an early version delays setting the completion flag by one wgmma group. When the current subtask finishes writing gu, it does not set the flag right away. Instead, it immediately issues the first wgmma group of the next subtask, and sets the previous subtask's completion flag only after that next subtask's wait_group<0> (see Chapter 5, Section 5) completes. A CTA's final gate/up subtask has no next gate/up subtask to wait on, so it issues its flag right before entering the down-projection phase, guaranteeing that every flag awaited by the down projection has been issued. Under the specification, the delayed release still comes after the gu writes in program order, so visibility does not change. The idea that "gu has already drained to L2 by then" is only a speed argument, and the specification makes no guarantee about drain timing. Compared with the 4-kernel baseline, this version saved 20.50 μs20.50\ \mu\text{s}20.50 μs when first measured; see the first chart of Section 9 for the final kernel's total saving. The cost is that the down-projection phase sees each flag one wgmma group later.

Step 2: publishing activation-gather readiness at kernel entry switches to a cross-proxy fence. Normal thread loads and stores travel through the generic proxy, whereas asynchronous TMA and wgmma reads travel through the async proxy; bridging the two takes fence.proxy.async (see Chapter 3, Section 3). On the reader side, the thread issuing TMA executes fence.proxy.async.global after ld.acquire.gpu and before issuing TMA (both when the gate/up projection reads gathered activations and when the down projection reads gu). On the writer side, 16 consumer warps write gathered activations into the global buffer at kernel entry, where previously every thread executed fence.acq_rel.gpu (5 SASS instructions). Now each thread executes only a single-instruction fence.proxy.async.global, and after a CTA barrier, thread 0 issues a single red.release.gpu; by cumulativity (Chapter 2, Section 6), this suffices (see the chart below for the speedup). For safety, we placed this cross-proxy fence on both the writer and reader sides; what happens if the writer-side fence is removed was not measured.

Step 3: consumers perform only an on-chip CTA-scope release and delegate the GPU-scope release to a dedicated release thread. This replaces the deferred-flag approach of Step 1. Each time consumers finish a gate/up subtask, they issue red.release.cta on a shared-memory counter; a dedicated thread polls the counter with ld.acquire.cta and, once the count reaches the target, issues a single red.release.gpu on behalf of the CTA for each subtask in order (including the final gate/up subtask; down-projection subtasks do not emit completion flags). When the dedicated thread observes the counter via acquire, it also observes all writes performed by the consumers before their release. When it then issues a GPU-scope release, it publishes all writes it has observed—cumulativity holds across scopes as well (see Chapter 2, Section 6). After warp 17 in the down projection observes the flag via ld.acquire.gpu, it likewise executes fence.proxy.async.global before issuing TMA (see Step 2). Because all gate/up subtasks precede all down-projection subtasks in the global subtask table, by the ordering invariant of Section 10 this wait cannot deadlock either.

Step 4: give the dedicated release thread its own dedicated release warp. Initially, the release thread lived on lane 1 of weight-producer warp 16. However, all 32 threads of a warp share a single instruction stream (see Chapter 4, Section 4): when stalled on a memory fence, the entire warp stalls, and while polling, lane 0 and lane 1 take turns occupying that single instruction stream, keeping lane 0 from issuing the next round of weight TMA loads promptly. We therefore add 1 extra warp per CTA (warp 18, expanding the CTA from 576 to 608 threads) and move the release thread there. At T=256T = 256T=256, deleting MEMBAR in place without moving the thread to a separate warp saves much less time (see the chart below), showing that most of the gain comes from no longer blocking lane 0. The cost is 32 extra threads per CTA (608 threads are still billed as 640 threads at the same 96-register per-thread cap from Section 9). Conversely, having this dedicated thread also emit per-phase signals to wake the post-expert RMSNorm kernel early does not pay off: the upper bound of tail latency that could be hidden is only 1.06–2.21 μs1.06\text{–}2.21\ \mu\text{s}1.06–2.21 μs, while emitting the signal itself costs 2.2–3.2 μs2.2\text{–}3.2\ \mu\text{s}2.2–3.2 μs, so every signaling variant tested ran slower.

There is also a correctness fix. Consumers must not arrive on the weight ring's empty barrier until compute instructions have consumed the data loaded from the slot; otherwise the producer's next TMA transfer can overwrite a slot that is still being read (see Chapter 3, Section 5 for the arrival rule). In the code, mbarrier.arrive.shared::cta uses the default .release.cta semantics. By the PTX specification, the default release should order prior shared-memory reads before the arrival, yet the compiled arrival instruction did not wait for the scoreboard of preceding shared-memory reads (see Chapter 4, Section 2 for scoreboards). In the single-operator version, moving the arrival after the wait on the activation ring's full barrier (Section 9) reduced data races from 551 occurrences across ~4.58 million calls to 0, at the cost of slowing Stage 6 by 0.4–1.6 μs0.4\text{–}1.6\ \mu\text{s}0.4–1.6 μs (this is a correctness requirement, not an optional optimization).

Waiting on the activation ring's full barrier, however, has no data dependency on the weight reads. In the compiled T=256T = 256T=256 full-layer version of Chapter 9, the compiler sank the decoding instructions that consume the weight registers past the arrival instruction, so moving the arrival position in source code was no longer enough; we therefore added an explicit fence.acq_rel.cta before the arrival. In SASS, this fence compiles to an instruction that waits for pending shared-memory reads to return, reducing outstanding reads at all arrival points from 24 to 0. The default release did not emit that wait instruction. By the specification the two should be equivalent, and the reason for the difference was not determined; this is an empirical behavior of the current compiler (Section 8). The race count of the fence version was not measured separately.

12Before Each CUDA Graph Replay, Who Zeros the Completion Counters?

Maintain even and odd counter arrays alternated by launch index; after griddepcontrol.wait returns, idle producer threads zero the opposite array for the next launch.

The completion flags in Section 11 are an array of global counters; on every CUDA Graph replay (see Chapter 1, Section 2), the next launch has to see all zeros. Previously, before each launch finished, every CTA ran an exit sequence (one device-wide memory barrier, two CTA barriers, one atomic increment, and several zeroing stores) so the last-exiting CTA could zero the counters. That exit sequence sat right on the critical path of the last-exiting CTA.

To get that cleanup off the tail, we switch to an even-odd ledger (ping-pong counter array): the counter buffer in device memory is doubled and split into an even ledger and an odd ledger (see Figure 8-11 for indices and buffer sizes). Before triggering the successor kernel, thread 0 of each CTA runs atom.inc on a global counter to claim a ticket ttt (see Chapter 2, Section 7 for atomic ticket numbers). Because that instruction carries the upper limit 2G−12G - 12G−1 (where GGG is the number of CTAs per launch), hardware wraps the counter back to 0 once it hits the limit, keeping every ticket ttt between 000 and 2G−12G - 12G−1. Taking ⌊t/G⌋\lfloor t / G \rfloor⌊t/G⌋ gives 0 or 1 to pick which ledger this launch uses: each launch claims GGG tickets that all land on the same ledger, and the next launch switches to the opposite ledger. Lanes 1–31 of the weight-producer warp are otherwise idle; after griddepcontrol.wait (see Chapter 1, Section 4; Section 8 of this chapter) returns and before the successor is triggered, they zero the inactive ledger for the next launch. The K-halves readiness flags and dynamic work-claiming counter from Section 10 are zeroed together inside the same even-odd ledger.

Why do tickets from two consecutive launches not interleave, and why does zeroing the opposite ledger not collide with the previous or next launch? Two preconditions guarantee this. First, every launch uses the same GGG. Second, every PDL-launched kernel on the same CUDA stream executes its wait before exiting, and claims its ticket and touches the ledger only after its own griddepcontrol.wait returns (see Chapter 7, Section 12 for this invariant). In the single-operator benchmark, this expert kernel runs without PDL and enters only after the preceding post-expert RMSNorm kernel finishes, which enforces the same ordering. Look backward first: the previous user of the opposite ledger is this expert kernel from the previous launch. By the time the current expert kernel's wait returns, the immediately preceding post-expert RMSNorm kernel has already exited; that kernel exited only after its own wait returned, by which point the kernel ahead of it had already exited. Walking backward along the PDL chain, the expert kernel from the previous launch has already exited completely and will not claim another ticket or touch that ledger. Now look forward: the next launch likewise claims tickets and touches the ledger only after its own wait returns, by which time the current launch (including its zeroing stores) has already finished, so neither tickets nor zeroing writes collide across launches.

Deleting the exit sequence from the tail of the kernel removes one device-wide memory barrier and two CTA barriers on the tail path, saving about 0.3 μs0.3\ \mu\text{s}0.3 μs in Stage 6 at T=256T = 256T=256 (see the chart below). The cost of the even-odd ledger is 4 KiB4\text{ KiB}4 KiB of extra device memory while shifting the zeroing stores onto the idle threads of the producer warp; whether any workload loses performance was not measured.

13What Bottlenecks the Gap Between Subtasks, and Why Does Folding the Scale into the Exponent Save Instructions?

The gap between subtasks is spent in the gate/up epilogue's SwiGLU, which is issue-slot bound; folding the tensor scale into the exponent argument and denominator cuts instructions from 9 to 7 per element.

Every subtask switch in the gate/up and down projections (including the tile epilogue; see Chapter 1, Section 3) takes about 1.31.31.3 and 1.8 μs1.8\ \mu\text{s}1.8 μs, adding up to about 12.7 μs12.7\ \mu\text{s}12.7 μs across all switches of a CTA (6.1%6.1\%6.1% of total kernel runtime). In m4's main loop, we alternate 2 register buffers for decoded weights (operand A) to get the inputs for the next wgmma group ready ahead of time. At first we suspected that this subtask gap was waiting on data, so we tried adding a third operand-A register buffer (wait_group<2>; see Chapter 5, Section 5) to keep one more wgmma group in flight and hide the gap. That gave zero gain, showing data supply was not the bottleneck. Counting the cycles of a single subtask epilogue tells us why: the 4 consumer warps on one SMSP take 932 issue cycles in total, more than the 768 cycles of the SFU (MUFU instructions). That means the epilogue is bottlenecked by the issue slot, which can issue at most one instruction per cycle (see Chapter 4, Section 1), rather than by SFU throughput (see Chapter 5, Section 1).

Here we also answer the question left open in Section 1: why do the gate half and the up-projection half of each expert share a single tensor scale sss? In the original model, the two halves have separate tensor scales sgs_gsg​ and sus_usu​; let r=su/sgr = s_u / s_gr=su​/sg​. Because SwiGLU is linear in the up projection uuu, changing uuu's scale from sus_usu​ to the gate scale sgs_gsg​ only multiplies the down-projection output yyy by a positive constant 1/r=sg/su1/r = s_g / s_u1/r=sg​/su​. And in Step 4 of Section 1, each expert runs its own RMSNorm right after the down projection and before the weighted accumulation across experts. Because RMSNorm divides a vector by its own root mean square, any positive constant c>0c > 0c>0 cancels out between numerator and denominator: ignoring the tiny constant ϵ\epsilonϵ, rmsnorm(c z)=rmsnorm(z)\mathrm{rmsnorm}(c\,z) = \mathrm{rmsnorm}(z)rmsnorm(cz)=rmsnorm(z). Each expert's gate/up projection therefore stores only a single tensor scale s=sgs = s_gs=sg​ (models without this per-expert normalization must store two separate scales).

Because instruction count is the bottleneck, we use that shared scale sss to fold instructions algebraically. Let dg,dud_g, d_udg​,du​ be the unscaled accumulator values in registers before multiplying by sss (g=s dgg = s\,d_gg=sdg​, u=s duu = s\,d_uu=sdu​), and substitute them into SwiGLU:

silu(g) u=s dg1+e−s dg s du=dg duk+k⋅2 dg⋅(−slog⁡2e),k=1/s2.\mathrm{silu}(g)\,u = \frac{s\,d_g}{1 + e^{-s\,d_g}}\, s\,d_u = \frac{d_g\, d_u}{k + k \cdot 2^{\,d_g \cdot (-s \log_2 e)}},\qquad k = 1/s^2 .silu(g)u=1+e−sdg​sdg​​sdu​=k+k⋅2dg​⋅(−slog2​e)dg​du​​,k=1/s2.

Here both −slog⁡2e-s \log_2 e−slog2​e and kkk are constants per expert: multiplying once when computing the exponent argument and evaluating the denominator with a single FFMA(e, k, k) absorbs both multiplications by sss. That cuts the epilogue from 9 instructions per element down to 7, saving about 0.6 μs0.6\ \mu\text{s}0.6 μs in Stage 6 at T=256T = 256T=256. Using ex2.approx.ftz (flushing subnormal numbers to 0; see Chapter 6, Section 3) then removes the fixup branch when the exponential result falls below 2−1262^{-126}2−126, saving another 48 instructions when each thread processes 8 tokens (see the chart below).

What epilogue scale folding costs is storing two precomputed constants (−slog⁡2e-s\log_2 e−slog2​e and kkk) per expert, and relying on the gate and up projections sharing a single scale. It helps only when the epilogue is issue-slot bound: it yields no gain in the small-batch kernel for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, and when ported to the full-layer expert kernels (m3 and m4) in Chapter 9, it cuts epilogue instructions by 22%–41%22\%\text{–}41\%22%–41%. Inside the full layer, however, the expert kernels are bottlenecked by scoreboard and barrier waits rather than issue slots, leaving single-layer latency unchanged (0.999×0.999\times0.999×).

14When All 32 Experts Are Busy in Prefill, How Large Should the Grid Be and Who Dispatches Tiles to SMs?

m5 truncates the main grid at twice the average local hit-pair count (about TTT) plus padding and hands overflow to a persistent fallback kernel, while launching 9,216 standard CTAs for down projection scheduled by the hardware block distributor.

The kernels in the preceding sections all target Me<58M_e < 58Me​<58, whereas prefill at T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 and 16,38416{,}38416,384 crosses 58 (T=753T = 753T=753 sits around 24, still below the line). The fifth generation (m5) is the grouped GEMM built for prefill, and every optimization below is measured in paired ABBA runs against the immediately preceding version of m5 itself (m4 and m5 were not benchmarked against each other on the same shape). Three names appear throughout this section. The route-alignment kernel reorders hit pairs by expert, pads each expert up to a multiple of the tile height BMBMBM, and outputs the reordered token table and per-tile expert IDs. gemm1 is the gate and up projection (Step 1 of Section 1, computing SwiGLU in its epilogue). gemm2 is the down projection (Step 3 of Section 1).

Step 1 keeps only tiles belonging to this GPU: the route-alignment kernel outputs tiles only for the 32 local experts on this GPU, filtering out non-local slots at the source. The cost is pre-allocating a fixed-size worst-case buffer in device memory that CUDA Graph reuses on every replay (Chapter 1, Section 2). How much extra memory that buffer takes and when it would lose performance were not measured separately.

Step 2 sets the grid size. CUDA Graph requires grid dimensions to be fixed at capture time (see Chapter 1, Section 2), before the actual number of local hits is known. Originally, the grid was sized for the worst case: all 8 slots of every token landing on this GPU, plus one padding tile for each of the 32 local experts (1,056 tiles in total at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384). Counted under the busiest-GPU benchmark workload at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, 77% of the CTAs find no work upon entry and exit immediately, implying that only about 1,056×0.23≈2431{,}056 \times 0.23 \approx 2431,056×0.23≈243 tiles have actual work (see Figure 8-13). Across 8 GPUs, each GPU receives an average of 8T/8=T8T / 8 = T8T/8=T hit pairs regardless of routing skew. m5 takes twice the average as routing-skew headroom, adds at most 127 padding rows per expert (truncation is enabled only for T>3,012T > 3{,}012T>3,012, where m5 uses 128-row tiles; see Section 15), and truncates the grid at ⌈(2T+32×127)/128⌉\lceil (2T + 32 \times 127) / 128 \rceil⌈(2T+32×127)/128⌉ tiles. At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, that caps the grid at 288 tiles, about 20% above the estimated ~243 active tiles (Figure 8-13). This factor of 2 is a design choice and was not calibrated against measured worst-case skew.

Any tiles exceeding the truncation cap are handed over to a persistent fallback kernel launched with 1 CTA per SM (132 CTAs in total). Under our benchmark routing distributions, no overflow occurs, and the empty fallback kernel takes about 1.25 μs1.25\ \mu\text{s}1.25 μs and runs only when truncation is active; how fast the fallback kernel runs when overflow occurs, and whether enabling truncation for T≤3,012T \le 3{,}012T≤3,012 pays off, were not measured.

Step 3 decides who dispatches down-projection tiles. Earlier, gemm2 was written as a 264-CTA (2×1322 \times 1322×132) persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1) that claimed tiles at a fixed stride. At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, tile completion times vary widely, and fixed-stride claiming cannot shift work from slow SMs to fast SMs: the profiler recorded 60.3 μs60.3\ \mu\text{s}60.3 μs of intra-kernel SM idle time. Reverting to a non-persistent grid launches 288×32=9,216288 \times 32 = 9{,}216288×32=9,216 standard CTAs (288 row tiles × 32 column tiles) so the hardware block distributor (see Chapter 2, Section 1) dispatches the next tile to whichever SM frees up first, cutting intra-kernel SM idle time from 60.3 μs60.3\ \mu\text{s}60.3 μs down to 18.6 μs18.6\ \mu\text{s}18.6 μs. That wins at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, where tiles are numerous and completion times vary. It is the exact flip side of the rule in Section 10: when tasks are long and numerous, the hardware block distributor acts as zero-barrier dynamic work claiming.

15Why Does the Main Loop Split into Two Paths Between T = 753 and T ≥ 3,012?

At T=753T = 753T=753, m5 selects 64-row tiles, and per-SM occupancy rises from 2 to 3 CTAs; at T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012, it takes the 128-row tile path and sets aside 4 gather warps to gather activations.

Both paths share the same skeleton (dispatched in code between T≤1,024T \le 1{,}024T≤1,024 and T>1,024T > 1{,}024T>1,024): 4-bit weights are decoded to BF16 in register buffers and fed directly as operand A of wgmma (RS mode; Section 3), while tokens sit on the operand-B side in shared memory. Both paths pair 4 rotating operand-A register buffers (whereas m4 in Section 13 uses 2) with wait_group<2> so that 2 wgmma commit groups stay in flight concurrently (see Chapter 5, Section 5).

At T=753T = 753T=753 (Me≈24M_e \approx 24Me​≈24), the tile height is set to 64 (see Section 5 for how tile height relates to MeM_eMe​), and each CTA has 128 threads (1 consumer warpgroup). Instead of threads issuing cp.async to load weights, the consumer warpgroup issues TMA loads directly. Dropping the copy-address registers lowers registers per thread from 180 to 152 (3×128×152=58,368≤65,5363 \times 128 \times 152 = 58{,}368 \le 65{,}5363×128×152=58,368≤65,536), raising per-SM occupancy from 2 to 3 CTAs (see Chapter 3, Section 1). A single weight decode is shared across up to 64 hit pairs (averaging about 24 at T=753T = 753T=753, with the rest being padding rows from Section 5; see Figure 8-14), speeding up single-layer latency by about 4%4\%4% (see the chart below). The tradeoff is that consumers issue extra memory-transfer instructions: applying this scheme to 128-row tiles at T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 makes execution slower, and conversely, forcing 128-row tiles with two consumer warpgroups at T=753T = 753T=753 leaves 24 tokens unable to fill 128 rows and runs slower too (see the chart below).

Next, for T≤1,024T \le 1{,}024T≤1,024, we apply single-grid fusion: folding gemm1, SwiGLU, and gemm2 into the same 64-row-tiled grid eliminates the tail drain and launch boundary between the two kernels. Registers per thread are capped at 128, fitting 4 resident CTAs per SM (4×128×128=65,5364 \times 128 \times 128 = 65{,}5364×128×128=65,536). Work assignment uses ticket numbers: each CTA claims a ticket upon entry (see Chapter 2, Section 7), where lower-numbered tickets execute gemm1 tiles first and higher-numbered tickets execute gemm2 tiles. A gemm2 tile acquires the completion counters of the specific gemm1 tiles it needs and starts as soon as they arrive, without waiting for the entire gemm1 phase to finish (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for acquire). Because each CTA claims its ticket via atomic add only after being scheduled onto an SM (see Chapter 2, Sections 6–7), the lower-numbered gemm1 tiles are guaranteed to be running already, so higher-numbered gemm2 tiles waiting on those completion counters cannot deadlock.

At T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012 (Me≈94M_e \approx 94Me​≈94 and 512512512), we step the tile height up to 128. Those 128 token rows are scattered across the original sequence: the reordered token table stores each hit pair's pairpairpair index (hit-pair index) pair=tok×8+slotpair = tok \times 8 + slotpair=tok×8+slot, which maps back to token index ⌊pair/8⌋\lfloor pair / 8 \rfloor⌊pair/8⌋. Because TMA cannot gather rows through an index table (see Chapter 3, Section 3), gemm1 carves out 4 gather warps (128 threads in total) to gather activations row by row with cp.async, while TMA streams contiguous weights into the 3-slot ring buffer (see Chapter 3, Section 4 for producer/consumer specialization). On this path, producers issue loads 2 steps ahead across all three 3-slot rings (activations, weight codewords, and block scales), paired with 4 rotating operand-A register buffers, speeding up single-layer latency by about 5%5\%5% at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384 (see the chart below). What the gather warps cost us is 128 threads and their registers. Skipping the dedicated gather warps and gathering activations in-kernel across wider token tiles disrupts the register budget and ring pipeline, buying zero gain at T=753T = 753T=753 and slowing execution at T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 (see the chart below).

Three further steps refine the T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012 path. First, we merge the 2 CTA barriers per K-step in gemm1's main loop into 1. Second, we turn gemm1 into a persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1) and add a tile-completion mbarrier so the gather warps start gathering the next tile's activations while the consumers are still executing the current tile's epilogue. Third, full tiles of gemm2 also use a 2-slot ring buffer with 1 TMA producer warp and 4 consumer warps (capped at 128 registers per thread).

Both the 64-row and 128-row paths also apply the tail-tile trimming from Section 5. We measure waste as the average number of rows issued per valid hit pair, where 1.0 means zero wasted rows. The larger MeM_eMe​ gets, the smaller the gain: a single layer runs about 5%5\%5% faster at T=753T = 753T=753, but only about 1%1\%1% faster at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384 (see the second chart below). In the implementation, a single scalar load plus a uniform branch (a conditional jump where all 32 lanes of the warp take the same path) checks whether every row from row rrr onward is padding; that keeps the ring-slot counters in uniform registers (UR; see Chapter 7, Section 7). Switching to an intra-CTA reduction forces those counters back into per-thread general-purpose registers and adds 34 instructions per K-step.

16Why Is the Prefill gemm1 Epilogue Slowed Down by Type Conversion?

Scalar FP32-to-BF16 conversion (F2F) and the exponential instruction MUFU.EX2 both run on the SFU; switching to paired packed rounding (F2FP) moves the conversion to the ALU pipeline and cuts kernel-wide SFU utilization by nearly half.

For T>1,024T > 1{,}024T>1,024, SwiGLU in gemm1's epilogue (see Chapter 1, Section 3) computes exponentials (MUFU.EX2) and then runs scalar FP32-to-BF16 type conversions (F2F) before writing out. On Hopper, F2F and MUFU.EX2 queue on the same SFU pipeline (the SFU accepts only 1 warp instruction every 8 cycles; see Chapter 5, Section 1 for pipeline definitions), stretching out the epilogue window.

The fix uses cvt.rn.bf16x2.f32 to round two FP32 values together into a packed pair of BF16 values, which compiles to F2FP (paired packed conversion) and runs on the regular ALU pipeline without occupying the SFU. Replacing most of the scalar conversions in the epilogue with paired packed conversions cuts the profiler's kernel-wide average SFU utilization from 5.74%5.74\%5.74% down to 3.08%3.08\%3.08% and speeds up single-layer latency by about 0.3%0.3\%0.3% (see the chart below). Kernel-wide average SFU utilization is only a few percent because the main matrix-multiplication loop does not use the SFU, so the SFU is busy only during the epilogue. The cost of paired packed conversion is running shift and bitwise-AND instructions before the store to unpack the two BF16 halfwords packed in the same register into their respective output lanes (adding a few ALU instructions). When the SFU is not the bottleneck in the epilogue, this change buys no speedup (it was not measured on the decode and verify kernels).

Stage 6 Routed-Expert Evolution Chain (m0 → m5)

Section 1 laid out how we dispatch across the three kernel families by TTT; here is the complete evolution chain from start to finish (see the charts below for step-by-step latency):

  • m0: Per-expert loop that decompresses weights to FP32 in HBM and reads them back (Section 2; m0 in the 60-layer total chart).
  • m1: Single grouped-GEMM launch per projection that decodes 4-bit weights in registers and reads them only once (m1a, ~80× faster), followed by gate/up row interleaving, branchless decoding, and PDL (Section 2; m1 in the 60-layer total chart).
  • m2: Pipelined wgmma tiling, Split-K, multi-slot weight ring buffer, pinned occupancy, and tail-tile M-dimension trimming, running ~2.0× faster than the baseline SGLang implementation (Sections 3–5; m2a..m2 in the 60-layer total chart).
  • m3 (for T≤32T \le 32T≤32): Persistent kernel, 8-token virtual passes, two PDL-chained kernels, and entry staggering, compressing the 60-layer total to about 6.12 ms6.12\text{ ms}6.12 ms by m3b (Sections 6–7; the two compiler fixes in Section 8 and the fifth optimization in Section 10 were measured only on the standalone Stage 6 operator).
  • m4 (for T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256): Persistent wgmma kernel (saving about 22 μs22\ \mu\text{s}22 μs in Stage 6 at T=256T = 256T=256), tail balancing, one-group deferred flag setting (subsequently replaced by the dedicated release thread in Section 11), even-odd ledger, and epilogue scale folding, bringing the 60-layer total of m3 + m4 to ~2.5× faster than the baseline (Sections 9–13; Steps 3 and 4 of Section 11 were measured only on the standalone operator).
  • m5 (for prefill T=753,3,012,16,384T = 753, 3{,}012, 16{,}384T=753,3,012,16,384): Grouped GEMM for prefill; at the grid-truncation step, the two GEMMs total 4,207 μs4{,}207\ \mu\text{s}4,207 μs (about 2.5%2.5\%2.5% faster than before truncation), while subsequent steps were measured only as single-layer percentage speedups (charts in Sections 14–16).

If we line both ends up against their physical lower bounds, decode and verify in the m3 + m4 build sit at about 1.75× the weight-read lower bound, while prefill at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384 in the grid-truncation build sits at about 2.5× the compute lower bound. Both ratios come from those respective intermediate builds—later optimizations were measured only as individual relative speedups, and the final combined version was not re-measured against the absolute lower bound. In Chapter 10, we will see how to track down, level by level, where most of the remaining gap goes.

Takeaway: An expert kernel has to adapt to the number of tokens MeM_eMe​ routed to each expert: below about 58, strip away HBM round trips, synchronization waits, and launch overhead; above it, keep the Tensor Cores and instruction pipelines fed.

Next chapter's question: Now that we have both attention and the routed experts in hand, how do we wire the remaining dense projections (Stages 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7) together with the normalizations and gated residuals into a single-layer pipeline—and how do we squeeze the critical path down to its minimum? → Chapter 9

Chapter 9

When Scheduling a Single Layer's Kernels Across 132 SMs, Where Does the Time Above the Lower Bound Go, and How Much Can Scheduling and Kernel Handoffs Recover?
