The previous chapter left us with one question: how do dense projections, normalizations, and gated residuals connect with attention and experts to form a single-layer pipeline? In Primer 2, we drew all eight stages on one GPU as a directed acyclic graph (DAG; see Primer 2, Section 3 and Figure P2-3) and derived the lower bound for the layer (counting dense weights in BF16; see Primer 2, Sections 4 and 5). Here we call the task-specified single-layer lower bound for each scenario the reference bound: 40.0 µs for the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer, 44.2 µs for the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer, and 62.3 / 66.4 µs for the T=8T = 8T=8 sliding-window / full-attention layer. That reference bound is not a lower bound on the bytes that any variant actually reads. Chapters 1–8 already made each stage's kernel fast on its own, yet when we chain those kernels together along the DAG and replay them as a CUDA Graph, the baseline l0 still takes 71.4 µs on the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer. This chapter answers only one question: Where does the time above the reference bound go, and how much can scheduling and kernel handoffs recover?

1Baseline l0: How Does a Single Layer's DAG Map to a Sequence of Kernels and Two CUDA Streams, and Where Does the Time Go?

l0 runs the forked branches in parallel across two CUDA streams; after subtracting ~5.4 µs of CUDA Graph replay overhead, the ~26 µs excess above the 40.0 µs reference bound is lost entirely inside the layer—within the kernels themselves and the handoffs between them.

When we talk about a single layer here, we mean the eight stages running on one GPU. A real 8-GPU run also does three cross-GPU collectives in every layer: an all-reduce after Stage 3 o, an all-reduce after Stage 6, and for T≤8T \le 8T≤8, an all-gather of columns across GPUs after Stage 7 (see Primer 2, Section 2). None of the single-layer measurements in this chapter include those collectives.

To see where a single layer spends its time, let's define the critical path: the longest chain of "must wait for the previous step to finish" dependency edges from layer entry to layer exit. Single-layer latency is simply the length of that critical path plus one CUDA graph replay overhead (~5.4 µs; see below). As long as side-stream kernels use only the SMs and bandwidth left idle by the main chain and finish before the join point, they add nothing to single-layer latency. Because all 132 SMs and HBM bandwidth are shared across the chip, however, the moment a side-stream kernel competes with the main chain for SMs or bandwidth, it stretches the critical path instead (see Section 7).

We measure l0–l3 by starting from l3 and turning off the changes from Sections 4, 3, and 2 one by one in reverse order. That way, each step's delta shows what that section contributes when earlier sections are on and later sections are off. Section 5 then adds one visibility fix on top of l3 to give the final version of this chapter.

On the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer, l0 already fuses adjacent small steps and turns on PDL across part of the chain (we finish the rest in Section 4). In total, it launches 12 kernels per layer: 10 on the main CUDA stream and 2 on a second stream, in the order shown in Figure 9-1. Stage 3 and Stage 8 each end with a boundary kernel that updates the FP32 residual stream stream and then runs the next stage's RMSNorm across all 8,192 columns (see Primer 2, Section 2 for the formula). Stage 5 normalization also sits in its own kernel in l0 (we remove it in Section 3), and attention merge stays a separate kernel rather than using the fused version from Chapter 7, Section 12.

Stage 3's output h forks into two branches here. We call the second CUDA stream the side stream, and use it to launch kernels that do not depend on the current step of the main CUDA stream. The two streams synchronize through CUDA event (inter-stream event) markers—an event recorded on one stream that the other stream waits for. After the Stage 3 boundary kernel finishes, the main stream records an event. Once the side stream sees that event, it runs router to score all 256 experts, then runs the Top-8 kernel to pick the 8 largest scores, normalize their weights, write out topk_ids and topk_weights, and record a second event. Back on the main stream, experts waits for that side-stream event before reading the routing results.

Why does this pay off at T=1T = 1T=1? Because at T=1T = 1T=1, pooler on the main stream launches only 64 CTAs—1 resident CTA per SM—leaving 68 of the 132 SMs (see Primer 3, Section 1) sitting idle. While pooler streams its weights (~50 MB in 12-bit format), router and Top-8 run on the side stream across those 68 idle SMs.

The price of the side stream is recording two extra events per layer, plus the requirement that kernels from both streams can co-reside on the chip at the same time (see Chapter 3, Section 1). Once the main kernel fills all 132 SMs, the side-stream kernels can only steal SMs from it (see Section 7). The timeline of l0 was not measured separately; in the version with PDL enabled across the full chain, the side branch finishes earlier than pooler (see Section 4). Whether pooler saturates bandwidth at T=1T = 1T=1, what happens if you turn off the side stream, and how much recording two events costs were not measured.

Every step in this chapter's evolution chain is measured the same way (see Primer 3, Section 5): we record the single layer into a CUDA Graph, flush L2 before each replay, time a full-graph replay with CUDA events, and take the median. The sliding-window layer attends over 2,048 historical tokens and the full-attention layer over 80,000 tokens, matching the reference bounds in Primer 2, Section 5. Every measured number includes ~5.4 µs of CUDA graph replay overhead—replaying a graph with just 1 empty kernel already takes that long. Production serving records all 62 layers into one graph so the full model amortizes that cost, and the reference bound leaves it out. The 4.96 µs figure cited in Chapter 6 came from a separate batch of empty-graph replay measurements of the same class of overhead; the two numbers come from different experiments, and the cause of the difference was not determined.

The noise band for the single-layer evolution chain is ~0.5 µs, and the paired ABBA noise band for multi-token and prefill runs is ~0.5%; we report any delta smaller than that as "within the noise band" (defined in Chapter 4, Section 6 and Chapter 7, Section 1).

Follow the evolution chain and that ~26 µs leaks out in four places: projections that read too many bytes or launch grids too small to fill a wave (Section 2); a standalone kernel that exists only to sum across a full row, and a device-wide memory barrier that waits for all of a thread's prior writes to reach L2 (see Chapter 8, Section 11 and Section 3 of this chapter); handoffs between kernels (Sections 4–5); and each kernel's main body plus its slowest-CTA tail duration (Section 6). The first leak sits inside the projections themselves.

2l0 → l1: Once Projection Kernels Are Placed Inside a Single Layer, How Can They Read the Fewest Bytes and Fill All 132 SMs?

Because projections are bandwidth-bound, latency equals bytes read divided by achieved bandwidth; l1 reduces bytes read and sizes small-batch grids to fill a full wave.

Let's start with the 12-bit weight layout and decoding at T=1T = 1T=1. Reading fewer bytes comes from 12-bit weights, which take 3/43/43/4 the bytes of 16-bit weights (see Chapter 6, Section 1); saturating bandwidth comes from putting enough SMs to work and keeping enough bytes in flight on each SM (see Chapter 2, Section 3). In l0 at T=1T = 1T=1, qkv_gate and pooler already read 12-bit weights, while the unpooler slice reads 16-bit weights. Compared with 16-bit weights, l0 reads 25.9 MB less, lowering the bound by ~5.4 µs, so its own byte lower bound is ~34.6 µs; counted against that bound, the 26 µs in Section 1 becomes ~31 µs. This 5.4 µs has the same numeric value as the graph replay overhead in Section 1, but it is not the same thing. To make the four versions easy to compare, this chapter still uses 40.0 µs throughout as the reference. In l0, those two 12-bit weight matrices still use the old weight layout and decoder, and l1 does two things to them: it switches to the 9-instruction decoder from Chapter 6, Section 2, and it reorders the pooler weight layout so that at every KKK-step the whole GPU reads a contiguous address range. The bytes read stay the same, and the time drops.

Now look at SM occupancy and 12-bit weights at T=8T = 8T=8. For T≤8T \le 8T≤8, each GPU computes only its own 1,024 output columns of unpooler, a [1024, 4096][1024,\ 4096][1024, 4096] weight slice that takes 8.4 MB in 16-bit format (see Primer 2, Section 1). At T=8T = 8T=8, l0 still leaves this unpooler slice in 16-bit format, cuts the 1,024 rows into 16 tiles of 64 rows each, and splits KKK into 4 segments to launch only 16×4=6416 \times 4 = 6416×4=64 CTAs (Figure 9-2). That leaves 68 SMs sitting idle and falls short of HBM bandwidth. Variant l1 compresses this weight slice to 12-bit format—shrinking it from 8.4 MB to 6.3 MB—and splits KKK into 8 segments instead, so 128 CTAs fill 128 SMs. The Stage 8 boundary kernel then sums the 8 FP32 partial sums for each output, without needing an extra reduction kernel launch (for Split-K, see Chapter 2, Section 5).

At T=8T = 8T=8, qkv_gate in l0 also uses 16-bit weights. Variant l1 compresses it to 12-bit format, slices the 2,304 output rows into 36 tiles of 64 rows each, and splits KKK into 3 segments to launch 36×3=10836 \times 3 = 10836×3=108 CTAs. The grid and register math is the same as in Chapter 6, Section 8: each SM holds 1 resident CTA, so 108 CTAs fit in a single wave, whereas splitting into 4 segments would launch 144>132144 > 132144>132 CTAs and spill into an extra tail wave (see Chapter 2, Section 1).

The T=8T = 8T=8 numbers also include a zero-column shortcut that only works in single-GPU benchmarks. In the Stage 8 boundary kernel, the residual stream update is stream_out=α2⊙stream_mid+β2⊙RMSNorm(f⊙(1+wpost_ffn))\mathrm{stream\_out} = \alpha_2 \odot \mathrm{stream\_mid} + \beta_2 \odot \mathrm{RMSNorm}(f \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{post\_ffn}}))stream_out=α2​⊙stream_mid+β2​⊙RMSNorm(f⊙(1+wpost_ffn​)) (see Primer 2, Section 2 for the formula). In a single-GPU benchmark, the 7,168 output columns of fff owned by the other 7 GPUs are identically 0, so on those columns stream_out\mathrm{stream\_out}stream_out is just α2⊙stream_mid\alpha_2 \odot \mathrm{stream\_mid}α2​⊙stream_mid and does not depend on the experts or unpooler. Because α2\alpha_2α2​ is a fixed vector, the Stage 3 boundary kernel can precompute the sum of squares for those columns on the spot while writing stream_mid\mathrm{stream\_mid}stream_mid; the Stage 8 boundary kernel then sums the squares across only this GPU's 1,024 columns and adds the number saved at Stage 3 to finish the RMSNorm. In a real 8-GPU run, an all-gather after Stage 7 first assembles all 8 GPUs' columns into 8,192 non-zero columns, so you cannot take this shortcut.

We get the biggest saving at T=8T = 8T=8 (~3.5 µs), though part of that comes from the single-GPU-only zero-column shortcut. If you look at the sliced unpooler kernel on its own, switching to 12-bit weights and expanding the grid to 128 CTAs cuts ~1.7 µs off its runtime (see the two charts below).

What do we pay for these changes? For every 8 weights decoded, each thread runs 9 integer instructions (~18 ALU cycles), uses 3 temporary registers, and applies escaped-weight corrections from the side table (see Chapter 6, Section 2). At T=8T = 8T=8, the 8-way Split-K also writes and re-reads 8×8×1,024×4 B=262,144 B≈0.26 MB8 \times 8 \times 1{,}024 \times 4\text{ B} = 262{,}144\text{ B} \approx 0.26\text{ MB}8×8×1,024×4 B=262,144 B≈0.26 MB of FP32 partial sums—still a small fraction of the 2.1 MB saved on weights. Once T≥128T \ge 128T≥128, 12-bit weights start to lose (see Chapter 6, Section 4; the trade-off at T=64T = 64T=64 was not measured), and the 1,024-column slice is used only for T≤8T \le 8T≤8 (see Primer 2, Section 1).

One more projection scheduling change shows up at larger batch sizes, outside the four l0 → l1 scenarios. When the batch size grows to T=32T = 32T=32, pooler launches only 64 CTAs (1 per SM) and streams its weights through a TMA ring buffer. By Chapter 3, Section 4, when all 132 SMs read at once, each SM needs ~48 KiB in flight; when only 64 SMs read, each of them has to keep 48×132/64≈9948 \times 132 / 64 \approx 9948×132/64≈99 KiB in flight. Out of 6 slots, 1 is being read by the consumer and the other 5 are in flight, totaling 80 KiB; with 7 slots, 6 are in flight for 96 KiB, making the standalone kernel ~0.55 µs faster (see the chart below; why it still falls short of the byte lower bound was not measured). The cost is one extra slot of shared memory per CTA, while occupancy stays at 1 CTA per SM; for the counterexample where we cut the ring shallower, see Section 7.

Now that we have plugged the leaks inside the projections, the next piece of overhead sits right between two projections: every cross-CTA full-row reduction for RMSNorm.

3l1 → l2: How Can a Cross-CTA Full-Row Reduction Avoid Paying for an Extra Kernel or a Device-Wide Memory Barrier?

Cross-kernel normalization splits column-wise gain and row-wise scaling across the preceding and succeeding kernels, while intra-cluster reduction uses direct remote SMEM writes (st.async) and local mbarrier.

Pre-Expert RMSNorm: Cross-Kernel Full-Row Reduction

Setting aside the full-row normalizations in the Stage 3 and Stage 8 boundary kernels, every other normalization in the layer has already been folded into a neighboring kernel—except Stage 5 pre-expert RMSNorm (pre_expert_norm) (see Primer 2, Section 2; for Q/K and gated-output normalizations see Chapter 7, Sections 11–12, and for intra-expert normalizations see Chapter 8, Section 1). At T=1T = 1T=1, it still sits in a standalone kernel in l0 and l1. At T=8T = 8T=8, all versions already use the split we are about to describe: the pooler epilogue multiplies by the column gain and accumulates the sum of squares, leaving the per-row scale factor to be multiplied later without launching a standalone kernel.

Let xpool=h Wpooler⊤x_{\mathrm{pool}} = h\,W_{\mathrm{pooler}}^{\top}xpool​=hWpooler⊤​ be the result before Stage 5 normalization, with shape xpool :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{x_{\mathrm{pool}}}{T,\;4096}{BF16}xpool​:[T,4096]BF16; the reciprocal root mean square of row mmm is

rm=114096∑kxpool[m,k]2+10−5r_m = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{4096}\sum_k x_{\mathrm{pool}}[m,k]^2 + 10^{-5}}}rm​=40961​∑k​xpool​[m,k]2+10−5​1​

and the normalized output is

p[m,k]=rm⋅xpool[m,k]⋅(1+wk)p[m,k] = r_m \cdot x_{\mathrm{pool}}[m,k] \cdot (1 + w_k)p[m,k]=rm​⋅xpool​[m,k]⋅(1+wk​)

The model stores normalization weights as offsets relative to 1, so the applied gain is 1+wk1 + w_k1+wk​; the 10−510^{-5}10−5 term in the denominator prevents division by zero.

Why can't pooler finish computing p[m,k]p[m,k]p[m,k] directly inside its own epilogue? Because pooler partitions the 4,096 output columns across different CTAs: each CTA holds only its own column segment of row mmm, and no single CTA can see the full-row sum of squares ∑kxpool[m,k]2\sum_k x_{\mathrm{pool}}[m,k]^2∑k​xpool​[m,k]2 across all 4,096 columns.

The way out comes from the linearity of matrix multiplication under row scaling: (rm xm) W⊤=rm (xm W⊤)(r_m\, x_m)\,W^{\top} = r_m\,(x_m\, W^{\top})(rm​xm​)W⊤=rm​(xm​W⊤): scaling a row before matrix multiplication is equivalent to multiplying by the matrix first and scaling the resulting row afterward. Look at the two factors in p[m,k]p[m,k]p[m,k]. The gain 1+wk1 + w_k1+wk​ depends only on the column index kkk, and each pooler CTA already has the finished values for the columns it computes, so pooler can multiply by 1+wk1 + w_k1+wk​ right in its output epilogue (see Chapter 1, Section 3). Meanwhile, rmr_mrm​ depends only on the row index mmm, so the experts kernel can run its entire KKK loop first and then multiply its full-row FP32 accumulators (see Chapter 5, Section 6) by rmr_mrm​.

We have to do this scaling before SwiGLU, because silu(r a)≠r silu(a)\mathrm{silu}(r\,a) \ne r\,\mathrm{silu}(a)silu(ra)=rsilu(a) (for SwiGLU, see Primer 2, Section 2). In exact arithmetic the two orders give the exact same result; in BF16 the rounding point moves from ppp to xpool⋅(1+wk)x_{\mathrm{pool}} \cdot (1 + w_k)xpool​⋅(1+wk​), and the single-layer output still passes verification.

At T=1T = 1T=1 (Figure 9-3 Mode 1), each pooler CTA writes out xpool⋅(1+w)x_{\mathrm{pool}} \cdot (1 + w)xpool​⋅(1+w) and at the same time uses one atomic add (see Chapter 2, Section 6) to add its column segment's partial sum of squares into a single shared FP32 slot in global memory; once the PDL wait call returns, the experts kernel reads that slot and multiplies by rmr_mrm​. That slot must be FP32 because scalar BF16 atomic adds degrade into a slow retry loop (see Chapter 6, Section 8). We zero the slot after the wait call of the Stage 3 boundary kernel (by which time the previous round's experts has already finished), and we place the atomic add after the wait call of pooler, so the order is always: previous read complete → zero → current accumulation (see Chapter 1, Section 4). That takes one kernel and the handoff in front of it off the critical path, cutting single-layer kernel launches from 12 down to 11.

What this split saves changes with the token count TTT. At T=1T = 1T=1, it saves one kernel handoff. By T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 (Figure 9-3 Mode 2), what it saves is an HBM round trip: a standalone normalization kernel has to read 24.7 MB of xpoolx_{\mathrm{pool}}xpool​ and write it back out, taking ~14 µs (see the chart below) and showing that those bytes go to HBM. Once we split the normalization, pooler divides the 4,096 columns into 16 column segments and each segment writes one partial sum of squares per row—producing a small partial-sum table rs :  [T,  16]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{rs}}{T,\;16}{FP32}rs:[T,16]FP32 that totals just 0.39 MB across the write and the read.

In the middle batch sizes, the gain is small or even negative: at T=753T = 753T=753, the intermediate tensor stays in L2 so the standalone kernel takes only ~3.7 µs, and at T=128T = 128T=128 and 256 splitting is actually 0.5%–1.0% slower, so those two shapes keep the standalone kernel.

The price of splitting is that the pooler epilogue does one extra atomic add (or writes a 0.19 MB partial-sum table), and the experts kernel does one extra load plus a full-row scaling step. And because atomic-add arrival order is not fixed, the least significant bits of the output may change from run to run (see Chapter 2, Section 7).

Boundary Kernels: Intra-Cluster Full-Row Reduction

Now look at the Stage 3 and Stage 8 boundary kernels. For T≤8T \le 8T≤8, each boundary kernel splits the 8,192 columns of each row across the 8 CTAs of a single thread block cluster, with 1,024 columns per CTA (see Chapter 7, Section 12), and every CTA needs the partial sums of squares from the other 7 CTAs. Variant l1 exchanges those partial sums with a release-semantics cluster barrier. Because the 8 CTAs run on different SMs whose L1 caches are not coherent with each other, global data only becomes coherent at L2. That forces the cluster barrier to wait until prior writes reach L2 (see Chapter 2, Section 6), which on H200 compiles down to a device-wide memory barrier (see the barrier.cluster row of Appendix B, Quick Reference 3). When the profiler samples warps at fixed cycle intervals and records why they cannot issue an instruction, 36%–46% of stalled samples are stuck waiting on this barrier (for stall sampling share, see Chapter 10, Section 7).

Variant l2 (Figure 9-3 Mode 3) replaces that barrier with st.async, writing each partial sum of squares directly into each peer CTA's shared memory while each receiver waits on its own local mbarrier (see Chapter 3, Section 5) until the expected byte count arrives (see Chapter 7, Section 12 for the mechanism). Now synchronization waits only for those 8 partial sums to arrive—7 from peers plus 1 written to itself—which saves 0.86–0.99 µs per call in isolated boundary-kernel benchmarks. Because the CTAs exchange only the partial sums in shared memory, and each CTA writes its own assigned columns into stream without reading any peer CTA's global writes, we no longer need that device-wide memory barrier here; the next kernel sees stream through the inter-kernel handoff.

The catch with direct remote-SMEM exchange is that it is easier to get wrong: our first implementation reused the same shared-memory buffer across two row reductions, and the shared-memory read/write hazard checker (see Chapter 10, Section 4) caught 8 write-after-read hazards (WAR; see Chapter 3, Section 5), which we fixed by giving each reduction its own buffer. Where this approach would start to lose was not measured.

Putting both changes together gives l1 → l2, saving ~1.8 µs on the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer (see the chart below for all four scenarios). At T=8T = 8T=8, pre-expert RMSNorm was already split (see the start of this section), and Stage 8 already takes the zero-column shortcut. Once we put the changes back into the single layer, only the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window delta clears the noise band. In the other three scenarios, the expected savings do not show up: the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer likewise drops one pre-expert RMSNorm kernel and the handoff in front of it, and switches both boundary kernels to direct writes; at T=8T = 8T=8, only the Stage 3 boundary kernel changes, saving ~0.9 µs per call when measured on its own. The cause was not determined.

4l2 → l3: How Can Every Inter-Kernel Handoff Be Hidden Inside the Preceding Kernel's Epilogue?

l3 enables PDL across the entire chain so successor kernels enter early to prefetch weights; using PDL safely requires two rules: pair predecessor and successor calls, and place the trigger point according to how many SMs are free.

PDL lets a successor kernel enter SMs early while the preceding kernel is wrapping up, and then pause at wait until the preceding kernel finishes and its writes become visible (see Chapter 1, Section 4). Inside a layer, dense projection weights are already fixed before the layer starts and do not depend on the previous step's activations, so the next dense projection kernel can start reading its own weights without waiting for the previous kernel to finish. Routed experts are the one exception: which expert weights to read depends on Top-8's output (see Section 5).

In l2, some edges already have PDL turned on, but qkv_gate → attention, attention → o, and the main-chain edges after the Stage 3 boundary kernel still do not: on those edges, each successor still waits for the preceding kernel to exit completely before launching. Variant l3 (Figure 9-4 Mode 1) adds the PDL launch attribute to every successor kernel along the chain, letting it pull its first batch of weights into registers or shared memory before wait. In particular, the o projection issues the hardware prefetch instruction prefetch.global.L2 (see Appendix B, Quick Reference 2): the instruction only tells the hardware to move that weight tile from HBM into L2, taking none of this thread's registers. Once wait returns, o reads the tile from L2 into registers.

To get PDL right across a full layer, we have to follow two rules.

Rule 1: PDL must be paired across predecessor and successor kernels. Along a multi-kernel chain, every middle kernel is both the successor of the previous step and the predecessor of the next step: the predecessor kernel has to fire its trigger call on time, and the successor has to launch with the PDL attribute and call wait before reading dependent data. Leave out either half, and the successor waits until the predecessor exits completely before launching—so by the time it hits wait, there is nothing left to overlap. On the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer, attention runs as a split-KV kernel followed by a separate merge kernel (see Chapter 7, Section 12). An earlier version left out the launch attribute and trigger call on the split-KV and merge kernels, so neither edge overlapped; putting the missing halves in makes the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer ~1.2 µs faster (paired ABBA measurement; see the chart below). You can only see this cross-kernel overlap in a full-layer replay (see Chapter 10, Section 1).

Rule 2: Where to place the trigger call depends on how many SMs the predecessor kernel frees up. Back in Chapter 1, Section 4, we placed the trigger call after the main loop because early-entering successor CTAs take up SMs and hold onto registers and shared memory while they wait (see Chapter 3, Section 1). That only hurts, however, when all the SMs on the chip are already full. As we saw in Section 1, pooler at T=1T = 1T=1 uses only 64 of the 132 SMs and leaves 68 SMs idle. Variant l3 (Figure 9-4 Mode 2) therefore sets the 132-CTA experts kernel as the PDL successor of pooler and has pooler fire its trigger call right at kernel entry. By design, experts is also supposed to wait for Top-8 on the side stream to join, yet on measured timelines experts enters ~2.65 µs before pooler finishes and even slightly before Top-8 finishes—for reasons we will unpack in Section 5. Its first 68 CTAs land on the idle SMs and start running prologue setup work right away: compacting local expert IDs, initializing barriers, and loading the first weight tile. The other 64 CTAs enter as pooler CTAs exit.

We measured full-chain PDL and early entry of the experts kernel together: l2 → l3 saves the most on the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer (~3.6 µs), with all four scenarios shown in the chart below.

The price of this handoff optimization is that early-entering successor CTAs hold onto their registers and shared memory the whole time they wait. Even after every CTA of the preceding kernel exits, the hardware still has to confirm that all prior writes have reached L2 before it lets the successor's wait call return; Section 6 measures how long that handoff gap takes. And if a successor enters too early and fights the predecessor kernel for SM resources, the whole pair runs slower instead—see Chapter 1, Section 4 and Chapter 7, Section 11 for counterexamples.

There is a catch, though: that prologue setup work reads topk_ids—written by Top-8 on the side stream—before wait, and that cross-stream read steps across a memory-visibility boundary.

5l3 → Fixed: What Can an Early-Entering Kernel Read Before wait?

Before wait, a kernel may in general read only data unmodified during the current graph replay (i.e., static weights); reading the predecessor's output before wait requires the predecessor to execute a gpu-scope release fence before issuing the trigger call.

When two kernels touch the same memory location, at least one of them writes, and nothing guarantees which happens first, you have a data race. In PTX, the trigger call is written griddepcontrol.launch_dependents and the wait call is written griddepcontrol.wait (see Chapter 1, Section 4 and Chapter 8, Section 8).

By the PTX specification, there are only two valid visibility paths that guarantee a predecessor kernel's writes are visible to its successor. Path 1: every writing thread in the predecessor kernel first runs fence.release.gpu (a gpu-scope release fence; or the threads can pass through an intra-CTA barrier first and let one thread run the fence for the whole CTA, as in Chapter 2, Section 6) and then calls launch_dependents in program order. As long as both grids sit in the same memory synchronization domain, the spec says this release fence synchronizes with the start of the successor grid, so the successor sees those writes the moment it launches. A memory synchronization domain is a tag CUDA attaches to each kernel launch; this book uses the default setting throughout, which puts all kernels in the same domain. Path 2: in every other case, writes are guaranteed to become visible only after the successor's griddepcontrol.wait returns (for release, acquire, and memory scope, see Chapter 2, Section 6). Because every kernel along the chain finishes only after its own wait returns, waiting for the immediately preceding kernel to finish also waits for every earlier kernel along the chain. Whenever you do not take Path 1, code before wait may read only data that nobody modifies during the current replay—in other words, static weights. Code before wait must also never write to any buffer that an earlier kernel (the immediately preceding kernel included) might still be reading. That is why Section 3 zeroes the FP32 accumulation slot only after wait returns; otherwise the previous round's experts kernel might still be reading it. Adding a release fence in the predecessor kernel does not change that rule.

Why did reading topk_ids before wait in l3 look safe at first? Because the main stream carrying experts first waits on the completion event recorded after Top-8 on the side stream, and an event join ordinarily waits for the entire Top-8 grid to finish. In eager mode—where the CPU launches kernels one by one without capturing a graph—that is indeed what happens. Once you capture the chain into a CUDA Graph, however, as soon as experts carries the PDL launch attribute, that cross-stream event-join edge changes how it runs. It executes as a programmatic dependent edge: the successor may launch before the predecessor finishes and waits only at wait, so experts can enter SMs before Top-8 is done. Public CUDA documentation does not mention this; we found it by testing: in a controlled experiment where Top-8 fires its trigger call at kernel entry, eager mode fails 0 times out of 50 runs, whereas graph mode fails 50 times out of 50 runs (giving wrong outputs).

A CUDA Graph reuses the same topk_ids buffer on every replay. When Top-8 triggers at kernel entry (Figure 9-5 Mode ①), experts beats it to the buffer every time and reads the previous replay's expert IDs—which look completely valid—so the single-layer output comes out wrong on every run with a relative error of 0.63–1.09. Moving Top-8's trigger point to kernel exit (Figure 9-5 Mode ②, i.e., l3) gives 0 errors across 240 standard replay tests (0 errors gives only an upper bound on the failure rate; see Chapter 10, Section 4 for the derivation). Because the exit trigger has no fence.release.gpu in front of it, though, it still falls outside the two guaranteed visibility paths; it just fails less often. launch_dependents is not a memory write and carries no release semantics of its own, so without a preceding fence.release.gpu, the spec guarantees no ordering between it and earlier writes to topk_ids—the successor can still launch before the written data is visible (see Chapter 2, Section 6).

Once we scale the replay count past 550,000 runs per shape and per version across multiple H200 GPUs (see the chart below), the race shows up clearly. Define a severe numerical corruption as a single-layer output that fails verification, meaning a relative error above 0.01. One GPU in our test pool failed far more often than the rest, so we separated it out of the tally; with that outlier GPU removed, l3 on the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer still hits 1 severe numerical corruption roughly every 11,000 replays, and the chart below shows the failure rates across the other three scenarios. That failure rate stays flat during steady-state execution, so it is not a warm-up effect. We also had CTA 0 of experts log the expert IDs it read before wait (see Chapter 10, Section 5 for the logging method): it repeatedly read IDs that did not match the current replay's routing, and every single mismatch we checked matched the exact IDs from the previous replay.

As we noted in Section 4, Top-8 decides which experts experts reads, so its entire prologue setup depends on topk_ids: compacting the local indices that land in this GPU's 32 local experts, initializing barriers, and loading the first weight tile. Corresponding to the two visibility paths at the start of this section, there are two ways to fix the race: Fix (a) moves the topk_ids read and all the prologue setup work that depends on it to after wait (Figure 9-5 Mode ③); Fix (b) has every Top-8 CTA pass through an intra-CTA barrier after writing, let one thread execute fence.release.gpu, and then explicitly call launch_dependents. Fix (b) relies on that undocumented graph-capture behavior; this book's final single-layer implementation uses Fix (a).

With Fix (a) in place, ~2.26 million total replays across all four shapes ran with 0 severe numerical corruptions. Aside from severe numerical corruptions, a separate class of small deviations (relative error ~0.003) that still pass single-layer verification shows up just as often before and after the fix, so it does not come from the topk_ids race (its cause was not determined). The fix in this chapter modifies the expert kernel used for T≤8T \le 8T≤8. At T=16T = 16T=16, the layer uses a different early-entering expert kernel—the virtual-pass variant from Chapter 8, Section 6—which also reads topk_ids before wait. We did not modify that kernel; the same fix should apply there too, though neither the fix nor its failure rate was measured.

At T=8T = 8T=8, l3 originally failed only once every ~840,000 runs, so running ~560,000 error-free replays on the fixed version cannot prove the fix by count alone (see Chapter 10, Section 4 for the derivation). Instead, safety at T=8T = 8T=8 comes straight from the spec: whether that cross-stream edge runs as a regular event edge or as a programmatic dependent edge, Top-8 is done and its writes are visible once wait returns, so reading after wait is always safe.

Moving the 3.2 µs prologue setup after wait slows down the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer by only ~1.35 µs (see the chart below for all four scenarios). After this fix, when the experts kernel enters SMs early, it no longer runs its prologue setup ahead of time. Variant l2 and the fixed version were not timed in the same experiment, and how much the PDL edges vs. early expert entry each contributed—as well as how fast Fix (b) runs—was not measured.

Take the ~5.4 µs CUDA graph replay overhead off the fixed version's 67.8 µs, and the single layer still sits ~22 µs above the 40.0 µs reference bound. Is that remaining time sitting in the handoffs between kernels, or inside the kernels themselves?

6How Much Time Can Fusing a Single Layer into a Megakernel Recover?

Very little: replacing kernel boundaries with device-wide counter handoffs saves at most ~0.66 µs, and fusing multiple stages into a megakernel is ~10% slower on the weighted score; most of the excess time lies inside each kernel's main body and tail.

First, let's see where the time goes. Here we dissect a slightly earlier build of the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer with PDL enabled and the data race unfixed, which takes 68.2 µs without timestamp probes. Because this is a different build from l3 in Section 4, you cannot compare their total latencies directly. Every CTA records three timestamps: when it enters, when wait returns, and when it exits (see Chapter 10, Section 5 for the method).

These timestamps split the waiting between kernels and the waiting inside each kernel into two numbers: the handoff gap, which is the time on the critical path from the last CTA exit of the preceding kernel to the first wait return in the next kernel; and the tail duration (CTA exit skew), which inside a single kernel is the time from the median CTA exit to the last CTA exit. Even if you fused multiple stages into a persistent full-chip megakernel, at most you could ever win back those two pieces—totaling ~12.5 µs.

Break that 68.2 µs total apart (see the chart below) and you see right away that the bulk of the time sits in the ~50 µs of kernel main bodies—roughly 1.25× the 40.0 µs reference bound. Handoff gaps and tail durations each take only ~6 µs, where each handoff gap includes acknowledging that every CTA of the previous grid has exited and flushing prior writes to L2. In this build, the experts stage (Chapter 8) has a byte lower bound of ~11.8 µs (reading 2 full local experts); its main body runs ~6.6 µs above that bound, and its tail duration alone makes up more than half of the entire layer's tail duration. The chart values already have the probe overhead factored out (Figure 9-6).

Now let's do the math on what fusing into a megakernel actually costs. Within a single layer, every output of y=Wxy = Wxy=Wx depends on the entire input vector xxx written in segments across all CTAs of the previous stage; thus every CTA of the next stage must wait for all CTAs of the previous stage to finish writing. If you marked individual tiles ready so the next stage could consume each tile as soon as it arrived, you could in theory hide part of the tail duration, at the price of per-tile acquire polling and finer-grained synchronization (this approach was not measured). When a megakernel hands off stages through a device-wide counter (working the same way as the grid barrier in Chapter 8, Section 6), the next stage still has to wait for the slowest producer CTA to finish writing xxx, so the tail duration does not go away; and the SMs that free up during the tail are already busy prefetching weights, so there is no extra work left to pack into them. To shrink each kernel's tail duration, you have to balance the load inside the heavy kernels themselves (see Chapter 7 for attention and Chapter 8 for experts).

We built a synthetic memory-streaming chain: for each of the six weight-reading stages in a single layer, it reads one segment of that stage's byte count (qkv_gate and pooler at 12-bit, o and the unpooler slice at 16-bit, router at FP32, and experts at 4-bit), ~169 MB in total. Because this chain reads 2 full local experts instead of the ~1.87 local experts that the reference bound assumes for the busiest GPU under the task workload, the chain's byte lower bound is higher than l0's byte lower bound in Section 2. On this chain, each device-wide counter handoff adds 1.08 µs. Out of the 8 handoff gaps in the layer, only the two entering attention merge and pooler are longer than that, and each one saves ~0.33 µs (these gaps come from subtracting timestamps recorded on different SMs, and the skew between SMs was not measured; see Chapter 10, Section 5). In total, that saves at most 0.66 µs, or about 1% of the layer (see the chart below).

That same 6-stage synthetic memory-streaming chain also isolates the cost of the persistent kernel structure itself: when we write those exact same 6 stages as a persistent kernel that does zero waiting between stages (see Chapter 3, Section 1), it still runs 8.3 µs slower than a standard launch reading the same bytes (see the chart below). The cause was not determined, and the overhead when scaled up to the full single layer was not measured. Because this control kernel does no inter-stage synchronization, its numerical results are wrong—it is only there to measure the structural cost of persistence itself. On top of that, every stage fused into a single kernel has to share one compile-time register and shared-memory budget, which forces lightweight stages to run under the occupancy cap of the heaviest stage (see Chapter 3, Section 1).

We also tried actually fusing Stages 6 through 8 (from experts through the Stage 8 boundary kernel) and adjacent steps of Stages 2–3 into megakernels; weighted across the 6 decode and verify shapes (see Chapter 8, Section 1) using the model's 46 sliding-window to 16 full-attention layer ratio, the fused versions ran ~10% slower.

Packing a small kernel into the epilogue of the preceding kernel (see Chapter 1, Section 3) is also slower. With PDL, that small kernel has already entered early on other SMs; once you pack it into the epilogue, it gives up that early entry, and the entire merge step gets serialized onto the last CTA. On the T=256T = 256T=256 sliding-window layer (called verify 32-request sliding window in Chapter 7), folding the attention merge step into the last CTA of the split-KV kernel makes the single layer 6.75 µs slower. For this shape, Chapter 7, Section 12 ends up taking the third path: CTAs in the same cluster write their partial results directly into one another's shared memory, without waiting for the last CTA of the whole kernel. Chapter 7's second path (last-arriver merge) is used for 16- and 32-request decode: each row is wrapped up by that row's own last-arriving CTA, spreading the epilogue work across different CTAs.

At this point, the T=1T = 1T=1 layer is scheduled around its own shape. Once the batch size changes, the number of SMs occupied by pooler changes with it, and the trade-offs of the two earlier techniques flip as well.

7At Larger Batch Sizes: How Does the Number of Idle SMs Reshape the Schedule?

A side stream generally pays off only when the main kernel does not saturate HBM bandwidth and either leaves idle SMs or allows SM co-residency; the stream schedule must switch per TTT.

Once the main kernel saturates HBM bandwidth or fills all SMs, every extra byte read and every SM occupied by a side-stream kernel stretches the main kernel. As the token count TTT changes, both conditions shift together (Figure 9-7; for residency limits, see Chapter 3, Section 1).

At T=1T = 1T=1, pooler launches 64 CTAs and leaves 68 SMs idle, so router and Top-8 run on the side stream (Section 1) and the first 68 CTAs of experts enter SMs early (Section 4).

At T=128T = 128T=128, both router and pooler launch 128 CTAs: router's 4-slot ring buffer takes ~128 KiB of shared memory, and pooler's 8-slot ring buffer takes ~193 KiB of shared memory (for ring buffer slots, see Chapter 3, Section 4). Together they need 128+193>228 KiB128 + 193 > 228\text{ KiB}128+193>228 KiB, exceeding the per-SM shared-memory limit (see Chapter 3, Section 1), so the two kernels cannot co-reside on the same SM; pooler can only enter after router runs on its own and exits, and router's standalone run plus the handoff takes ~8.5 µs in total. Cutting pooler's ring buffer down to 4 slots to squeeze both onto the same SM makes the sliding-window layer 8.4 µs (T=128T = 128T=128) and 5.0 µs (T=256T = 256T=256) slower instead.

What actually works here is a merged launch. Because router and pooler read the exact same input tensor h, we can fold both stages into a single kernel: each CTA first computes its slice of router scores using the shared-memory ring buffer, and then goes straight into the pooler main loop. After merging, the total bytes read across the layer stay the same, while router's 8.4 MB of weights stream through the same ring buffer as pooler without paying for a separate launch and exit wait; the sliding-window single layer runs 1.30% faster (paired ABBA median; see the chart below). By T=256T = 256T=256, the change falls inside the ~0.5% paired noise band and shows no measurable gain, so we keep the two kernels separate there.

At T=753T = 753T=753, prefill pooler slices its output into 128×256128 \times 256128×256 tiles to launch 96 CTAs, leaving 36 SMs idle. Putting router, Top-8, and the route-alignment kernel—which sorts token indices by expert and pads each bucket to the tile size (see Chapter 8, Section 14)—on the side stream to run in parallel across those 36 idle SMs makes the single layer ~3.2% faster (see the chart below).

Step up to T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012, and pooler fills all 132 SMs. If we keep running pooler first with router on the side stream, the single layer runs 0.76% slower; launching router on the side stream right after the Stage 3 boundary kernel (without waiting for pooler) is also 1.01% slower. So at T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012, we put both router and pooler on the main stream in sequence.

At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, pooler has far more than 132 output tiles and keeps every SM full from start to finish. If pooler went first, router would have to wait until it finished before starting. So here we flip their order: router runs first on the main stream, and only the lightweight Top-8 and route-alignment kernels go on the side stream to overlap with pooler (the gain from flipping the order alone was not measured). This does not fully match the rule of this section: pooler occupies all 132 SMs and leaves no idle SMs, and how much Top-8 and the route-alignment kernel actually overlap with pooler on the side stream—and whether that overlap helps or hurts—was not measured separately.

Using idle SMs to take on the second-wave tiles of qkv_gate at T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 (see Chapter 2, Section 5) speeds up the isolated kernel by 8.7 µs, but once you put it back into the single layer, the sliding-window layer is only 0.18% faster and the full-attention layer is 0.10% slower—both inside the ~0.5% paired noise band—so we did not adopt it.

8Placing This Layer Back into All 62 Layers: Which Part of One Decode Step Do This Book's Measurements Cover?

Summing the 62 final single-layer latencies at T=1T = 1T=1 gives 4,329.2 µs, which overcounts 62 single-layer graph replay overheads and omits 186 cross-GPU collectives, token embedding, lm_head, and sampling.

The solid bars in Figure 9-8 are the 62-layer single-GPU body that this book measures (46 sliding-window layers and 16 full-attention layers).

Add up all 62 single-layer reference bounds and you get ~2.55 ms, which is higher than the ~1.87 ms number from Primer 1. The 2.55 ms sum adds the busiest GPU's expert weights plus the KV cache and activations, and leaves out lm_head (the chart below breaks out the three pieces).

How does the measured 4,329.2 µs sum (46×67.79+16×75.6846 \times 67.79 + 16 \times 75.6846×67.79+16×75.68) differ from a real one-step decode? On one hand, it counts the 5.4 µs single-layer graph replay overhead from Section 1 62 times, whereas real serving amortizes graph replay across one 62-layer graph (how much replay overhead remains after amortization was not measured). Layers 0 and 61 also store their experts in BF16 (see Primer 1, Section 2), while this sum treats every layer as 4-bit experts, biasing the total low (the difference was not measured separately).

On the other hand, the four light-gray segments in Figure 9-8 sit outside single-layer single-GPU benchmarking, and none of their latencies were measured. Before entering Layer 0, the vocabulary embedding table is split by rows across all 8 GPUs, so looking up the token is followed by an all-reduce across GPUs (see Primer 1, Section 1). Inside each layer, we have 3 cross-GPU collectives (see Section 1); at T=1T = 1T=1, each collective sends only a single row of 8,192 BF16 elements (16 KiB), so it is latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound, and all 186 collectives across the 62 layers sit right on the critical path. After Layer 61 and the final RMSNorm, this GPU's slice of lm_head reads 414.2 MB (an 86.3 µs byte lower bound at 4.8 TB/s; see Primer 1, Sections 3–4), followed by an all-gather of logits across GPUs and token sampling. If the serving engine uses speculative decoding, each step also adds the draft model plus a T=8T = 8T=8 verification pass (see Primer 1, Section 7; draft-model latency was not measured).

Chapter Evolution Chain (l0 → l1 → l2 → l3 → Fixed)

  • l0 (Section 1): baseline obtained by turning off the changes from Sections 2–4 in l3, with the main chain on one CUDA stream and router plus Top-8 on the side stream.
  • l0 → l1 (Section 2): projections switch to the 9-instruction decoder and new weight layout from Chapter 6; under 8-token verification, we compress qkv_gate and unpooler to 12-bit weights and widen their grids. At T=1T = 1T=1, qkv_gate and pooler already use 12-bit weights in l0.
  • l1 → l2 (Section 3): we split pre-expert RMSNorm across the pooler epilogue and expert accumulators, and boundary kernels exchange partial sums via direct remote-SMEM exchange.
  • l2 → l3 (Section 4): we enable PDL on every edge along the chain, and the first 68 CTAs of the experts kernel enter early on the SMs left idle by pooler (containing the data race analyzed in Section 5).
  • l3 → Fixed (Section 5): we move the topk_ids read in the T≤8T \le 8T≤8 experts kernel after wait, eliminating that cross-stream data race.

Takeaway: Most of a single layer's execution time sits inside the kernels themselves: scheduling and handoffs bring the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer down from 71.4 µs to 67.8 µs in the final version, and fusing the layer into a megakernel cannot recover the rest.
