Chapter 10

Given a Slow Kernel, How Do We Measure It Accurately and Diagnose Its Bottleneck Level by Level?

  • Preface
  • Primer 1
  • Primer 2
  • Primer 3
  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]
  • Chapter 3 [Level 3]
  • Chapter 4 [Level 4]
  • Chapter 5 [Level 5]
  • Chapter 6 [Level 6]
  • Chapters 7–9
  • Chapter 10: Performance Diagnostics
  • Appendices

The previous chapter ended with a question: when you get a brand-new slow kernel, how do you find out where it stalls level by level without guessing? Only two mistakes can fool you on a slow kernel: measuring it wrong, or looking at the wrong level. So this chapter starts by getting the timing right, and then walks the profiler level by level from the outside in. Before touching the code, we estimate the speedup upper bound; at the end, we list the four hardware limits on H200 that software can only work around. Throughout the chapter, we keep using single-request gemv to show the readings at each level, bringing in operators from Part II only when a phenomenon does not show up in gemv.

1Why Do CUDA Event Timing and the Profiler Report Two Different Latencies, and What Should Each Be Used to Read?

CUDA event timing includes launch and event-recording overhead, whereas the profiler measures only the kernel itself; use event timing to report microsecond speedups and the profiler to read bottleneck shares.

For kernel-level profiling in this book, we use Nsight Compute (NCU). It focuses on one kernel at a time and replays that kernel across multiple passes, collecting one set of hardware counters per pass. Because NCU flushes the caches between passes by default, those counters give you cold-cache readings. Its gpu__time_duration.sum metric clocks the pure GPU execution duration of the kernel from the moment the first CTA starts to the moment the last CTA exits.

Take gemv v8 from Chapter 4, Section 6 and measure it both ways: the CUDA event timing from Primer 3, Section 5 comes out ~2.8 µs longer than the gpu__time_duration.sum reported by NCU, as shown in the chart below.

Where does that extra ~2.8 µs in CUDA event timing go? Most of it is the launch command and event-recording overhead between the two timing events, which NCU does not measure. The two runs also did not use the exact same machines, and their SM clock frequencies may differ; the share of each of these two factors was not measured. Do not compare this 2.8 µs with the 4.6 µs from Primer 3, Section 5: the two numbers do not measure the same thing, because 4.6 µs also includes the GPU execution of the empty kernel itself.

By default, NCU locks the SM to a lower base clock. In this run, we disabled clock locking so the SM ran at ~1.96 GHz. The SM frequency during CUDA event timing was not recorded, and the effect of clock frequency on v8 latency was not measured separately.

So when you report how many microseconds an optimization saves, use only CUDA event timing, not NCU duration. To time a single kernel, wrap a single launch in CUDA events; to time a single layer, bracket one CUDA Graph replay with events. If you need to time an individual kernel inside a CUDA Graph replay, use NVIDIA's profiling interface CUPTI (CUDA Profiling Tools Interface): instead of replaying the kernel, it records only the start and end timestamps of each kernel on the GPU during graph replay. Conversely, when you want to know why a kernel is slow, switch to NCU to read the bandwidth share, stall sampling share, and instruction counts.

2Why Must We Read 512 MiB to Flush L2 Before Every Timed Run—and Why Only Read, Not Write?

A single operator's weights fit inside the 60 MiB L2 cache, so without a flush you measure warm-cache latency; if you flush L2 with writes, the measurement inverts the speed ranking of the versions.

Before every timed run, do a 512 MiB read flush outside the start and end timing events: read a buffer much larger than L2 once so you replace all the old data in L2 with clean cache lines.

Why do we have to flush L2? Compare Mode 1 and Mode 3 in Figure 10-1. The weights W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 of qkv_gate take up only 37.75 MB, which fits inside the 60 MiB L2 cache of the H200. If you run the same kernel back-to-back in a loop without flushing, most of WWW is already sitting in L2 from the second iteration onward; in production, however, L2 is cold when each layer reads its weights (see Chapter 2, Section 2).

A warm L2 and a cold L2 give very different readings. Take gemv v1 from Primer 3, Section 6: on the same H200 GPU and in the same process, timing without an L2 flush clocks in ~30% shorter than timing after a 512 MiB read flush, as shown in the chart below. If you pick an implementation based on warm-cache numbers, that choice may not hold up in production.

Why must the L2 flush only read and not write? If you flush L2 by writing a 512 MiB buffer (Figure 10-1 Mode 2), you leave the 60 MiB L2 cache full of modified dirty cache lines that have not yet been written back to HBM. When the tested kernel then goes to read WWW, L2 probably has to write each evicted dirty cache line back to HBM before pulling in a new cache line, eating into HBM bandwidth.

A write flush also flips the measured speed ranking of two versions. On the gemv evolution chain, v4 was withdrawn for this reason: it added the L2 residency hints from Chapter 2, Section 4 on top of v3 from Chapter 2, Section 8. When we flushed L2 by writing 512 MiB, v4 looked ~10% faster than v3 (see the first chart below). Once we switched to a 512 MiB read flush and tested in both forward and reverse orders across two H200 GPUs, all 4 medians of v4 came out higher than v3, averaging ~1 µs slower (see the second chart below). Compare the two charts and you can see why: the write flush slowed v3 down by ~5 µs while leaving v4 nearly unchanged. Tagging WWW in v4 with evict_first probably changed the dirty cache line eviction order.

So we do not count v4 as a step, and the evolution chain jumps straight from v3 to v5; for why v4 saves no time under a read flush, see Chapter 2, Section 4.

After a read flush, L2 is just as cold as when 62 layers rotate in production, and the interference from dirty cache line writeback is gone. The cost is an extra 512 MiB read outside the timing events on every iteration, which stretches the total runtime of the experiment (by how much was not measured). If an input is naturally warm in production—such as the activations just written by the preceding kernel inside the same layer—cold-flushing an isolated single kernel will measure it as artificially slow. When you time a single layer, bracket the entire layer in one CUDA Graph replay so warm intra-layer data stays in cache naturally (see Chapter 9, Section 1).

3How Much Must Two Versions Differ Before One Is Truly Faster?

Run the two versions alternately in A, B, B, A order within the same process to cancel linear drift. Then use an A/A null-hypothesis control to measure the operator's noise band; a delta counts only when it exceeds that band.

First, look at why you cannot time two versions on different machines and subtract the results directly, as shown in the chart below. When you run the exact same version of gemv on two different H200 GPUs using the same cold-L2 CUDA event timing, the medians across the two machines differ by up to 0.32 µs (excluding v0, which takes nearly 700 µs). Take v8 → v9 in Chapter 5, Section 8: across 4 paired comparison rounds, two rounds tied and two rounds came out slightly slower for v9; every delta was smaller than the span of v8's own 4-round medians, so the change in v9 sits inside measurement noise (see Chapter 4, Section 6 for the criterion).

Why does the A, B, B, A order from Chapter 7, Section 1 cancel drift? Even on the same machine, latency drifts slowly during a continuous run—from temperature, clock frequency, and other factors whose individual shares were not measured separately. If you run NNN back-to-back iterations of A followed by NNN back-to-back iterations of B as in Figure 10-2 Mode 1, the later B runs execute in a consistently slower state, mixing that drift straight into the delta. Switch to the alternating A, B, B, A order in Figure 10-2 Mode 2 and label the four runs in a group as timestamps 1,2,3,41, 2, 3, 41,2,3,4: the mean timestamp of A is (1+4)/2=2.5(1+4)/2 = 2.5(1+4)/2=2.5, and the mean timestamp of B is (2+3)/2=2.5(2+3)/2 = 2.5(2+3)/2=2.5. As long as the drift across those four runs is approximately linear, A and B see the same average drift, which cancels out when you subtract them. Run multiple consecutive groups and take the median of the group deltas, and you also suppress random jitter within individual groups.

Once linear drift is canceled, we run the A/A null-hypothesis control from Chapter 7, Section 1—feeding two identical copies of the code as A and B into the same paired ABBA benchmarking harness. On the dense projection kernels, the maximum delta is 0.13 µs, so we set the threshold at 0.15 µs; this threshold is the maximum observed A/A delta, not a statistical confidence interval.

You have to measure the noise band separately for each operator rather than applying a single constant across this book; the chart below shows the value for each operator.

What does paired ABBA benchmarking cost? Every group takes 4 runs, and both A and B have to live in the same process at the same time (see Section 5 for how to keep their device memory allocations from crowding each other and skewing the readings). Also, if a non-linear step change such as a sudden clock drop hits mid-run, the symmetric order cannot cancel it out (behavior under such sudden jumps was not measured). And if one side computes wrong outputs, paired ABBA benchmarking cannot make the timing delta meaningful either: verify outputs before timing (see Section 4).

4Before Timing, How Do We Verify That a Version's Output Is Correct—and Stays Correct Every Time?

A version with wrong outputs may appear faster because it skips work or changes power draw, so verify outputs before timing. Rare races need large replay counts: 0 errors in NNN runs can only show, with ~95% confidence, that the failure rate is below 3/N3/N3/N.

Feed your test with non-zero random numbers rather than all-zero tensors: all-zero inputs may give you artificially fast readings (the reason was not measured separately).

Timing a version that computes wrong outputs is meaningless. In one full-layer comparison, we ran A several times in a row and then B several times in a row, and B clocked in ~8.55% faster than A. Only when we checked the outputs did we discover that B's output was wrong. Two effects were mixed into that difference: B computed wrong outputs (corrupted values may alter chip power draw), and the benchmark ran A then B (mixing in drift; see Section 3); the share of each factor was not measured. Once we fixed the output and switched to 20 groups of paired ABBA benchmarking, the difference disappeared.

Even after a single-run output check passes, you still have to guard against intermittent concurrency data races. You can catch shared-memory read/write hazards and CTA barrier misuse with racecheck and synccheck in NVIDIA's runtime checking tool compute-sanitizer—but neither tool can see cross-kernel global-memory data races.

To catch an intermittent cross-kernel data race, you can only count errors across a large number of replays. Take the topk_ids data race in Chapter 9, Section 5: on a T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer, it showed up only about once every 11,000 CUDA Graph replays, and at T=8T = 8T=8 it took about 840,000 replays to trigger once.

So how many error-free replays does it take before we can say a data race is fixed? We bound the failure rate using the rule of three. If the true per-run failure rate is ppp, the probability of seeing zero errors across NNN consecutive runs is:

(1−p)N≈e−pN(1 - p)^N \approx e^{-pN}(1−p)N≈e−pN

Set that probability to 5%5\%5% and take the natural logarithm: ln⁡0.05≈−3\ln 0.05 \approx -3ln0.05≈−3, which gives pN≈3pN \approx 3pN≈3. Seeing 0 errors across NNN consecutive replays does not prove that zero bugs remain; it only shows with ~95%95\%95% confidence that the true failure rate ppp sits below 3/N3/N3/N. This upper bound assumes independent replays and an identical failure rate across GPUs; in Chapter 9, Section 5 one GPU failed far more often than the others, so this bound constrains the average failure rate across those GPUs.

Plug the numbers from Chapter 9, Section 5 into that formula: after the fix, 567,200 consecutive replays on the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer (including the outlier GPU) produced 0 severe numerical corruptions. By the rule of three, that pushes the upper bound on the severe numerical corruption rate down to 3/567,200≈5.3×10−63 / 567{,}200 \approx 5.3 \times 10^{-6}3/567,200≈5.3×10−6. Before the fix, the failure rate was ~9.2×10−59.2 \times 10^{-5}9.2×10−5—had the data race remained, those 567,200 replays would be expected to hit the race ~52 times, whereas the measured count was 0, proving the fix worked. Now look at T=8T = 8T=8: the original data race triggered only about once every 840,000 runs. After the fix, 556,000 runs produced 0 errors; even if the bug were unfixed, 556,000 runs would be expected to hit it only ~0.7 times, so that 0 proves nothing.

The cost of this check is that replay counting takes substantial time: bounding the failure rate below ppp requires at least ~3/p3/p3/p runs, and turning on compute-sanitizer also slows the kernel down a lot (the slowdown factor was not measured). When the trigger rate of an intermittent data race is extremely low—as in the T=8T = 8T=8 case above—the feasible replay count NNN is too small to push 3/N3/N3/N below the original failure rate. At that point, your only option is proving correctness from the memory-model specification itself (see Chapter 9, Section 5).

5How Do We Keep the Measurement Harness from Altering the Tested Kernel?

When probing timestamps, keep readings in registers until the end of the kernel; when comparing two versions, keep the device memory allocation layout identical.

CUDA event timing gives you only the end-to-end duration of the whole kernel. If you want to know how long a specific slice inside a kernel takes—such as the prologue or the reduction tail step—you have to insert a timestamp probe inside the kernel: a snippet of code that reads the clock and records stage-by-stage elapsed time. That probe reads %globaltimer, the device-wide 64-bit nanosecond timer register. Because all SMs read the same global timer, readings can by design be subtracted across CTAs. On H200, its minimum non-zero step size is 32 ns, which is only 1/25 of the ~0.8 µs gaps in Chapter 9, Section 6. Whether any skew exists across SM readings was not measured, so those sub-1 µs gaps should be treated only as estimates.

Write the probe the wrong way and it will directly stretch the code you are trying to measure. Recorded timestamps eventually have to be written out to a global memory buffer; if every timestamp point first loads that buffer's output address from global memory, each probe adds a global memory load, and the subsequent store has to wait for that load to return. We measured the elapsed time from function entry to the first useful compute instruction on a dense projection kernel, with the result shown in the chart below. A probe that loads the output pointer from global memory on every timestamp takes 0.576 µs longer than a probe that holds timestamps in registers and writes them out at exit—larger than the 0.06–0.4 µs prologue duration that the experiment was trying to measure. Holding timestamps in registers and writing them out at the end adds only a few register assignments inside the measured interval.

Next look at how device memory allocation affects neighboring operators. Allocating an extra 84.9 MB buffer for new weights during setup shifted the latencies of subsequent untouched neighboring operators by ±0.5%–1%—for example, unpooler at T=32T = 32T=32 slowed down by ~0.5%, enough to drown out small real speedups. Allocating an extra buffer probably shifts the virtual and physical addresses of subsequent tensors in the device memory allocator, changing which HBM partitions they land on (see Chapter 2, Section 2).

So when you compare two versions, do not alter the order or total byte count of device memory allocations. You can preserve the layout in two ways: either construct the new-format weights in place inside an old buffer that is no longer used, or use a fixed device memory pool from which all tensors are carved at fixed offsets out of a single pre-allocated block of device memory. Because every address inside a CUDA Graph is baked in at capture time and cannot change during replay (see Chapter 1, Section 2), any temporary workspace buffer used for timing must also be allocated and warmed up before capturing the graph.

The cost is that each 64-bit timestamp consumes two 32-bit registers, which in a kernel already near its register cap may reduce occupancy or trigger register spilling (actual impact not measured; see Chapter 3, Section 1). A fixed device memory layout is also more tedious to maintain and only keeps neighboring operators stable rather than making anything faster. When a single execution of the candidate code is shorter than 32 ns, in-kernel timestamp probing cannot resolve it accurately; as long as that code executes enough times for its total time to exceed the noise band, you can measure it from the outside using the perturbation test in Section 8.

6The Outer Three Levels (Levels 1–3): Which Metric Do We Check on the Timeline, the Full Chip, and a Single SM, and What Fix Does Each Point To?

Diagnose from outside in: are there gaps on the timeline? How many bytes did the full chip read, and is there a tail wave? Does a single SM spill registers or lack sufficient bytes in flight?

Until you rule out outer-level bottlenecks, a piece of code you optimize at an inner level may not even lie on the critical path (see Section 8).

Start at Level 1: Timeline (see Chapter 1, Section 1). Open the system-wide timeline profiler Nsight Systems: it plots CPU launches and the start and end of every kernel on the GPU along the same timeline, so you can see right away whether gaps sit between adjacent kernels. If tensor shapes are fixed and CPU launch gaps show up on the timeline, capture the chain into a CUDA Graph (see Chapter 1, Section 2). If hardware handoff gaps from the predecessor's tail still remain between adjacent graph nodes after graph capture, enable PDL so the dependent kernel enters early (see Chapter 1, Section 4). Only small kernels whose gaps even PDL cannot hide are worth fusing.

In Chapter 9, Section 6, fusing kernels that were already hidden—or merging stages into a megakernel—made execution slower instead. On the gemv chain, the step at this level is v2 (see Chapter 1, Section 5).

Once the timeline is packed tight, zoom in to Level 2: Full Chip (see Chapter 2, Sections 1–3). First put the measured latency next to the theoretical lower bound: for gemv, reading WWW once has a bandwidth lower bound of 7.86 µs (see Primer 2, Section 4). Next check two readings in NCU's Speed Of Light (SOL) panel: measured HBM bytes read (dram__bytes_read.sum) and achieved bandwidth as a percentage of peak. Those two numbers put you in one of three cases:

  • measured bytes read significantly exceed algorithmically required bytes: either your global loads are not coalesced, or the cache is getting flushed and reading the same bytes twice. Drop down to Level 3 to check coalescing and cache behavior.
  • measured bytes read equal required bytes, but achieved bandwidth is a low fraction of peak: you are not reading extra bytes—the problem is that bytes are not arriving fast enough. gemv v9 lands right here: NCU measures 37.78 MB read, nearly identical to the 37.75 MB of WWW, yet achieved bandwidth reaches only ~66% of peak. Its per-SM bytes in flight are already near the 64 KiB saturation line (see Chapter 2, Section 3 and Chapter 4, Section 3; that 66% is averaged across the whole kernel including ramp-up and tail, while steady-state bandwidth was not measured separately).
  • measured bytes read equal required bytes and achieved bandwidth is near peak: you have hit the physical ceiling of HBM. Tweaking the schedule will not squeeze out any more time, so the only way forward is to read fewer bytes—for example, by narrowing the weight bit-width as in Chapter 6, Section 4.

While you are at the full-chip level, also check whether all 132 SMs finish together. Probe %globaltimer and %smid (the current SM ID) at kernel entry and exit using the pattern from Section 5. If you see the final batch of CTAs dragging on across only a few SMs, you have a tail wave. In gemv v1, for example, we launch one CTA per row; after the first wave fills 2,112 CTAs, the remaining 192 CTAs form a tail wave (see Chapter 2, Section 1), and v3 splits each of those 192 rows into two half-row CTAs to flatten the tail wave (see Chapter 2, Section 8).

After you rule out the full-chip lower bound and tail waves, step into Level 3: Single SM (see Chapter 3) and check four readings in order:

  1. ptxas -v prints the register count and register-spill byte counts (spill stores / loads) for each kernel. Check first whether spilling is 0; the moment it is non-zero, register accesses degrade into local memory round trips (see Chapter 3, Sections 1 and 6).
  2. Next check whether each SM keeps enough bytes in flight. By Little's Law from Chapter 2, Section 3, when all 132 SMs read concurrently, ld.global requires ~64 KiB / SM and TMA requires ~48 KiB / SM (see Chapter 3, Section 4); when only half the SMs are reading, the bytes in flight that each SM must keep outstanding double. Both thresholds are calculated from loaded latency. Under lighter load, latency is shorter, so dipping slightly below the threshold costs little bandwidth. In Chapter 3, Section 9, v6 shrinks each CTA to 1 warp, dropping bytes in flight to 8.7 KiB / SM and slowing the kernel down.
  3. Open NCU's Memory Workload Analysis panel to check the fraction of bytes per global memory request that is actually used (see Chapter 3, Section 2) and whether shared memory runs into bank conflicts (see Chapter 3, Section 7).
  4. In the Launch Statistics and Occupancy panels, read the resident CTAs per SM and achieved occupancy (see Chapter 3, Section 1).

7The Inner Three Levels (Levels 4–6): Which Metric Do We Check on the Scheduler, Execution Pipelines, and SASS?

Check first whether the scheduler has an eligible warp each cycle and what stall reasons dominate, then check which execution pipeline or issue slot is saturated, and finally inspect SASS for compiler-inserted wait barriers or instruction reordering.

Follow the lower half of Figure 10-3 into Level 4: SMSP Scheduler (see Chapter 4). At a fixed cycle interval, the profiler samples a warp and records whether it issued an instruction on that cycle or why it could not issue. The fraction of non-issuing samples attributed to a given reason is its stall sampling share (the profiler counts not selected as one of the reasons). In the Scheduler Statistics panel, check the active issue-slot share and the share of cycles with no eligible warp; for the breakdown of stall reasons, check the Warp State panel; to map stalls back to source lines, open the Source Counters page after compiling with -lineinfo.

When issue slots are busy and the top warp state is not selected, your warps are already eligible and yielded that cycle's issue slot to another warp (see Chapter 4, Section 1). In that case, jump straight to Level 5. When the no eligible share is high instead, match the dominant stall reason against the list below:

  • long_scoreboard: warps are waiting for global memory loads to return because per-thread in-flight reads are too shallow or address calculations have serial dependencies (see Chapter 4, Section 2). On gemv, the reading to watch is the average stall cycles per issued instruction: v6 stalls for 12.9 cycles, and v7 drops to 8.1 once we expand per-thread in-flight reads to 8.
  • mio_throttle / short_scoreboard: MIO is the SM instruction queue that buffers shared-memory accesses, warp shuffles, and special functions; once it fills up, later instructions have to wait. short_scoreboard means a shared-memory load and the instruction that consumes its result sit too close together, which you fix by separating them (see Chapter 4, Section 2). mio_throttle means the MIO queue itself is full, which you fix by sending fewer instructions into that queue or offloading work to another pipeline.
  • barrier: warps arrive at the CTA barrier __syncthreads at uneven times (see Primer 3, Section 4). Fix it by balancing the work across warps or switching to a named barrier that waits only on a subset of threads (see Chapter 5, Section 7).
  • wait: warps are stalled on the fixed-latency stall count encoded by the compiler in the instruction control word (see Chapter 6, Section 5); the fix is to increase instruction-level parallelism or reorder instructions. For waits on asynchronous matrix multiplication wgmma.wait_group, see Chapter 5, Section 5; which stall category they fall under in NCU was not determined.

Once you confirm that the scheduler is issuing instructions every cycle, step into Level 5: Execution Pipelines (see Chapter 5). Open NCU's Compute Workload Analysis panel to read the utilization of each physical execution pipeline and the total executed instruction count:

  • one execution pipeline is near saturation while adjacent pipelines remain idle: rewrite the computation on the crowded pipeline into equivalent instructions that run on an idle neighbor (see Chapter 5, Section 1). In the prefill loop of Chapter 7, for example, online softmax pushed the 4-lane SFU to 77.3%, so we offloaded row sums and exponentials onto other pipelines (see Chapter 7, Sections 8–9).
  • no single execution pipeline is saturated, but issue slots are already busy: the bottleneck is issue slots, because each SMSP can issue only 1 instruction per cycle. Shuffling work between pipelines does not help here; you have to cut the total instruction count directly through algebraic folding and packed instructions—which is how we diagnosed the expert epilogue bottleneck in Chapter 8, Section 13.

The cautionary counterexample at this level is gemv v9 from Chapter 5, Section 8: v9 applies a Level 5 fix—breaking the accumulator dependency chain and cutting total executed instructions by ~24%—yet latency did not budge. The Level 2 reading from Section 6 tells you why: v9 is still bottlenecked at the memory level. Level 5 fixes help only after you have ruled out Levels 2–4.

Finally, drop down to Level 6: SASS (see Chapter 6, Section 5). Run cuobjdump --dump-sass to read the generated machine code directly, checking three things in particular:

  • Check whether the compiler inserted WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0 (a drain barrier) after every HGMMA. If it did, your async region has degraded into serialized execution; see Chapter 6, Section 6 for the cause and the ptxas performance warning.
  • Check whether the compiler sank your early prefetch ld.global.nc instructions past the PDL wait instruction from Chapter 1, Section 4, or repeatedly rematerialized loop invariants inside the inner loop. That is how we caught the rematerialization and instruction sinking regressions in SASS in Chapter 8, Section 8.
  • Check whether the consumer of an on-chip ring buffer still has pending shared-memory loads before arriving on empty[s]: if so, you have the write-after-read hazard (WAR) from Chapter 3, Section 5. After fixing it, scan the machine code to confirm that all shared-memory load instructions (LDS in SASS) have returned before each arrival.

On the gemv chain, the Level 6 step is v10's in-register 12-bit weight decoding in Chapter 6, Section 7 (see Chapter 6, Section 2 for the decoding instruction sequence).

8Is a Code Segment Truly on the Critical Path, and How Much Can Optimizing It Save at Most?

Skip the candidate code at runtime while keeping the machine code unchanged, then measure latency with paired ABBA benchmarking: unchanged latency shows that the main track hides the code, and the size of any latency drop is the speedup upper bound for fixing it.

On a GPU, HBM / TMA transfers, Tensor Cores, and normal arithmetic pipelines advance in parallel along separate tracks (see Chapter 5, Section 1). As long as a shorter arithmetic or synchronization branch overlaps with a slower main track, even cutting that branch all the way down to 0 clock cycles leaves total latency unchanged (see Chapter 4, Section 1).

How do you test this before you rewrite the code? Run the perturbation test (ablation test) in Figure 10-4. Keep the non-zero random inputs unchanged, and skip the candidate code using a runtime parameter switch opaque to compile-time dead-code elimination (set to execute in the baseline and to skip in the test version). Then use paired ABBA benchmarking to compare the CUDA event timing delta before and after the skip. Despite the "ablation" label, it is actually a runtime skip: the skipped instructions stay in the machine code, and you do not delete a single line of source.

If you delete a block of code in the source file, ptxas sees a different control-flow graph (see Chapter 6, Section 5). It then re-decides loop unrolling and register allocation across the whole kernel, so the compiled binary is no longer the same kernel. Take the expert kernel in Chapter 8, Section 9: how much can we save at most in the entry section where consumers gather activations xxx? Deleting that code in source bloated the machine code by ~12% and made the kernel 23–26 µs slower instead (see Figure 10-4 Mode 3). Once we switched to a runtime skip, the machine-code size stayed unchanged. At T=256T = 256T=256, we derived that the first HGMMA started 5–7 µs earlier. Yet the whole kernel sped up by only a measured 3.11 µs—that is the speedup upper bound for optimizing this section, and the chart below shows the upper bound at each TTT.

A perturbation test gives you one of two outcomes:

The first outcome is total latency unchanged: the candidate branch is completely hidden behind a slower main track, so optimizing it buys you nothing. This book has no example of a runtime skip leaving latency unchanged; the MUFU.TANH experiment below is a source-code modification and serves only as corroborating evidence. In one version of the Stage 6 expert kernel (Figure 10-4 Mode 1), the activation epilogue used the hardware hyperbolic tangent instruction MUFU.TANH to compute sigmoid(x)=0.5 (1+tanh⁡(x/2))\mathrm{sigmoid}(x) = 0.5\,(1 + \tanh(x / 2))sigmoid(x)=0.5(1+tanh(x/2)). Removing MUFU.TANH in source code (replacing it with a single FMA) changed latency by 0.0%, whereas replacing it with a multi-instruction polynomial approximation slowed execution by 0.4% (the machine-code lengths of the two variants were not measured), indicating indirectly that a single MUFU.TANH probably did not block the critical path. For the experiment showing that the epilogue is bound by issue-slot instruction count, see Chapter 8, Section 13.

The second outcome is total latency decreases, as shown in Figure 10-4 Mode 2 and the chart below. For Stage 5 pooler at T=256T = 256T=256, skipping the final cross-CTA reduction tail step at runtime cut latency by ~4.9 µs, setting the upper bound for optimizing that step. Only after confirming this upper bound did we rewrite the tail step as a TMA tile reduction following Chapter 5, Section 7; paired ABBA benchmarking measured a 2.66 µs speedup, staying below the upper bound.

Here are the trade-offs of a perturbation test:

  • What you gain: you find out whether a code segment is worth optimizing before spending time rewriting it.
  • What it costs: each suspect code segment requires compiling a separate binary with a runtime conditional switch and running a round of paired ABBA benchmarking; the runtime branch itself adds a few instructions, which sit in both the baseline and test runs and cancel out.
  • When it loses: when the skipped code produces data consumed by subsequent steps, the corrupted values may steer later code down a different control-flow path or alter power draw and clock frequency (see Section 4). Then the measured delta reflects more than just omitting that segment, and the upper bound can serve only as an estimate.

9What Does It Take for a Change to Count as a Real Win?

For an optimization to count, it must exceed the noise band under paired ABBA timing, keep the same sign on re-runs, and cause no regressions across all input shapes when integrated into the full layer.

The first rule is: fewer static instructions do not guarantee a speedup; the delta must exceed the operator's A/A noise band and keep the same sign on re-runs. In the Stage 6 persistent wgmma expert kernel of Chapter 8, Section 9, rewriting the second-stage writeback to use predicated execution cut the compiler-inserted branch reconvergence instruction BSSY (see Chapter 4, Section 4) from 123 instructions down to 58—more than a 50% reduction. Yet under paired ABBA benchmarking, all three measurements fell inside this kernel's noise band of about ±0.4 µs, and the two re-runs at T=256T = 256T=256 even flipped signs, as shown in the chart below; so this change gets credited with zero gain. If you look only at static instruction counts or run only a single pass, you will mistake random jitter for a real speedup.

The second rule is: after winning in an isolated kernel benchmark, a change must be re-tested inside the full layer across all input shapes. A change that wins when you benchmark the kernel in isolation does not necessarily win inside the full layer. SMs that were idle in isolation may be occupied by other kernels on parallel branches, occupancy may change, and cross-kernel handoffs may shift out of alignment. Chapter 9, Section 7 gives two examples: offloading the second-wave tiles of qkv_gate sped up the isolated kernel benchmark, but once placed back into the single layer its delta fell inside the paired noise band, so we did not adopt the change; likewise, whether concurrent stream scheduling wins or loses flips across token counts.

Whenever you report a speedup, state the measurement baseline explicitly: whether it is the isolated single-kernel cold benchmark from Section 2 of this chapter, or the single-layer CUDA Graph replay from Chapter 9, Section 1. Do not mix numbers from the two measurement baselines in the same evolution chain.

What does enforcing these two rules cost? Verification time: every change requires at least two rounds of paired ABBA benchmarking plus a full-layer re-run across all input shapes. Small changes whose true gain is smaller than the noise band are rejected by these rules; whether stacking multiple rejected small changes would cross the noise band was not measured.

10At the End of the Diagnostic Tree: Which Bottlenecks Cannot Be Fixed in Software?

After walking all six levels of the diagnostic tree, four fundamental H200 hardware limits remain that software can only work around rather than eliminate.

  1. Hardware Limit 1: Register file capacity (Level 3). Large-tile matrix-multiplication accumulators sit directly in the vector registers of the 4 warps, where they share each SM's pool of 65,536 32-bit registers with ordinary thread variables (see Chapter 3, Section 1). In Chapter 3, Section 6, we used setmaxnreg to squeeze the producer warpgroup down to 40 registers per thread and bring the consumer warpgroups up to 232 registers per thread just to fit 2 consumer warpgroups. In Chapter 8, Section 9, when we tried to launch 4 consumer warpgroups, no register reallocation could make them fit, so we had to cap each thread at 96 registers.
  2. Hardware Limit 2: Lockstep warpgroup issue (Levels 4–5). Asynchronous matrix multiplication wgmma carries .sync.aligned: all 4 warps in the same warpgroup must execute the same instruction, or behavior is undefined (see Chapter 5, Section 3 and Appendix A, Section 2). In the Stage 6 persistent wgmma expert kernel of Chapter 8, Section 9, 84%–94% of the measured non-issuing stall samples at each HGMMA land on warpgroup_arrive (the profiler's name for this stall reason: a warp stalled at the wgmma issue point). That reading alone cannot tell you whether a warp is waiting for the other warps in its warpgroup or waiting for data.
  3. Hardware Limit 3: 4-bit weight conversion (Level 6). Hopper has no hardware instruction to convert 4-bit floating-point NVFP4 directly into BF16. Unpacking every 8 four-bit weights takes 8 integer instructions, and you still have to multiply the unpacked values by the block scale before feeding them to mma.sync (see Chapter 6, Section 3). Of those unpacking instructions, 6 run on the ALU pipeline and 2 run on the FMA pipeline. Whenever decoding takes longer than loading weights and multiplying matrices, operand supply cannot keep up (see Chapter 6, Section 4 and Chapter 8, Section 3).
  4. Hardware Limit 4: Non-contiguous row gather (Level 3). TMA moves only rectangular tiles (see Chapter 3, Section 3), so it cannot gather scattered rows by row index. When we read non-contiguous KV rows through a page table in Chapter 7, Sections 5–6, we cannot use TMA and have to fall back to letting every thread compute its own addresses and issue cp.async.

Those four limits correspond directly to the four lines inside the endpoint box at the bottom of the diagnostic tree in Figure 10-3 (Readings point to hardware itself → Appendix A).

Takeaway: Measure accurately first, walk the profiler level by level from the outside in, and bound the maximum speedup before rewriting any code; only a change that clears the noise band and causes no regression inside the full layer counts as a win.

Appendix A

Four H200 Hardware Limits That Software Cannot Change: How Does Blackwell (B200) Change Them in Hardware?

  • Preface
  • Primer 1
  • Primer 2
  • Primer 3
  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]
  • Chapter 3 [Level 3]
  • Chapter 4 [Level 4]
  • Chapter 5 [Level 5]
  • Chapter 6 [Level 6]
  • Chapters 7–9
  • Chapter 10
  • Appendix A: From H200 to B200

Chapter 10, Section 10 left us with four hardware limits on H200 that software cannot change. Let's walk through how Blackwell (B200, target architecture sm_100a) changes the hardware at each one, compared against H200 (target architecture sm_90a).

B200 speeds up single-request decode through wider HBM, not through the four changes below. Divide the public 8-GPU node spec by 8, and a single B200 has about 8 TB/s of HBM bandwidth. On every forward pass, each GPU reads a fixed ~9.0 GB of dense and lm_head weights (see Primer 1, Section 4); counting only that read, the lower bound drops from ~1.87 ms on H200 to ~1.12 ms. That ratio compares weight-read lower bounds, not full decode latency. The lower bound leaves out the busiest GPU's expert weights and the KV. For handoff gaps and tail duration, see Chapter 9, Section 6; for CUDA Graph replay and the 186 cross-GPU collectives, see Chapter 9, Section 8.

All four hardware changes below live on-chip, and they help prefill, large-batch verify, large-batch expert computation, and attention loads of non-contiguous KV rows. Every measured result in this book comes from H200; latencies on B200 were not measured at all, so the trade-offs in each section are derived from the PTX ISA specification.

1Can Accumulators Avoid Occupying Vector Registers?

Blackwell adds a dedicated 256 KiB Tensor Memory (TMEM) per SM, where fifth-generation Tensor Core instructions write their accumulators directly.

We hit the H200 register file capacity limit in Chapter 10, Section 10: with the wgmma tile shape from Chapter 5, Section 3, splitting a 64×25664 \times 25664×256 FP32 accumulator (m64n256k16) evenly across 128 threads eats 64×256/128=64 \times 256 / 128 =64×256/128= 128 registers per thread, roughly half of the 255-register per-thread cap just for the accumulator alone (Figure A-1, Mode 1, left).

Blackwell fixes this by adding a dedicated TMEM (Tensor Memory) inside each SM, separate from the vector register file (see Figure A-1, Mode 1, right). Each SM's TMEM holds 128 rows × 512 columns of 32-bit cells, giving a total capacity of:

128×512×4 B=256 KiB128 \times 512 \times 4\ \mathrm{B} = 256\ \mathrm{KiB}128×512×4 B=256 KiB

At runtime, a CTA allocates TMEM columns from the hardware with tcgen05.alloc and frees them with tcgen05.dealloc when finished. Multiple CTAs resident on the same SM share those 512 columns. The fifth-generation Tensor Core MMA instruction tcgen05.mma places accumulator DDD directly in TMEM: left matrix AAA can come from SMEM or TMEM, and right matrix BBB comes from SMEM. Accumulator DDD no longer occupies the vector register file from Chapter 3, Section 1. This change helps the large-batch persistent wgmma expert kernel in Chapter 8, Section 9 and the large-tile matrix multiplications in prefill, both of which hit the register quota on H200.

Once the accumulator moves into TMEM, you can spend the freed vector registers on address calculation, prefetching, or higher occupancy. You pay three costs in return: the kernel must explicitly call tcgen05.alloc / tcgen05.dealloc to allocate and free TMEM; before the epilogue runs, it must first pull the results back into general-purpose registers via tcgen05.ld; and the hardware restricts each warp in a warpgroup to accessing only its own 32 rows of TMEM (128 rows split across 4 warps). At small shapes like T=8T = 8T=8, where the accumulator is already small and the vector registers are plenty, that extra round trip between TMEM and registers buys you nothing and adds only overhead.

2Can Matrix Multiplication Avoid Requiring 4 Warps to Issue in Lockstep?

wgmma requires 4 warps to issue in lockstep; tcgen05.mma is issued by a single thread.

Chapter 10, Section 10 showed the lockstep warpgroup issue limit on H200: on Hopper, the accumulator is spread across the registers of the 4 warps (128 threads) in one warpgroup (Figure A-1, Mode 2, left). The wgmma.mma_async instruction carries the .sync.aligned suffix. Under the PTX ISA specification, .aligned requires every participating thread to execute the same instruction—for wgmma.mma_async, all 4 warps in the warpgroup—or the behavior is undefined. Before issue, wgmma.fence orders the reads and writes; after issue, wgmma.wait_group waits for completion (see Chapter 5, Section 5).

With the accumulator living in TMEM (Section 1), Blackwell's tcgen05.mma switches to single-thread issue just like TMA in Chapter 3, Section 3 (Figure A-1, Mode 2, right): launching a matrix multiplication takes only 1 thread in 1 warp issuing 1 instruction. That thread waits on an mbarrier until the data is ready (see Chapter 3, Section 5), while the remaining warps do not have to execute the MMA instruction and can go compute addresses, run activation functions, or move data on their own. This change targets the large-batch persistent wgmma expert kernel in Chapter 8, Section 9 and the multi-warpgroup matrix multiplications in prefill attention in Chapter 7, Section 7.

The trade-off is that the single issuing thread has to manage mbarrier waits and completion notifications itself, and you have to repartition work in your kernel code to keep the freed warps busy. Moreover, the warpgroup_arrive stall does not tell you whether warps are waiting for peer warps in the warpgroup or waiting for data; if they are mainly waiting for data, switching to single-thread issue will not eliminate that wait either. How much each cause contributes was not measured on either H200 or B200.

3Can 4-Bit Weights Avoid Unpacking in Registers?

Blackwell Tensor Cores provide block-scaled MMA instructions that directly consume 4-bit weights and per-16-element scale factors, eliminating in-register integer unpacking.

We saw the 4-bit weight decompression limit on H200 in Chapter 10, Section 10: on Hopper, you have to unpack NVFP4 weights with integer instructions in general-purpose registers and multiply by their block scale factors before feeding them into left operand AAA of mma.sync (see Figure A-1, Mode 3, left, and Chapter 6, Section 3).

Blackwell's fifth-generation Tensor Core adds the block-scaled MMA instruction tcgen05.mma.kind::mxf4nvf4.block_scale (see Figure A-1, Mode 3, right): it takes 4-bit floating-point values and one block scale factor per 16 elements directly, scaling and multiply-accumulating inside the Tensor Core hardware with no integer unpacking in general-purpose registers. That maps straight to the Stage 6 expert computation in Chapter 8, where the weights sit in NVFP4 (see Primer 2, Section 1).

Hardware block-scaled MMA cuts out the in-register integer decoding instructions, so the ALU and FMA pipelines spend zero cycles decoding weights. You pay two costs: first, weights and block scale factors must follow the exact block size and memory layout the hardware expects, or else loading weights requires an extra layout permutation; second, this model's NVFP4 weights also carry one tensor scale per tensor (see Chapter 8, Section 1) that this instruction does not apply, so you still have to multiply by it separately in the epilogue. Whether this model's existing weight layout can feed this instruction directly was not measured.

In the T=1T = 1T=1 decode regime on H200, software decoding instructions hide behind the wait for weight bytes returning from HBM (see Chapter 6, Section 4). Because B200's estimated HBM bandwidth is ~1.67× that of H200, that latency-hiding window shrinks; whether decoding still stays hidden on B200 was not measured.

4Can TMA Gather Non-Contiguous Rows by Row Index?

Blackwell TMA adds .tile::gather4 mode: a single command specifies 4 row indices, and hardware gathers all 4 rows directly into one SMEM tile.

We saw the non-contiguous row gather limit on H200 in Chapter 10, Section 10: here, one row means a 128 B K row or V row. When each page holds only 1 token, those KV rows sit scattered across device memory, forcing Hopper to fall back to per-thread cp.async loads (see Figure A-1, Mode 4, left, and Chapter 7, Section 5).

On Blackwell, TMA adds .tile::gather4 mode (Figure A-1, Mode 4, right): one TMA command gives the hardware 4 non-contiguous row indices, and TMA gathers all 4 rows and packs them into the same SMEM tile, cutting out the per-thread address math and the string of cp.async instructions. This change targets Stage 2 attention in Chapter 7, Section 5, where decode and verify gather non-contiguous KV rows one row at a time.

With .tile::gather4, gathering non-contiguous rows by row index can also run through single-thread-issued TMA. The catch is that .tile::gather4 supports only 2D tensors, taking a fixed 4 row indices and 1 starting column index each time. Those row indices still have to be read from the page table first: the three-hop pointer wait for the page-table lookup in Chapter 7, Section 6 does not change, and gather4 saves only the per-thread issue after the row indices return. Each command moves only 4×128 B=512 B4 \times 128\ \mathrm{B} = 512\ \mathrm{B}4×128 B=512 B. By Little's Law (Chapter 2, Section 3), TMA on H200 needs ~48 KiB in flight per SM (Chapter 3, Section 4), which works out to ~96 commands. B200 has higher bandwidth and needs even more bytes in flight; whether 1 thread can issue commands that fast was not measured.

There are also cases where gather4 does not help: if the number of rows you need to gather is not a multiple of 4, the final request leaves some slots unused; and if each page holds multiple contiguous tokens, the rows within a page are already stored contiguously, so ordinary rectangular-tile TMA per page is all you need.

Takeaway: B200 addresses in hardware the four H200 limits that software can only work around, not remove. That mainly helps prefill, large batches, and non-contiguous row gather in attention; faster single-request decode still comes from wider HBM.

Where Does an Unfamiliar SASS Instruction Come From, Which Hardware Pipeline Does It Use, and Which Level Does It Belong To?

  • Preface

At the end of Appendix A, we asked: when you run into an unfamiliar SASS instruction, where does it come from, which hardware pipeline does it use, and which level does it belong to? This appendix covers only instructions whose PTX or source-code forms appear in the main text or figures, and the SASS column gives the mnemonics seen in the disassembly in this book. We group them by function into four quick-reference tables, followed by an alphabetical mnemonic index at the end.

We assign each entry to a level by the hardware it uses, and the "Where used in this book" column points to the section that explains or uses it:

  • Level 1: Grid launch and handoff, and grid-wide synchronization; see Chapter 1.
  • Level 2: Operations that act directly on the central L2 cache or across SMs, including L2 residency hints and prefetching, L2 atomics and reductions, device-wide memory barriers and release/acquire operations, and thread block clusters and DSMEM; see Chapter 2.
  • Level 3: Data paths and resources inside a single SM, including normal global loads and stores through the local SM L1 cache, SMEM, TMA, cp.async, mbarrier, setmaxnreg, and intra-CTA memory fences; see Chapter 3.
  • Level 4: SMSP scheduling, including CTA barriers and warp-level barriers, warp shuffles, warp votes, branches, scoreboard waits, and special-register reads such as clock counters and thread indices; see Chapter 4.
  • Level 5: Execution pipelines and Tensor Core, including FMA, ALU, and SFU arithmetic and transcendental instructions, as well as HMMA, HGMMA, and QGMMA; see Chapter 5.
  • Level 6: Bits and machine code, including bit permutation and packed type conversion, SASS encoding, and group flags encoded in the control bits; see Chapter 6.

1How Do We Dissect and Read a Single SASS Instruction?

A SASS mnemonic combines an opcode with modifier suffixes, followed by operands for the destination register, memory descriptor, and 64-bit address.

Getting from source code to machine code goes through three layers: CUDA C++ → PTX → the 128-bit (16 B) SASS instruction words emitted by ptxas (see Chapter 6, Section 5). Let's take Mode 1 in Figure B-1, LDG.E.EF.128 R8, desc[UR12][R8.64], and break it apart. This instruction is a 16 B-wide streaming global load with an L2 residency hint (see Chapter 2, Section 4 and Chapter 3, Section 8):

  • LDG: the opcode for a global memory load;
  • .E: an instruction modifier suffix that selects a 64-bit extended address;
  • .EF: the evict_first suffix for the local SM's L1; the L2 residency policy does not take an instruction suffix, and goes into the desc operand instead;
  • .128: each thread loads 128 bits (16 B) at once into four consecutive 32-bit vector registers R8..R11;
  • desc[UR12]: a 64-bit memory descriptor held in uniform register UR, which encodes the L2 residency hint from Chapter 2, Section 4 (created with createpolicy in PTX). UR is shared across the entire warp (see Chapter 7, Section 7), and instructions whose mnemonics start with U read and write it;
  • [R8.64]: a 64-bit byte address formed by the register pair R8:R9.

2Why Does One PTX Instruction Not Always Become One SASS Instruction with the Same Name?

ptxas may compile a single PTX instruction into zero standalone instructions, expand it into a multi-instruction sequence, or map it to a different mnemonic and operands.

  • Category 1: No standalone SASS instruction. Take wgmma.commit_group (see Chapter 5, Section 5 and Chapter 6, Section 6): it takes up no separate instruction word in SASS, and is encoded directly as the group flag at the end of the last HGMMA in that batch (see Quick Reference 3, Item 45).
  • Category 2: Expanded into a multi-instruction SASS sequence. A single-warp FP8 matrix multiplication mma.sync … e4m3 on sm_90a first uses F2FP to unpack FP8 into FP16 and then issues 2 back-to-back HMMA instructions (see Quick Reference 3, Item 41). Likewise, the cluster barrier (barrier.cluster.arrive/wait) in Chapter 9, Section 3 expands into a device-wide memory barrier (MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + CCTL.IVALL; see Quick Reference 3, Item 39).
  • Category 3: Renamed mnemonic or encoded as an operand/modifier. Cache modifiers on global loads turn into suffixes or descriptor operands in SASS—for instance, the L2 residency hint in Chapter 2, Section 4 becomes the desc[URn] operand on LDG in SASS (see Quick Reference 2, Item 24).

Why the mismatch? Because the PTX specification defines only semantics, not a fixed SASS instruction sequence. NVIDIA has not published hardware details for ERRBAR and CGAERRBAR inside the device-wide memory barrier; this book records only the sequence seen in sm_90a disassembly, so re-check the disassembly whenever you switch compiler versions.

3Quick Reference 1: Arithmetic, Transcendental Functions, and Type Conversions

When you look up an instruction in this group, check first which pipeline it runs on—FMA, ALU, or SFU (see Chapter 5, Section 1). Arithmetic and transcendental functions sit at Level 5, while bit permutation and packed type conversions sit at Level 6.

No. PTX SASS Pipeline · Level Where used in this book Source form and notes
1 fma.rn.f32 (same for mad.f32) FFMA FMA pipeline · Level 5 Primer 3, Section 1; Chapter 5, Section 1 fmaf(a,b,c), __fmaf_rn, or a*b+c with default contraction; compiles 1-to-1 into FFMA
2 add.f32; mul.f32 FADD, FMUL FMA pipeline · Level 5 Primer 3, Section 4; Chapter 5, Section 1 a+b, a*b, __fadd_rn, __fmul_rn; using __fadd_rn / __fmul_rn stops the compiler from contracting a*b+c into FFMA, at the cost of issuing 1 extra instruction
3 div.full.f32; div.approx.f32 MUFU.RCP, FMUL SFU + FMA pipelines · Level 5 Chapter 7, Section 3 __fdividef(a,b) or a/b with -use_fast_math enabled; 1 PTX instruction expands into approximate reciprocal MUFU.RCP plus multiplication FMUL, skipping the Newton-Raphson iterations and branches of standard division at the cost of lower precision than IEEE standard division
4 ex2.approx.f32; ex2.approx.ftz.f32 MUFU.EX2, FMUL, FSETP SFU pipeline · Level 5 Chapter 7, Section 9; Chapter 8, Section 13 exp2f(x), __expf(x), or inline PTX; .ftz flushes subnormal numbers to 0 (for subnormal numbers, see Chapter 6, Section 3) and compiles into a single bare MUFU.EX2; omitting .ftz adds two fixup instructions (FSETP + FMUL)
5 ex2.approx.f16x2 MUFU.EX2.F16, PRMT SFU + ALU pipelines · Level 5 Chapter 7, Section 8 h2exp2 or inline PTX; 1 PTX instruction expands into 2 scalar MUFU.EX2.F16 instructions plus 1 PRMT byte permute and cannot halve SFU cycles (see Chapter 7, Section 8; the SASS suffix for the bf16x2 form is unknown)
6 rcp.approx.ftz.f32; rsqrt.approx.ftz.f32; lg2.approx.ftz.f32 MUFU.RCP, MUFU.RSQ, MUFU.LG2 SFU pipeline · Level 5 Chapter 5, Section 1; Chapter 7, Section 3 rsqrtf(x), __log2f(x), or inline PTX; only the .approx.ftz form compiles into a single MUFU instruction, at the cost of higher approximation error than standard library functions
7 tanh.approx.f32 MUFU.TANH SFU pipeline · Level 5 Chapter 10, Section 8 Inline PTX (standard library tanhf is a software expansion); compiles 1-to-1 into MUFU.TANH
8 mul.rn.bf16x2; fma.rn.bf16x2 HMUL2, HFMA2 FMA pipeline · Level 5 Chapter 5, Section 1; Chapter 6, Section 3 __hmul2, __hfma2; packed BF16 instructions carry the .BF16_V2 suffix
9 mad.lo.s32; mad.wide.u32; mul.hi.u32 IMAD, IADD3 IMAD uses FMA; IADD3 uses ALU · Level 5 Chapter 5, Section 1; Chapter 6, Section 3 Integer a*b+c, pointer offset ptr + i*size; IMAD also handles register moves (IMAD.MOV), left shifts (IMAD.SHL), and 64-bit wide multiply-add (IMAD.WIDE)

4Quick Reference 2: Global and On-Chip Memory Access and Asynchronous Copy

Here the first question to ask is which path the data takes: LDG / STG moving data in and out of registers through the Load/Store Unit (LSU), LDGSTS writing directly into SMEM while bypassing registers, or TMA initiated by a single thread (for the differences among the three paths, see Chapter 3, Section 3).

Accesses that act directly on L2 sit at Level 2: loads and stores that bypass L1, L2 residency policies, and L2 atomic reductions. Normal global loads and stores through the local SM's L1, along with SMEM, TMA, and cp.async, sit at Level 3.

6Quick Reference 4: Warp Operations, Memory Fences, Atomic Operations, Grid Handoff, and Control Flow

The intra-warp collectives SHFL and VOTE sit at Level 4: SHFL goes through the MIO queue (see Chapter 4, Section 5 and Chapter 10, Section 7), and for VOTE see Chapter 7, Section 9 and Chapter 8, Section 6. Device-wide memory barriers, L2 atomics, and release/acquire handoffs sit at Level 2 (see Chapter 2, Section 6), while PDL grid handoffs and grid-wide synchronization sit at Level 1 (see Chapter 1, Section 4, Chapter 7, Section 12, and Chapter 8, Section 6).

55 fence.acq_rel.cta; fence.acq_rel.gpu; fence.sc.gpu MEMBAR.ALL.CTA, MEMBAR.ALL.GPU, MEMBAR.SC.GPU, ERRBAR, CGAERRBAR, CCTL.IVALL LSU / memory-system acknowledgment · Level 2 (.cta belongs to Level 3) Chapter 8, Section 11 __threadfence_block(), __threadfence() (compiled into fence.sc.gpu and expanded into 5 instructions: MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + MEMBAR.SC.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + CCTL.IVALL); when you need only acq_rel semantics, write inline fence.acq_rel.gpu. A device-wide memory barrier waits for prior writes to be acknowledged by L2 and invalidates the local SM L1. For one-way producer-consumer handoffs, acq_rel is sufficient; acq_rel does not prevent a store in this thread from reordering with a subsequent load from a different address, whereas when both sides first write their own flag and then read the other side's flag (the Dekker pattern), you need fence.sc to forbid that reordering
56 fence.release.gpu Not recorded in this book's disassembly LSU / memory-system acknowledgment · Level 2 Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 9, Section 5 Inline PTX; it defines ordering only: it orders this thread's prior reads and writes before subsequent strong writes or griddepcontrol.launch_dependents. A strong write is a store with a memory-ordering qualifier such as st.relaxed; a plain st is a weak write. Making prior writes visible to another thread requires pairing with one of two patterns: a subsequent strong write (such as st.relaxed to a flag paired with an acquire load on the receiving side; see Chapter 2, Section 6), or a griddepcontrol.launch_dependents ordered after it in program order (within the same memory synchronization domain, which is the default setting; see Chapter 9, Section 5). Supported starting from sm_90

60 griddepcontrol.wait; griddepcontrol.launch_dependents ACQBULK, PREEXIT Hardware grid distributor and SM · Level 1 Chapter 1, Section 4; Chapter 8, Section 8; Chapter 9, Section 5 cudaGridDependencySynchronize(), cudaTriggerProgrammaticLaunchCompletion(), or inline griddepcontrol (see Chapter 8, Section 8). wait → ACQBULK: blocks until the predecessor grid finishes and its writes are visible. launch_dependents → PREEXIT: once all CTAs issue it or exit, the hardware can schedule the dependent grid. Under the PTX specification, if a predecessor thread executes fence.release.gpu before launch_dependents (with both grids in the same memory synchronization domain, which is the default setting), its prior writes are visible from the start of the dependent grid; otherwise they are guaranteed to be visible only after the dependent grid executes griddepcontrol.wait (see Chapter 9, Section 5). Triggering too early makes the dependent grid occupy SMs while it waits idle (see Chapter 1, Section 4; Chapter 7, Section 11)

Takeaway: When you spot an unfamiliar SASS instruction, look up its mnemonic in this appendix to see what source pattern produced it, which pipeline it runs on, which level it belongs to, and which section of this book uses it. To trace an instruction back to a specific source line, compile with -lineinfo and check the source view in NCU (see Chapter 10, Section 7).
